My first thought is why do you need 5 tons. I completely admit that it is always my first thought on these questions. I just looked up Burbank weather. It doesn't look like you really need heat most of the time - compared to the national average. Your summer is also relatively mild (not compared to Santa Monica perhaps but national). 5 tons is an lot of BTUs for that space. The need for BTUs can be driven quite high with large uncovered windows - particularly facing west. I see no windows in your space so it becomes hard to see why you need so many BTUs. It is never just a simple square footage calculation. The tendency for HVAC contractors is to oversize and then you need large registers and ducts to move that air. As a point of comparison, I have 4 tons in 3800 sqft with 35 windows in Raleigh NC which is both way colder and more humid in the summer. You really need to do calculations to see what size registers you need - no one here can answer that. They look enormous to me. In more modest constuction, we tend to use 4x10 registers - very cheap. The room I am sitting in typing is about 35x20 with 10 foot ceilings. It has 5 registers - but mostly because it is on the coast with a massive SE facing window wall.

Hi, Jonathan, Controlling your home's indoor environment involves both conditioning air and distributing it throughout your home, too.   Without careful consideration of the distribution part, rooms can be uncomfortable.    Don't look to eliminate air supply ducts, but rather to locate them so they are less obtrusive.  If there is attic area behind the wall, it may be possible to relocate the ducts to that space.  If the attic is an unconditioned space, the insulation may need to be a higher R-value, but it's a trade off worth considering.

All farm sink cabinets are templated to the exact sink, and field cut on site. All farm sink cabinets. Fireclay shrinks as it is fired, and and does not have a consistent size, or shape. It can vary 3-5%. No manufacturer ever would take the risk that the sink  was 5% larger or  smaller than nominal, or one side was higher than another. And it does vary tremendously, which is why most installers hate fireclay sinks.  The installer always field customizes the sink base. At an additional labor charge, of course. Usually $600-$700 extra in the whole.

It still goes without saying that we don't have enough information to answer some of the questions. But moving a register a foot or two is generally fine. In tight modern construction, the placement of the registers is not all that important. Mostly you want them near windows because that is where the greatest gain is (and loss too). With shading and low SHGC windows, it isn't as important. It doesn't look like yours are near windows which may be why they have been designed so large - to get the air to the windows? Larger registers will always be quieter for a given air movement. The noise tolerated probably varies in certain markets and price points. Pros often get bent out of shape by "internet" knowledge. That often says more about them. That doesn't mean you should go all in claiming to have figured it all out. But, being able to expand your knowledge and ask better informed questions is the goal. There are often local considerations that the contractor knows about or owner expectations in certain markets. Someone in your area (or your contractor) could answer this - is a Manual D required? I sometimes find the "requirement" does not actually require a decent job. Throw some numbers in a report that an inspector just glances at.

Almonds are very picky about their environment.  In the United States they only grow in the deserts around Southern California where they are irrigated.  Without irrigation they quickly die due to lack of water.  No pest, fungal disease, or humidity. Occasionally you will hear of someone having one somewhere else, but they never make a crop due to rain during the fruiting season or freezing since they also bloom really early in the spring, really in late winter.  And this is in areas that get 30 inches or less of rain each year.  In southern Cal they get rain only in the fall and winter and have no rain in the summer months.  Almonds do not like rain or even humidity.  And those that do grow probably have been grafted with a root stock that will tolerate soils that otherwise would be too wet. Honestly, I think it would be nearly impossible to grow almonds in your climate.  You said you got the seed from Israel,  another area that is arid with little to no rainfall in the summer months.  That is probably the only type of place that they will actually produce any fruit.

The natural beauty of stone can't be copied. It's been used for over 2,000 years. Stone provides a look and feel of elegance. "has seen changes in color within a day or two of installation." "The second, runs from the attic." What is this wire connected to in the attic? You wrote that the black wire from the circuit breaker is connected to laundry room switches in addition to this one. Is there an outlet or switch in the attic that also receives its power from this circuit? If so, then follow the Single-Pole instructions:

One of your black wires feeds the kitchen light and another black wire feeds the attic.  The third black wire is the power from the breaker panel.  To find out which is which, if you are comfortable  doing so, you can remove the dimmer and separate the three blacks and make sure they don't touch each other nor anything else.  Make sure no kids or pets are around, and turn the circuit breaker back on.  Check CAREFULLY which one of the three blacks is hot.  CAREFULLY mark this wire, and shut the power off.  Connect one of the two remaining blacks with the one you just marked, and turn power back on.  Note what is now on: kitchen light or attic.  Turn power off. Identify this wire accordingly.  The remaining black wire feeds whichever did not get power in the previous step. The wire that you have identified as feeding the attic should be twisted together with the black wire you have identified as the power from the circuit breaker and the black wire from the dimmer switch.  The red from the dimmer switch should be twisted together with the remaining black wire.  Keep the red with a white stripe capped and the green/yellow connected with the bare ground wire.

If you have softened water, watermarks (actually mineral deposits left over when the water evaporates) are not a problem. If you don't have treated water, then you should look into it IF you local plumbing code allows water softeners. If you don't have treated water, then matte finish tiles will not show spots as readily as a polished finish - not to mention fingerprints, etc. Be careful with the word "porcelain" when buying tile. You don't need what American tile companies call porcelain - another name for tile graded impervious. Impervious tile is only needed outdoors where there is a hard winter freeze. Hello Mark,  if the interior walls are plastered then to add electrical wiring and plumbing will be exactly the same process as if you home was brick construction with plastered interiors. Cost would also be the same as the trenching and re-flushing will be the same process. If your concrete internal walls are exposed however (same as in modern rammed earth walls or precast concrete walls today) then you would have to consider three options as to how to add electrical or plumbing lines and these would also have different costs depending on what you do. One option would be again to trench these in, and then cement over the trench when finished, however this would leave an obvious scar on the walls wherever the trenching is done. The other option would be to trench and then fill as-well-as then plaster over the entire wall that was effected; changing the exposed concrete appearance to a plastered appearance ready to paint. (instead of plastering you could alternatively wall-paper or use some other type of covering. The other option would be to run cable inside Trunking which is fixed and left exposed on the face of your walls, where this is often done in industrial style interior fit-outs and is also done in some heritage buildings. These really depend on what your walls are, how they have been finished already, and what you want them to look like when you finish renovating.       Hope this helps, Malcolm.

Here's what we do to prevent damping off.  After I plant the seeds, I use a fungicide. I put a heaping teaspoon of Captan in about a cup of water and shake it up good (it will settle back out). I water the seedling, making sure all of the soil is touched by the fungicide. That usually controls damping off for us. Also, don't keep your seedlings too moist. Once ours go outside (we grow under lights) and they are not sitting in a tray that doesn't drain, we can water them all we want. But when they are in the house in a tray that holds water, they don't like to stay too moist. I would rather they be a little dry than too moist I hope you get your damping off under control. It's really disappointing to see those little seedlings falling over. Nancy

You would need a 80 inch round table to seat 10 people comfortably, and adding three feet all around for chair space, your room is not wide enough. Furthermore, there is a tremendous amount of wasted space in the middle of the table. A rectangular table 96 inches in length will seat 10 comfortably with 4 on each side and one at each end. You don't need to get the table that is 96" long, just get a table that has two leaves, and with the two leaves added will be 96" long. At 96" it will extend beyond the strict length of the dining room, but it is not a big deal for the table to extend past the doorway just for the duration of the meal. After the meal is over, you will take out the leaves and the table will be short again. It is most important for your guests to be comfortable while dining. You also want the table to be sufficiently wide, try for a table that is 45-48 inches. Any narrower than that and you may not have sufficient room for serving pieces, centerpieces, candles, etc. This is especially important when you do not plan to have other furniture in the room such as a buffet.

Just wanted to comment on paint finishes in general since there seems to be a fair amount of confusion.  For Benjamin Moore or Sherwin Williams, you can always go to the TDS sheet for any paint and it will give you the amount of sheen as a % at a certain angle.  This is much more accurate than the store sample display. The amount of sheen varies between brands and different lines within each brand.  For example, Benjamin Moore "eggshell" in their contractor grade of "Ultra Spec 500", is lower than in their designer grade of Regal or Aura.  Also, less scrubbable and harder to "touch up". To make it more confusing, their newer paint - Scuff X - (which I really like) is part of their Ultra Spec line! I believe SW paint has their TDS sheets posted on line as well.  I have never used SW paint, but read many comments that SW sheens are lower compared to Benjamin Moore and others.  This is most likely due to "lower solids".  % of solids is also listed on the TDS, so easy to compare. If your builder lets you pick the exact paint, always go for the best quality paint.  The labor is the most expensive part, and should be the same regardless. Cheap paint isn't cheap when it doesn't last.

It's likely the underlying cause for the spoiled foliage is too much water in the grow medium, and it's typical that symptoms of stress are first made manifest in the lighter tissues of variegated plants. That said, the repotting at this time of year is likely an unnecessary stress as the best way to stop the spoiled leaves is by getting to a place where watering intervals are appropriate. Keep in mind that damp/moist are the operational words for how much water should be in the medium; and, if your pot is deeper than about 5", the commonly offered advice to "water when the top inch or two of the soil feels dry to your touch" is inappropriate, as it is a recipe for over-watering. Using a wooden tell you can make for next to nothing from a wooden dowel rod (any hardware or home improvement store) will help you add the "appropriate" part to appropriate watering intervals, something essential to maintaining the vitality of your plant. There is some chance that the spoiled foliage is from under-watering or a high level of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from fertilizer solutions and the minerals dissolved in tapwater, but there isn't enough information to determine that yet. Still the advice I offered about getting watering intervals right applies. If you water while you can still detect some moisture in the medium either by visual confirmation or testing it with a finger, you're not under-watering. Also, if you haven't noticed the plant wilting, it's very unlikely under-watering is to blame. It would be a good idea to flush the soil (next time the plant needs water) and probably fertilize at that time, but before that's decided we should see an image of the plant and its pot, please. Certain trees and plants may succeed in wet saturated soil, but they cannot stop sheetflow of water, nor cannot "soak up" more water quicker than the surrounding grade's saturation point. Not a good homeowner solution in directing and managing problem water. Nor is introducing detention areas with gravel and native plants that would be a different visual and functional "island" unto itself competing with your landscaping concept and the neighborhood in general. You need to direct the sheetflow of water, that is, the water running on top of the grade and walk. You can leave the walk, just remove some of the edging plantings (or lower them) so the water can exit to the sides. It looks like there is a "dip" about where the YELLOW circled area is anyway. The swale's "vee" would be in RED to direct water around to the sides. The grade should be sloped in BLUE towards the swales, and that includes a portion sloping down from the house to the swale. Realize a swale is not steep like a ditch, but just gradual sloped sides that still allows a mower's deck width to work. Your house is basically in the way of where the water wants to go (which explains why you needed some basement fixes). In a situation with minor standing water, swales should do it. If you are in a heavy rain climate and still not getting results, in the future then you could add a french drain at the 'vee' of the swale to "quicken" it's capacity by collecting some underground water too.

From a thermodynamics standpoint, the wood flooring may slow the transfer of heat a bit, which will result in a little more lag, but heat is not going to be "lost." My neighbor and I have essentially the same house design,  with hydronic heating of bare concrete floors downstairs and plywood subfloors with carpeting upstairs. About a year ago my neighbor replaced all his carpeting upstairs with  engineered flooring and has reported no problems. With any radiant heating there is always a lag as the heat source first heats up the surrrounding materials, and it can be a long time for concrete to heat back up once it's cooled. In fact, if I lose power for an extended period of time in winter the house cools slowly, but it can take almost 8 hours for the house to get back up to normal temperature when the power comes back on.  That's why we don't have a night setback thermostat since the swings in temp are so slow. Having said that, I don't think what you're  contemplating will create major problems and should work ok, and you may have less lag with your setup than I do with my  concrete floors.

@Joanne, The latch lever is probably hidden behind a panel that opens upward between the control panel and oven door.  Lift the panel, move the lever fully to the right to lock. I would do something really simple that I've used many times.  Buy four of the cheapest white muslin twin flat sheets you can find.  (Walmart used to sell flats and fitteds separately, but I don't know if they still do.)  Sheets are long enough to go floor to ceiling and they come with nice wide hems already sewn on one end.  Hold them up against the rods so the wide hem just clears the floor and mark on the other end where the top of the rod is.  Turn that end down that amount (narrow hem and all) and sew across to make a rod pocket.  (You can do two rows of stitching a little more than the rod width apart if you would like a ruffle at the top, above the rod.  Measure each sheet separately; they often vary in out-of-the-package length.  If you don't sew, you could use iron-on mending tape.)  Tie them back at the top of the lower sash with something decorative that relates to the room colors. These would be stationary curtains (although you could release the tiebacks at night to let them hang straight down).  Cheap sheets will typically have a low thread count, which is good because they look nice and airy and light comes through them, so it's okay that they cover part of the window during the day.  (As you said, you have the blinds for light blocking if/when needed.)  And sheets are wide enough to look nice and full on the rod. I think if the curtains basically don't extend beyond the window trim, the two windows will look the same width and the asymmetry in the window placement won't be disturbing. Damping Off. Common fungal problem for seedlings when the soil is too wet for too long. If you look closely at the base of the seedling close to the soil line you will see the young stem is considerably narrower and stringy and brown. That is the location where the fungus hits the the delicate stem and cuts of the supply of water and nutrients to the seedling and keels over. Possible solutions are to use sterile mix, keep the surface dry (better air flow), use well draining mix (suitable for seedlings), anti-fungal spray before the seeds germinate.

Concrete and water are perfectly fine together. You could submerge concrete under water and it will be fine. Having a wet towel sitting on concrete does nothing but be gross over time and attract bugs. The water should be clear being filtered through the deep grade outside, however, when something is wet, airborne particles (and dirty stuff from before) stick to it, which is what any mold growth would feed on. You can scrub the area clean and it 'should' remain clear water when entering. There is no interior surface cover that would stop the water - like paint - water is still entering behind that paint, and it will find a way in (note the difference between water and moisture). The best thing to start addressing this is looking outside. Where are your downspouts discharging? Is grade sloped away from the house? Do you have thick mulch beds or a lot of plantings right up against the house? If there are some improvements outside to be made, they could at best eliminate, or maybe reduce the seepage to just a trickle on high rain days. The sump set up needs some more investigation: - First, with a new house purchase, I would have thought you would have gotten a radon test. The first thing done is seal all openings, which would include a tight sump pit cover. - Second, if there is no french drain connected to it, what water is it discharging? With an original sump pit, the house would assume to have a footing drain tile on the exterior (which is a french drain down below the slab height) which would cross through/under the footing to this sump pit. There also could have been interior french drains added later when they had water problems, but that would have been routed to a newly installed sump pit. They also could have later installed just a sump crock with perforations for a high water table, but I would think there would be a french drain somewhere with that. So what french drains are you talking about that go nowhere? I see you spent a chunk of change replacing the battery backup pedestal pump with a water powered one.

I've been working on rooting roses for a couple yrs now. I'm in zone 9a. I discovered last yr, I simply cannot do it from about May 1st thru Sept 1st. We had triple digits almost that whole time. Tried putting the pots inside, but still was too hot for them. Fall and spring are the best times for me. Nov and Dec were unusually colder than normal this time around, and the cuttings have taken a LOT longer to root. Upside is they don't rot or fail as fast as in the heat. All you can do is just give it a try. Don't do like I tend to do tho, and pull them before they are ready!! I keep thinking they HAVE to be rooted after about 6wks... But... it's taking them about 8-10wks or longer in the colder temps. But now we are experiencing unusually WARM temps, and even ones I potted up back in early November are just beginning to callous, let alone form roots! Most everything is eventually working tho. Just gotta be patient!! It's all a crap-shoot. Some suggestions... try potting them up in clear plastic containers, like soda bottles or juice bottles. I cut the tops off and put drain holes in the bottom. You can see when the roots have formed. It's fun to experiment. And I use Hormex #8 rooting powder mixed with some cinnamon to prevent rot. When you water, try to avoid getting water on the leaves or anywhere where it can collect in any cupped leaves or nooks/crannies. Fungal spores need a continual source of moisture over varying periods to activate.  This is the disease tetrahedron. All 4 of the requirements must be met for a pathogen to infect the plant. By denying fungal spores the amount of TIME they need be continually wet, you eliminate one side ot the tetrahedron, which is all that's needed to prevent a pathogenic attack. This applies to plants other than succulents as well, which is why you so often see the advice to 'water in the morning' (so the water dries up quickly in the warmth and normally increased air movement that occurs during the daytime hours. When you water, be sure the entire soil column has been moistened and at least 20% of the entire volume of water used during the session exits the drain hole. This ensures there can be no excessive build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the grow medium, which can affect root health and root function. A healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Al

The whiter quartzites can be very porous (that doesn’t define whether they’re a true quartzite, per numerous threads by our resident geologist) and this edge staining has been theorized to be either silicone bleed or water during fabrication that’s trying to push its way out months later, or a combo of both. I personally lean toward silicone bleed because it seems to happen to some installed slabs and not others.  I have what I think is the identical stone but I do NOT have this edge staining.  Our fabricator was very experienced working with quartzite and HAD heard of this happening within the industry (I ran from one fabricator who claimed he’d never heard of it and denied it was a risk).  We had multiple discussions with our (amazing) fabricator about how best to mitigate silicone bleed and he confirmed that they use high quality non-bleeding adhesive.  We also did not have mitered edges (3cm stone), and we had them seal our faucet hole after drilling it out.  So far, so good, but who knows if our luck will eventually run out a few years down the road.  But we have very realistic expectations about the potential for it to occur and we know we did everything possible to minimize it. I’m very sorry this took you by surprise and I hope you’re able to lessen the edge staining using many of the techniques in the threads linked by @vinmarks. Wall cavities can be insulated after drywall is installed using injection foam insulation.  It expands differently than spray foam insulation and applies less force to the backside of the drywall than spray foam would.  It can be installed from the exterior after removing a few courses of siding and drilling holes in the sheathing which is the route I'd recommend.  It's not a job for an amateur.  Spend time vetting the insulation contractor and don't settle for some fly-by-night outfit.    A post installation quality check should consist of a visual inspection of the drywall to ensure it isn't "bulging" and an IR camera to show any spots where insulation is missing.  Those can then be treated on an exception basis.

text: In principle you CAN grow roots from pepper stems, just not necessarily from everywhere on the stem like for tomatoes. That's why you can grow cuttings from peppers. The roots will usually emerge more reliably from just below the node where the leaves join the stem. So, in  principle, you can cut off the lowest leaves and bury to just above that node. I suspect, however, that it isn't going to make much of a difference.

I generally bury pepper plants 1-2" below the existing soil line. As @daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa) mentioned, the stems will root somewhat, but nothing like the heavy full-length rooting seen in tomatoes. While I don't see any negative consequences of burying peppers a little deep, I suspect it doesn't contribute much additional vitality. It may, however, provide additional support & reduce the chances of the plants being tipped over as the peppers take on weight. I do see quite a few branches emerge from the soil line, which contribute to the overall bushiness of the plants... but can't say for certain if that is caused by burying deep.

The only way to do this right is to test the paint colors in your space. You need large samples and you need to look at them with your furnishings and finishes. I have a system for choosing a whole home color palette. It begins with a walk through of your home.   I determine what rooms connect to each other and how the visual flow works from room to room. I then determine what must stay.   (Other than a new build we almost always have things that we are not willing to change either because we like the item or we can't afford to change it). This may be flooring, countertops, cabinets, wood trim, appliances, furniture . . .  It may also include some personal pieces of art or sculpture. I draw out the rooms in order of how they flow and note the colors that must stay for each room. The second step is to figure out the colors.   Those actual colors (vs neutrals) that make your heart sing.   Do you love fall colors with the deep greens and golds and orange reds or do you love cornflower blue and peach?   Everyone has a few colors that dominate their wardrobe and are the colors they are drawn to when they pick art or décor items.   Seeing those colors makes you feel happy.  We love colors that are associated with happy memories. Think about how you want to use those colors in your home.  How to make those colors flow from one room to the next.  How to bring joy into each room through color. Now you can pick your neutrals and your whites.   They have to work with what is already there and with the colors you love. For some taupe (pink/purple/beige/gray) will never work.  For others greige (green/beige/gray) undertones don't work and for some neither is going to work well - they need a clearer creamy color or a steel blue gray. You can select one white and use it for walls, ceiling and trim throughout your home or pick lighter versions for trim and doors than for the walls.   You can vary walls from one room to the next using lighter and darker versions of your neutral.

You can have two very large firm cushions made that span the length of the bed and go up 16-18 ", your preference and have them made out of quite dense foam wrapped in batting. No down needed here, and the children should not be able to feel the rails behind them. (Now your daughter is gentle floral. In 5 years she may be animal patterns, and 5 years after that she may be into goth!) You can also have ties made to tie the cushions on to the rails so they don't slip and slip. Velcro works, but after a while, it gets weird in the wash. Since girls often have sleep-overs, a trundle day-bed is a great idea, and the top mattress can be a full size and the bottom one can be a twin. See if you can find one where the lower one pops up to the same level as the upper one, it is so much nicer. Rather than the cheapo furniture that is sold nowadays, why not go to a Goodwill or similar store and purchase a well-made solid wood triple dresser and nightstand and paint them. If you ask in the smaller lumberyards and hardware stores you can often find men that do these sorts of projects. I would get a really good closet system, one that will grow with her. What I mean by "grow with her" is one that is adjustable, that you can adjust the height of the various elements, etc without paying someone else a fortune to do so, that you can use your own tools, not the package's special;y sized wrench or whatever you 3 years later goodness knows where you stashed it. Also, you want a reputable brand or company that will stay in business so that if you want to add on and buy more parts, they will still be in business. The cheapo one at a dollar store or discount store may look just as good now, but later, it will be useless. You can build in a desk under the window, to be used for both crafts and schoolwork. You can use a formica laminate that you get from IKEA or someplace like Home Depot or wood. That can be attached to the wall and the height changed as she grows. You can get a set of drawers for one side for craft supplies and a two-drawer file cabinet for her papers and files. As others have mentioned, a bookshelf is important, but maybe only one book shelf. Children don't use that many school books anymore, many of their school "books" are on- line. At this time, since she may not have that many books, you can use the book shelves to store her toys and games and dolls. If you can't afford to buy a bookshelf, don't worry, you can use a thick wooden board and cinderblocks, and it will more than do the job, and it will be much sturdier than any particle board shelving unit from IKEA! And you can always paint the wooden shelf, even the cinderblock if you want. Just like brushing teeth, now is the time to inculcate good habits like orderliness. Children can't put things away if they don't know where they are supposed to go. Those TV shows that show a row of baskets or opaque bins are the most stupid things ever if one expects a pre-literate child to clean up after him/herself. First go through all your daughter's possessions,  & keep, donate, or discard. If donation centers are not taking donations due to COVID, don't wait for COVID to be over, just trash it. The way I got my daughter to part with things was two pronged: 1. Indoor space is finite, she can't get more until she gets rid of a significant amount of what she has 2. As much as I love her chefs-d’œuvre, I can't possible keep every piece of paper she has touched with a pen, pencil or brush. I purchased a big portfolio and once a year she went throught her things and selected the things she wanted me to keep for her. 3. Her books were really piling up and she inherited the book-hoarding gene. This tactic worked- "Think of all the poor children who can't afford to buy books..." And we did donate them.Purchase transparent plastic containers for your daughter's possessions of a size that will separate things by type. e.g.  dolls together, building blocks together, each type in it's own baggie, etc. Then, if you prefer opaque containers, you can put the transparent containers in the opaque containers and label the opaque containers with what is inside, either with words if your daughter can read well, or with photographs. I felt that was too many extra steps. I just used transparent plastic and labels. Don't stack too much, use those wire shelves that they sell for the kitchen to separate stacks of plates, otherwise when your daughter reaches for one thing, everything will come tumbling down. If you are going to have a television in her room, it can be wall-mounted on a mount that is adjustable so that the TV can be turned and raised or lowered so she can see the TV from her bed or her desk or even the floor. (Oh, the days when it was comfortable to sit on the floor!) Use vertical space as much as possible. For example, you can have a shelf over the window and have decorative boxes there. Either buy pretty floral hatboxes and rectangular boxes, etc or buy plain ones and you and she can cover them with gift paper you buy yourselves. Way up there is a great place for things you or she don't use that often, like the fancy hats for holidays, certain types of craft supplies, maybe clothes that are too big for her that she has received as gifts or hand-me-downs. You might want to use ModPodge on top of the wrapping paper surface if you DIY. If you put clothes in those boxes make sure they are clean and dry and tuck in several silica gel dessicant packets. Don't use flour-water paste, that will attract bugs. You can even gussy the boxes up with brass corners , handles and label holders.

In reverse order: A decent hood blower (internal or remote) is unlikely to reduce house pressure relative to the outside by more than a few inches of water column.  At that point the blower is gagged and no air is actually flowing.  MUA serves two purposes.  The first, which should be obvious from the above remark, is to allow the blower to actually move the CFM needed for ventilation.  The second is to ameliorate a safety hazard of low house pressure back drafting combustion appliances, if any, and pulling moisture and dust through wall crevices. You didn't address what is above the range location.  You could run a duct to the roof, depending what is up there.  You could use an island hood, or as you note, fill in the wall opening and mount a hood to the wall. Pro range effluent plumes are not going to be successfully captured and contained with a downdraft system when cooking anything involving hot (vapor point) oil or grease.  The plume momentum will be too large to divert into going the other direction.  Search this forum for "downdraft" for examples of negative commentary.  "Pro" ranges require "pro" hood systems, plus MUA systems of some minor or major complexity. I suggest you sear some meat and see how well your existing 'ventilation' works at plume capture.

Its not the pilot light, primarily, it is the use of efficient heat transfer that makes the exhaust gas nearly room temperature, and hence the appliance has very little draft.  Very low pressure differences with the outside will cause the exhaust to be pulled into the house.  This can happen at 0.03 inches, w.c.  (1 inch w.c. = 0.036 psi)  Fully sealed units with their own source of outside MUA, or those in areas exposed to the outside, will not be susceptible.  I presume your attic is ventilated to the outside. Suppose you built out the wall somewhat to allow an 8-inch duct?  Or you mounted a chimney hood to the 2 x 4 wall and put a chase (or cabinet) above the hood to cover its duct and allow room for a bend into the joist space.  An 8-inch round duct transitioning to an 8 x 10 rectangular duct could probably tolerate a 90-degree bend rectangular duct section. In any case, once the hood configuration is determined, an estimate of the duct pressure loss, the baffle pressure loss, and the MUA pressure loss (you may be able to use a simple passive MUA system), will allow you to determine what blower to use to achieve the desired CFM at that pressure loss. Start with the range size, then the hood size, then the desired flow rate, then the duct size, etc.  I may use Wolf Design Guide listed hoods for analysis, but you will find seemingly endless hoods exist for every niche and pocketbook.  Just keep in mind that in the trade space of performance, aesthetics, and affordability, one either balances these or chooses two to maximize.

I grow about half (if not more) of my roses in pots and the others in the ground.  All are on own root except for one.  We get (as I always say), hotter than Hades here in the summer.  We are typically over 100 F from June (sometimes May), until October.  Last summer we got to 116 F again.  It is misery. I use BIG pots for my roses.  They have them at Sam's Club this time of year.  They are at least 22 inches in diameter and are resin pots.  They are much thicker than "regular" plastic ones and help to protect the roots from the heat and sun.  I have them on caddies with wheels that will hold over 100 lbs.  Great as they get very heavy between the potting mix, rose and the water.  I also have them on drip and water them daily during the summer for one minute each day.  I also have them in morning sun and afternoon shade from about 3 PM or so.  I don't really feed them from about the end of May until at least the middle of September.  It is too hot and they are just trying to survive.  I want them to survive and not waste energy trying to grow flowers when it is that hot. Now, that being said, the best ones for my pots has been my NOID (no ID) which is a rose I grew from one of Roseseek's seeds--that name is what I call it--it does have an "official" name of initials of its parental units--no ID is easier for me.  Others include Peppermint Parfait--a wonderful Ralph Moore rose.  It is first to bloom this year (Already! A month early!).  Minnie Mouse is another great rose that does very, very well.  Violet Hour does great and is gorgeous!  Ah, too early in the morning to think of what else I have out there....I have several "experiments" this year. My other roses are on their own in the ground.  I find hybrid perpetuals tend to do well for me on their own root.  Probably my star rose is Vick's Caprice.  Portland from Glendora has done well.  Also Alice Hamilton (I love this rose!).  They are all on drip. Others that do well for me are Ralph Moore's Sequoia Gold, and Halo Sweetie.  A Burling rose Flamingo Dancer is an all star rose as well. For DA roses--Munstead Wood, Pretty Jessica, Mary Magdalene, Princess Alexandra of Kent and Jubilee Celebration do OK.  I have been slowly getting rid of my DA roses as they just are not wild about the heat here.  Probably the best for heat is Pretty Jessica (if you can still find her) and Mary Magdalene (if you can still find her). I just moved Jubilee to a different location where she will get full sun all day, so we shall see how she does.  I am keeping my fingers crossed. My roses that are in the ground are all on drip.  I have water restrictions where I live and can only (during the summer) water 2 or 3 days a week and only during certain hours.  For about half of the year, I can only water one day a week.  Mother Nature does the rest of the watering (and she hasn't been around much over the past several years during winter and is not around at all from May through October).  I am thinking of putting up sunscreen over my roses that get full sun during the day and see if that helps.  I think the homeowners association will probably complain as well as my neighbors, so the jury is out as to whether or not I do this in the front and side yards.  People in Tucson do this with their roses (which many are in pots due to soil, etc., there). Hope that helps!

You probably are going have to install some type of support to keep the return pipe off the fins. You can try using zip ties wrap around each of the brackets. There are ties rated up to 180F degrees which should be sufficient. If you need something with more heat resistance then look at using soft solid bare copper wire. If you use a metal wire then I recommend it be copper. Using a dissimilar metal could cause long term problems. The pipe has to be pulled up so it doesn't touch the fins but it should touch the brackets either.

The return pipe may be contributing to the noises, and should not lay on the fins. I imagine it would certainly affect the efficiency of heat transfer to the room. In my home, when our baseboards get noisy, it usually indicates air trapped in the system and needs to be bled.

I would try using heavy nylon zip ties to support the pipe - looping it through the gap in the brackets that are every foot or so. You only need about an 1/8 of an inch gap. If the heat from the pipe is an issue for the nylon ties, any type of thermal break (cardboard) would limit the heat transfer.

Horticulturally speaking, planting multiple trees in the same hole is not a sound practice. Root competition and crowding will result in trees consistently under stress with subsequent increased vulnerability to pests and diseases. And with poor fruit production. Multi-graft apples are widely available from most major vendors so that is the easiest option. However, you do not always have your choice of apple varieties and usually have to stick with what the grower provides, generally those that will successfully pollinate each other. Typically you can pick from as few as 2 different apples to as many as 5 or 7 (semi dwarf or standard only). As to what apples to choose, your county extension service is best able to help you with that. Not all apples will grow well or be equally productive in all areas, so best to get local recommendations on what does best in your specific locale.

Since we don't really know the growing conditions, it is hard to speculate on what is the problem (if any). I would suggest that instead of watering on a weekly schedule, water only when you need to. And that will be determined by the potting media and indoor conditions. I have copied Al's (tapla) great instructions for using a "tell" to determine when to water. By far the best method to judge watering needs if not very familiar with both the plant and the media. "Start using a 'tell' to 'tell' you when it's time to water and things will probably straighten out. It won't be over-night, but you should start to see a difference right away. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoidit is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a veryimportant factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue."

There is a tab in the center of the socket at the bottom, and sometimes those don't quite make contact with the bulb.  It happens with other fixtures, like lamps, too.  A quick way to check this is to make sure the power is off, get a small screwdriver, and use it to bend the metal tab up from the bottom of the socket just a little bit more.  Then re-try the bulb.  If that doesn't work, you can get an identical replacement for that porcelain socket for about $5-6 at your local hardware store. Just make sure the power is off before switching the wires to the new socket. And of course, before buying a replacement, you can turn off the power, undo the two screws, and pull the socket down to make sure there is no loose wire. Whatever is wrong, I can't see that it poses a hazard unless you decide to work on it without having cut the power to it.

Hi, Elaine, If your home were an air-sealed box and fresh air was introduced only via the HRV you could design a system with a high-efficiency filter for the HRV to be used when wildfires occur.   But most homes don't behave like air-sealed boxes.  Instead, they operate at negative pressures due to the combination of wind, stack effect, and HVAC systems with undersized return air flows.  Air is drawn into the home though penetrations, cracks around windows and doors, etc.  For that reason, and given that wildfires are (hopefully) infrequent, I suggest you invest in air sealing your home to the extent practical, and balancing of your home's HVAC supply and return air flows.   When wildfires occur, turn off the HRV and use portable room air cleaners to filter ambient smoke inside your home.  You can move them from room to room as needed.

Be careful about using straight rubbing alcohol, it can strip cuticular wax from the leaf surfaces, which increases water loss through leaves and provides an entry point where pathogens can more easily enter the plant. You don't mention where you live, but should it be too cold to spray the plant outdoors now, my suggestion would be to treat the plant with a soil drench that contains Imidacloprid, which will take care of both issues.  Add 2 teaspoons of the 1.47% solution to a quart or liter of distilled water to which 1 teaspoon of white vinegar has been added. The reason for the distilled water and vinegar is, Imidacloprid is degraded by alkaline hydrolysis, and almost all tapwater is alkaline. Using distilled water or water from a r/o filtration system that has been acidified with white vinegar ensures it will be free of bicarbonates and slightly acidic. If it IS warm enough that the spraying can be done outdoors where the plant can be left to dry, Bayer 3-in-1 for Insects, Disease, and Mites will work better and faster, and it covers 3 bases.  Follow mixing directions and spray the plant so all surfaces of leaves and branches are made wet, then allow it to dry outdoors out of wind. This product should similarly be mixed with distilled water and acidified with vinegar to work best. Be sure to purchase the product with a label which lists Imidacloprid as an active ingredient. They make 2 products with the same label and only 1 contains the systemic insecticide Imidacloprid. If you're not happy with your plants level of vitality (health), and if you wish, we can talk about how to tailor a care regimen to the plant, and talk more about repotting. If you live in the Northern Hemisphere, the best way to proceed is * Flush the soil thoroughly * (probably) Fertilize with an appropriate soluble synthetic fertilizer (Foliage-Pro 9-3-6 is great) * Make sure your watering intervals are appropriate by using a wooden 'tell' to 'tell' you when it's time to water. * Move the plant outdoors into dappled or open shade as soon as night temps are reliably above 55* * Plan to repot and do any essential pruning in June My plan isn't to leave you stranded with some generalized suggestions. If you decide you think there is merit in my reasoning, we can work together on a care plan and I'll provide more specific suggestions - like how to go about repotting, how to flush the soil, why I suggest you wait until June to repot and do any other stressful work  ........... More on using a tell: Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

See if there is a correlation between your rust spot locations and the locations of the clips holding your sink in place. If so, the clips are rusting, bleeding, and will eventuraly fail. Disconnect the plumbing and drive a stiff scraper between the sink flange and the stone bottom (if you can't access the clips with a screwdriver); pound until the clips fail. Poultice out the rust, seal, and you should be fine.

Walls are built over the sub floor.  For 9' ceiling framing would consist of a pre-cut 104 5/8" stud, bottom plate 1 1/2" thick and double top plates 3" thick.  Total height would be 109 1/8".  Subtracting 5/8" for ceiling sheet rock the height would then be 108 1/2".  The thickness of the finished floor would  determine finial height. 3/4" wood flooring would be a 1/4" short of 9 feet so to get exactly 9' you could only use a finished floor that was 1/2" thick.  This is the standard for 9' ceilings and your builder will understand without question and work off the blueprints. If you decide on 3/4" wood flooring and want that extra 1/4" of head room, or a few extra inches then 10' studs would need to be purchased and cut down but will more expensive  because of materials and extra labor.   So ask your wife if a 1/4" matters and if she'd be happier with a few extra inches, and if height is important you may want to think about 10' ceilings.

Problem with the water inlet valve ...  hot or cold side, whichever.  Could be a bit of debris is obstructing the diaphram from seating fully closed.  Or the valve has just gone bad due to an internal problem with the diaphram, plunger, or spring.  You can identify which side of the valve by turning off the cold supply faucet to see if the dripping stops.  If not, then turn off the hot supply faucet.  Valves years past could be disassembled to clear debris or even replace internal parts but nowadays they're usually sealed and can't be disassembled, must replace.  It's not a large repair.  Sometimes debris will loosen and flush through by tapping on the solenoid while it's on ... but sometimes not.  Safest recourse is replace the valve assembly.  The drip can get worse over time.

I had a top shelf about 6 feet tall where I stashed unbreakable, easy to grab items like cereal boxes and paper towels. From what Ive been reading a stark white trim will bring out the undertones in otger whites, and therefore to avoid pairing something like simply white with a white trim? A lot to unpack there. :) First, colors don't possess or inherently *have* undertones. Undertones are just someone's subjective opinion of what a color looks like - to them - under a random light source and in a particular context. Undertones aren't facts of color. They're subjective judgments. And they don't scale beyond the individual making that judgment about what a color looks like. Every color of white belongs to a hue family. If two colors of white belong to different hue families, there is going to be a degree of contrast in terms of hue and your eyeballs may register the tension of that contrast. Depending on the specific color relationship, each could enhance the colorfulness of the other. If two colors of white belong to the same hue family, there will be less contrast. Less contrast means less tension between the two colors for your eyeballs to discern and less contrasting energy to feel. So a statement like "a stark white will bring out undertones" requires qualifying exactly what they mean.... a lot of qualifying.

I struggle. I have 3 'mothers'....one my real mother, one my gf's mother and one a woman I worked with for many years.  My real mom is gone, but the other two are still alive and in their late 90s.  They have all showed me how to deal with aging and loss with grace.  They have all suffered serious loss in their lives:  My mom lost dad and son to suicide; my GF's mom lost her husband and her ability to leave her bed; my friend from work lost her husband, her daughter and her ability to leave her bed.  Yet all of them stay(ed) focused on feeling good, upbeat, cheerful and open to whatever life has brought them.  Laughter is always sought after and comes easily.  It is never hard to visit with them as they are always so welcoming and pleasant to be with.  They are still the giving and loving people they always were.  Though life has brought them such suffering and constricted them in so many ways, they will still offer whatever they can to make life better for all. How they've walk(ed) their path is so admirable, so courageous, so hard, and yet they've all accomplished it with such grace.  I am ever grateful for them, for showing me it can be done. Here I am, 30 years younger and already haven't come close to what they've achieved.  I have yet to find that grit, that resilience.  I already see how my heart has hardened to loss and suffering...I already feel how joy has been sapped and capped by the knowledge that boundless love means boundless suffering...and so I hold back.  And while change is inevitable, I so fear the negative changes to come and how much pain and stress they will cause that every task seems fraught with risks almost too hard to bear lest it lead to harm. I can't become a victim of my own fears especially when I have no power to change the inevitable.  When I have been open, I have been rewarded with unexpected pleasures and joy.  So it's there, available to me.  But it's more than choosing to be open.  It's finding that grit, that persistence, that will, discipline and focus to shed the fear, loss and suffering like a snake sheds its skin, as often as necessary, so that joys of living emerge renewed again and again. And so I struggle. May this year be the year when I stop trying and just do...like these brave women before me have.

I had a 6-burner Dacor gas cooktop with a separate downdraft unit.  I've almost completed a kitchen refresh that involved changing the gas cooktop to induction.  I bought a Bosch Benchmark 36" induction cooktop with a Zephyr 36" separate downdraft unit.  Like you, there was no possibility of using a hood.  I had to stick with the downdraft. Not optimal, but it was what it was. Here is what I learned in the process.  Both the Best and Zephyr downdrafts telescope up to 18" making a larger area for drawing.  That's the biggest available.  They both come with a led light that lights up your cooking surface.  That's a surprisingly nice benefit.  While not perfect, it's better than what I had in the past with a 8" telescoping unit. When you repotted your tree, did you remove the old medium from the roots or just leave the medium in place? If you left the medium in place, then you wind up with two different drainage patterns for your well draining mix and the original soil. Not a good situation. I would repot the tree, remove the old medium, and place the tree in new. Then submerge the pot so that the whole rootball gets soaked, or conversely run a hose through it until no more bubbles appear. Also, I would beware my moisture meter. Different moisture meters are calibrated in different soils, therefore they can be off if you're using them in a soil different than they were made for. If you want to use the moisture meter you need to "calibrate" it for yourself by figuring out what it reads as dry and wet for your soil. Use a chopstick or a wood skewer stuck down into the soil and feel the wood. Then put your meter in the soil and see what it reads. If the stick is wet, then whatever the meter is reading is "wet" if dry, then the meter is reading "dry". Use this to get a feel for when to water.

I'm no expert at telling the various cucurbits apart at this stage, but it is definitely a cucurbit. Personally I can't guess accurately at this stage if it's cucumber, melon or squash. Are you using homemade compost? One tip is that cucumbers we buy generally have immature seeds and are less likely to volunteer from the compost (because fully ripe cucumbers get sour and seedy and less good to eat). Melons and winter squash we buy and eat have ripe seeds which are very good at volunteering in compost. If a gardener lets  cucumbers stay on the vine too long, their seeds are viable. Many people online strongly recommend against growing on seeds that grow from garden vegetables, with an extreme fear that they might be from hybrids or cross-pollinations. But most cucurbits except Cucurbita pepo are fine. I've done it, and the science/logic is fine. They won't have the special properties the hybrid was bred for, but they will produce edible and maybe delicious melons, cukes, winter squash, because most of these have one general type per species, so cross pollination within the species will still produce plants producing that general type. For example a seed from a cantaloupe/muskmelon will surely produce a cantaloupe/muskmelon, and it will likely be a yummy one if it gets time to ripen, but it won't have the special disease resistant or other properties of the mother plant the seed came from. Same with cucumbers and C. maxima winter squash. C. pepo species is problematic because zucchini, spaghetti squash, delicata, acorn squash, and bitter toxic ornamental gourds are all in this species, so crosses may actually be weird or unusable, and if bitter, then they're toxic.

It could be whiteflies or spider mites. If the leaves are sticky, it's whiteflies. Look on the undersides of the leaves for small, white flies/moths. They also make holes in the leaves. The white areas look like mealy bugs to me.  You should realize that Majesty palms are notoriously difficult as "houseplants". They only reason HD sells so many of them is because they grow so fast so can be sold inexpensively. You can spray it with insecticidal soup, readily available. These ARE NOT like most palms in that they DO NOT appreciate drying between waterings, so feel free to ignore the one size fits all for watering palms that suggests that they need to dry out between waterings...., they would even occasionally appreciate sitting in a shallow saucer of water. Higher indoor humidity is good, ventilation, keeping it on the cooler side, and putting it outside for the growing season (depending on where you are). But honestly, coconut palms are easier inside. Good luck! P.S., You might also add a bit of more soil to cover the exposed roots but don't over do it.

"They’re like a hospital hallway with how blue and bright they are." As shown in the photo below, the color temperature (in Kelvin or "K") determines the warmth or coldness of the light. In general I will say the following: float a couch in the living room with the back towards the kitchen (with two feet behind the couch). That will create a visual "room", separating the two spaces. Items in a store look smaller than they will look in your house. Get seated pieces with narrow armrests. Wide armrests take up too much room. If you need storage in the living room, get some either stand alone tall pieces (and bolt them to the wall) or built ins. Closed pieces with doors and drawers are best. Seeds differ in their requirements -- some need light, some darkness; some need cool soil temps other warm temps.  You won't be successful if you don't give the seeds what they require. A lot of your question hinges on whether you use the lights to generate the warmth needed to heat the seeds or whether the warmth is coming from elsewhere (e.g. heat mat, placing on top of the fridge, etc).  I don't use supplemental heat, so when I start under lights, the light is as close to the top of the seed tray as I can get it; this usually generates enough warmth for germination.  Note I use florescent bulbs, not LEDs; I don't think LEDs would generate enough warmth. For seeds that require darkness to germinate, covering with potting medium is usually sufficient, but there are a few where covering with something that blocks all light is beneficial (annual phlox comes to mind); something like black plastic will do. It's not hard to germinate seeds and grow seedlings under lights, not at all; you just need to understand the basic principles of it. I can't recommend this book highly enough:  The New Seed-Starter's Handbook by Nancy Bubel | Goodreads It taught me pretty much all I needed to know about seed starting, and even though it's old, the info in it is still sound. You DO NOT NEED special "grow lights"; cheap fluro tubes work just fine, and a mix of warm and cool bulbs works best IME.

I just noticed you mentioned you use bottom heat.  In that case, you don't need to put the lights as closely as I do, and if you're using fluros you shouldn't -- you might end up cooking them.  A couple-few inches above the seed tray should probably be sufficient -- it's the light + the heat that's needed.  After they germinate the light level is going to be more critical.

I have used flourescents, have largely moved on to tube style LED that are similar and use less power. For 1 flat (22") I use a single 24" dual tube unit (19W total) that provides 1200 lumens. Each light 'tube' contains a single string of Leds about 1/2" apart.  Perhaps you can use this to estimate how to apply the led light strings to your grow table.

Speed Queen TC5003: "Check standpipe height. The recommended height for the standpipe is 36 inches [914 mm]. Standpipes higher than 4 feet [1220 mm] are not recommended" LG WT7305CW or WT7005CW: "Do not install the drain hose with the end lower than 29.5 inches (75 cm) or higher than 96 inches (244 cm) above the bottom of the washer or more than 60 inches (152 cm) away from the washer."

>>>"Would my drain height be an issue?"<<< Depends on which model SQ washer you have your heart set on. Basically, higher standpipe drains result in slower draining which is a bigger problem for some SQ models than others. The slower draining seems to be a major issue for the TC5 model (so-called "classic" top-load model).  That's the one with a manual "recommending" against standpipes higher than 4 feet. For SQ's TR series top-load models (the "agi-tub top load" models designated as as TR7, TR5 and TR3) the manuals say: "Standpipes higher than 4 feet [1220 mm] will result in slower draining and may extend cycle times. ... NOTE: Machine will not drain if standpipe is higher than 8 feet [2438 mm]." For SQ's current FF7 front load models, the manual has a chart listing the  drainage flow rate for standpipe heights ranging from 3 feet  up to 8 feet.  The machine is rated to pump out 8.6 gallons-per-minute/32 liters-per-minute with a 36"/0.9m high standpipe with the rate declining down to 4 gallons-per-minute/15.2 liter-per-minute with a standpipe at 8 ft./2.4 m. above floor level. As best I could tell when I looked into this a year and something ago, an FF7 with an 8 foot tall standpipe might take about 5 to 10 minutes longer to run a washload than one hooked to a 3 foot tall standpipe, depending on how many rinses you've selected..

@katesullivan73  --- If you want to consider lowering your standpipe -- or alternative plumbing solutions ---  it can be worth consulting a plumber as opaone suggested. That is because of technical code requirements that govern the height, diameter and positioning of new and revised washing machine drain lines. From that, you can compare costs for getting what you want versus buying something else that can drain to the existing standpipe. For something that is somewhat like the SQ TC-5 but which could drain to the existing  6-foot high drainpipe --- have you looked at the Maytag Commercial MVWP575gw model? It seems to be an often discussed (sometimes touted, sometimes panned) residential/commercial alternative to the SQ TC-5. My own house also has a tall standpipe in the basement laundry room. I found I could not lower the existing standpipe drain below 68" high. That proved to be the minimum height needed to meet code requirements for the minimum height of vertical pipe above the code-required p-trap where the line transitions to a horizontal run over to where it connects with the house's drain waste line when sloped at the code required ¼-inch per foot.  The constraint was how and where the 1910 builders placed the main waste line to the sewer. Short of digging and installing whole new and much lower main waste line out to the sewer --- a huge and unaffordable expense for me --- the existing standpipe cannot go any lower.  YMMV, so it may be worth your while to check with plumbers if you aren't code-savvy. FWIW, I found the more affordable solutions to my house's plumbing constraints came down to: (a) limiting my washer choices to models with drain pumps rated to drain up to an 8-foot/96"/2.4m high standpipe; or (b) installing a large laundry sink (one large enough to hold all the wash water draining from a cycle) and installing and wiring in a lift pump rated for draining a laundry sink, an example being a SaniFlow SaniVITE. (There are plenty of other models, that just happens to be the one I researched.)

Step 1: Cut the individual colors out of the sheet they are in so you can see the color directly against the stone. White borders are useful when viewing a sample on a color you are going to be painting over, but not useful when comparing a color to an element that is staying. Step 2: Throw out any samples that clearly don't work with the stone Step 3: View the samples at different times of day and under daylight and artificial light. Throw out any samples that clearly don't work at each viewing. Step 4: Put the samples on the floor. Do they work with your floor? Throw out any that don't work. Step 5: Move the samples around the room. View them on vertical surfaces, not just flat on your counter. Throw out some more. Step 5: If you are keeping wall and trim color, test the remaining samples against those and throw out any remaining ones that don't work. If there are any other elements you are concerned about playing well with the cabinets, do the same for them. Step 6: Now with a much smaller pool of candidates, order large swatches (or sample paint so you can paint your own). Repeat steps 2 through 5 with the large samples. Step 7: Pick your favorite. If you can't pick a favorite by this time, they are all fine; throw a dart and don't stress.

My houses have been of 1930s vintage with high quality 6 over 6 singe pane windows with integrated weather stripping. It would cost a fortune to replace these windows with new windows of comparable quality. I believe that any replacement materials should be of similar quality to original My current house has triple track storm windows and I have no interior condensation issues. When the exterior drops quickly or gets below zero, a couple storms will get condensation but itsn't a serious problem to me.The previous house had french doors on the main floor which had matching wooden storms and screens. The second floor wood storms were still in storage but not used since a previous owner installed aluminum storms. When the storms are painted the same color as the windows, they aren't obvious. We did not change out the screens on the main floor except for four storm door panels and the only double hung on the main floor. The changeout took about 45 minutes spring and fall and didn't require a ladder. I know a couple homeowners chose to install interior wood storms and they were satisfied with that approach. I am not a member of the replacement window lovers club. New windows have a different and very obvious appearance.

What I see here is BIG and EMPTY ... this room needs more than shelves; it needs personality.  My thoughts -- in no particular order: - Paint or wallpaper that back wall with an accent color /pattern -- I'd say something pretty bright /no neutrals.  Consider repeating that color somewhere on the other end of the room -- the whole "door wall"?  Maybe just around the shower?  I would not do an upper-half accent -- that doesn't seem right for this room.  Something like this provides color, yet also plays second fiddle to what you already have, and won't be hard to live with after a couple years:  - Crown molding would add a new dimension /a more finished /polished look to the whole room.  - I'd think about a single shelf -- black, to match the countertop -- above the toilet.  Place a fairly large piece of artwork (with a black or black-accented frame) above that shelf /a small plant and curio or a little basket on the shelf.  Today's trends head towards rustic, and I don't see that fitting into your room -- you need something a bit more polished.  Do consider how the shelf looks FROM THE SIDE.  In your space, it will show from the side. Alternately, a train rack would work for you -- and would give you space to stack some small towels /bring in color. Another alternate:  Two large pictures stacked, though personally I like the dimension that the shelf brings in.      - You need artwork on the wall straight ahead of the door -- I'd lean towards a collection of four moderate-sized pictures hung together in a big rectangle.  I like that this example is "wide" instead of "tall".  I think it'd fit better in your space.   - I'd add a piece of artwork on the wall next to the right-side sink too.  This example picture was rather hard to find -- this particular example is actually a concealed medicine cabinet /it opens up and gives more storage.  Note that this art is important in that it reflects in the mirror /shows up twice.   - Add towel bars on each end of the tub /bring in color through towels.  If you're thinking of a towel warmer, I'd put it on the shower half-wall.  Be super-careful not to permeate the shower's waterproofing as you hang anything on this half-wall. - With no good place to hang a hand towel for the left-side sink, I'd get a countertop fingertip towel stand.  Or two ... those sinks are too far apart to share a hand towel.   - You need something in the space dead-ahead of the door, and you need a small stool, table, whatever near the tub to hold a book, a candle, a drink -- I'd choose something small, which would sit against the wall by the tub.  This will give you something to fill that space that isn't just flat on the wall.  I'd go with something black /to tie into the countertop.  Another idea for this space would be a hamper.  Or a chair.   - Another thing to consider near the tub:  a standing candle holder. - You need bath mats for comfort -- but with such a large space, I am concerned that they'll look like a couple sprinkles on a great big sundae.  Not sure how to handle this.  Maybe one long mat for the sinks?  Big baths aren't easy.  The sink /shower door area will be the hardest, and they're right by the door, which might catch the mat as it opens. - Consider ditching the Hollywood lights. - I see lights above the vanity and a light in the shower -- I like to read in the tub, so I'd really care about a light over the tub.  Alternately, a carefully place sconce might fit between the window and the wall -- not sure based upon these pictures. - Are you attached to those vanity faucets?  If you change them, go with a wide-set that's easier to clean /doesn't require "flossing".  - Add window treatments above the tub to bring in color, pattern and softness. - Add a frame to the large mirror -- this will make a big difference and is very inexpensive.  - A full-length mirror is always nice in the bathroom -- but the only place I see to put it is the back side of the door. - Finally, add some greenery and something woven -- a hamper or a trash can?  These "finishing touches" help every bathroom.

ProMix HP is peat based....very heavily peat based. And peat based potting media is excessively water retentive. It is not surprising that after a week (or more) the soil is still showing signs of being overly wet. Despite claims to the contrary about "fast" or improved drainage, it is really very little different than using Miracle Gro potting soil. I would strongly urge you to find or make a bark based potting media. A custom mix like the 5-1-1 is ideal but there are commercial mixes available that are primarily bark (often labeled as 'recycled forest products') but they tend to be somewhat regional in their nature....not necessarily national brands. And there are a couple of statements in the previous comment that need some clarification. When you water containerized plants (indoors or out), you don't use a proscribed amount like a cup. You flush the media fully until it runs freely from any drainage holes. This is to fully hydrate the soil mass as well as flush out any soluble salts that might be present. Drain completely, then you do not water again until a 'tell' - or the plant - tells you it is time. "i dont understand root pruning ... peeps seem to do it" "peeps seem to do it" because it is absolutely necessary to maintain root health over time and to keep plant size in check if you do not wish to up pot to a larger size container. Rootbound plants are stressed and will eventually die if not attended to in a timely manner.

Overwatering is the #1 cause of death of these plants.     It  pays to keep it in a pot with soil amended with perlite or pulmace or both.     Some of my Aloes I keep in a 50/50 mix of potting soil and perlite.      From what I can see, it still looks good.     Give it all the indoor sun you can.

I use 6500K T8 fluorescent bulbs, in a 6-bulb high-bay fixture. The high-bay fixtures are more expensive, but usually have better reflective backing than shop lights... so more efficient light transfer. Not as uneconomical as it might first appear either, given that one 6-bulb fixture will cover the same area as 2-3 standard shop lights. When I bought mine, the fixtures (without bulbs) were about $85, but they have gone up considerably since then. High bay LED fixtures, though, have become cheaper... and can be amazingly bright. IMO high bay fixtures are too often overlooked as plant lights. While I agree that the light spectrum is important, so is the light output. When shopping for bulbs, look for the output (usually expressed in Lumens). Sadly, most of the T8 bulbs sold in local big box stores focus on energy efficiency - but have very low light output. A couple of exterior doors are a minor annoyance and often special doors are installed late in the process. Garage doors can be 7 months from order depending on model and manufacturer. We keep our homes heated above 50 degrees at this point for quality and of course paint manufacturers instructions. The other issues are unrelated to paint, but a concern. Okay, got tired of guessing, so I painted a piece of drywall. Put a primer coat on Taped off and painted a black stripe across then entire piece. I used Benjamin Moore Regal Select base 1 eggshell without tint added. One coat was not enough to completely cover a black stripe, but two coats make the stripe undetectable.
