I would hazard to guess that the rest of the trim in your house was brush painted and if it was done well you hardly even tell. Having a background in historic preservation, I prefer the brush technique anyway. Minimizing brush strokes though is all about the quality of the painter, their paint, and their brushes. Don't let anyone roll this though; the texture won't be convincing that it is all wood like I assume you want it to appear. As far as the tight joints, any joint can be caulked, but a narrow joint may be more difficult to get a proper caulk bead and may crack with the change of the seasons. The back side of the panel molding against the stiles and rails may also be difficult to caulk without losing the sharp shape of the molding the way those pieces come together. It's definitely much easier to embrace the tight joints here if you can handle it.

Cloud white and simply white do not have that .20ish difference in chrome which had me worried. You're right they don't. They're very similar overall. Simply White is more neutral because it has a smidge less Chroma. And it's also a tiny bit closer to the Green-Yellow hue family. It's that pocket of the color wheel - the GY region - where we find colors that read as being most neutral, the least discernible hue bias.   Cloud White is slightly darker and more in the middle of the Yellow hue family. A smidge more Chroma and darker means it's more of a color when compared directly to Simply White. Bottom line, I think it would be difficult to distinguish that these are two different colors once installed. So it comes down to pretty and function. Which one looks the prettiest to you and which one has the better hide, takes fewer coats; a lot depends on product but my guess is Cloud White will be the one with better hide.

Your mirror should be silver unless it was made decades before the house was built. Mercury stopped before the 1900's. Silver was used in the 20's. Even if it were mercury, after a centry off gassing wouldn't be an issue anymore. But still, mirror licking should be discouraged regardless of what the backing material is.

The vapor pressure of metallic mercury at room temperature is pretty much zero, I don't think "off-gassing" is much of a concern. Also metallic mercury is pretty unreactive, the real toxicity comes with organic mercury compounds that can penetrate and interact with biological targets. Real mercury backed mirrors are very rare these days and quite beautiful. A much richer look than the silver used now.

You need stripper to remove the polish and get down to your original urethane finish. You could buy a container of commercial non-ammoniated wax stripper but they're usually sold in large quantities. A more viable option is to use an OTC wax stripper like Armstrong New Beginning. The recommendation was to do small areas at a time to avoid getting it down in the grooves. It would be best to apply sparingly with a sponge, let it work, then remove with sponges and clean water. Grout sponges are excellent for this type of work. If you have wet/dry vac it could be used after to suck up any residual water. Start in an inconspicuous area to make sure there's no unexpected reaction and to determine how heavy it needs to be applied and how long it needs to sit. You know it's working when you rub it with your thumbnail and you can see it gelling. After removing the polish, use an approved cleaner like Bona. Ordered from Build*com in September/October- for a range and refrigerator for delivery in 6-10 weeks. Almost a $20K order, so not insignificant. When that came and went (Dec) it was delayed to May 2022.  I immediately put out feelers for other retailers, and found the refrigerator at Home Depot, and range at ABT Appliances in IL (I think that's who it was), which they air freighted here to TX.  Both appliances were delivered to my house within about 2 weeks from that date, whereas I would still be waiting on Build. All manufacturers are having delays, and they are shipping periodically, but they aren't able to meet all the demand so they are shipping fewer units than ordered, and allocating their orders to their customers (this is what some retailers told me).  So you may order from someone who truly expects to get it in 6-10 weeks, but when 6-10 weeks come they get 20% of the volume of what they thought, so they too then have to allocate the limited number of units to their customers.  Some get their order filled, the others get "order delayed" email like I did. At that point, I reached out to several retailers for each appliance and got on their notification list.  As soon as an item came in stock I immediately called them to place the order (vs ordering online).  For the refrigerator, I actually had someone at HD call the warehouse and confirm that the item was physically in stock, and that one of the was allocated to my order.  Maybe I got lucky and had a really good customer service agent, but that's how I ended up with appliances. Our builder also told us that larger customers (like HD, etc) get priority allocation on some of the orders, so they get what they order (or don't get cut back as much as smaller customers).

Every hurricane reference I find discusses 12 inches as typical with statements like - "if you have over 12 inches".... But I have found some saying stay less than 20 inches or 24 inches. Matt, the most commonly encountered Southern Magnolia cultivars sold in our area include; Edith Bogue, Victoria, and Bracken's Brown.  I have Bogues and Victorias and they are good with heavy, WET snow loads and wind. I also have Majestic Beauty, they are not as readily sold in the area but they have had no issues with snow for me.  Sometimes you see Little Gems, I have a few of those, but they are not known for superior cold hardiness.  The only ones I really have had issues with, are the strong vertical growers (such as Alta), as our sticky, heavy weight snows get caught between the branches and trunk, and the branches just snap.  In our area, heavy snow load is much more of a factor than cold tolerance. 1) Short answer is "yes."  A small distance outside of the clear aperture may also be effective.  In the case of my Wolf Pro Island hood, I count the inch at each end and back, but not the higher curved part that adds to the specified dimensions.  I count an inch of the light bar zone also, which is significantly larger.  This is really in the noise, though, given the ability to estimate baffle pressure loss, among other things. 2) Not me. 3) It doesn't help if containment is perfect (which is our goal) if some of the effluent plume is not captured.  To the extent feasible, determine the contour of the largest pans you might use on all your burners.  Determine your hood height above the pan bases and multiply by the tangent of 10 degrees.  (This is the minimum; somewhat larger angles can be argued for in various circumstances.)  Extend the outside edge of the pan contour all around by this height x tangent value.  Your hood capture area should encompass this larger area. In your case, the back is a wall and the hood need not go any farther. Larger containment volumes (significantly larger than residential hoods provide) allow averaging of the highest velocity plumes over the baffle space allowing commercial hoods to get away with somewhat lower CFM for a given capture aperture area. 4) @opaone's noise charts.  I don't have an iphone to use to contribute values with. If you use an external or in-line but distant blower, and install a silencer such as Fantech makes in the path from hood to blower, the blower blade tip noise and upper duct turbulence noise will be significantly reduced.  My roof-mounted Wolf/Broan 1500 CFM rated (at zero static pressure) blower pulling an actual ~ 100 ft/min across my hood capture aperture is fairly well attenuated such that the dominant kitchen noise in the voice band is baffle hiss.  This might vary with baffle design. 5) I can't answer specifically, but with my hood blower on full power one can converse at normal talking level with someone on the other side of the hood or a few feet away.  From the cook's point of view, Intelligibility of a TV in the open room on the other side of the peninsula requires a modest volume level increase over listening with no blower flow. In my opinion, find a hood that best solves your optimization of the trade space of capture, aesthetics, cost and use an appropriate remote blower with a silencer, and you will find the noise is attenuated enough.  If you follow the general "prescription" of @opaone's commercial setup, you may be able to run lower flow rates from a large enough blower that the noise is negligible for most cooking tasks.  Opaone has discoursed on this in a number of threads that should be reviewed. 6) The more the hood design approaches a commercial configuration, the more volume below the baffles you will have.  See this thread for a relatively practical quasi-commercial solution. https://www.houzz.com/discussions/6204496/range-hood-questions#n=8

One of reasons we use skirting boards is because plaster is weakest at its edge. If the edge is exposed even light taps like those from a vacuum will cause it to break and fall off as well as leave scuff marks. Skirting board covers this delicate edge. If the skirting is removed you need some other way to protect the edge this is usually done with a stop bead. I have seen examples of houses where they have been plastered to the floor without any stop bead, but these are ultra modern minimalist new builds. No idea what it looks like once people (and a vacuum cleaner) have lived there. If your house is concrete floors and brick walls like these new builds, you should be able to do it without the stop bead. Otherwise probably better to keep it off the floor.

My house is somewhat old.  It was built in the 80’s.  It is 2 story with actually 4 attics, but really 2 main ones. When I replaced the ceiling, I thought I did not want foam on the rafters for the reasons I indicated.  So I, aparantly mistakenly, had foam put on the bottom of the downstairs attic.  But the foam vendor did a very poor job and many of the sections between rafters are less than half full of foam.  Its a disaster.  I actually had one vendor tell me that I needed to remove that foam and he quoted me $40,000 to remove the old foam and do foam on the rafters.  Not doing that, for sure. The other main attic which is upstairs came with blown in-insulation, but not well installed and lots of under coverage.  So, what I did was is to scoop up some of the blown in and move it from one section to the next, leaving some sections completely uninsulated.  Then put in R-19 batts in the spaces I cleared out. I suspect your drawer boxes were already warped and this is largely a problem with reusing drawer boxes. ---- Handles do a lot of the heavy lifting in the connection of drawer fronts to frames, however, people still open and close drawers without using the handle.  Thin panel material has no screw holding strength so the panel should be thickened rather than shimmed in this situation. The cabinet maker should either build the drawer panels out of thicker material so the back of the panel is even with the back of the frame, or place (preferably glue) in a piece of wood between the drawer box and the drawer front to bridge that gap. ---- In order to work up the courage to try to pass that mistaken drawer size off as correct, I would have to slam my nuggets in it repeatedly. LOL at these classic Houzz answers - you ask a question about something you like, and people instead answer with what they like. I had an integrated Corian bathroom sink, and it was great.  No seams, no cracks, a perfect surface.  The glacier white solid surface lends itself extremely well to clean-line modern looks, though obviously there are other styles for other tastes. The term integrated can be used various ways, though.  When Corian says "integrated," they mean a truly seamless surface, where the countertop and sink are fused together as one.  This can only really be done with a solid surface material.  All the vendors you listed are solid surface, just like Corian. The reason they can be fused with the sink is because solid surface is made up of plastic resin, which can be essentially melted together. Quartz, marble, granite, etc, cannot be fused together the same way solid surface can.  Sometimes people will still refer to the sink as integrated, though.  Perhaps they made the sink out of a matching quartz to the countertop, and it LOOKS like they are one piece.  But close examination will reveal a seam.  Stone fabricators can make sinks, so if it's the LOOK you are after, it can be achieved (not inexpensively, though).  But if it is the totally seamless practicality, that only comes from solid surface. (Well, technically, you could carve a sink into a thick slab of stone, but holy millions, batman).  Your fabricator may be able to integrate your Corian sink to other materials, or Corian countertop to other materials, but one material needs to be solid surface.  And I can guarantee there are requirements of the material they are integrating with. If you google Corian kitchen sink, you will see there are kitchen sink options available. Regarding colors - Corian and similar companies offer premade solid surface sinks, that your fabricator then fuses to the countertop.  Those stock sinks are only available in white and biscuit type colors.  You can, however, ask your fabricator to MAKE you a sink in any color and size.  That sink can again be seamlessly fused.  But the custom sink is obviously much more expensive than simply buying the stock options.

There are many ways to implement HVAC zoning. However, for residential application a zone is best described as a floor or level when thinking of zoning via equipment. Meaning that each system is zoned for a particular floor. Large expansive areas on a single level can be zoned with additional equipment as well. If an area is so large it may make sense to have more than one system, zoned to a particular area of the structure. Even if that area is on the same floor. When the focus is on one area and zoning via controls with one HVAC system it's best to consider a zone as an area of the structure with 4 walls and a door, windows are optional.  Zoning an open area with 2 seperate zones is more in the realm of staging or staggering. That being said you can incorporate more than one room on a single zone, typically zoning using controls tied to a single HVAC system is to alleviate hot / cold spots when designing it from the room to room level. Unintended consequences come into play when you have a smaller zone tied to a larger HVAC system. Air conditioning capacity is primarily achieved by moving air. A smaller zone won't require as much as a larger zone. If tied to a 5 ton system, the system is going to require in the realm of 2000 cfm of air. If the room or zone in question only needs 400 cfm of air (essentially 1 ton of AC) that other 4 tons of AC in a 5 ton AC system has to go somewhere. This is why HVAC zoning via controls can be a nightmare. It's really simple to those that think you can close a damper and think that air flow is going to magically go somewhere with no room to go. LOL. So imagine if the zone in question only needs 250 CFM of air. Some structures zoning isn't the better choice. It is what it is sometimes. Zoning via controls is a tool that should only be chosen when it's appropriate. It really is done best when it can be achieved elegantly. You (the designer) are painting the canvas with comfort... or I say should be (that's how I approach it - I'm not in the business to sell garbage if you can't afford what I offer you're better to save your beans until you can.) Most of the time I see nothing but horse crap. Gee I wonder why it doesn't work? I call it like I see it. I'm not in the junk refurbishing business. I know when to walk away, I can tell you that much. If the goal is just to cram it in a closet, hide it, bury it / disguise it --- probably not going to turn out anywhere close to what you think. If the system in question is in a closet now? uh, better open that wallet up wide. Design is the magic here and that includes everything, equipment selection, controls selection, thermostat selection -- If you don't have that knowledge it's a long and winding road. 28 years in HVAC talking here from doing, not just yacking. Because I am a straight shooter, tell it like is kind of guy based on my experience is primarily why people call me in the Katy, Texas area. Some of what I put here isn't necessarily for you Boe Dillard. It's for others who may read this thread days, weeks and sometimes months or even years later.

In such a wide open space, how do you intend to have more than one zone? With zoned HVAC, you typically have barriers (i.e., walls /doors/floors/ceilings) that allow the thermostat for that area to maintain a certain temperature.  When you have no barriers, the heating/cooling supplied quickly mixes throughout the space, making the idea of zones pointless.  While you will likely need more than one supply duct for that big an area to achieve overall comfort, that's unconnected to the idea of zones.

No dimensions on this so of course we don't really know how big it is. But using stair and hall width as basis for sizing, it really isn't that big. As Kudzu mentioned, you don't use HVAC for cooking issues - you vent. I suppose in a massive window situation with very cold exterior temps or very bad glass (either with solar gain or insulation), you could have some temperature stratification in this space. But the real answer is to fix the losses rather than zone the HVAC. Austin gives some good insight to the challenges of zoning but there are ways to do it right. Are you used to zoning in some prior structure? Because zoning an open area in residential construction just isn't done. You zone floors and sometimes large suites. The reality is that a well done modern structure has small losses which make temperatures more stable than historic structures. The challenge sometimes is that sun loading or window losses in one area give some stratification but there is no air flow because the HVAC isn't needed. Zoning can help that but not with typical HVAC systems - probably minis. Case in point. I don't need to run the upstairs heat because heat rises and the upstairs is mostly fully heated from below. But, in one room with 2 north windows and an east window, it will get cold if the door is closed for long periods of time. The other rooms are either on the south side or have a person sleeping in them for a time so they are warm enough for those reasons. If I had a poorly insulated structures, the HVAC would run and probably even this out better.

Staging and or staggering is primarily used in unique structures with grand entrances, large scenic open areas with possible walls of glass over looking something else. Where are you in that structure? The ceilings might be 30-40 ft high as an example. The more air volume, the more it will cost / take for you to be comfortable. By zoning areas like this gives you some choices, which can make your HVAC system more efficient, there by making you more comfortable. You can't control something with 'no control'. What are you Ray some sort of *control* freak. Yeah you could say that. LOL. No two structures are exaclty alike, nor are two people. This comment is to clarify better what, how, why staging and or staggering might be used. It would be unnecessary for most structures.

Paint has measured colour attributes which paint companies use as a target to ensure consistency from batch to batch. But the colour target can often be achieved in mutiple ways. Somtimes a shot of a particular colourant maybe so small, even in a large can, that it becomes too difficult to reproduce as an even smaller percentage, for a sample can. So they combine other colourant proportions to achieve the same measured target colour. That’s why examining formulas for colourant ratios is a waste of time. They can be  different depending upon the size of can. Most often, if a colour doesn’t appear in a particular space as you imagine it should? It is due to the quality of available light & the context of the room in which you paint it. ’Change the light + you change the colour.’ Less often colours are mixed incorrectly at the store.

yato,  I'm going to ask this question but I expect no answer from you.  The answer will only be important to you.  How old are you?  The reason for the question is: I believe there are no plants, or at best only a very few plants that you can carry out a meaningful hybridizing program with in a short period of time.   Having been associated with a nursery that had a sizeable orchid breeding program, many years ago, the average time for most orchids to reach blooming size from seed sowing, was about 7 years.  Adenium's are a bit faster growing than that, but from seed sowing to first blooms will still be measured in years. Another critical point is record keeping.  Excruciatiatingly detailed and accurate records must be kept of everything you do in the breeding process, especially if you intend to sell your plants.  It is more than embarrassing to grow a crop of seedlings that you think, and advertise will produce white blooms, for instance, and then a couple of years after the sale your customers begin to come to you complaining their plants are all producing beautiful red blooms.    Now, if you  just want to cross pollinate a few of your own plants just to see what you will get, forget everything I have said, do it, and have fun. Some very basics of genetics.  If you have two plants that are true species, crossing the two plants, or selfing(using pollen from one plant to produce a seed pod on that plant) either one of them should produce seedlings that look like the parent(s).  However, just for the fun of it, lets say that one of your "species" isn't.  We'll say it is the product of a long line of breeding, but several generations back a plant was used to make a cross that the breeder thought was the species but was not, we'll say it was dominant for the characteristics of your intended species, but still carried the genes of the mystery plant as recessive genes.   In this case, your seedlings could very well bloom with some completely unexpected characteristics. Basically, you cross a white and a red (both species) you should get some whites, some reds, with the majority something in between.  Caution: If either parent you used is a long line hybrid with plants with different characteristics, "grandparents", "great-grandparents" and on and on back will all have an influence on your outcome. You will see results (flowers) at each generation.  Pollinate the flower, when the pod matures and opens, harvest the seeds, plant them, grow them to maturity, and they will bloom.  That's a generation.  It's that simple.  Good luck, and most of all, have fun. Bill

As has been pointed out, what you wind up with depends on the genetics of the parents and luck.  The more unusual flowered hybrids out there are generally the result of random mutations which the grower capitalized on.  Often they will self such a plant to increase the odds of getting more similar to it.  To get at least an idea of what is most likely to result from your crosses, you might do a search to see if anyone has listed what traits tend to be dominant.  (For example, with Cattleya orchids, lavender tends to be dominant over any other colors.  So a plant with deep red flowers crossed with one with lavender flowers is most likely just going to have lavender flowers.)   However, with most plants, flower traits are rarely simple dominant and recessive interactions. Instead, there is often a spectrum of "partial dominance" or multiple genes which are involved. If you decide to get more seriously into hybridizing, as Bill pointed out, keep very detailed notes and LABEL every offspring/pot/tray. If you  have the plants outside, then another step would be to emasculate (remove the stamen before they mature) the flower you are going to pollinate to reduce the chance of self-pollinating.  After hand pollinating, "bag" the pollinated flower with cheese clothe or other light breathable material to prevent an insect or other animal from also pollinating the flower.

Crassula and most other succulents suffering from chronic under-watering die primarily from the top down, secondarily from the root tips back to the basal portion (base) of the stem, and the last part of the plant to forfeit its viability would be the root-to-shoot transition zone. Chronically over-watered plants generally shed the finest roots first, and continuing intervals of complete or partial soil saturation cause larger and larger roots to succumb to cultural conditions the plant is not (genetically) programmed to deal with. It's very common that the first symptom presented by over-watered succulents and noticed by the grower is a plant that simply toppled from the pot when it was bumped during watering or otherwise jostled - reason being dieback of roots to the degree that insufficient anchorage destroyed the plants anchorage to the pot and grow medium. A tip: If you want a plant with 3 trunks, it's better to to start with a cutting that has rooted, then cut it back late spring/ early summer (in the US, think summer solstice or Father's Day to Independence day) so only 2 nodes are above the soil. This should produce 4 new branches/trunks, one of which can be rubbed off, leaving 3. OR, you can lay a branch on its side as seen in the next 3 images of a cutting started this past summer with the intent of becoming a raft-style planting:   I made the pruning cut (closest part of the cutting above) at an angle so the scar would be less noticeable. The cutting is about as thick as a fifty cent piece.    This raft cutting, a pruning resultant of removing the top of another larger specimen, can be developed so it has any number of trunks. It will now be left to grow unencumbered by pruning for a couple of years before I decide what to keep/build on and what needs to go, in terms of potential trunks. The plant is Portulacaria afra (commonly mini-jade, elephant bush, spekboom), but because it has the same growth habit and cultural wants as your jade, it might as well be one. If you're after a planting meant to evoke a sense of it being a miniature tree, one of the upright forms of Portulacaria might be the better direction, as its leaves would be much more in scale to the size of the plant. The leaves of jades don't reduce well (in size), so except for very large specimens (30"+) with trunks as thick as a Mason Jar there's always going to be the issue of the leaf size appearing disproportionately large for all but very large plants. When pots are deeper than 4-5", we can get an accurate read on whether or not the plant needs water by using digital testers (our fingers). The top 2" of a pot 10" deep can feel dry even while the bottom 6" are completely saturated with water. What's most important is what moisture levels are deep in the pot. "Water meters/gauges" don't work because they measure electrical conductivity, not moisture. A wooden tell that can be made by cutting a 1/4 or 5/16 wooden dowel rod in half and sharpening the ends in a pencil sharpener provides an accurate sense of when it's time to water. more on that below. Also, note the grow medium I use. Growing things immediately becomes less trying and more rewarding once we get to the point where we are no longer forced to battle our grow medium for control over our plants' vitality (health). Al

The UCLs are not supposed to be installed toward the back.  They’re supposed to be installed toward the front of the upper cabinets, just behind the light rail.  That way, the light is shed onto the middle of the counter where it is supposed to be.  And the lighting is pointed straight down onto the counter.  The UCLs are not supposed to be ”illuminating the backsplash”.  They are supposed to provide task lighting onto the counter which would otherwise not receive task lighting from your ceiling lights because the upper cabinets overshadow the counters. If you install the UCLs correctly toward the front of the upper cabinets, they will still provide some light onto the backsplash.  But to install them toward the back so that they shed light mostly onto the backsplash is a big waste of the money you spent on them. Furthermore, if you install the UCLs at the back rather than toward the front, you will be able see them from a seated position which is glaring.  That is another reason why the correct installation of UCLs is toward the front of the upper cabinets.

If your contractor answers “cement board” when you ask what waterproofing system he plans to use, then get another contractor.  It is not your job to teach a lazy contractor how to waterproof a shower.  There are too many things he can do wrong with the waterproofing systems that could cause leaks.  You want a contractor who knows what they are doing.  One who has a certification from the manufacturer (like Schluter or Wendi) is ideal.

Looks like wallpaper to me :) I prefer repairs that resemble the original install method but you can also look into specific repair systems with plaster washers, or even use drywall and mud. You'll want to remove all the paper (steamer, or whatever method work ok), and anything loose.  A lathe/plaster wall relies on the mechanical hold of "keys" through the lathe.  Basically, the scratch coat is pushed through the lathe, and those blobs harden and hold it in place.  So, you'll need to remove anything that is cracked and the surrounding area.  You'll know you can stop removing once you see the keys through the lathe (ie ones that haven't broken off). The actual repair would be a pretty long post, but your basic options for further googling are: 1. scratch/brown/finish, known as a 3-coat plaster (probably what you have already).  Products aren't usually carried at big-box stores, so call around to plaster suppliers or masonry/stucco suppliers.  They'll be able to help you with product selection. 2. Drywall patch - a sort of 2-coat plaster system.  Cut a drywall patch to fit the new hole (not too thick, might only need 1/4" drywall).  Use durabond to mud it in.  Finish coat with durabond. 3. Look into repairing with plaster washers (I'm not familiar myself).

If you are building a new house then a basement requires at least (1) emergency escape and rescue window in addition to the egress route up the stairs. If you have sleeping rooms in the basement, then each room requires an emergency escape and rescue window within the bedroom. If you are remodeling an existing basement without an emergency escape and rescue window, then usually the existing small windows can remain grandfathered, unless you are adding a sleeping room, which would then require an emergency escape and rescue window. However it can vary per locale, as if you are finishing an unfinished basement (defined as storage), a locale may interpret code as a change of occupancy (to a habitable space) and require one installed.

It seems unlikely a drywell would have been placed so close to your home. But something is undermining your paving stones. Commercially built drywells are either concrete or high density plastic with a life expectancy of 30 years, but homemade drywells can be made of metal or plastic barrels surrounded by and sometimes filled with coarse stones to allow collected water to seep into surrounding soil. These may have a shorter lifespan. Do you have any plumbing lines that run under this paving? Even a small leak could cause the shifting of base materials. Do you have a high water table? Gravel and paving tends to sink into consistently wet ground. I would try to find out where outdoor supply and drainage lines run. Fixing the problem usually requires removing the paving stones that are settling, filling in more sand or gravel to support the stones, then replacing them. Start at the loosest stone, and use a spade to tip up one edge. Ideally you would have a level to raise up any subsidence, a tamper to pack down additional sand or gravel, and a rubber mallet to tap the pavers back into place. But you could use any straight stiff item like a pipe to eyeball low spots. You can use a wide flat board, even an old cutting board, laid over the fill and walked on. Use a short piece of wood placed between the paver and a regular hammer to protect the paver from chipping. It can be very difficult to find someone to make minor repairs; they generally want to completely replace the pavers. Here is an article with video on doing it yourself.

Most likely it is the flame roll out sensor shutting down the furnace. The furnace has to be examined carefully as to why this is happening. It could caused by a cracked heat exchanger which is a serious problem. The furnace does not look old so hopefully it is something else. This can't be diagnosed remotely. Hopefully your HVAC company will respond quickly to a no heat service call.

I agree with Mike, a roll-out sensor is what first came to mind. When there is sufficient restriction in the combustion area or exhaust stack, the heat and/or flames from the burners can 'roll out' into the surrounding area. The roll out sensors are temperature snap switches that sense this increased temp/heat and shut the furnace down. It can be caused by furnace issues or a restricted flue/chimney as well.

Are you familiar with the LRV ratings for paint?  It is a measure of the light reflecting value.  The higher the number the lighter the color. 855 Cloud Cover - LRV 81.80 856 Silver Satin - LRV 76.35 857 Sheep's Wool - LRV 74.52 Instead of using 50% of Sheep's Wool you should try Cloud Cover and/or Silver Satin. 869 Oxford White- LRV 88.85 870 Mountainscape (next darker version of Oxford White) has some green in it, so Oxford White probably does too. If you want a really white white for trim you should be looking at OC-17 White Dove, Super White OC-152 or OC-65 Chantilly Lace.  White Dove has a slight gray undertone.  The LRVs are on BM's website. I always find the color looks darker on a wall than on a swatch.  Patricia is right in that lighting has a big effect on any wall color.  But you're looking at the samples in the light that is in the room you're going to paint, so what you see is what you get. While sampling is very useful as it will help you eliminate a color that clearly looks wrong, sometimes getting to the one that is exactly right is difficult.  I just painted my master bedroom and I sampled five colors.  Usually the best I do is only sampling three and there was one time I think I sampled ten.  Also, not that this helps, but when you paint the whole room it will look different than you're expecting too.  Sometimes better, sometimes worse.  BM paint frequent covers in one coat, so if it doesn't turn out exactly the way you were expecting another coat of something close should do it.

I'm with Jonathan. We sanded the original pine floors in our 1930s house when we moved in 9 years ago. It looked lovely and I do like the rustic, characterful look. But. Pine flooring isn't designed to be a final floor finish - it's too soft. So you end up with dents all over the place, just from shoes coming in, which get grubby. The only way to clean them is down on your hands and knees (because a mop doesn't get down into the dents), and you need to do that very often to keep it looking clean. It's quite soul destroying! The floor boards are also draughty - on cold days you can feel the coldness seeping up from the floor. And because the boards weren't designed to be the finished floor level, you have gaps under the doors which are also draughty and mean noise travels through the house. We're just about to have engineered wood flooring laid throughout the ground floor, though we are also adding a tiled boot room and utility room and I envisage muddy shoes to come through there rather than the engineered wood hallway. If the hall is going to be your main entry point into the house, I'd go with tiles there, for robustness, and then transition to engineered wood in the living areas.

Looks like mealy bugs and/or scale.  Wipe off as much as you can and spray.  Quarantine from other plants, unless all your plants are infested.  Since scale (if it is scale) has a waxy shell that resists pesticides, you may have to repeat. With persistent wiping, you can eliminate either pest, but it requires wiping every part of the plant where they are.  Not too hard in plants with a few big leaves (I successfully cured an Amaryllis), tough in plants with many leaves and stems. Look up mealy bugs and scale and look at your leaves with a magnifying glass, because diagnosis via the internet is uncertain.

eep Ok.....here's my "Hybrid technique" that I often tell our Customers. Not trying to "Toot my Horn", but my walls at home are flawless....🤓😁 * I work in 3' wide sections. 4' is too wide. * Assuming 8' walls, use a fully loaded White-Dove roller-cover, & start at the top left. * Use the "Slanted N or W" pattern to spread out the paint in a 2' high rectangle. * Load the cover for EACH block in the column. * Overall pattern: you're "filling-in" a vertical column of 4 2' high x 3' wide "blocks"! * Here's the REAL difference-maker..... after the column is filled in, bring your roller immediately to the top left, & do a light, continuous "Sweep" down to the bottom. * Lightly lift off the roller at the bottom, & do another light top-down sweep. ALWAYS Top-to-bottom. Think of a plane taking-off here! * Should be about 4 top-down sweeps per 3' column using a 9" cover. 2 things are happening here: 1) This technique "GETS ENOUGH PAINT" on the wall, without being too thick OR thin. 2) The vertical sweep is the REAL IMPORTANT part. You're evening-out the thick & thin areas....AND, more importantly, the paint is now "Leaning" the same way. Modern paints start setting up fairly fast. Most TV commercials show people painting willy-nilly in the middle of the wall. I have to shake my head 🤔😬😬 This scattershot way of doing it leaves all kinds of varying thickness areas across a wall!! Plus, you get the visible "roller-path" when you go back 1 minute later to fill in a "thin spot". Why is this??? Because, the paint is a little more "set", leaning in a different direction, & also with a different thickness. You'll always see it.... Remember.....you asked.....🤓🤪😉 Faron

Arbordave, I modified it to say, "within reason", and that is obviously something people aren't going to agree on!  Respect your opinion even if different from mine. And yes I noticed the start of heart rot but didn't mention it because, in a sense, (the sense in which I see the issue) it's immaterial. My lot had 1 huge white oak that towered above the canopy of the other trees on all the adjacent lots .  It was a tree when everything else was farmland.  About 10 years ago it fell on its own on a bright clear windy day  (fortunately, away from my lot) because its trunk was full of rot.   In my opinion it would make more sense to calculate which lots have the healthiest mix of eastern forest species undergoing normal forest succession, and ecological/site factors likely to permit long term continued development/succession  (e.g., not being surrounded by high rises or whatnot) and prioritize those lots for permanent preservation.  Not to say singular "landmark trees" above a certain size and age should be preserved.  Feels a bit like someone traveled to the PNW or coastal California and has "big tree envy" LOL.   Well, guess what?  The PNW doesn't have derechos, hurricanes,tornadoes or microburst thunderstorms.

davidrt28, I totally agree that the preservation of lots/parcels having a healthy "mix of [native] forest species undergoing normal forest succession" should be prioritized, but I also think that the science does indeed support the claim that big trees (especially native trees on relatively undisturbed sites) provide significant environmental and ecological benefits that are often overlooked or undervalued. Planting a bunch of nursery grown landscape trees after the native soil has been removed and the natural site conditions permanently altered can't really compensate for the loss. I'd rather see 1 huge old white oak preserved (even though it may have some defects and a finite life span) by reconfiguring the development of the site, than to watch it be removed and "replaced" by one or more red maples, honeylocusts, callery pears, etc (IME often whatever the landscaper can find cheap locally).

In addition to what G & S Floor Service said, you need to understand one thing, moisture enters concrete in many ways, i.e from humidity in the air, ground, and moisture in the concrete itself that was added to it. Moisture leaves concrete one way and that is through the surface. Under-slab moisture barrier is installed, but it also could be punctured during the concrete pour, some laborers if there is no supervision can purposely puncture moisture barrier for the water to escape so they can float the surface faster, etc so there is no real reassurance that the moisture barrier under there will prevent any moisture from getting into the concrete. Like G&S mentioned contact the manufacturer and see what they will tell you.

The kitchen is on the backside of the wall this return vent is in, so not sure why it needs moved and which wall you want to move it to. This return utilizes the 14 1/2" stud space cavity, where it has a duct connected either at a hole in the top plate (to duct to an attic unit) or to a hole in the bottom plate (to duct to a basement unit). The duct can be moved to an adjacent stud space cavity pretty easily. But to move it to another wall, depends on how far you are able to extend the return duct (or alter a branch) above or below this floor, whether the wall is interior or exterior, and how close/opposite you will be to the supply register for the room.

If the petunias were blooming well, why worry about aphids?  One pot with a few plants is not much to rely on if one wants to attract any kind of wildlife.  If you have the discipline to change the sugar water daily, a hummingbird feeder is an ideal way to get a good look at hummers.  I have hundreds of various nectar-producing blooms in my yard on a given day during the warm part of the year but hummers go to the feeders much more often than any Lantana, milkweed, Salvia, or other single type of nectar plant.  I am not saying don't put nectar plants in your yard, but relying on a few snapdragons in a pot for the sole purpose of attracting hummers may not be as rewarding as you hope.  Having a few snapdragons in a pot because you love them and hope you might see a hummer visiting them is a great idea. National Audubon Society has published this warning about using neem oil outside on blooming plants: * A note on the use of neem oil, which is an insect growth inhibitor and non-toxic to birds. Because neem oil prevents insects from developing further, it can prevent bee larvae from developing if adult bees feed them neem oil-coated pollen they've brought back to the hive. For that reason, you should avoid using neem oil on flowers or remove open flowers from plants you're treating with neem oil. https://www.audubon.org/news/bird-friendly-plants-faq  (Question 20)

"I had no idea there was Poncirus growing anywhere in NYC," The reason you don't see them is because they are so freakin' THORNY and the fruit is extremely sour, but apparently you can find recipes online to make something from the fruits. I first saw this species as a sizable tree in Longwood Gardens decades ago (which apparently, over the years went from a Zone 6b to 7a).  It was loaded with fruit. I recognized it immediately as a some kind of citrus (apparently, there is still some debate to include them in Citrus or Poncirus (their own genus but closely related to Citrus). I can hardly tolerate the thorns on my Seville/Bitter/Sour Oranges.  Frankly, I don't know how any tree can survive in Manhattan!  Most trees will suffer from..., urban pollution, road salts, urban heat island heat, soil compression, etc... Which is one reason that particular tree from the Jurassic dominates Manhattan Island today..., Gingko! If you just want something exotic, try Musa basjoo, Japanese fiber bananas, I see house around me with groves of them.  They die down after the first frost but will come up again from the roots. Alternatively, 7 feet should enough width that you could put both toilet and vanity on the wall opposite the bath, or to put them facing each other with the bath/shower on the current sink wall -- that would give you space for a much wider vanity. It is the velocity of the rising and expanding cooking effluent plumes that determines the velocity of the hood air needed to entrain the effluent into the baffles.   One burner cooking at the vapor point of peanut oil, grape seed oil, or just grease will have an upward velocity of the order of a meter per second.  With residential style hoods having minimal reservoir volume below the baffles, this effluent needs to be immediately entrained into the baffle flow.  Commercial hoods with large reservoir volume can average out the plume(s) over the baffle space and operate on lower CFM depending on cooking conditions.  See figure 4 of https://www.tagengineering.ca/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/KVSApplDesign_catalog.pdf Velocity of hood air integrated over the hood aperture determines the CFM being moved.  Multiplying 90 ft/min times the hood entry area in square feet and multiplying the result by 1.5 to make up for not doing a proper pressure loss analysis (assuming decent MUA) will yield the rated zero static pressure flow rate (CFM) of a suitable blower. Hood entry area should overlap the burners in both directions -- side to side and front to back.

tropicreezent, I’m sure this is not the answer you were hoping to hear, but the truth is, in orchid breeding, the name is really the weak link in the entire chain of events. There are a fairly large number of closely related species, and other hybrids, that will breed with Oncidium, and in our never ending quest to generate something “new” that will generate sales, means that we will continue to do this kind of breeding until we have tried all the combinations that will produce viable seeds. The Royal Horticultural Society in England tried to keep all this mess straight and orderly (as the British are want to do), but when the Asian market started breeding, and cloning,  with no record keeping, the task became impossible, so today you can purchase orchids in any big box store with no name attached. And only if the plant really looks like a Cattleya, or Phalaenopsis, you have no idea what it is…..Oh, my bad, it could be a Brassolaeliacattleya,  or perhaps a Doritinopsis. One of these looks like a Cattleya, and the other like a Phalaenopsis, but neither is. When you are dealing with multigeneric long line hybrids, all of the possibly a million seeds in a pod will produce a genetically different plant. And without a name tag, identification is simply impossible. You have a beautiful blooming orchid plant. Enjoy it. Bill

For starters, your cabinetmaker is measuring the aisle widths incorrectly.  Aisle widths are measured to/from the items that stick out into the aisle the farthest -- counter overhangs (1.5" beyond cabinets), appliance handles, etc.  They are NOT measured to/from cabinets like your layout shows.  The 24-inch cabinet depth only includes the cabinet box, it does not include the doors/drawer fronts or the counter overhangs. This means your aisles are at least 3" narrower than they look -- even narrower in front of the range. Is the refrigerator a true built-in refrigerator?  Or, is it a counter-depth?  Counter-depth refrigerators are around 31" deep, not including any required air clearances behind them.   In addition to deeper depths, the doors of counter-depth refrigerators must extend out past all surrounding items (walls, counters, cabinets, etc.) to allow them to be opened fully for full access and cleaning.  (The term "counter-depth" only refers to the refrigerator's box/carcass -- it does not refer to the overall depth including doors & handles.) Does your island have the minimum recommended seating overhang of 15"?  It looks less than that.

If the pilot lights while depressing the gas valve, it's not a pilot gas line. If the pilot won't stay lit when releasing the gas valve, the broken 'hose' may be a broken thermocouple tube; the thermocouple must be intact and working for the pilot to stay lit. Your picture shows the 'hose' leading back to where the pilot flame and thermocouple sensing head should be located. The purpose of the thermocouple is to give the gas valve a signal that the pilot flame is lit. That's it, no natural gas or propane is carried within the thermocouple, it only sends a signal to the gas valve. This make it safe for the DIY'er to replace a failed thermocouple themselves. Replacement thermocouples are available at a hardware or box store, they are generic and interchangeable, the only issue being the tube length. don't buy too short a one, longer and the excess tube can be coiled. To change one is fairly easy and requires only simple hand tools, maybe including nut drivers and some small wrenches. I don't know about those fingernails, though! They may get in the way. There is no danger of gas leaks, etc. when changing a thermocouple, they either work or they don't, at which point the gas valve shuts the gas off. https://www.homedepot.com/c/ah/how-to-replace-a-thermocouple/9ba683603be9fa5395fab901ced3a679

I concur. They are getting too much water. The buds will open when the plant variety deems that it is appropriate. Many Camellia japonicas will start to bloom anywhere from December to March/April. Cold temps may also cause it to temporarily stop opening blooms and start again a few weeks later. Regarding oedema, water less frequently during winter if the soil remains moist and there is enough rainfall to maintain the soil moist to a depth of 4". Once oedema has occurred, the affected leaves should not be picked off. If outdoor plants show signs of oedema, check the soil for waterlogging and improve the soil texture by incorporating organic matter such as leaf mould. For plants growing in permanent containers, decrease watering and try to improve drainage by using bigger drainage holes, new pots or repotting with new potting mix, if necessary. I have observed leaf damage similar to picture to #2 in some japonicas that get too much sun (they should get shade by 10-11am).

Water doesn't 'get in', it comes up through the concrete. Concrete is porous, like a very fine sponge. Moisture can be wicked up from the soil or whatever is underneath. When it reaches the inside surface, warm dry air (such as, in winter) will evaporate it right at the surface so there is no visible moisture. But it carries salts out of the concrete, which are left behind when the water evaporates. Voila, efflorescence. If it only happens in part of the house, there is either a difference in the flooring or moisture barrier, or a difference in the concrete (different batch), a difference in the soil or gravel underneath in terms of holding water against the concrete, or a difference in the water level itself (such as a low spot that is more wet). Obviously some of those can be fixed easier than others. Amazing that a floor installer wouldn't consider that a moisture barrier should be used on top of a concrete slab.

There is a sensitivity setting for when the plinth filter (the black sponge looking filter behind the door on the bottem left of the dryer) needs to be cleaned. As fine lint builds up on the filter less air moves past the filter per minute.  The dryer has logic that determines when the filter is getting loaded.  When the set point is reached the display on the dryer will show ”Clean Plinth Filter” There is a ”sensitivity” setting that can be adjusted that allows the customer to determine how quickly this is displayed.  If it is going off more than tou would like it is possible to change the setting to reduce the frequency.  The downside is that drying cycles may take a little longer. How quickly this occurs really depends on the type of textiles you dry and what they are made of.  Lots of fine lint being shed will clog the filter more quickly. In our house we usually get 15-20 cycles before needing to clean the filter.  We primarily dry woven cotton and some poly type shirts.  Few, if any, loose weave or knot items.  Our towels are all loop terry cloth with no cut ends.

Hi Marissa, and it’s good to see Jane out and about also.  Now, Marissa, where are you located? The reason for the question is because Jane lives in southern Florida. What she is saying in her post is absolutely correct for her growing location, which is tropical and dependably hot and wet-orchids love that. Jane has been at this orchid growing stuff for a long time, and puts out good information. I, on the other hand am located in the upper central part of South Carolina and here our weather is far from dependable at any season-orchids struggle to adapt here. A few weeks ago, we had several nights with heavy frosts, then day before yesterday it was 80+ degrees. I just checked the calendar, and yes, it is December!   Where I live, Phalaenopsis plants don’t seem to have much of a clue what they are supposed to do, so they just do what they want to do, when the notion strikes them. I have a plant (photo attached, I hope) that was given to a friend of mine when she had surgery over 2 years ago. She was absolutely certain she was going to kill the thing within the next 30 minutes, so she gave it to me. When I got it, it had just lost two blooms out of a beautiful double spike of blooms. It kept a respectable show of blooms on it until about Sept. of this year-two years. At that time, I removed all the spikes with the intent of repotting it, since it was still in the containers it was purchased in (a clear plastic slotted inner pot with a non-draining ceramic outer pot). When I took a close look at the plant, there was about a 3-inch bloom spike tucked between two of its leaves. I decided not to repot-yet-, and put it back on the shelf.  A new leaf quickly followed the bloom spike, so no potting for a while. Now, all this verbiage to say this.  Orchids are really tough, but adaptable plants. On forums like this, there are folks who love to help others who are struggling with their plants, be it their first, or their second greenhouse full. Some of these folks really know what they are talking about, some mean well, but don’t. Suggestion: get a book or two on orchid culture- (I guess today you would use the internet) the kind of orchids you want to grow-and find out where your type of orchid grows in the wild, and what kind of environment it really likes. It probably would prefer some place other than a kitchen window, but it will adapt, if you work with it. When you have a problem, or a question, and come to a place like this for help, find out a bit about the person who is offering assistance. Tissues pretty much disintigrate when wet (ever tried to clean something wet with one?)... three tissues are not going be a disaster, even if you have septic. Even all flushed at once, I'm not sure they'd create a clog. If you had a clog, your toilet would be emptying poorly or backing up (and the solution would be a plunger). Yes, it is normal for water pressure at any single faucet to be reduced if you open all the taps at once; that's just physics.

If you have a septic system, you might have a problem over time, but even septic systems can handle the correct type of tissue. I have a regular sewer system and have been throwing tissues into my toilets for 50 years and have never had a problem yet. I guess if you had a huge number of tissues and wadded them up into a big ball you might have a problem...just like you would have with a huge wad of toilet paper. And, as pointed out above, this has nothing to do with water pressure. When you have multiple taps running, you're putting a demand on your supply to provide more volume, and the flow won't be as strong as when you only have one tap open. This is true to some extent in almost all domestic plumbing unless the supply pipes are large, the pipes aren't internally corroded, and your water pressure is strong.

I'm in IT - and our stuff is ALWAYS thought of last. I've been with some customers where we actually are brought in first and no matter what a CEO, a secretary, a janitor always ends up taking the space we designate for the server room and the room goes to a closet with a slop sink and a mop bucket in it. I consider the MEP room to be the server room of the house and realize if I do it wrong I may have a loud HVAC, unbalanced air flow,, I may spend more on the system to compensate for location or inadequate ducts, etc. Yeah so you're well aware of the problem with HVAC then, not to mention other mechanical things that can make or break a structure. You understand the value of room... dedicated space for whatever. So that's a good thing. I can't tell you how many jobs I've lost because there was no room at the inn for what was needed to be done. Typically it isn't the lack of room for me, but the cost to get her done. Room = money (land etc) vs Lack of Room = money for HVAC solutions. The lack of room thing = higher labor and more trade offs. Try working in a room with no room. LOL. Can't be any more clear than that. In terms of loud, there's really nothing inherrently loud today. But noise is subjective. A unit running produces *some noise* vs a unit that is off. Equipment made today is much quieter than HVAC units of the past 20-30 years ago. Any brand pretty much. Obviously if a system doesn't have adequate return air / supply air to handle volume -- the equipment can get the shakes and other types of odd noises. I rarely see those kinds of problems any more. I only say "rarely" because if I said never I might be proven wrong within a day or two. LOL. This is a job of variety, lots of similar type problems but there's odd ball problems that come as well. Any thoughts on how to deal with the large room in the center of the house (short of moving the room) in a duel HVAC house? Best to have it controlled via one system. How is the orientation of the house? Is the larger room area facing East & West or North & South? East and West facings have higher heat loads in summer due to trajectory of the sun everday. Windows, more of them and larger over looking some scenic thing in the yard (sticks, water, hills & in some cases mountains) If this large expansive room faces north and south rather then East and West problems will affect other areas of the home. I don't believe your climate in Maine is as much of a deal as it is for us southern folk. (AC mode) --- heating depending on type has it's own issues. But mechanical cooling is in a league all it's own most of the time. What is the heat load of the entire structure? if it comes in at 4 tons total or 3 tons total your options are less than if the load comes in at 5 ton or 6 ton. Say total load comes in at 5 ton. You could choose 3 ton for one side and 2 ton for the other. 6 tons and it could be 4ton and a two ton. So in these kinds of examples your cut of the house wouldn't be cut exactly in half, but where ever that cut is -- the hvac system for that area (whatever it is) the hvac system is placed in the central part of that area or as close to it as possible. The large expansive area, depending on how you use it, may at some point be better to be zoned. I think if it were me, I would seperate the master suite from the large area. I would include the larger area in the equipment zoned for other kid / guest bedrooms and then be prepared to potentially zone that system later with controls. Not necessarily every room, but maybe a 2 zone set up with one zone being that larger area and another zone controling the bedrooms on that side which ever side the kids bedrooms are on. I'm not sure how you have perfectly equal lengths unless my house is round and I diidn't hire Axel Foley to design the place :) It won't be exactly perfect. The idea is to cut out long runs and minimize temperature differences. There will still be some disparities the idea is to lessen them so they aren't noticeable. A few degrees one way or the other. But always plan for the what ifs. Putting it on paper doesn't always measure up in real world. Considering these things now, you're miles ahead of most.

The origins of steampunk go back to the speculative fiction and related illustrative art of the late 19th c. (Jules Verne, HG Wells), and also alternative history/future fictional technologies. The term itself originated in the 1980s but the ideas of such, things looking steampunk/being in fiction, predate this, the show Wild, Wild West (1965), and movie Brazil (1985) The sets and devices of The Time Machine (1960) and 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea (1954) are steampunk. The ideas really have a presence in Japanese literature and movies back to the 1940s. The Arts et Metiers metro station (1994) is steampunk--a thirty year old design, really.  The Waterstone wheel faucet qualifies as steampunk, I think, (retail $5000-6000) and I think this has been around 10 + years because back in the old days of "Design Around  . . . ." this was used in a steampunk round of that activity on the old GW and that had to be ten years ago anyway, because I lived in a different house.  So I don't really think that it is a "trend" or a "fad" as much as it is an alternative design/literature philosophy that has paralleled more mainstream design for at least a couple decades (much like the goth movement and other punk movements) that occasionally intersects with more mainstream design, but never really caught the fancy of the larger public particularly in residential settings.

Dulux Caspar White Quarter is a crisp very slightly cool white that may work. After much testing using the Dulux A4 colour swatches, we gave this throughout our house. I highly recommend using the swatches to figure it out in your own unique setting. They are samples of the actual paint so really help to make a good choice.

When you have an idea of a colour you like, you can go to the Dulux website and see the details of the colour: light reflectance and the ratio of red to green to blue. Then pick some similar colours - I generally go for something slightly darker and something lighter but the same or similar colour. Alternatively you could go for same tone but slightly different colours - cooler or warmer. Order these 3 or 4 in the large A4 swatches and then use blu tack to put them on the walls you plan to paint. It is amazing how different these will look in different areas and at different times of the day. I number each one on the back and keep a record of my preferred colour in north, south, east & west facing spots in morning & afternoon light. The choice then comes down to which colour I picked most often.

Given that the space between the sitting room and garage is described as ‘alleyway’, I assume this and the WC and Utility room were previously / are outbuildings?  As mentioned above the footings for the garage will probably require significant work and money in order to be able to build on top.  I would therefore knock the garage, hall, WC and utility (as it will probably be cheaper to start from scratch) and do a full two story extension on the side and open up the current sitting room and kitchen diner into each other and the extension.  The living room could then become a formal sitting room. Depending on whether you need a garage, you could have a beautiful huge open plan living area utility & WC and upstairs you could either extend bedrooms 2,3 &4 and add a couple of en-suites, or an additional bedroom, or change that side into a fabulous master, with it’s own full bathroom and walk-in wardrobes. Radiant heated floors are fully compatible with some engineered woods. WAY more than they are with laminate. What you're asking is difficult to impossible to answer.  Paint color on the walls should be the last item that you choose, after all the permanent fixtures are in.  I know builders want to paint first, but that makes it frustrating to homeowners.  Color changes with the light, and is influenced by everything else in the room.  When we built our home, we had everything painted white.  If we wanted to paint the walls a different color at a later date, we did that ourselves and had time to consider what the best color would be. But if you're really focused on getting the best gray color, you need to get very large samples, or paint posterboard yourself with the actual color, and then see how it looks in your room with your lighting.  Gray Screen is in the blue/green color family, so it makes sense that it tends to look cooler than Repose Gray which is in the yellow color family.  Both colors are very neutral, which means that they can morph and change greatly with changes in the light.  There's no substitute for making this decision in situ.

@HU-840490612 nice catch, but I don't think the 3" lintel bearing (4" min, 6" recommended) would cause all 3 different locations of cracks (maybe the one adjacent to it), because the lintel is bolted to the wood header. So this problem should be put back on the builder to rectify, but you should always be armed with as much information as possible when conflicts arise. So I am postulating about what may have caused this, which is only an assumption based on 2 pictures, but it could help direct someone in what to look for or engage you to stand your ground on the matter: - I would guess you'll find no stress cracks in the foundation stem wall, and no evidence of poor footings or settling. I say that because of the confined cracks in the middle of the door jamb and above the opening, and the stress cracks have routed through a couple bricks. - It looks like you have an attempt at a portal frame, where the LVL header extends to the outer wall. Sheathing is then closely fastened to create a very stiff 'L' leg, but I am guessing they didn't do this. - Consider that the header should not only be sized for the roof (and lateral) loads, but the weight of the masonry. There is not a lot of psf of brick above the opening, however, the LVL is designed, and allowed, to have a certain amount of deflection (a 16' span @ L/240 = 3/4"). - The steel lintel is attached to this LVL. Even so, the lintel could be undersized. I would expect a L6x4x3/8". - The bricks are then attached to the sheathing, most often by using the corrugated strap version of ties, where they will allow some movement, but not if they were angled high above the course joint. So picture the LVL naturally deflecting, it has a stiff enough connection at the ends, the ties didn't allow the brick differential movement, and you get stress cracks at these locations:   Things to look into then: - foundation - LVL size and deflection - portal frame or not - masonry ties (weeps and flashing while you're at it) - lintel size and fastening to LVL - whether repair of the mortar joints will crack again in the future from varying loads on the LVL changing it's deflection amount

text: I consider roses growing in a comparable zone to my zone 5/6*, Pittsburgh, PA, that start to show black spot damage from September and on, no earlier, and primarily on the oldest, lowest leaves of a bush, with no black spotted leaves anywhere on a bush from spring until then, a very black spot resistant bush.  Such bushes are keepers, IMHO. Black spot damage from September on is not really weakening the bush much.  It primarily attacks the leaves lowest down on the canes. They are the oldest  (by now 5+ months old), least BS resistant leaves on the bush, due to their advanced age and lower disease fighting ability.  These work horse old leaves performed their duty and their service is no longer needed.  The growing season is winding down by then and upper growth has slowed considerably.  This kind of  late season black spot damage is mostly cosmetic damage, of little negative consequences that I can determine. They are the black spot infested bushes whose leaves started black spotting in late May, and are miserable looking by July 4th., that are the primary candidates for removal from the garden.  Replacing them with well researched new, black spot resistant/free bushes, especially those selected from among the ADR winners is the ticket to success. Now a days we are so fortunate to have so many choices of fungicide spray-free rose bushes from which to choose roses for our gardens. ............... ............... *zone 5/6....May I explain why I put my zone as zone 5/6 in my identifying info after my name, Moses.  I am technically in zone 6, 6b specifically.  If I grow anything listed as hardy to zone 6, it invariably dies out over my zone 6b winters.  This goes for all flora species, especially Butterfly Bushes, Buddleia davidii.  In spite of climate changes occurring, zone 6 hardy plants don't make it here.  They have to be listed by the powers that be, as hardy to zone 5.  Then my chances of success are pretty good. Moses

We had radiant in-floor heat on both levels of our home - main level was on a slab and they poured a thin layer of Gypcrete over the tubes on the 2nd floor - I wouldn’t have had it any other way! (Our primary BR was on the 2nd floor).  Put a separate thermostat in the bathrooms (from the bedrooms - as folks typically want the bedrooms to be a bit cooler when they sleep).  This was a mountain home in CO, so there was no need for A/C.

If you are using a forced air heating and cooling system on the main floor of the house, radiant heat in the basement works great because it’s too hard to regulate the forced air heat down there. (Usually the supplies are in the ceiling and to get the heat to go down to the floor is contrary to thermal dynamics).  Forced air systems are usually very cost effective and gives the option for air conditioning, so I would use that for the majority of the house and use radiant in floor hot water heat with an electric boiler for the basement. (It will also give you a drier basement, especially if you open the A/C vents in the summer).

Unfinished basement - air sealed from the remainder of the house? What else is in the mechanical room? For me, the air handler makes the same amount of noise - but I am sure this varies based on design. The air handler runs a lot more often. If you are super sensitive to noise, your answer is to make sure the acoustics of the mechanical room are done right. Presumably, you would need that for the air handler (if you have one). I'd also be super critical about HVAC design (again if you have one and probably more than 90% do) since air movement through vents can be really poorly designed and this is by far the worst noise that I hear in new houses - even mine in a few areas.

David, I’m not sure you understand me and I’m not sure I understand you. Radiant in floor heat in the basement will give you a warmer and drier basement because the heat is at your feet, moving upward and the warm slab is drying out one of the dampest surfaces in the basement. If the basement is used only for storage and tornados, then it’s an expensive upgrade, but if you plan on spending any time in the winter down there, it’s well worth it.I would hope in the summer the radiant system would be turned off and the forced air A/C ducts opened to allow some dehumidification of that space, there again, the dampest part of a house in the summer months.The question was if they should put radiant heat in just the basement or the basement and the main floor. It looks like you have a basement and a wood framed structure. Your 3/4" plywood floor sheathing and joists are not designed for heavy equipment, nor when those loads shift with the tires (or tracks) as a careless operator rotates, stops, or maneuvers. You will be removing lots of topsoil + subsoil (clay). They will probably use a mini-excavator to dig, and a skid steer to remove the spoils (a conveyor might be an option rather than the skid steer). A mini-excavator and skid steer each weigh from 4,000-10,000lbs depending on the capacity they want (or already own). That's like parking a full-size truck (or two) on your floor. A skid steer's bucket holds from 3/4-1 cubic yard. A 20'x15'x4' deep pool is 45 cubic yards of material to dig out. That's 45 trips over your wood framing. A yard of soil in the bucket adds another 2,000lbs or so. If you build a temporary bridge, I would suggest steel beams from foundation wall to foundation wall with the cribbing on top of those. Many times you strike a deal with the neighbor to use part of their yard to go around. So remove any fence, etc, lay gravel, etc. Then repair it afterward at your cost. Unless you have a moat, your house cannot be built right up to a creek. There must be some room, at least 5'. A skid steer is about 6'-6" wide. They might use a crawler instead of a full-size skid steer, those are about 4' wide, but will take really long to remove spoils. It may be worth building a temporary retaining wall to widen a slope. Actually, if you hire landscape maintenance their mowers will be from 48" to 75" wide anyway, so maybe you should think about permanent side access to the rear. You also have to think about how long this would delay finishing the house. And how long it will take to build the entire courtyard, as they have to bring in pallets of tile/stone/pavers, 2" caliper trees, whatever.

It does look like cold damage.  It is not the fault of the store unless all the plants there looked similar.  Cut off the damaged leaves and it should recover provided you give it what it needs to thrive. My sister in law and her husband visited us in Atlanta one January long ago.  The weather was in the 70's on Saturday and short sleeve weather.  My wife took them to our local chain nursery where they bought a "corn plant" in great health. This is the recipe that I use: Biscotti Position a rack in the center of the oven and preheat the oven to 350°.  Line a baking sheet with parchment or silpat and set aside. Put the flour, sugar, baking powder, cardamom, and salt in a large bowl and stir with a rubber spatula to mix. Stir in the almonds. Whisk the eggs and vanilla together in a small bowl; then stir them into the flour mixture. The dough will be loose at first but will come together during the kneading process. Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured work surface and knead, folding it over onto itself until it is smooth. Divide the dough in half and shape each half into a 12 inch long log. Gently press down on the logs to flatten them until they are about 2 inches wide and 1 inch high. Transfer them to the prepared pan. First Baking Bake the logs for about 30 minutes, or until they are slightly risen and firm to the touch. Slide the logs off the baking sheet and onto a cooling rack. The logs must be completely cool before you can continue with the recipe. Since they will take about 30 minutes to cool, you can either turn the oven off or leave it on for the next step. You can bake the biscotti up to this point several days ahead. Wrap the logs well in plastic and continue when it is convenient.  Second Baking When the logs have cooled completely, preheat the oven to 350°F, if necessary. With a sharp serrated knife, cut the cooled logs diagonally into 3/8 to 1/2 inch thick slices. Place the sliced cookies cut side down on the pans and bake for 15 to 25 minutes, or until the biscotti are crisp and golden. Cool on the pans.  Thicker slices will take longer to get crisp.  You can slice them as thin as 1/4” thick, if preferred.  Melt the chocolate in the top of a double boiler.  Dip flat side of cooled cookie into the chocolate and return it to the pan to cool again.  If you have chocolate left over, you use a metal spatula to add more to the cookies or drizzle it over.

Hi, Abhish, Stucco can indeed wick up moisture as Kevin notes above.  You should ensure the perimeter of your home is properly graded to ensure rain water is directed away from the foundation.  The code in our area requires 6 inches of fall in 10 ft or a 5% grade; yours may be different.   Hopefully, that's the only issue and grading fixes the problem.  In the event it's not, keep in mind that wicking of moisture is not the only way moisture can get into a wall assembly with stucco cladding and you may need to do something else to mitigate it. Since your home was constructed around 1950 (assuming no remodeling of the exterior stucco) I assume you have a traditional, 3-coat cementitious stucco installed over metal lath installed over asphalt-saturated felt (a.k.a., tar paper.)  Best practice is to use two layers of 15 lb. felt to create some drainage channels between the layers, but a single layer of 30 lb. felt was a permitted alternative when I built a home with cementitious stucco 22 years ago. Traditional cementitious stucco is a "reservoir cladding" meaning it has the capacity to store water.   Cementitious stucco, once wetted, would dry both to the exterior and to the interior of your home, albeit at different rates depending on interior and exterior conditions and the properties of the felt.  Exterior conditions that may increase wetting include orientations more susceptible to wind-driven rains, and walls which dry more slowly due to shading.  The condition of the stucco (e.g., cracks) can also contribute to increased wetting. Just like us, (wives aging like fine wines being the notable exception) asphalt-saturated felt deteriorates over time.   Homes I've remodeled which were constructed in the 1950s generally have pretty thin felt and it's usually pretty brittle (for the record, 70 years of service life is more than you should expect from many synthetic materials, too.)  The deterioration changes the properties of the felt and allows more moisture to move to the interior side.  That can increase the relative humidity in the wall cavities and the adjacent living areas since it is drying to the interior.  In the event it is, you'll want to get things dried out before mold/mildew becomes an issue.  Running a dehumidifier is a good idea.  Another way to deal with the deteriorating felt layer is to reduce water absorption by the stucco by painting it.  You'll need to use a vapor-permeable paint (permeance greater than 10) which will slow absorption, but still allow drying to the exterior. Best wishes for a successful fix.
