Are you sure they are sugar maples? Not that common a species here in the PNW. If they are sugar maples, 20 years old is just barely out of their teens for a tree that can live into the 100's, and not a valid reason to have them removed. As to a close proximity to a structure, as long as the trees are structurally sound and the canopy high enough not to interfere with the siding or the roof, there is really not a pressing issue nor any immediate need for removal. The PNW is home to many very large growing native tree species - Doug firs, western red cedars, bigleaf maples, madrones, etc. - and in more suburban/rural settings, these are sometimes sited very close to structures, either intentionally or because the house was built to accommodate their existing placement. Again, if the tree is in sound health, there is generally no issue. I have a 60'+ Doug fir growing within 15 feet of my house and it's been there longer than the house has! The other issue is that if you have these trees removed, it will be many years - possibly even decades - before replacements grow sufficiently tall enough to provide the shade you are looking for.

Go to your local big box store and check their pre-hung doors and you will probably find plenty that are cracked.  It is the nature of hollow core pre-hung doors and is not difficult to repair properly. Store everything where you use it, and consider the kids will grow up and may add to the number of workers in the kitchen so create separate Work Zones. Features you may wish to consider but certified kitchen designer will offer you these ideas and more - gas cooktop zone with bank of drawers under it (for cooking utensils & pot holders/pots & pans/wire rack for lids); 6”- 9” wide spice rollout lower cab - or spice rack in upper cab - or lying down in top drawer - if you usually add spices while cooking; very quiet low decibel vent hood without a microwave; vent hood can be a feature or can be under upper cabs; at least 12” counter on 1 side and 15” counter on other side; you don’t need a pot filler if you will be carrying the heavy pot of boiling water to drain it in the sink anyway; don’t put open shelves in cooktop area because things will get grimy and greasy. Baking zone with oven in lower cab or in wall at waist height is better for lifting heavy pans; don’t do range/oven/cooktop combo if there is more than 1 cook; need counter space for mixing ingredients and rolling out dough; drawers underneath (for oven mitts/ bakeware/meat thermometer/mixing bowls & utensils/ measuring cup/hand held mixer; upright sectional storage above - or rollout lower cab - for cookie sheets, cooling racks, waffle maker, etc. stored on their sides. Some ovens come with a warming drawer if that would be useful; under cab door with lift-up shelf if you use a heavy mixer machine. Appliance garage with outlets for often used small appliances you can use right there (blender, toaster, food processor); under cab shelf or pantry storage for crock pot/pasta maker/bread maker/air fryer/popcorn popper. Sink within a few steps of pantry and fridge for efficient prep zone; DWs by sink and next to storage for dishes/bowls/glasses/silverware; if dishes are in a drawer then a top shallow drawer for knives that slides back to reveal dishes underneath and vertical pegs to hold dishes in place; if glasses are in drawer there are spacers for them; keep colander by sink. Some microwaves have convection feature to act as a second oven; need storage for pot holders and microwave-safe bakeware you use. A good spot for fridges and microwaves is at end of the cabinet run so people grabbing quick snacks don’t enter the sink and main cooking areas. Consider a fridge with water dispenser if you drink lots of water; a mini beverage fridge if you drink lots of canned or bottled drinks; a shallow fridge drawer if you buy weekly pizza; a fridge with 2 ice storage areas - or separate undercounter ice maker - if you use a lot of ice. Consider a freezer chest if you need more freezer space than fridge offers. You need somewhere other than under the sink for trash and recycle if more than 1 worker in the kitchen (haha, someone is always at the sink when the other needs to toss something). A shallow pantry with narrow shelves - or a tall rollout pantry beside the fridge - or pantry of drawers are easier to grab things than pantry closet with deep shelves. Consider storage needed for your serving items and counter space for plating your food and serving buffet-style. Consider where you will keep mop/broom/toxic cleaning supplies, they make tall shallow kitchen cabs for them now. Consider everything at waist height to be prime real estate and store your lesser used items down low or up high.

You didn't exactly specify, but it sure sounds like an existing garage you'd like to modify. There is much more involved to widening an existing garage door than you might think. A new header, cutting the foundation walls and portion of slab, pouring new slab, are the walls combatting shear for the structure, the width of the driveway, etc. A 20' door is offered for a residential stamped panel, but 18' is the more common oversized width chosen. What is critical is the amount of space adjacent to the cars, not so much the space in between (you may walk by them both to get outside, access shelves, whatever many times a day vs getting out of 1 of the cars 2 or 4 times a day). Unfortunately, @i3igdmsu, you have more of a hope than a plan.  Hood system, MUA system, and cooking appliance should be configured as an integrated whole. With your stated goal, you will have to cook anything that releases oil vapor, grease vapor, or fat entrained in moisture on the back middle burner unless you make the hood wider and deeper, and for the latter it needs to be higher to reduce head impact.  The hood should encompass the rising and expanding cooking plumes from front burners. I would put the hood at 36-inches high, or even slightly higher, and expand the hood canopy in both horizontal directions sufficiently to reasonably capture all plumes.  @User's comment is a good one as you need the wall space.  CFM calculations, duct size calculations, and MUA issues are described in scores of my messages here, many recent.  Noise issues are important for many and suggestions are also in these threads.  Air quality issues are addressed, inter alia, in @opaone's https://bamasotan.us/range-exhaust-hood-faq/ For examples of adequate hoods, please view the canopy hood portions of the Wolf Design Guide (available from their website).  Many other hood sources exist and may be lower in cost.  But the Wolf guide is a little easier to digest initially than the vast array of hoods on, e.g., AJMadison's web site. Homeowners often need to be their own HVAC engineers when it comes to specifying their kitchen ventilation systems due to lack of well-informed contractors who work on kitchen renovations. you need to apply more caulk INTO the crack.  use a knife to remove the existing caulk.  then very carefully apply painters tape very close (~1/16") to the edge of each surface on either side of the crack.  Then apply a fresh bead of caulk along the crack.  Then take something with a square edge (like a shim) and run it along the crack which pushes the caulk into the crack and leaves it flush with the adjacent surfaces.  The carefully remove the painters tape which will have excess caulk on it and let the caulk set.  Painters take will not damage the finish on cabinetry or painted surfaces.  This is time consuming but it's the only way I know of to get a perfect caulk bead every time.

The best growing period here is December-March when day temps will rarely ever get near 80. I find that many years we get an early hot spell and that will blast the tulips as they flower and they last but a day or three.  Only occasionally have I had tulips bloom a second year, and then only in the ground somewhere they get part shade, and then with much smaller flowers. Growing in pots, my best year was when I followed the Sunset garden Book method of planting out in large pots (15") in early December and holding the pots in deep shade covered in mulch (oak leaves) until leaves show. Your 'fail' may be just fine. IMPE, whole wheat flour can make for a more dense result. I recall something about the bran affecting the strands of gluten so they're not as long. I beat that very well, then cover and let rise in a warm place for 1-1 1/2 hours, then add another cup of flour a little at a time and knead into a smooth dough and cover to let rise again for another 1-1 1/2 hours before shaping, rising and baking.

Try to find some old house forums and/or local people who do plaster repair.    Beware that people whose skill set is drywall are going to tell you that it all needs to come out.  Very rarely does all plaster have to come out unless its been neglected or water damaged over a period of time.  It may be you use a range of different techniques depending on what kind of damage.  You may find that some walls have only minor cracks that can be simpy filled ,while some walls may have major bowing and large loose areas.   arger damaged areas can either be re-done using old methods OR.... just attach drywall patches and fill in gaps with plaster (using bonding agent to get old plaster to adhere to new plaster). Whatever you do, please dont do the thing of putting drywall OVER the old plaster and butting it up against the baseboard and window and door trim. Thats just plain ugly Ceilings might be the one surface you decide to have drywalled - looks like we are seeing ceilings in your pics?  Gravity has greater effect on ceilings, so damage can be a lot worse than walls. And, since theres no trim to contend with up there, its a lot easier. If you want to start a thread and post some pics over on the old house forum, I think youd find a lot of us could advise in more detail.

When was the wiring and plumbing last inspected or replaced?  Can most of the wiring be seen beneath the floor and/or in the attic? Have you had any problems with any electrical outlets or lighting?  If so, after you remove the drywall in the room(s), would be a good time to check any problems and, for safety sake, make   any needed repairs before hanging the replacement drywall ... whether sheet rock or paneling. If there are no small children in the home, you might consider removing all of it and replacing it with paneling one room at a time. On a budget?  If you're considering whether to use sheet rock or paneling, take into consideration the cost of having sheet rock finished and the time involved as you compare that cost with the cost of paneling. If most or the walls have cracks, it could be that the house itself is settling and covering up the problem  with more sheet rock will certainly not solve the problem -- only waste money as the problem reoccurs.  Can you get into the crawl space beneath the house to inspect it --   or have that done?

Another plus for plaster is the surface is harder and doesn't get dings and damage nearly as easily as drywall. Removing cracked plaster is not an upgrade.We have had good luck with drilling holes through the plaster, squirting construction adhesive between the lathe and the back of the plaster and then screwing the plaster pieces to the lathe. After the adhesive dries, you can remove the screws and then patch the holes and cracks. If you choose to drywall any ceilings,  use lots of adhesive and longer screws and go right over the plaster if the plaster is not crumbling.

Have not one fat clue why someone would say Bleeker Beige isn't an option for a classic orange barrel tile roof. My guess is because they think it has "xyz undertones" and have shared that opinion without  qualifying their subjective opinion - for example, under what light source? Or if they're lookin' at a chip at their kitchen table, on a laptop, or where exactly? But I can tell you - and show you - why it's worth sampling to see if it's the look you're after. It works because - factually - it's an analogous color scheme. Bleeker Beige sits inside the warmer side of the Yellow Hue family. It leans towards the Yellow-Red hue family (aka orange). We can qualify warm and cool on The Color Strategist Color Wheel because of the color notation; paint colors have to be compared to thousands of other colors in the system in order to categorize them by hue, value, and chroma. The order system provides context and you need context to judge warm or cool. A warm and cool comparison happens organically within a notated color system. The warm/cool designation isn't a measurement like hue/value/chroma but it holds true. (I've never seen it not hold true, let me put it that way - and I've been looking for it to not work for a very long time, tens of thousands of colors.)

I don't think Bleeker Beige DOESN'T go with orange. It's in the orange-yellow color family, so with the roof you have an analogous color scheme. If people don't like it with orange, it may just be that the roof color is pretty assertive, and folks who don't like Bleeker Beige with it may just prefer that the orange be the star and want to pair it with colors that are lighter/less assertive. If you look up a color on the Benjamin Moore site, there is usually a "goes with" option. I picked a couple BM color that looked close to your roof color (Topaz, Pennies from Heaven) and looked at their suggested palettes. The Senora Gray in the third palette is actually quite close to Pashmina. The Chatsworth Cream is very similar to what I've seen in a lot of Mediterranean-style homes. It doesn't seem like the direction you want to go, but I think it's popular because it works well with the orange tile.

Several years ago, and a few years apart, I bought, on speculation, two travel memoirs by the same author because they looked like books I might enjoy. In December I finally cracked one open and read it, and liked it so much that I have just finished the other one. The author was British novelist Jenny Diski, whom I had never heard of before. I loved how she could write books about fairly uneventful voyages and still make them interesting without being long-winded. Much of that has to do with her elegant prose, and the way she makes perfectly ordinary people seem like extraordinary characters. A less skilful writer would have written two boring books or two forgettable articles from the material. Both books concern trips she took. One is about a trip to Antarctica (Skating to Antarctica), ostensibly to find quiet, characterised by the all-surrounding whiteness of snow (she finds more grey and blue), but really about coming to terms with her troubled childhood and examining if she can forgive her mother for past transgressions. The other book, the one I just finished (Stranger on a Train), is about two trips by train, one most of the way across, and the other around the perimeter of, the continental USA. On the surface, these train journeys were taken to meet interesting people in the train smoking spaces and to be alone with herself, but are really about mulling over aspects of her past life and experiences. These are the kinds of trips I sometimes take myself - for the journey itself rather than any specific destination. I know if I come across her other non-fiction books, I will want to read those as well. My current read is Voyage of the Basilisk by Marie Brennan, the third in a series that combines three of my favourite genres: fantasy, historical novel and travel. They take place in a fantasy realm that is decidedly Victorianesque and describe the voyages of a woman naturalist whose interest is in dragons. I decided to buy all the books in their analogue formats, because I love the beautiful artwork on the covers.

It works fairly well, but there are a few things I've noticed. 1. You need to make sure that the tip of the branch is angled towards the ground or your branching will grow weird and it will produce growth from the tip of that branch. 2. You need to stay ahead of the new growth. This means that any time a branch gets big and long, wire it AS SOON as you can and while it is soft. You have a lot more leeway with the branch while it is soft and rubbery than when it hardens. Make sure to stay ahead of the new growth. 3. If you're doing this outside, use something that won't heat up, or fabric wrapped wire so that it doesn't heat up and damage the tree. Or paint it white. You can also use Jute to pull down the tips of branches, tied off the trunk. I did that in the early years with my Nagami before I got the wire. If done right you can really get some nice shape from a tree without removing a ton of branches and without significant pruning.

I have...opinions about Benjamin Moore. They're expensive (especially their samples) and their matte is gorgeous but too matte (as in, marks easily, difficult to clean). I've painted a ton and have had just as good results with the higher tier of Behr and Sherwin Williams. Their matte is not as flat, but it still looks great and is easier to care for. If you require really good assistance with color and advice, go to a Sherwin Williams store instead of a hardware store. Choosing paint is really specific to what kind of natural light you have and also how you light it at night. You have a ton of trees, so look around during the day and see if they reflect a green cast into the rooms? Then you might need an off white with an undertone more on the pinkish end of the spectrum (not yellow), such as SW Paper Kraft. A good off white should come off as warm and creamy but not noticeably pink or yellow. When you narrow down to a few favorites, get samples and paint big swatches (you can do this on cardboard if you don't want to paint the walls). Matte is best for walls (I only choose satin for damp spaces like bathrooms). If you don't need to worry about green cast, the sky is your limit. To keep things easy: choose the same white for trim and ceiling (a brighter white than the walls).  Satin for the trim and matte for the ceiling.

The pump filter is in a similar location as models that have an access hatch, there just isn't a hatch.  So, yes, the machine typically must be disassembled to get to it. In some cases the bottom panel of the machine is partially open and the pump/filter can be accessed from beneath ... but not always, and the access can be tight if it is possible. Remove the top panel (screws at the rear corners).  The control panel typically must come off, with unplugging of wires involved, unless it can be positioned to sit atop the tub / outer cabinet frame without removing the wires.  Sometimes there are snap-on trim pieces that must be removed to reveal hidden anchor screws. Then detach the outer spring/wire around the tub gasket that anchors it to the machine front panel, and remove the front panel.  The door latch mechanism may need to be detached from the front, or the wires taken off of the latch for room to maneuver the front if the wires are too short to move it aside.  It's best not to attempt separately removing the door but the front panel will be heavy and awkward to handle with the door swinging.  Note that getting the gasket spring/wire back in place can be a challenge. There will be some residual water spill out when the pump filter is opened. If you want get a general view of the filter location, find the model number of your machine on the tag visible when the door is open.  Look up the model at online parts sources that have breakdown diagrams, such as AppliancePartsPros.com or SearsPartsDirect.com.  Find the diagram that shows the pump, which is generally the picture that has the tub and drum. It's always best to cite the model number when asking appliance questions.  A year reference is not sufficient, there may be different machine designs among the various models of a given year.

I'm in North Carolina. Not a super expensive market but not the least expensive either. Licensed architects are professionals. Bottom line, you engaged a professional without a contract clearly delineating deliverables. Always get it in writing with clear expectations including billing cycles. If the pro hesitates to do this, move on to someone else. The architect I worked with on my remodel speced some windows out incorrectly on the materials plans. The markup is likely on their wholesale or designer-discounted price.  The decorating designers I work with mark up between 25%-35%.  Their pricing is similar to most retailers who sell the same products, but they have access to many more options than a single retail store.  They charge an hourly fee to make the selections, but do not charge an hourly fee to manage the order once it has been placed.  The markup covers the cost/time to manage the order.  When you purchase from a designer, they often deal with any issues, like repairs or delays, directly.  They are also responsible for reviewing the final order they receive from the manufacturer or showroom.  When you order furniture on your own, you take on that risk. If you are buying good quality furniture, it could absolutely be of value for you to work with a designer.  If you are looking for lower-quality or disposable furniture, then you may not feel the need to pay a professional to mitigate the risk of making a mistake.

OK, where was I? First, one needs to determine the size of the hood's capture aperture.  This can be found by the following process.  Assume that each burner has the largest pot/pan that is likely to be used.  Determine the outer boundary of the contour that these circles represent.  Add one inch for the gas flames and their combustion products.  Add plume expansion.  For this value, take the height of the hood over the pan (a variable for now) and multiply that number by the tangent of 10 degrees (0.176).  Consider drafts and occupant movement causing turbulence and bias to the plume and add for that also, if necessary. Using stick figure drawings, consider how high the hood should be for good site lines and head clearance.  Take into account what is available off the shelf, or which can be economically (heh) constructed as a custom hood.  This sets the height parameter and hence the size of the desired aperture.  Note that this is recursive with the steps in this paragraph, and higher reduces visual impact but costs more due to size. This resulting rectangle should have 90 ft/min at full hood blower power, so the required CFM is the product of 90 ft/min and entry area in square feet. Blower size depends on various pressure losses from kitchen to outside and back to kitchen, and this in turn depends on the make-up air scheme, not further addressed in this particular message.  The approximation value for selecting blower rated CFM is 1.5 times the CFM calculated in the previous paragraph. Duct size should be such that full power air velocity lie in the 1000 to 2000 ft/min range. With an attic and the option to angle the duct to a best point on the roof for an external blower, there should be room for a silencer.  This will greatly help to keep noise down. Excluding commercial hood designs, the best residential island hood configuration is represented by the Wolf Pro line, in my opinion.  See the Wolf Design Guide that is available for download.  The farther a hood design deviates from this tilted baffle, pyramidal design, the greater the likely deviation from good efficiency and good performance. Thin hood forms can have unequal flow across the filter space unless the filters are fairly restrictive. Mesh filters are fairly restrictive, especially when dirty.  Baffles are better except perhaps at low specific (per square foot) air flow levels.  Low air flow is only applicable to poaching, simmering, and maybe quiet bacon frying. Slotted hood schemes may prove to fail to fully capture energetic plumes because conservation of momentum applies to air also, and reflection happens where plumes meet metal. The example hoods are marginal, front-to-back distance, for island use.  The chimney cover tends to be visually significant, so I'm not sure you gain a lot over a conventional pyramidal hood. All that said, one has to trade among many variables in each of these cases, keeping in mind that one can't simultaneously optimize performance, aesthetics, and affordability .

Keep in mind that a hood is an appliance for your and others health, not just a decorative element. If you always have windows open for fresh air or don't do a lot of cooking and especially not a lot of pan frying or other stuff that creates a lot of effluent then any of those might be fine. Otherwise you should consider a proper hood. More: https://bamasotan.us/range-exhaust-hood-faq/

My Dripping Springs lows are generally 5º colder than forecasts for Austin. However, Austin has colder and warmer spots due to elevation, tree coverage and development density. Austin is listed as zone 8b (lows 15-20º) but, Dripping Springs straddles the 8a/8b divide and our entire area could easily fall either way. It's a microclimate difference between halfway up a south-facing hill versus a north-facing valley. Pansies and ornamental cabbage and kale are THE reliable winter annuals. Others that work well are snapdragons, dianthus (perennial species: gratianopolitanus, plumarius, and armeria; annual species: chinensis, cv. Diamond or Ideal series), and sweet alyssum. When planted from seed in fall, stocks (Mathiola incana) and pot marigold (Calendula) will bloom very early. These will all take zone 8 temperatures, though ice storms can leave them looking pitiful. In my personal experience, the only perennial dianthus species that can take our summer heat is gratianopolitanus. Christmas rose (Helleborus niger) is a winter blooming perennial best placed in groups beneath a deciduous tree in moist soil. There are many evergreen mahonia species that produce yellow flowers in winter or spring with fruit following. Various species range from ground cover to tree sized.

HU….it’s my understanding that the hot surface ignitor will not read voltage until that step in the sequence of opeations is reached, and prior steps have been satisfied. In this case…the thermostat has called for heat (or heat is jumped out), the inducer motor has started and the pressure switch has closed. You mentioned that you have recently replaced the pressure switch. You also mentioned that the draft motor starts for a second, stops and restarts. I have never witnessed this hapening before. Does your inducer motor have a limit switch built into its’ housing? My gut feeling is that there may be an issue with your inducer motor. Maybe some sort of blockage? If it does have a limit switch built in check to see it that is working? Can you confirm that the air pressure switch is proving? You won’t see voltage at the gas valve either or hear the click until that step in the sequence is reached and all other prior sequence of operatoins satisfied. If your ignitor never recieves voltage it won’t tell the board to send voltage to the gas valve. If I’m off here I aplogize. I’m still learning but wanted to share what I though may be the issue.

Good news! Problem solved. I was getting a reverse polarity code on the ignitor module. It turns out the the furnace was wired "backwards" for 30 years.....neutral and hot were reversed. Does anyone know why it would have worked all these years? It suddently stopped working this year. After a lot of troubleshooting, I realized what was wrong, switched the hot and neutral to the correct positions and...it works! What could of changed in the furnace or the house to have caused this problem? Thx!!!!

The furnace housing is usually not connected to the neutral connection so swapping the hot and neutral wires should not matter. The original 50E47 module failed after 30 years, but the Universal 50E47-843 does not work with swapped wiring. I can't think of a reason why it would not. You would have to study the schematic of the module for a possible reason. Good work at troubleshooting the problem and coming up with a solution. Sorry I wasn't more of a help. I actually enjoy trying to solve problems like this.

Thx for your help. The only logical explanation is that the 50E47-70 failed for whatever reason but was not sensitive to reversed polarity of the line voltage. Once i repaced it with the 50E47-843 the original problem was likely solved but….this newer controller has the polarity sensitivity. Once i corrected the input line polarity (connecting hot to hot and neutral to neutral right where the line comes  into the furnace) the furnace operated normally. Without the yellow flashing error code on the  new -843  controller i never would have thought about polarity and never would have found it. Gotta  love technology!

Talk with your professional tile installer.  There are different qualities.  Density of the stone is one differentiation.  The source (quarry/origin/and part of the quarry) makes a difference. Quality and  quarry source origin are the big differences. Iron inclusions and subsequent rust is far more common in Indian and Chinese sourced ”carrarra“.  Even some of the Turkish rusty marbles are being labeled carrarra. True Carrarra only comes from Italy in the Carrarra region. High grade Carrarra isnt as cheap as any of that either. It isn’t the muddy gray that most low quality marble labeled that looks like.  Its a mostly white, with bluish gray veining. There’s a lot of bad, muddy, gray,  ”carrarra” out there. A big name, large direct importer, like Daltile, gets the better quality picks. That doesn't mean it is statue or slab A+ quality though. If it were, it wouldn't be being cut into tiles. It just isn’t D- quality.

dark stains + dry = dirt or dust  ---- dark stains + damp (or wet) = mold potential. Filtration: the better filter you use, the less dirt goes thru -- however a too restrictive filter and your system won't work or you cut the capacity of the system and your light bill goes up. funky smells and Texas go hand in hand. When you switch from heat to cool and then from cool to heat like we've been doing here lately --- it's not uncommon for funky smells to rear up. Especially when humidity levels start going back up. Bacteria -- is what causes the smells most often, not mold. Mold often will make you sick first no smells and discovered after you get sick and start investigating. Bacteria usually gives off smells when heated, but if you have a heat pump not uncommon to get funky smells in heating mode or AC mode after recently interchanging between the two. Why does that happen? Humidity plays a role in that. Especially when you run the AC in more mild like humid type conditions the AC doesn't run long enough to pull it out. The pictures you show are about as common as the day is long. What can you do? Set your temperature set points higher or lower forcing the equipment to run longer. If the smells don't go away after several hours of run time (heat or AC) then you may need to have the E-coil professionally cleaned as this is where the bacteria grows. Shut the system off, avoid using it during times like this in our climate. Bacteria needs the moisture of the AC cycle to grow. Heat cycle kills it, so when it dies it gives off smells. You can put in UV bulbs and a whole conglomeration of other gadgets, but if you're not prepared to replace these parts on an annual maintenance plan then keep your money in your wallet. It is argumentative that these sorts of products do much of anything. If you are an alergy sufferer there are products for that -- but there are additional costs to maintain those on an annual basis. Here's what the code for Virginia says: M1503.4 Makeup Air RequiredExhaust hood systems capable of exhausting more than 400 cubic feet per minute (0.19 m3/s) shall be provided with makeup air at a rate approximately equal to the exhaust air rate in excess of 400 cubic feet per minute (0.19 m3/s). Such makeup air systems shall be equipped with a means of closure and shall be automatically controlled to start and operate simultaneously with the exhaust system.Exception: Intentional openings for makeup air are not required for kitchen exhaust systems capable of exhausting not greater than 600 cubic feet per minute (0.28 m3/s) provided that one of the following conditions is met:

Beyond the safety issues expressed in the code, no air leaves the kitchen via the hood system that isn't replaced somehow.  One can't just drain the house volume of air.  Further, if the hood system has to lower the house pressure to get enough air from house leakage, the hood air flow rate will be degraded, and stuff in the walls may find its way into the living areas. If you search this forum for "MUA" you will find various ideas and conditions for adopting them.  Depending on the type of combustion appliances in your house that are within the "air barrier," you may need a blower-driven MUA path (active MUA) or a large duct (passive MUA).  Both will need some form of heating and filtering. You may notice that active vs. passive is not explicitly called out in the code text listed above, nor is there an explicit demand for a particular pressure balance.  Once review of the material here leads you to feel comfortable with the issues, you might want to discuss your MUA system plan with your local code enforcement to ensure that you are both on the same page. Alternatively, finding an informed HVAC contractor may be sufficient.

Hi, Justin, I don't share the concern about the addition of weep holes introducing moisture into the void space between the brick veneer and sheathing.  Adding the weeps provides a path for liquid water to exit the space.  Albeit without flashing, providing a path is positive, in my opinion. The concern about moisture in the stud cavities is valid.  In our climate zone, (I design, build and remodel homes in zone 4c,) I believe the best strategy is to enable the structure to dry to both the interior and the exterior.  I'd avoid any vapor retarder other than latex paint on the interior.  With regard to insulation, the objective is to fill the entire volume of each stud cavity to prevent a void in which condensation could occur.  Blowing in cellulose insulation is likely to fall short of that objective.  I'd favor the use of a retrofit/injection foam insulation to fill the void volume completely.

The most common method to lower pH or acidify soil is to apply agricultural sulfur. But it is not a fast process as the chemical reaction that causes the change takes time - 3-12 months - to occur, depending on soil type. And not really necessary if growing in containers. Commercial container/potting soil is buffered to have a pH of just around neutral or slightly under, typically 6.5 - 6.9. But you can address nutrient inaccessibility - the primary reason for pH requirements - through fertilization. Or you can use a potting soil formulated specifically for acid loving plants (Dr. Earth, Coast of Maine, EB Stone, Fox Farms all provide such a product). Hard or alkaline tap or irrigation water can also be neutralized or acidified by using plain old table vinegar, 1 tablespoon to a gallon of water. This is a common practice in areas with hard water and container growing things like blueberries, rhododendrons or Japanese maples.

If they're known and respected and the price is what you would expect -- chances are the art is what they say. If you open the oven door, you will see that the range sides - without the door - are made to be flush to the cabinets for most ranges in the U.S. market.  That way the sides are not showing.  But the oven door sits proud of the adjacent cabinets for fire safety and so that the cabinets don’t get burn marks from the heat of the oven.  The counter usually does not come out as far as the range oven doors, though some people do opt for deep counters overall (about 27-28” deep with that option), but that is not what you are asking. Actually, what I have read on this forum over many years is that the Bluestar open burners are the best cooking applyancevyou can have in a home kitchen. (1) waterproofing membranes are often not perfect as small punctures are possible and having a substrate that doesn't fail from insignificant amount of water is good.  (2) drywall is not rigid enough to be a good substrate for many tile applications. Since they chose to use drywall, there is no repair that can be acceptably done.  If the kerdi was appropriately adhered to the drywall removing the tile after a week is going to destroy the drywall.  Since they can't get to an undamaged section there is no overlap avaliable for the patch.

You really must go to the countertop layout at the fabricator's to see the various options of where the seam will be. The first thing to do is avoid terms like "rotted floor".  If an OSB subfloor has been wet long enough, its bending strength is reduced so it feels spongy under foot.  Unless its treated or plywood, It also swells and doesn't completely shrink back when dried. This is not necessarily wood decay from fungal growth. If the subfloor is Advantech, it would be pretty well protected. So, describe the material and condition of the floor and post photos.  Don't approach the contractor with half baked assumptions.

See here. Your nose knows! Take a look in attics and basement corners.  A knife blade into suspect wood framing will reveal the extent of wood rot.  Peeling paint and wallpaper are giveaways too. As @Charles Ross Homes says, your Architect and Designer will likely have a questionnaire that gets at the info that they think is most pertinent. But that doesn't mean that it will collect the info that you think is most important. My most successful renos have happened when I prepared my own proposal outline for the renovator to guide our conversations. It gives them a very good idea of my level of knowledge and engagement, as well as ensuring that I get all my questions asked. I don't have a template for my proposals. But they usually have the following sections: Once I have sketched out the above info, I refine and clarify it. I try to put the tasks in the order that they'll probably happen. And I add any comments or questions I might have.  For example, this is one of the tasks on my recent bathroom reno proposal: This lets the designer know that I want my closet to change and that I have a couple of options in mind but that I'd like their advice. Not including pictures, the whole thing is about 3 pages. I send it to the renovator ahead of our first meeting. And I have a printed copy that I revise as needed during our meetings. Once the official quote with scope of work has been sent to me, I compare it to my (revised) proposal to make sure that the renovator and I both have the same understanding of what will be done.

I would also recommend exploring other more usual sources of odor in old houses than dry studs. I have never heard of dry plaster having a smell. For example, wax rings around toilets will need to be replaced periodically and may cause toilet water slow leaks around the toilets. Also, drain pipes in areas with low use may have the p trap dried out, allowing sewer gas to pervade the house. This is a general bad smell that is hard to source. I have 2 laundry areas, one of which is not in use now and the trap dries out every few months and it starts to smell. Do you have any drain traps that may just need a cup of water added to them? The previous owners to my own house noticed a terrible smell and it turns out that my house's sewage pipe had not been connected and years of blackwater were draining into a pit under my house. This is obviously extreme but just an example. Did you check the attic area for evidence of bat guano, raccoon nests etc. These can get pretty smelly, especially the bigger animals will cause soaking of the wood/insulation or paper facing of the ceiling below with urine.feces. I am sure others will have other suggestions of hidden sources of stink.

Musty smells often come from the basement or crawlspace.  There could be a small plumbing leak or standing water that's not draining properly, or something similar that's causing mold/mildew.  Have you checked all those possibilities? In my experience with 2 old houses, both in need of renovation/restoration, when we first walked in, they smelled musty.  After occupying them for a while, using the HVAC, getting some ventilation, and fixing plumbing, the mustiness went away.

If there are no basement or crawl space issues, drywall and paint should encapsulate the odor.  We had a similar situation (an abandoned 1903 cabin that had been home to many happy mammals for ten or twenty years) and we tore out all wood products - cabinets and doors. The smell was unbearable. Once we dry walled and painted it was fine.  A few years later we were renovating and opened one of the old walls - the old, awful smell was still there.  It seemed encapsulating worked for our situation.

There is no "standard." It's whatever the electrician did to accomplish the most efficient wiring runs, which would typically mean fairly direct horizontal runs between receptacles.  I think the risk of hitting wiring is minimal, especially if you are drilling the wall close to the floor.  If you are really nervous, you just need to be smart about drilling. You should know what the depth of the brick is and you can put a piece of masking tape on the masonry bit equivalent to this dimension. That way you can ease up as you are getting close to breaking through so you don't shove the bit tip way into the cavity when you do break through.  Once you have that hole drilled, you can use a small dowel of a piece of wire to probe to confirm there is nothing that feels like wire in the way of the hole; then finish the job.  Additionally, you can also buy yourself a cheap boroscope on Amazon; they start at about $40.  These are mini cameras on the end of a cable which you can slip into a small hole and get a video of what is inside.

I am a fabricator.  Quartz (i.e. engineered stone) is definitely more susceptible to heat damage than most natural stones.  I have had several repair calls over the years where a guest with granite at home scorched a quartz countertop by placing a hot item on quartz counter like they do in their own home.  Heat damage to a quartz top is usually damage to the resin component of the material.  Unfortunately it takes an unusual level of skill to repair a scorched area if it's even possible.  Natural stone can be damaged by heat but is it far less common.  I have had only 2 incidents of obvious granite heat damage in 21 years in the business; one was a fireplace hearth that cracked and the other was cracks in a brand new countertop when the homeowner had a "lefsa" party where the lefsa cookers heated spots in the granite over a period of several hours.  In the fab shop we sometimes use propane torches right on the stone to dry it out when doing a chip repair so I don't consider heat damage much of a risk for natural stone.  I know not everyone will agree with my assessment but I'm going by my experience with many thousands of stone and quartz projects.

Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Oedema Oedema (aka edema) is a physiological disorder that can affect all terrestrial plants. It occurs when the plant takes up more water than it can rid itself of via the process of transpiration. The word itself means 'swelling', which is usually the first symptom, and comes in the form of pale blisters or water-filled bumps on foliage. Under a variety of circumstances/cultural conditions, a plant's internal water pressure (turgidity) can become so high that some leaf cells rupture and leak their contents into inter-cellular spaces in leaf tissue, creating wet or weepy areas. Symptoms vary by plant, but as the malady progresses, areas of the leaf turn yellow, brown, brown with reddish overtones or even black, with older damage appearing as corky/ scaly/ ridged patches, or wart/gall-like bumpy growth. Symptoms are seen more frequently in plants that are fleshy, are usually more pronounced on the underside of leaves, and older/lower leaves are more likely to be affected than younger/upper leaves. Oedema is most common in houseplants during the winter/early spring months, is driven primarily by excessive water retention in the soil, and can be intensified via several additional cultural influences. Cool temperatures, high humidity levels, low light conditions, or partial defoliation can individually or collectively act to intensify the problem, as can anything else that slows transpiration. Nutritional deficiencies of Ca and Mg are also known contributors to the malady. Some things that can help you prevent oedema: * Increase light levels and temperature * Monitor water needs carefully – avoid over-watering. I'd heartily recommend a soil with drainage so sharp (fast) that when you to water to beyond the saturation point you needn't worry about prolonged periods of soil saturation wrecking root health/function. Your soil choice should be a key that unlocks the solutions to many potential problems. * Avoid misting or getting water on foliage. It slows transpiration and increases turgidity. * Water as soon as you get up in the AM. When stomata close in preparation for the dark cycle, turgidity builds. If you water early in the day, it gives the plant an opportunity to remove (for its own needs) some of the excess water in the soil. * Put a fan in the room or otherwise increase air flow/circulation. Avoid over-crowding your plants. Al

The pit itself can be anywhere, but it's usually close to where the pipe comes through the foundation wall. Plus, the pit will have one or more incoming pipes leading to the tile drainage around your foundation, and ideally that run is as short as feasible too. Either way, you'll want to maintain easy access to check it every now and then. You'll want to know it's working (often just the satisfying hum of the pump running every now and then, but not constantly), and you'll want to be able to get in there fairly quick if something goes wrong. I've had cases where the float gets stuck, and the pit fills up. So at least once I year I pop the cover and jiggle things around to make sure everything's sliding & working. I also always recommend a high-level alarm. You can get a sensor to tie into your home alarm if you have one, or something separate. But pumps do fail, and you'll want a secondary warning other than sloshing through ankle-deep water. You'd best consult with a plumber or foundation drainage contractor to make sure you're doing it right.

You are wise to consider adding a pit if you're lowering your floor 2 feet. It's very difficult to determine for sure if you need to or not, but better to put one in than find out a bit later that you're 6" below the high-water line. "Normally" the pipe runs straight up, one right angle, and through the wall to outside (below the typical frost line where you are, or 3'ish feet below grade so it won't freeze), then angled down to where it comes out the other end. But since the water is being pumped, you can have additional bends. Make sure you have a reverse-flow valve (so water can't come back in via that pipe). And yeah, you can have a cabinet that hides it, as long as it's set up so that you can get access in a pinch. Sumps are often things you ignore, until that fateful day you suddenly can't. One small tip is when you build the cabinet, have some air gaps such that the pipes aren't touching the cabinet itself. The pump will have a bit of a "hum" to it, and that slight vibration might transfer to the cabinet (think sub-woofer) and drive you nuts with the low drone every time it comes on. As to the radon mention, just double-check that your local code doesn't require radon pre-mitigation since you're pouring a new floor. Ours does on any new/replaced floors. Radon finds its way through cracks and openings in the floor and walls. Pressurization (like stack effect) is a strong force, pulling the air through openings you cannot even see. So merely the presence of a concrete slab, gravel, insulation, and vapor barrier is not enough to stop radon. Passive radon mitigation is merely a pipe stuck through the slab, with the open end allowing the air filtering through the dirt or gravel underneath the slab to escape into the pipe and be exhausted above the roof. When you seal all areas that air can rise into the basement, like drains, slab edges, sump covers, except for this one pipe, the air escapes via convective rise on its own (lower subslab pressure vs higher indoor pressure), and sometimes can be adequate to lower radon levels. If not, then you add a mechanical fan to pull the air out. AARST CCAH-2020 standards recommend that new construction either have 4" gravel or a 4" perforated pipe loop running under the slab. In the same way you are lowering your risk by installing a sump pump, a surge protector, or pre-wiring low voltage for some unknown future electronic device, for radon you should install the 4" pipe loop when you have the chance. If you've seen installation of radon systems, you understand that "communication" (meaning the success of pulling the air through the gravel or dirt) is part-n-parcel of mitigating radon, and there are always issues with the gravel and dirt. Avoid that by putting in a pipe which allows air to move unhindered. This simple to install, cheap corrugated pipe would connect to a vertical 4" PVC pipe with a Tee. The 4" PVC can be a stub located where it could route up through the roof or out the side of house later, or you can install it vertically complete now. 100' of 4" perforated corrugated pipe runs about $50. Polyurethane sealant runs about $5 tube. This is cheap insurance to make it much easier later if you find out you have to. AARST also says to short-term test within 60 days after construction, but I'd wait 6mos to a year or so, if fine, then retest after a few years.

A primer coat will be splotchy looking because it's primer and not top coat. And it is a temporary kind of thing; primer is intended for a top coat sooner than later because it starts to break down rather quickly. Rather quickly being relative I suppose. It depends on the product how quickly it starts to break down but I wouldn't let it go more than 4 to 6 weeks max. Kilz is yet another topic. If it's a water based product from Kilz it will do nothing to block residual wallpaper adhesive. All it does is reactivate it. When you paint over this newly created brew of water based primer and adhesive with water based paint, it will reactivate the adhesive again but this time when it dries it will crackle the paint film. That's how you get alligatoring. The best product to use over wallpaper adhesive to block and make sure it doesn't reactivate under your new top coats is GARDZ. Stinky and runny but 1000% worth the effort because it works. GARDZ is also the best product to use to prep walls for installing wallpaper. Because it provides amazing slip to position the wallpaper and when it's time to strip the paper, it will peel off easily. https://www.rustoleum.com/product-catalog/consumer-brands/zinsser-products/specialty-water-base-primers/gardz-problem-surface-sealer

Disconnect the power cord from the wall receptacle for 1 minute, or longer to be sure the machine's control circuitry is completely drained of residual power. Reconnect the power cord. Open/close the lid 6 times within 12 seconds.  Open the lid far enough each time to disengage the lid switch, then close it fully to re-engage the lid switch. Smoky Fire Crackers 2 Seven ounce bags oyster crackers 1 cup butter, melted 3 tbls brown sugar 1 tbls garlic powder 1 tbls smoked paprika 1 tsp crushed red pepper flakes 1 tsp dried oregano 1/2 tsp salt (which I omit because I always use salted butter) 1/2 tsp freshly cracked black pepper Preheat the oven to 300F. Place the crackers  into a big roaster or dutch oven, etc.  Something big enough to hold them and still stir.  Melt the butter, stir the rest of the ingredients.  Pour over the crackers, stir well.  Place into the oven and bake 15 minutes, stir, bake 15 more, stir, bake 15 more.  They will still seem soft when you take them out of the oven, but they will crisp as they cool. To answer your question, no, the offset recommendation is not due to weight concern.  The primary concern is lippage which occurs more frequently with large format tile (where one edge is greater than 15").  Minimal lippage is more frequent in larger tiles due to the manufacturing process.  To avoid excessive lippage upon installation, a qualified tile installer will not only recommend the appropriate layout, consistent with industry standards and manufacturer recommendations, but use proper methods and tools (appropriate notch trowel size, mortar coverage, substrate prep, grout joint size, etc.) as well as consider the effects of lighting.  Industry standards recommend any off-set pattern for large format tile to not exceed 33%.  In other words,  50% offset is not recommended.   Your choice of a stacked pattern would not be in conflict with the recommendation (it is not an "offset pattern").    Recommend you have this conversation with your professional installer as there are various considerations for a quality result.

text: My advice is: 1. Do your pruning first. My pruning start is a couple weeks off still.  The daffodils and forsytha are not yet in bloom here in Pittsburgh. 2. Next, put down your systemic insecticide for midge fly right after pruning.  It needs a couple weeks to kick into action. The Bayer 12 month soil drench is the go to product.  I plan to put down the Bonide Annual Tree & Shrub (1.47% Imidacloprid).  It's a bit cheaper. 3. I will still spray for black spot and powdery mildew, every two weeks after the new shoots are 3-4" long.  Since I am slowly working on transitioning to mostly BS and PM resistant/free/minimally affected rose bushes, I will not have to spray every bush. Controlling the fungi by soil (drench or dry broadcasting or granules), is a several times a season procedure, which means having to "jiggle-around," the mulch at every treatment, and that's not practical in my 18' x 8', one and only rose bed....too much probable bush damage, so I opt out of this method. 4. Now put down your manure, fertilizer, and any other soil amendments.  You can scratch it in a bit.  I use aged pigeon manure from my loft.  I have found no difference in the roses' growth response from the pigeon manure whether it is just laid on the soil surface or scratched in/dug in a bit. 5. Now place your mulch.   Pine bark is my favorite mulch.  It decomposes slowly, looks beautiful, and only needs topped off every year.  I like the nuggets (bigger pieces...2"- 4"), best.  The finer pine bark mulch is still v. good, but it doesn't let air get to the soil surface as easily as the bigger pieces of mulch do.  The nugget size mulch makes it easier to get the 6 week systemic fungus/insect applied granules to the soil surface. Just scatter it and water in.  It will wash down to the soil surface. Now get to work! 😁 Moses

One option is to move the oven all the way to the left. Then place your cleanup sink in the center of the counter. This takes it away from directly under the window. A sink under a window is an anachronism from the time when families hand washed dinner dishes and needed a view to pass the time. You'd also lose an upper. But you could have wide 3 drawer lowers on that and other runs. A 24" undermount sink with a 21" interior width will fit in a 24" sink base. Lots of actual usable space.

You might consider just doing a range with a double oven. The top oven is just below counter height and super easy to use - likely the oven you'd use most. Then the bottom oven can be used less often for larger things (turkeys, roasts, etc.). Personally I'm not a fan of my wall ovens and wish I had a range. If you insist on a wall oven, I might consider switching the fridge and oven locations, and putting a counter depth fridge where the red box is (with appropriate fillers). Right now your fridge door opens into a wall (won't be able to fully open). And 3'-6" between cabs is already tight - standing in front of an open fridge will just make this tighter (you'll be closer to 3, maybe less, when considering the fridge depth). Better to have the oven there than the fridge IMO. Fridges need more room than ovens do, and that way no one will come into the cooking zone to grab something from the fridge.

Just to update this thread for other folks, Larson no longer offers the SCS, they have normal, double strength or tempered glass options only.  So if one wants laminated glass, MonRay is the only option.  I did view MonRay, QuantaPanel and ProVia IRL and there is a huge difference. The main plus of ProVia is they have a very good lifetime warranty, however it is not sealed nearly to the degree of Quanta and MonRay.  The folks at Provia were adamant they've never done any STC test and never would.  If you have an old house and really do *need* storms, I think your only options are Quanta and MonRay.  When comparing the most noise-abatement efficient / historic home appropriate product of both (500 series / 504),  the main difference is MonRay is flat (with a slight bump if you get 1/4" glass) and Quanta has a bump out.  Quanta's aluminum has stripes on it and MonRay's is flat.  MonRay has these stainless steel do-dads (look like a volume control knob) that can be used to open a double hung whereas Quanta has normal finger latches.   Both have an interlocking seal between the two panels of the doublehung. Both have 'marine grade'  glazing, both feel like they are made of a very hard metal (MonRay talks a lot about this).  Quanta was much easier to get in contact with, to get info from and allows for homeowners to order themselves. Quanta is more affordable. They use different types of painting processes, MonRay will do a custom color for about 3k Quanta will do one for 6k.  Otherways MonRay has a very limited selection of standard colors, Quanta has about 100 standard colors. Personally, I liked the feel of the Quanta more, and I enjoyed speaking to the folks at the shop they were extremely helpful.  I wish they offered laminated glass. I also contacted Velv-a-lume storm windows (owned by West Windows) which no one has discussed on here but are targeted for a historic home, and they don't offer laminated glass.

Where you live is an essential piece of information if you're looking for advice tailored to your specific situation. I'll assume you're living in the Northern Hemisphere and not within 20* (latitude) from the equator. Here are the steps I wold take to improve your plant's level of vitality and what I would do to cut it back to something you can build on in terms of the plant's shape: Step 1) Flush the soil thoroughly by slowly pouring through the soil a volume of water equal to at least 10X the volume of the pot the plant is in. This will reset the fertility level of the soil solution as close to 0 as possible. 2) Immediately after flushing the soil, fertilize with a production strength solution of Foliage-Pro 9-3-6 fertilizer. This fertilizer will serve you well as a complete nutritional supplementation program as a single source; and it provides several other notable advantages as well.  3) Get in the habit of flushing the soil each time you water and checking the moisture level of the soil deep in the pot through use of a 'tell', which will allow you to determine what the appropriate intervals between waterings are. This is important as over or under-watering can be very limiting. See below for more about making/using a 'tell'. 4) Move the plant outdoors as soon as night temps are reliably above 55*; or; move the tree in and out to take advantage of the added light and temps above 55* and protecting it from colder temperatures. The added light and air movement will cause the plant to respond with more growth and and improve its o/a level of vitality. In turn, the boost in it's metabolic rate will a) increase the enthusiasm with which the plant responds to the pruning I'm about to describe, and b) decrease the amount of time it takes to recover from the pruning (and the repot if it needs one) 5)  Assuming again you live in the Northern Hemisphere, I would plan on pruning the plant around Father's Day or the Summer Solstice (21 June). The pruning would go like this a) prune all primary and secondary branches back to 2 leaves, so every branch will have 2 leaves left on it.  This ficus cutting ^^^ has been cut back to 2 leaves. Notice the new BRANCHES that are forming in the leaf axil (crotch). If your tree is healthy and growing well when you cut it back, the same thing should happen to your tree. During the remainder of the summer, when the 3rd leaf on any branch Is starting to open, prune that branch back to 2 leaves. When you follow this habit of pinching, it rapidly increases the fullness and ramification (branch and leaf density) of the tree. Follow the pinching schedule to about mid-Sep, then stip pinching and just allow the tree to grow all winter. Next June, you'll be able to identify the winter growth because internodes (distance between the leaves) will be very long. All winter growth should be cut back (every June) to the previous summer's growth. This ensures that only the tightest growth and shortest internodes remain as part of the composition. 6) When it's time to do the pruning (June), lift the plant from the pot. If the root/soil mass comes out intact (doesn't fall apart), the plant will benefit from repotting, which consists of bare-rooting, root pruning, and a change of existing soil to fresh soil; and, hopefully it will be a medium that allows you to flush the soil at will w/o you needing top worry the soil will re,main saturated for a n interval long enough that it conspicuously limits root function, or worse, wreaks havoc of root health. What you choose as a grow medium has much influence over what kind of opportunity you'll be able to offer your plants to realize as much of their genetic potential as possible. An inappropriate grow medium can rob your plant of more than 90% of its potential in terms of growth rate, vitality level, eye appeal, and yields where applicable, so it's worth getting right. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. ..... questions or concerns? Al

Either the attic is inside the building envelope or it isn’t. In old homes typically the attic is well vented so is essentially the outside temperature so condensation is minimized. This is helped by super insulating the ceiling of the top floor so heat from the living spaces doesn’t migrate into the attic. Alternatively the attic is conditioned- lately this is done by sealing all external penetrations and spray foaming the underside of the roof deck as well as any attic gable walls. Both techniques are fine but you can’t mix them.

  • The appliances are 30" deep but kitchen cabinets* are only 24" deep and 35" high so you'd have to mount such cabinets away from the wall and on legs or a plinth. Or buy deeper and taller cabinets.
  • The countertop would have to stretch over two 27" wide appliances. Support may be needed between the appliances.
  • You'd have to make cutouts on the back of the countertop for the pipes and cables.
  • It would be harder to service or replace the appliances unless the countertop were removable.
  • You could mount a drop-in or undermount sink in a kitchen cabinet frame but the sink wouldn't be as large as the one you have now.
  • Of course you could mount shelves and drawers in the cabinets.

Per plant growth with LowE coatings, look at page 29 of the Cardinal glass guide for more information. https://www.cardinalcorp.com/source/pdf/TGG_V3.0_Final_11-20-2020.pdf For reference, the SmartSun option that you are considering is Cardinal's LoE³-366, a triple-silver layer coating. Sun coating is LoE²-272, a dual-silver layer which is also listed on the chart. Adding Heatlock will lower visible light transmittance by a percent or two compared on what's on the chart. Even in a heating dominated climate like Ontario blocking solar heat from west-facing windows is generally good advice; what you might lose in winter is more than offset by what you don't gain the rest of the year, so using SmartSun on west facing windows is not a bad idea. However, like WoW said, I would be more inclined to use LoE coatings that allow more solar heat gain in your other windows if for no other reason that it feels good on cold winter days but also because it can be a nice supplement to the heat provided by your furnace. Heat-lock is a surface 4 (inside glass surface that you can touch) coating that improves the U-factor value of your windows by reflecting interior heat back into the room; heat that would have escaped to the outdoors otherwise. The upside of the surface 4 coating, besides the improvement in U-factor, is that because it reflects the heat back into the room, it can feel noticeably warmer when sitting in front of the window on a cold day. The downside is that because it reflects heat before the glass can absorb it, the glass is colder making it more prone to winter condensation if the outside it cold and the inside has a high enough level of moisture in the air. This doesn't mean that condensation is inevitable, the glass is still warmer than a dual pane without a LowE coating for example, but it does mean that you will have to pay more attention to managing your indoor humidity levels when it's really cold.

I too have long liked a number of the Monkees' songs but they have to be taken with open eyes for what they were, it was a show of actors chosen to portray musicians, not a band or musicians cast for a TV show. And most songs were written by top composers of the day. I'm A Believer, as an example, was written by Neil Diamond. I saw Nesmith live in concert a few times (including a show just a few years ago) and a unique part of his shows was his habit of offering a preface to songs he'd written to explain either what he had in mind in writing the song, or a fictional scene he imagined having taken place that the song was intended to describe. Two examples, not dissimilar sentiments, as I remember what he said. Different Drum, the song that brought Linda Ronstadt to the public's attention, was described by him as a scene of a man and woman at a table in a Paris cafe. The couple had known each other for a while but the male had concluded that the relationship wasn't working and it needed to end. The lyrics tell of how he tried to gently share his feelings and the reasons for them, to explain why he believed they'd each be better off if apart. Joanne represented the pleasant memory of a brief relationship with a young woman that had long since ended. Why things didn't work out and the settings in the countryside where they spent time together. These were two very exceptional songs in my view and it's puzzling that the rest of his composing output didn't include many more such outstanding songs. For interested fans, he wrote an autobiography a few years ago. HELP! MY SHOWER IS LEAKING! Many times, a leaking tiled shower can be the result of an unqualified person performing the work. A leaking shower can damage other areas of the bathroom or even the room below the shower. There are multiple reasons why this could happen. Your first line of defense should be to have your plumber check for leaks in the: · shower control valve and/or pipe to the shower head · water supply lines · drain and trap Your second line of defense should be to have your shower door installer check for leaks in: · the door track mounted on the curb (if present) · the vinyl sweep on the bottom of the door · between the vertical metal frame and the tiled wall · between the door and the metal frame attached to the tiled wall What evidence do you see of a leaking shower? 1. The ceiling in the room below my shower has water stains and/or water is dripping from the ceiling Potential Causes · Hole or leak in the pan liner under the tile · Clogged weep holes in the drain assembly · No or incorrectly applied waterproofing on the curb, walls, niches, and seats · Post-tile installation: installed grab bars, soap dishes, or other screw-attached items – not properly sealed 2. The floor tile just outside my shower is wet, damp, and/or discolored Potential Causes · Shower curb is not sloped properly toward the drain and water is running onto outside floor · Shower pan membrane/liner not properly installed over the entire curb and continuing to the floor outside the shower · Pan liner pierced during shower door installation 3. The tile on the inside of my shower walls, floor or curb is loose, the grout is cracking or there is a mineral deposit build up at grout/caulk lines Potential Causes · Blocked weep holes at drain · Breach or incorrect installation of shower pan membrane/liner · Improper or lack of waterproofing at wall to curb and/or other changes in plane · Improper materials used under the tile · Lack of proper ventilation (ceiling fan) 4. The tile on the curb is cracked and/or loose and/or the walls next to the curb are deteriorating. Potential Causes · The curb was not properly constructed and/or waterproofed · Backer board was nailed or screwed through the shower pan liner and into the curb. No waterproofing was applied · The curb does not have the proper slope toward the drain · The shower door was improperly installed (door installer error) o Holes drilled into the curb or the floor on a barrier free shower o Holes drilled into the wall and not properly sealed 5. The walls outside my shower are damp and spongy, drywall is bubbling, or damaged. There is evidence of moisture damage and mold/mildew on the wall(s) on the other side of the shower. Potential Causes · The shower pan liner was not correctly installed · The shower drain was not properly installed · The shower drain weep holes are clogged · Improper or lack of waterproofing on walls up to the shower head · Fasteners were placed through the tiled surface and not sealed 6. My shower has a terrible odor Potential Causes · Incorrect drain installed · The floor under the shower pan liner was not properly sloped toward the drain · The shower drain weep holes are clogged · The lower part of the drain body (below the tile surface) was incorrectly installed higher than the surrounding floor and will not drain · Stagnant water and organic shower products (soap, shampoo, body wash, and body oil are trapped below the tile allowing mold to grow Unless otherwise indicated (such as plumber or glass installer), it is important that you seek the help of an industry QUALIFIED tile professional who uses tile industry standards and approved best practices for shower installations and strictly follows the material manufacturer’s specifications and instructions. It’s helpful to understand this about showers: A properly constructed shower manages and directs all the water that flows through it to the drain, and nowhere else. The shower “fixture” needs to be water tight, utilizing one of the two basic types of showers: a "Water In, Water Out" shower system, which is constructed with a clamping ring drain and waterproof shower pan liner or a "Sealed System" which employs a bonding flange drain and a waterproofing membrane that extends to the shower head.  Both systems require that the walls, seats, ledges, niches, and curbs be treated with the appropriate waterproofing product.  If the waterproofing, drain components, or any part of the shower system is not installed properly, is damaged, punctured, or compromised during installation, a leak can and will result in failure. PLEASE NOTE: Beware of the claims that a leaking shower can be eliminated by using grout or caulking repairs/replacement or the application of a sealer or coating. These actions will, at best, provide only a temporary fix. Beware of individuals and companies who are NOT insured, licensed where required, or certified by the tile industry.  Wisely consider, interview, and hire dedicated tile professionals who have received proper training and have experience in the process of providing a long-lasting and trouble-free shower installation. A qualified tile professional will perform work in accordance with the Tile Council of North America (TCNA) HandbookMethods, American National Standards Institute (ANSI) Standards, and the manufacturer’s written instructions.
