But how do you know your contractor is qualified? We have surveyed homeowners, designers, contractors and other construction industry experts to compile a list of questions every homeowner should ask an installer before starting a project. To help ensure the tile contractor you hire is the right fit, start with these 13 questions: 1.  Are you licensed in your area? Verify. Some states do not require tile contractors to be licensed 2. How many years have you/your team been working exclusively as tile installers? It takes many years to become proficient as a dedicated, qualified tile professional. Five years or more would be an expected minimum. 3. How were you trained? Do you participate in on-going professional training from organizations and/or manufacturers, and specifically what? Tile installers who have completed an apprenticeship under a Qualified Tile Installer/Organization and participate in industry training are generally more likely to follow standards and industry recommendations and stay current with products, materials, and industry updates. 4. Tell me about your favorite tile installation project and why. What project(s) were challenging for you and what did you do to overcome those challenges? Get to know the tile professional as part of your project team. Do they take pride in their work? If you have a General Contractor (GC) or Designer who is hiring the tile installer, it may make sense to request meeting with the GC/Designer and tile installer in advance of the installation to plan and answer your questions. 5. Do you have a company website or social media pages with photos of your work? Professionals will have a public presence that is available to consumers so you can review their work and customer reviews. Lack of a traceable, legitimate, and experienced business should be a deterrent to hiring. 6. Can I speak with recent customers and view photos of those projects? Qualified, experienced tile contractors will have a history of satisfied clients that are happy to recommend them and share their experience.There are professional standards for 7. Are YOU FAMILIAR WITH THE TCNA HANDBOOK and ANSI STANDARDS? DOES YOUR WORK FOLLOW THESE INDUSTRY RECOMMENDATIONS? The TCNA Handbook coupled with the ANSI Standards are the industry recognized guidelines for the installation of tile for a wide range of applications. A qualified tile professional installer will be familiar with and know how to specify and use these reference tools. 8. Do you have successful experience working with the type of tile I plan to use? There are different methods, materials and considerations when planning and installing various tile products such as ceramic, porcelain, large format tile, handmade tile, mosaics, natural stone or glass. Verify their experience and training with the tile product you have chosen for your project. 9. What manufacturer’s products do you use and do you comply with manufacturer instructions? There are many manufacturers of quality tile setting materials. Most perform well with use of approved methods and adherence to manufacturer specifications. Most qualified tile installers will be well versed on the methods and systems they prefer and should be able to answer your questions about their process and materials and associated warranties. 10. If wet areas (showers/baths) are to be included in the work performed, what approved system/methods will you use to assure a long-lasting installation? Tile installations in wet areas require some very important preparation to avoid leaks and unwanted moisture problems. Unapproved methods, and the use of materials inappropriate for this application can contribute to a very costly and unwanted result that too often requires complete removal and replacement by a qualified professional. A quality installation should last decades or longer. 11. Do you have liability insurance, and if you have employees, are they covered with Worker’s Compensation Insurance? Make sure you can verify appropriate insurance coverage. 12. Do you belong to professional organizations like NTCA (National Tile Contractor’s Association)? Industry involvement is one indication of a tile installation company’s commitment to their craft. It gives them access to education, technical information, and other resources to assist them in professionally serving you. 13.  Are you a Certified Tile Installer (Certified Tile Education Foundation, CTI) or do you have Certified Tile Installers on your team? The certification of tile installers is an important step forward for the consumer and is “one” indication of professionalism. The industry has established a process to certify tile installers. Certification identifies an installer as being a dedicated and knowledgeable professional whose competence in installing tile has been verified to meet specific tile industry standards.

I'm not recommending this, but offering a suggestion on how to reduce size of materials. I learned this when I was doing a lot of drapery work. Here goes...if you need to reduce the size of something, don't take the total reduction off one end or one side. Split the required amount in half and reduce two sides or top and bottom. Doing it that way,  it's not as visually obvious that you have made a reduction. So in your case, you need a 3" reduction. Take 1.5 inches off the top and 1.5 inches off the bottom. This only works if you aren't damaging the structural integrity of the thing you are cutting. If there is black/brown mold at your undermounted sink, it's because your sink is leaking. Not drip-type leaking, but capillary action type leaking. The tiny gap between the sink flange and the stone bottom is sucking in dirty sink water. You cannot topically caulk your way out of this. The sink must be dropped, the flange and stone bottom cleaned and resiliconed, the clips abandoned, and the sink strapped in place. That fix is permanent. Black/brown crud is no reason to get a top mount sink.

Why don't you try an LED bulb in the 3000K to 4000K range and with more lumens than the bulb you are currently using and see what happens? (A standard 60 watt incandescent bulb produces 800 lumens, a 100 watt produces 1600 lumens.) Because even though that is a hallway and not a kitchen, the glass cover of the fixture may obscure some of the light from the bulb making the hallway seem very dark. Light color or appearance is measured on the Kelvin (K) temperature scale, and it's the difference in soft white versus daylight bulbs. Lower Kelvin numbers mean more yellow light; the higher the Kelvin number, the whiter or bluer the light.

Sit on the chair with your feet on the floor and your back very straight. Have your helper measure the distance between your back and the back of the chair in the middle of the back of the chair. That distance is what you need to overcome. Since you are not going to grow any taller, pillows will have to suffice. Lumbar pillows will not do the trick, since they will only take up the distance at your lower back (lumbar section) and the rest of your back will have no support whatsoever and you will be in pain rather soon. So the other distance you need to measure is the distance from the seat of the chair to almost your shoulders. Your helper can do this too. The odds are, no pillow you buy will be firm enough to support you, at least not for very long. Especially if you have a bad back. What you want to do is go to a place that sells foam and get a piece of foam that is high density, extra firm. You have to see what the store sells. If they sell 6 inch thick foam and that's what you need, marvelous. It's expensive, but it makes more sense than getting 2inch foam and making up three pillows. Depending on the thickness they sell, you need to figure out how many pillows you need to make up the distance between the back of the chair and your back, and then you have them cut the foam to the height you measured from the seat of the chair to just below your shoulder and horizontally a good width would be from one elbow to to other while you are seated and your arms are bent, around 26." Then get some batting for around the foam, then a muslin cover. Then a fabric cover that zips off and is machine washable, dryable and permanent press. And make a few extra covers, because there is a monster in some washing machines. But do yourself a favor, go to a seamstress or upholsterer and let them do it, unless you know how to sew. if you are getting machine washable fabric, wash it first and put it in the dryer to allow it to shrink as much as it needs to before it is sewn.

There are so many decisions that should be made carefully to determine what are the appropriate and inappropriate improvements to make. Your home should bring you joy, but that must be tempered against the other things in life that bring you joy, and your joy bucket only gets what is left over after necessities and responsibilities. How long you will be in the home is probably the first question you should ask yourself.   The length of time that you will enjoy the upgrades makes a difference in how much you should spend. Determine how your home compares to the other homes in your neighborhood.  If you over improve you get a far lower ROI than if you stay within the norms for a neighborhood. How much of your home improvement budget needs to be set aside for the not fun maintenance that will need to be done during your tenure in the home.  (HVAC/Roof, electrical, plumbing . . .) How well does the home function?   What items are causing angst vs neutral response vs bringing joy. Once you figure out how much you should spend then you can decide where to spend the money. You will need to know how much of what you spend you will get back when you sell and how much will be gifted to the next owner.  (ROI - return on investment) https://www.remodeling.hw.net/cost-vs-value/2021/ Planning well can keep you from making costly mistakes and having to redo work along the way. Often renovating one room leads to having to renovate another room because the two don't work together, then another and another and people go way over their anticipated budget trying to make everything work together when good planning could have prevented the problem. Knowing what style works for your lifestyle and is aesthetically pleasing to you and developing a whole home color palette is part of that planning.    Knowing generally what you will update over the next 5 years and keeping those changes in mind while you renovate the other parts of the home will leave you with a cohesive, harmonious end result.  Doing one room at a time often ends with disjointed rooms that don't speak to each other.

Youre NOT understsnding cabinet installation at all. If the *floor* is the sloping issue, that doesn’t ever  show up on the *ceiling*. Base cabinets tops must be shimmed level to a 34 1/2” line above the high spot on the floor. Wall cabinets are hung at a bottom alignment line at 54” above the high spot in the floor. None of that out if level floor gets transferred to the ceiling. It’s only if the *ceiling* is out of level do you need a scribed horizontal filler there, and then you have to the math for that, based on the ceiling slope.

The entire house is the sloping issue. The 91-3/4” from floor to ceiling is consistent. But since I have to shim up the cabinets at the low spot 3/4” so that it sits level with the high spot, then that puts that area at 35-1/4” from the floor. Add 1-1/2” for countertop, 18” of space, and then 36” for the upper and you’re at 90-3/4” or 1” from the ceiling.

@Jackie Kemper, It should be obvious, but "water saving" is a standard that never applies to a tub fixture. If it takes 50 gallons to fill a tub, for example, slowing down the water flow doesn't save water... it still takes 50 gallons.  There are no "government restrictions" on the flow rates applied to tubs. So when they say that, they are either very ignorant or they are covering for their mistake. Plumbing fixture manufacturers are also very aware of tub fill speeds. Nobody designed a TUB valve that would take 19 minutes to fill a standard tub. Again, assuming that it's 50 gal to fill your tub to "normal" bath volume, that's about 2.6 gallons a minute (gpm). That's approximately the flow rate for a typical water saving shower (2.5 gpm). Standard flow rates for a tub valve (not a big soaker tub) are 4.5 - 6 gpm. You need to get a lot more precise about this. Get a 5 gallon pail from the hardware store (you may even have to measure 1  gallon of water at a time and mark that level on the pail). Then fill it from your tub spout and time it for 1 minute. You should be able to fill the 5 gallon pail in just about 1 minute. Be sure to use about the same mix of hot and cold water that you would use to fill the tub in case it's a problem with the hot or cold water. Assuming that your test shows something significantly less than 5 gpm, there are a few possible reasons: 1. Debris from the inside of the plumbing clogging up the valve (this is common on new work or repairs) 2. Wrong valve 3. A pressure / flow problem in the house (not applicable here since the previous tub did not have the same issue) Here's the thing: It's not your problem to figure out, or to fix, or to put up with. They should rule out #1 by turning off the water, removing the insides of the valves and flushing them out.  I've seen crud stuck in valve bodies that I've had to break up to flush out. I've had to cut the pipes in the basement and use compressed air to blow things out backwards. I've even had to replace a brand new sink faucet that I couldn't get cleared out. If the issue is #2 above then it's going to get very expensive for them to fix. The will have to replace the valve and re-do all the tile work unless they can do it from the back. Stick to your guns. It's not fixed until you are getting very close to 5 gpm and you really will have to measure that with a 5 gallon bucket and a timer.

I get emails all the time asking the same thing, you're definitely not the only who has noticed. The discrepancy is because those are subjective opinions. Based on nothing more than what some person thinks a color looks like to them under some random light source in some random context. And, frankly, in many cases I think some people are making that stuff up as they go based on what they see online; never as much as looked at an actual color chip. There is one way and one way only to define and describe color appearance and that way is to measure color using a standard that strives to quantify how the human eye - a real person with normal color vision - sees color. That data is where numeric color definitions and descriptions come from. This is the exact same color standard of measuring color that the paint companies use to make paint colors in the first place. All over the place, conflicting color reviews is why I created The Color DNA Table of factual hue, value, chroma and LRV color notations. May be a shameless plug right there but it's true. Crazy pants color reviews and descriptions are a major pain point - for everyone - and I decided to do something about it. This is what you need to know about Silver Satin. Because of the factual notation, we know it's a low Chroma color from the middle of the yellow hue family and so we know it could actually show up with moments of greenishness. If there's a fair amount of light, it will actually show up as a subtle greige - more color and warmth than a flat gray. We also know that low Chroma colors in this hue family region can shift and look purple. So, all three can be true: greenish, purplish, or more neutral with no discernible hue bias. Without an orderly factual hue/value/chroma notation to start with, there's no way track how paint colors actually show up under different light sources, in different contexts. Indoors, we can never achieve photo load offered by full sun outdoors. The primary reasons are A) some of the light energy is turned to heat as light is partially absorbed by the glass. Even a single lite of single strength window glass can reduce the amount of light that passes through the window by 20% or more. Insulating glass windows, tinted windows, and windows with pyrolytic coatings designed to reflect each work individually or collectively to reduce available light, and B) winter sun is less 'intense' because as the earth tilts on its axis, light has to travel a much greater distance through the atmosphere before it reaches the earth's surface. Every dust particle and droplet of moisture cause reflection and refraction which cause light to be reflected or change direction such that a significant amount refracted and reflected photons once on a direct course toward earth never reach the earth's surface. BTW - The angle at which the sunlight strikes a surface has a big influence on how much light  energy is reflected. When the sun is lowest in the sky (winter equinox - 21 Dec), it is much closer to being perpendicular to the a vertical surface of your window (0* angle of incidence) which ensures the best opportunity for light transmission. so the trouble with winter sun isn't how low it is in the sky, it's how far it has to travel through the atmosphere, as noted in B above. What determines whether or not it does need repotting is how congested the roots are, and there is nothing in the info you supplied to cause anyone to conclude the roots are congested. The best way to tell is by lifting the plant from its pot. If the root/soil mass remains completely intact, it needs repotting; however, that doesn't mean it's essential or a good idea to do it when recovery will be lengthened considerably due to limitations on the plant's metabolic processes due to it being winter - low light, dry air, often cool temps. There is a difference between repotting and potting up. Repotting includes bare-rooting, root pruning or dividing, and a change of the grow medium. for you, the best time to repot would be around the summer solstice (21 Jun) - or Father's Day. If you feel like you really need to 'do something', even if it only makes you feel better, it makes more sense to pot up to a slightly larger pot and plan and plan ahead for the Jun repot. Using a digital device (a finger) as the tool that decides whether or not it's appropriate to water works reasonably well if your pot isn't too deep, maybe 5" or less. IF the pot is deeper than that, say 10", the top 2" could feel completely dry even while the bottom 6" of the soil column is still 100% saturated; so, unless your pot is quite small, the advice to follow the 2" finger test is pretty much a recipe for over-watering. I'd suggest you save cutting any roots for the Jun repot. Our plants' level of vitality varies significantly over the course of an annual growth cycle. Serious work like repotting and any heavy pruning or roots OR shoots should be timed so the plant has a high level of energy reserves and its ability to make food (during photosynthesis the plant makes its own food - sugar/glucose) is about to peak. That occurs around the summer solstice/Father's Day. This occurs when A) there is not enough Ca in the medium and available for uptake, or B) a cultural influence is limiting the plant's ability to take up Ca, even though it might be represented in the grow medium at adequate/appropriate levels. B is a VERY common issue, and can occur whenever there is too much water in the grow medium, the medium is badly compacted, or when there is inadequate light, humidity is high, or temps are cool. The primary driver of a culturally induced Ca deficiency is over-watering. My suggestions: * When the plant next needs water, flush the soil thoroughly. First, water with room temperature water until the soil is completely saturated. Allow the planting to rest for 15 minutes to an hour to allow as much of any salt that has accumulated in the soil to go into solution. Then pour a volume of room temp water equal to at least 10X the volume of the pot the plant is in slowly through the soil. This will remove most of any accumulation of offending salts and resolve any skewing of nutrient ratios. Residual salts in the medium from tapwater and fertilizer solutions can limit water and nutrient uptake. Also, lift the pot so it sits above any effluent that collects in the collection saucer. This eliminates the current pathway by which the effluent can make its way back into the soil.  * After flushing the soil, fertilize immediately. I highly recommend using Foliage-Pro 9-3-6 as your 'go to' produce for nutritional supplementation. Thereafter, make sure you're watering to beyond the point of saturation, so you're flushing the soil as you water. The entire soil column should be saturated and at least 20% of the water you apply should exit the drain hole. Fertilize about every 4th or 5th time you water. I use FP 9-3-6 for virtually everything I grow and the reasons are numerous. Ask, if you want a rundown. * Start using a 'tell' to 'tell' you when it's time to water. See below, 'Using a Tell'. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. I never did it full-time, and that may be because it's easier for most people to go to a business -type area rather than a home in the suburbs. It's just easier to stop at the seamstress's business if it's near the post office, or the grocery store, or other businesses. Getting people to drive out to someone's house may be a deal breaker if there's more convenient options on the way home. Most of my clients were friends and acquaintances, and they referred other customers to me. Occasionally there were people I didn't know - none gave me the heebie-jeebies. The only potential customer who did creep me out contacted me by email. I actually wondered if someone was trying to set me up: The writer wanted loose, floor length nightgowns out of 100% linen, with real fabric ties at the neck, waist, and wrists. All things deemed safety hazards for children's clothes, which was why he or she couldn't find what he wanted in the stores. The obsession with little girls' nightwear was weird and off-putting. Of course you have a neat area set aside for customers; if possible, one where you don't have to lead them through your entire house to get to. Another woman I met doing that sort of work actually set up a small outbuilding (These days, it'd be called a she-shed) and saw her customers and did her work there. It also made it easy to justify her expenses for tax purposes- the square footage was separate from her living area- and it's been a while but she may have had a separate electrical service for the shed. I would say be ruthless in tracking your expenses - shipping for supplies can eat up profit and actual trips to the store not only costs money for your supplies but also the wear and tear on your vehicle, and your time.  Know your worth - don't be surprised if you run into people who expect your to work for minimum wage. Know how long it takes for you to do common tasks, and charge a wage worthy of professional work. It's tempting to "start out low and raise your prices later" but it's a failing tactic. The people who patronize you for your low prices will dump you when you raise them - and they won't sing your praises, they'll just say you were 'okay until she started overcharging.' Working for eight or ten dollars an hour won't be profitable, and will teach your customers that "women's work" isn't worth a living wage. People who insist on doing that make it that much harder for professionals to earn a living. I would advise in particular for special occasion dresses: ask customers to bring the bra, undergarments, slip  and shoes they will wear with the dress. Take bust, waist, and hip measurements at the first fitting, and measure the heels of the shoes as well. Write them on your sales or alteration form. You won't have to re-alter often, but you don't want someone to have a breast augmentation and complain you took it in too much, or not mention that she's pregnant.  BTW, if she was wearing four-inch heels and is now going barefoot, don't assume you can hem the dress four inches shorter; it doesn't work like that. And yes, all these things have happened. And yes, I have charged for a re-alter under those circumstances. When someone says "Just shorten this to 29" inseam" I write PCR (per customer request) on the form. It's also okay to say, "I need to see this on you." I used to hate saying no, but better that than going against my better judgement and disappointing someone. If it seems like a bad idea to me, I won't do it. I now have no problem referring a customer to somebody else.  Need a shirt made out of a scarf? custom silk pants? Need a knee length swing coat made into a hip length fitted jacket? "No, I don't have the pattern-making skills. Here's the numbers for Ruby, Yolanda, and Adele. They'd love a project like that."

Thanks for your question Carol. This is a good-sized challenge. My suggestion is to create a product that falls somewhere between an opaque paint and a perfectly transparent stain. Start with some scrap wood that is similar in color to your ceiling. (Or, plan to sand your new coating off of any area of the ceiling that you coat but don’t like.) It’s likely impossible to altogether hide the red and orange tones without hiding most of the original grain pattern, however, I wouldn’t want to discourage you from trying. If you have access to General Finishes or to SamaN stains, I encourage you to experiment with some of their water-based stains. Scuff sand the surface of your ceiling and before you brush on the stain. (These products are unique in that they allow you to coat a surface that has already been stained/sealed.) Start with a color of your choice as well as some of their “natural” or untinted stain. Intermix the color and the uncolored stain until you come up with a sufficient level of translucency that will cover your objectionable tones without altogether obscuring the grain. Whether or not you obscure the grain, you might choose to add a second layer of stain that’s more translucent and slightly darker. When you brush this on, you’ll create the look of grain lines.   Let me know if you have questions.

Maidenhair ferns sold as houseplants tend to be almost exclusively selections of Adiantum raddianum. And one of the trickier houseplants to grow well indoors. Lack of humidify and any mistimed watering can do them in pretty rapidly. This is a tropical maidenhair (Central America, West Indies) so not very cold hardy. If you live in zone 9b and above, you can expect it to survive outdoors, even more likely if grown in a container and moved into protection if colder than normal weather is anticipated. How much 'hardening off' is required will depend on your location and current temps. And it's a fern for heaven's sake, so of course no direct sun!!

Hi, Amanda. Because of the sudden reduction in the amount of water your plant will actually need, maintaining appropriate moisture levels has just been moved to the forefront in terms of criticality. The easiest way and arguably the best way to monitor moisture levels deep in the pot, where it counts most is by using a wooden 'tell', which can be very easily made from a 1/4 or 5/16" wooden dowel rod. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Are you left with any additional questions or concerns? Al

text: Well, it is a little odd that you're only seeing this problem in some plants. That is, you'd think any deficiency would be common for everyone in the bed. There are many strategies for adding these nutrients Certainly just applying some broad spectrum fertilizer like MiracleGro can't hurt. But if you're serious about gardening, I'd recommend that you get a soil test done. Then you can work with facts. Now, I don't believe CA extension services do these tests, so you'll have to find another provider. Maybe someone from CA could weigh in here. FWIW, pure seaweed fertilizer has ZERO phosphorus. I'd look at the NPK rating on it, and see what it's got. Because of that, phosphorus is sometimes added to make it more complete. As to water, you don't want soggy soil, but Brassicas do like moist soil. Now, overwatering in a grow bag is kind of hard to do. They drain readily.

The white paint borders around the edges of the floors were lead paint too. We ended up refinishing them taking precautions for lead paint. We bought a HEPA vacuum and sanders that could attach to the vacuum to control the dust. We wore p100 masks throughout all the work, taped up all doorways, and tried to keep any dust from our feet as contained in the area as possible. We taped off all HVAC vents and shut the system off to keep it from getting in there (it was January in new England, this sucked lol). We initially wet mopped the floors and HEPA vacuumed to get as much off as possible. We used a belt sander a bit but most of it was done with a random orbital hand sander (this is because the floors are uneven and a drum sander would have torn through them. We also wanted to take as little off as possible). We took as much of the solid lead paint off as possible before sanding. Did multiple passes with different grits. We dug out between each groove in the floor and vacuumed the 150 years work of crap that came out up. Once floors were ready for stain we started cleanup. We wet mopped the floors again and HEPA vacuumed again. Cleaned other areas of the house to get rid of any dust we might have tracked through there. We used TSP (turns lead into lead phosphate. Carcinogenic but not immediately harmful) on all the walls, baseboards, doors, window trim, everything. Wiped off with water. Put a coat of stain down and then 3 coats of oil based poly. We chose oil based because it's more durable than water based. the entire point was to encapsulate the floors. There is likely no way we could have cleaned up every little speck of lead dust (and it could have even soaked into the wood itself) so encapsulating it was the only way to ensure it won't be harmful to us. Oil poly is much more durable than water based poly, so it is less likely that the finish will come up and expose us to anything that we might have missed in cleanup. Many people don't like to use poly on antique floors but with the lead element it was really the only way we could safely use them. We then cleaned other areas of the house again just in case we got some more in there. When everything was totally done we did have the ducts cleaned too just in case. We've done lead tests on the floors, in dusty corners, and near HVAC vents since, and all have come up negative. Our process does appear to have worked! It is a lot of extra time and effort to keep the lead contained and cleaned up, but thankfully it was worth it in the end. If you're doing it yourself, drink lots of milk too! Calcium can help prevent your body from absorbing the lead if you accidentally get some in you. If you have any questions, want to know what products we used, anything, please let me know! It was a crappy time trying to figure this all out so I'm very happy to help with anything you need. Edit: here's an imgur album with before, during, and after: https://imgur.com/a/iDpEngZ

Not all Kitchens can support an island.  My Kitchen is 11'0" deep and I tried for so long to shoehorn in an island, but in the end I accepted the inevitable -- any Kitchen narrower than around 12'6" is just too narrow to get a functional/useful island and still have enough room to be able to maneuver around the island and through the Kitchen. I ended up with a shallow "U" with two open peninsulas (one each leg of the "U") with seating for 2 on one peninsula and no seats on the other (it was on a busy aisle and I wanted  more space inside the "U").  There is also a row of cabinets opposite the base of "U". I absolutely LOVE my Kitchen and am so glad that the folks here patiently worked with me to help me realize a functional/useful island just wasn't possible with my Kitchen. That said, if you are OK with a very narrow island and narrow aisles, an island can be shoehorned into your Kitchen.  Personally, I do not recommend it, but it's your Kitchen. (1)  What's your family composition?  Children?  (If so, I feel even more strongly about not recommending an island since children are active and running around and it can be an issue with narrow aisles.) (2)  How high off the floor are your bay windows? (3)  How deep is the bay window well?  It looks like 18", but when "box counting", guessing partial boxes is guessing game.  (That's why we request ALL dimensions be clearly labeled, even when using graph paper and to-scale.  A scale of 1 box = 1' is even worse for estimation -- 1 box = 6" is much better.) (4)  Does the office have another door?  If not, could one be added on another wall? (5)  Do you have a separate Dining Room?  Or, is this your only table space?

FYI...here's my Kitchen, in case it helps you.  As I said, I love it!  I keep telling my DH that it's going with us when we move! The shallow "U" helps protect anyone prepping and/or cooking and/or baking from through-traffic (the Dining Room is on the left, the Family Room & Garage are on the right, and the Foyer is "below" the Kitchen)        (We also ended up having to build out the back wall 6" to hide some plumbing that couldn't be easily moved -- I now have a Kitchen 10'6" deep -- but that was discovered after we finalized the design and had no bearing on the layout decisions.)

It really is brand specific. Delta and Moen are high quality brands. They actually have fixtures that are quite expensive as cost depends on the style and the finish. Delta and Moen make upgraded styles and finishes and the price reflects that even though they might be less expensive than more upscale brands. 13 QUESTIONS TO FIND THE RIGHT TILE INSTALLER Qualified tile contractors have the verifiable experience and use proper methods and materials. But how do you know your contractor is qualified? We have surveyed homeowners, designers, contractors and other construction industry experts to compile a list of questions every homeowner should ask an installer before starting a project. To help ensure the tile contractor you hire is the right fit, start with these 13 questions: 1.  Are you licensed in your area? Verify. Some states do not require tile contractors to be licensed. 2. How many years have you/your team been working exclusively as tile installers? It takes many years to become proficient as a dedicated, qualified tile professional. Five years or more would be an expected minimum. 3. How were you trained? Do you participate in on-going professional training from organizations and/or manufacturers, and specifically what? Tile installers who have completed an apprenticeship under a Qualified Tile Installer/Organization and participate in industry training are generally more likely to follow standards and industry recommendations and stay current with products, materials, and industry updates. 4. Tell me about your favorite tile installation project and why. What project(s) were challenging for you and what did you do to overcome those challenges? Get to know the tile professional as part of your project team. Do they take pride in their work? If you have a General Contractor (GC) or Designer who is hiring the tile installer, it may make sense to request meeting with the GC/Designer and tile installer in advance of the installation to plan and answer your questions. 5. Do you have a company website or social media pages with photos of your work? Professionals will have a public presence that is available to consumers so you can review their work and customer reviews. Lack of a traceable, legitimate, and experienced business should be a deterrent to hiring. 6. Can I speak with recent customers and view photos of those projects? Qualified, experienced tile contractors will have a history of satisfied clients that are happy to recommend them and share their experience. 7. Are YOU FAMILIAR WITH THE TCNA HANDBOOK and ANSI STANDARDS? DOES YOUR WORK FOLLOW THESE INDUSTRY RECOMMENDATIONS? The TCNA Handbook coupled with the ANSI Standards are the industry recognized guidelines for the installation of tile for a wide range of applications. A qualified tile professional installer will be familiar with and know how to specify and use these reference tools. 8. Do you have successful experience working with the type of tile I plan to use? There are different methods, materials and considerations when planning and installing various tile products such as ceramic, porcelain, large format tile, handmade tile, mosaics, natural stone or glass. Verify their experience and training with the tile product you have chosen for your project. 9. What manufacturer’s products do you use and do you comply with manufacturer instructions? There are many manufacturers of quality tile setting materials. Most perform well with use of approved methods and adherence to manufacturer specifications. Most qualified tile installers will be well versed on the methods and systems they prefer and should be able to answer your questions about their process and materials and associated warranties. 10. If wet areas (showers/baths) are to be included in the work performed, what approved system/methods will you use to assure a long-lasting installation? Tile installations in wet areas require some very important preparation to avoid leaks and unwanted moisture problems. Unapproved methods, and the use of materials inappropriate for this application can contribute to a very costly and unwanted result that too often requires complete removal and replacement by a qualified professional. A quality installation should last decades or longer. 11. Do you have liability insurance, and if you have employees, are they covered with Worker’s Compensation Insurance? Make sure you can verify appropriate insurance coverage. 12. Do you belong to professional organizations like NTCA (National Tile Contractor’s Association)? Industry involvement is one indication of a tile installation company’s commitment to their craft. It gives them access to education, technical information, and other resources to assist them in professionally serving you. 13.  Are you a Certified Tile Installer (Certified Tile Education Foundation, CTI) or do you have Certified Tile Installers on your team? The certification of tile installers is an important step forward for the consumer and is “one” indication of professionalism. The industry has established a process to certify tile installers. Certification identifies an installer as being a dedicated and knowledgeable professional whose competence in installing tile has been verified to meet specific tile industry standards.

As you can see from Patricia Colwell’s post, MCM landscape is not the usual mixed border foundation planting. It’s generally minimalist and architectural with structured looking plants, and devoid of lots of floral color. If this is the look you want, I’d remove all material and choose a single shade tolerant tailored-looking plant that grows not more than 4’ high, to be placed along the left and right sides along the front of the house (depending on width, maybe 3 on each side). A row of small ornamental grass, perhaps with foliage that’s not straight green can line the front railed area (if you don’t like grasses maybe some strappy liriope-not sure about your zone and sun). To the left of that ‘porch’, in front of the innermost 4’ shrub, consider one unusual accent plant, perhaps slimmer than the shrubs, and with different texture than fine grasses (think bold leaves, or variegated, or sculpted, or just distinctly different from the leaves of the shrubs and grasses/liriope). A low groundcover in front of the remaining 4’ shrubs is all you need. Whether evergreen, woody or perennial, it, too, needs to contrast with the other foliage texture but create a pleasant coordination. A flowering groundcover would be nice but fleeting, as are most flowering plants. I repeatedly state on landscape posts that less is more. If you don’t need to hide your foundation or scale a tall facade, don’t swallow your house up with too many plantings. So, finally, use a large gorgeous planter on the porch, to the left of the door, with flowers and tall material to bring floral color to the space. Have fun changing it up in different seasons. If this is too austere for you, then you need to redefine the look you’re going for. Adding in perennials is another exercise in timing and color, and comes with more maintenance. Non-rhizomatic irises are tidy and architectural enough to blend with MCM but fluffy perennials conjure up a whole other feel. I’m not familiar with your growing area, so hopefully others can recommend specific plant material. If you go to a nursery be sure to tell them that you get only partial sun. Shade plants that get your morning sun would probably do better than sun plants that tolerate shade. Know your soil, also.

@qam999 and @mcarroll16, notice I did not call out specific items good/bad or agree/disagree, just a general statement. It does feel that the OP is getting hammered by some of the same repeated comments that are stamped to suburban U.S. houses, which may not be warranted here, especially with so little information. Also not that either of you have here, but often so many commenters say their piece but they cannot even read drawings or understand why things are the way they are, and some of them even consider themselves "Pro." So I will tell you what I saw that countered some comments, causing me to jump in originally: - I see a narrow lot of about 50', with a zero lot line on one side. Apparently an urban area, with some adjacent constraints. That can limit the shape of the footprint and opening up the side walls. - I see wet bathrooms, a common occurence in Europe and Asia. The little triangle represents a showerhead, so the Guest has a full bath, the Powder does not have a shower. - I see wardrobe cabinets, not built-in closets, a common occurence in Europe and Asia. - I see a kitchen that follows many utilitarian designs across the globe. Cabinets are furniture, and sometimes still travel with you. Some appliances are cabinet/appliance combos. Kitchens are not necessarily the central congregration area like in the U.S. Pantries are not huge as stocking up is not the norm. Laundries are not tasks to be celebrated, often there is a small combo condensing washer/dryer. Storage is not as critical as in the U.S., as other cultures just don't buy stuff, stuff, and more stuff to take care of their stuff. - I see a Living area that is not grouped to Dining and Kitchen. The U.S. way of living is to have large, open, communicating functions, not necessariy the norm in other parts of the world. - I see a small outside backhouse area and cafe table sized patio. Probably just for a burner to keep smells out of the house, hang laundry, and a table area that fits the lifestyle of just morning coffee. Many urban areas don't prioritize huge outdoor living/eating areas for huge parties. So, there are many things pointed out in the comments that can be improved with this plan, as I alluded to originally. But when commenting on a design, sometimes you have to shift gears to what, where, and why it is for that particular location, not just site, but country and culture. Even in the U.S., there are obvious differences comparing a typical suburban house located in Florida, California, Arizona, the Midwest, or the Northeast. It may be what an architect only does, but you have to get in the same mindset as the homeowner, or at least understand it.

I wrote a piece comparing peat and pine bark to coir and coco husks a while back. You'll find some interesting facts and observations in it that should be helpful. Peat vs. Coir Sphagnum peat and coir have nearly identical water retention curves. They both retain about 90-95% of their volume in water at saturation and release it over approximately the same curve until they both lock water up so tightly it's unavailable for plant uptake at about 30-33% saturation. Coir actually has less loft than sphagnum peat, and therefore, less aeration. Because of this propensity, coir should be used in mixes at lower %s than peat. Because of the tendency to compact, in the greenhouse industry coir is primarily used in containers in sub-irrigation (bottom-watering) situations. Many sources produce coir that is high in soluble salts, so this can also be an issue. Using coir as the primary component of container media virtually eliminates lime or dolomitic lime as a possible Ca source because of coir's high pH (6+). Gypsum should be used as a Ca source, which eliminates coir's low S content. All coir products are very high in K, very low in Ca, and have a potentially high Mn content, which can interfere with the uptake of Fe. Several studies have also shown that the significant presence of  phenolic allelopathic chemicals in fresh coir can be very problematic for a high % of plants, causing poor growth and reduced yields. I haven't tested coir thoroughly, but I have done some testing of CHCs (coconut husk chips) with some loose controls in place. After very thoroughly leaching and rinsing the chips, I made a 5:1:1 soil of pine bark:peat:perlite (which I know to be very productive) and a 5:1:1 mix of CHCs:peat:perlite. I planted 6 cuttings of snapdragon and 6 cuttings of Coleus (each from the same plant to help reduce genetic influences) in containers (same size/shape) of the different soils. I added dolomitic lime to the bark soil and gypsum to the CHC soil. After the cuttings struck, I eliminated all but the three strongest in each of the 4 containers. I watered each container with a weak solution of MG 12-4-8 with STEM added at each watering, and watered on an 'as needed basis', not on a schedule. The only difference in the fertilizer regimen was the fact that I included a small amount of MgSO4 (Epsom salts) to provide MG (the dolomitic lime in the bark soil contained the MG, while the gypsum (CaSO4) in the CHC soil did not. This difference was necessary because or the high pH of CHCs and coir.) for the CHC soil. The results were startling. In both cases, the cuttings grown in the CHC's exhibited < 1/2 the biomass at summers end as the plants in the bark mix. If Prakash still has his trees, it should be helpful, if not, A) I already have most of the info saved as word documents, so it takes but a few minutes to post the info. B) I know people regularly search for resolution for problems they are dealing with in their own plants, and come across threads like this one. The cause of chlorotic foliage is far from being linked exclusively to over-watering. Over-watering, under-watering, a high level of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil solution, nutritional deficiencies (especially of nitrogen, phosphorous, potassium, or magnesium), nutritional toxicities, soil compaction, root congestion, inappropriate irrigation water, natural senescence (aging), low light, too much light (especially sudden increases), low temperatures, sudden chill, insect herbivory, disease pathogens, and more, are other potential causes. The key element supporting the over-watering theory is not that leaves are yellowing; rather, it's due to the fact the plant presents evidence of a physiological disorder called oedema/ edema. I'll leave something about that below. The best course forward should include making sure you're watering correctly, getting watering intervals under control, and making sure the irrigation water is appropriate. (Is the water you use for the plants routed through an ionic exchange water softening system [uses salt])? Fertilizing regularly should also be a part of the care regimen, Watering about every 4th time you water in winter and about every 3rd time in summer, with an appropriate fertilizer (Foliage-Pro 9-3-6 is an excellent product for trees and houseplants). If you still need help or more clarity, just ask. About Oedema Oedema (aka edema) is a physiological disorder that can affect all terrestrial plants. It occurs when the plant takes up more water than it can rid itself of via the process of transpiration. The word itself means 'swelling', which is usually the first symptom, and comes in the form of pale blisters or water-filled bumps on foliage. Under a variety of circumstances/cultural conditions, a plant's internal water pressure (turgidity) can become so high that some leaf cells rupture and leak their contents into inter-cellular spaces in leaf tissue, creating wet or weepy areas. Symptoms vary by plant, but as the malady progresses, areas of the leaf turn yellow, brown, brown with reddish overtones or even black, with older damage appearing as corky/ scaly/ ridged patches, or wart/gall-like bumpy growth. Symptoms are seen more frequently in plants that are fleshy, are usually more pronounced on the underside of leaves, and older/lower leaves are more likely to be affected than younger/upper leaves. Oedema is most common in houseplants during the winter/early spring months, is driven primarily by excessive water retention in the soil, and can be intensified via several additional cultural influences. Cool temperatures, high humidity levels, low light conditions, or partial defoliation can individually or collectively act to intensify the problem, as can anything else that slows transpiration. Nutritional deficiencies of Ca and Mg are also known contributors to the malady. Some things that can help you prevent oedema: * Increase light levels and temperature * Monitor water needs carefully – avoid over-watering. I'd heartily recommend a soil with drainage so sharp (fast) that when you to water to beyond the saturation point you needn't worry about prolonged periods of soil saturation wrecking root health/function. Your soil choice should be a key that unlocks the solutions to many potential problems. * Avoid misting or getting water on foliage. It slows transpiration and increases turgidity. * Water as soon as you get up in the AM. When stomata close in preparation for the dark cycle, turgidity builds. If you water early in the day, it gives the plant an opportunity to remove (for its own needs) some of the excess water in the soil. * Put a fan in the room or otherwise increase air flow/circulation. Avoid over-crowding your plants. Getting Watering Intervals Under Control Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

Mealybugs have been the bane of my existence for over two years.  They are pervasive.  I have found nothing to eliminate them.  Because even if you get them off of one plant, they will be on another and eventually move from it.  Also, they hang out on crevices of pots and wood as well.  I have found them in the inner rim of pots, on wooden candle stands (that i use to add height for some potted plants), and even a chunk of petrified wood that I had on a shelf for decoration.  They are insidious. The systemic granules that contain imidacloprid unfortunately are not a panacea.  Yes, I use them because I try everything I can to get rid of them and I think it's often best to attack from several angles. But they have yet to solve my problem. I have a theory about systemic granules.  Hear me out.  They are dependent upon the plant taking up the poison into its blood stream for lack of the botanical words.  So, I believe they work best on plants that are very thirsty and have more water in their stems, petioles, etc.  But hoyas are not very thirsty and also tend to have more woody stems.  They take and use less water.  I have this theory that is why the systemics don't work as well on hoyas as they do on some other plants (think syngoniums, where they do work well). One other thing I will mention is that Bonide sells a large jug of the granules and a smaller one that has a label that says "houseplants".  The formula is identical.  It's just a packaging difference.  So buy the big one.  It's less expensive and you'll probably use it.

text: Just a note - depending on your situation, fluorescent lights can be useful, compared with LEDs. I went through a little of this with a college aged niece-like young lady.  She had no science background and wasn't a great critical thinker.  I started by just chatting about the protein contents of various vegetables and plant meat-alternatives, and gave her a big jar of nutritional yeast with the B-12 talk.  I also let slip some gentle scorn for vegans who fill up on sweets and don't eat their vegetables.  Then there's the young women more than anyone need iron talk, and the quantities of dark green leafies she needed no matter what.  And the sheer quantity of food, especially vegetables, vegans need to consume for adequate nourishment.  All of that was well spread out, however, and layered in discussion of planning meals and recipes, clothes, boys, school, etc. The fact is, being a responsible and well nourished vegan is a lot of work.  She was getting a lot of social pressure from people she was living with.  She spent a long weekend with friends of her parents who fed her up with delicious home cooking which she couldn't refuse as a guest, and was meat at most meals.  She decided she didn't want to be a vegan and that meat makes her feel good.  She had to come to it herself, but having to look after her own nutrition and do the cooking, seeing the junk her friends were eating, put her off of being vegan.  It did teach her some of the importance of eating vegetables and making healthy food choices.  She’s grown up now, cooks, and eats well. So, if that wasn't clear, I think what worked, no matter the final outcome, viz-a-viz animal or not, was to gently push knowledge and help her be vegan, when that's what she wanted.  Vegan can't be about no animal products.  That leads to cupcakes for dinner.  It has to be about pursuing a healthy diet no matter what restrictions there are.

You can die from a shock of just 6 stray volts stepping out onto wet grass or a patio that has unbonded, conductive material underneath. To be honest, setting a swim spa over this same area could be less than safe for the same reason. Swim spas are often not installed with the most ideal safety considerations when it comes to equipotential bonding. Consult an electricial who specializes in pool bonding to verify. If you can safely annul the threat of underground steel, San Juan Pools makes a couple of small pool fiberglass models that can be installed completely above ground, the Sedona, Canyon Lake, and Canyon Lake Deep. They will ship you the shell only if you cannot find a local dealer of San Juan. Alternately, I would not install an in-ground fiberglass pool prior to removal of the steel shell because you will not have room for proper plumbing and backfill, plus the ground may not be secure enough to prevent shifting under lateral pressure of the new inground installation.

The control system on these machines is sensitive to the electrical resistance and voltage values of the various component parts.  A pump gone to off-spec resistance as may occur from water damage to the windings if it leaks or electrically fails can damage the board.  The fuse kit is a retrofit included with replacement pumps to protect the board from future pump failures.  There should be an included instruction sheet detailing how to install it.  You didn't get a sheet?  What was your source for the replacement pump? --> Was the machine completely dead when it stopped without draining?  Or was the panel powered but the pump just wouldn't run?  The pump has thermal overheat protection so may not run until it cools and the protector resets.  Did you try waiting a while when the failure occurred, then manually draining by advancing the cycle to the final spin? Does the pump run now if you advance to the final spin? A board damaged by a bad pump may evidence failure on other components than the pump circuit.  There normally are fault codes triggered if the water valve solenoids go bad.  The cold valve fault normally takes precedence over hot if both are bad, and the fault typically will trigger immediately on plugging in the power cord as the board checks those circuits when it boots-up to standby mode.  It's possible the valve codes don't trigger if the board is damaged on the valve circuits. Have you tested the hot and cold valves via diagnostic mode?

I don't think the preceding comment is a complete answer. In order to have "instant" hot water, there may be a fair amount of plumbing work required to be done to do it the best way. OP, you've used the right words, what you need is a recirculating pump. In order for water to "recirculate", there needs to be a circular loop that starts where the water leaves the water heater, passes by the fixtures where you want hot water, and then returns to the water heater to be reheated. Such a system keeps water in the loop hot so that when you turn on a fixture, the hot water is right there. The product linked pumps water around the loop but at this point, you don't have a loop. You likely have a one-way passage right now with no return route to the water heater. It may be difficult/cost prohibitive, to run those additional pipes to create a loop. A cheapo solution that some use that I think is inferior dumps cooled hot water heater back into the cold supply at the fixtures and does away with the need for a return pipe system. The problem with this approach is that it puts water that previously passed through the water heating system (whether a tank or tankless) into the cold-water system. Water in heaters often picks up minerals and other substances that can adversely affect the flavor of the cold water if put into that system. I experienced that myself when visiting a friend's vacation house that he'd retrofitted with such a system. Good luck

Fixtures designed and sourced from China will most likely not have a UL certification. Most of them contain a mark of CE compliance, which is for the European Union and does not require safety certification by a 3rd party or to comply with extensive safety and manufacturing standards and codes as does a UL process of certification. And, manufacturing in China is still like the wild west, where the sticker may say anything they want, CE, UL, or some other "official" sounding acronym, but doesn't necessarily mean anything. It is hard to decipher what is legitimate, unless you know you have a U.S. company backing a product, because unlike many other countries, in the U.S. a company can be held liable for their product. And these standards are not just whether a fixture may spark or overheat, but other concerns like how much lead or formaldehyde is contained in the materials. Note that fixtures designed in the U.S., but manufactured in China, would still have to follow UL guidelines and procedures to obtain their UL certification. However, most of these fixtures would not be selling on Alibaba. You may find on their website exact or similar products to expensive ones in the U.S., but the factory owner might very well be using the same tooling or parts as they make for a U.S.-market company, but selling off-hand in the Chinese market for much cheaper because they don't have the overhead (read: safety regulations, red tape, and financial heirarchy) or substitute lesser materials. You will also find that CE-listed Edison-socket fixtures are made for certain European-sized 'bulbs,' which are compatible with similar U.S.-sized 'bulbs,' but just slightly different to be bothersome.

Hi there! Hi, Rachel. I'll sort through your discussion and make comments as I go. Long story short, I obtained 3 separate FLFs growing in one  14" pot and was advised to separate and repot them. The best time to repot is just before the summer solstice (21 Jun - think Father's Day). Repotting in fall sets you/the plant up for a recovery period measured in months rather than weeks, as would be the case if the plant was healthy and repotted in Jun. I hesitated for a  while because they seemed happy and had new growth, but about 3 months  ago I finally pulled the trigger because they were pushing each other to  lean waaay out of the pot. A more appropriate response to a leaning plant is to get out ahead of the lean through directional pruning. The growth habit of Ficus is such that their leaves grow grow from the branch in sort of a spiral or helix. From above looking down, the first leaf would be at the 12 o'clock position, the next one at 3, then 6 then 9 (roughly) then repeat. By pruning just beyond a leaf facing the direction you want a new branch to grow, you can chance the direction any trunk/ branch is growing.   In the figure above, a cut above the top leaf would produce a branch that would grow to the left and back. The middle leaf, as you can see, has produced a new branch growing to the right and back. Had the stem been pruned above the lowest leaf, it would have produced a branch growing to the left and forward, and the unseen leaf below the lowest leaf is almost certainly growing right/ forward. By choosing where the branch is pruned, you can change it's direction. Also, The best pruning response (most enthusiasm from the plant) occurs in summer. If you prune now, you get a winters worth of lanky growth that you really don't want to keep. It's best to prune in Jun. That way, you get a full summer of tight growth and short internodes, followed bt more lanky growth in winter. The fix for that is to remove the winter growth every year in Jun. That way you keep only the tightest growth, so you have a fuller and more compact tree. Questions? I repotted the largest one in it's own pot (it's doing well!) and  potted the other two together using a 65/35(ish) mix of Fox Farm  potting soil and perlite. Initially all 3 FLFs lost a couple of leaves  from the shock, but ultimately were doing well until their first  watering about 2 weeks after repotting. A couple days after watering,  all of the leaves on the upper half of the left tree in the photo began  to droop dramatically and fell off one by one over the following week  (all of the leaves were newer but of comparable size to the ones on the  upper right tree). It was very upsetting, but I knew the damage was  irreversible - although I still don't know exactly what  happened  - so I just left them alone and this is where we are now. Hard to say, given the info provided. Was the tree outdoors for the summer? Odds are heavy it was either a response to a decrease in light or over-watering. The tree on  the right never reacted negatively, and the one on the left seems to be  done with his tantrum. The upper half of the trunk where the leaves dropped has  shriveled up and seemingly died from what I can tell, along with a tiny  little branch you can see on the bottom right. My question is: do I need  to wait until the late spring to prune off the shriveled/dead parts, or  can I cut off some of it now so it doesn't look quite so grim? Either is ok. Start cutting segments of the branch at its tip. Keep cutting segments until you find living/ green tissue or the entire branch has been removed. I live in zone 7 and know not to prune or notch for new growth  until next year, but since the upper part is (very likely) dead, I don't  think pruning it in the winter will trigger any new growth? Right? Removing dead tissue can't and won't stimulate back-budding; and your tree(s) won't grow until the volume of the root system is able to support new growth. This, because the plant is programmed to spend energy on roots BEFORE it spends energy on shoots. That's why the first growth from a seed is the root radicle (taproot). It sounds like it might be a while before the root system is able to support more top growth; and, you have the short days and diminished light intensity working against you until spring. Al

Besides, unless you are removing all MEP, you won't be able to sister. Blocking is required for lateral restraint to prevent the joist from rotating, not fireblocking. This occurs at the bearing ends of a joist, so the rim joist takes care of it on the outside wall, and down the middle of the house you need 2x8 in between each joist over the beam. Joist bridging somewhere at midspan is not really needed here, as the rotational moment is not as great in the smaller section of a 2x8 joist (rather that a taller joist like a 2x12) and the shorter 12'-3" span. Adding blocking over the beam is adequate. The tilting needs more info and pics whether that can have a fix. The squeaking can be alleviated by screwing the T&G subfloor into the joists. As others have mentioned, the minimum recommended knee space is: 12" is too shallow unless you and everyone in your family has very short legs. Regarding # of seats: Each seat needs a minimum of 24" of linear space for counter-height & bar-height seating. Table-height seating needs 24" to 30" of linear space per seat. I can give you most of the information you'll need to reason through what's happening, but given what we know at this point, it will be up to you to decide what the likely cause of the wilting is. Plants in containers are always "stressed" because container gardening is inherently stressful to plants; too, stress comes in many forms and directions, and to varying degrees. "Stress" simply means the plant is growing under the influence of  imperfect cultural conditions, or, perhaps more accurately, stress occurs when the plant is growing at or near the limits of what it is genetically programmed to tolerate. The key issue isn't whether or not a plant is stressed; rather, the questions are to what degree it's stressed and what is the CAUSE of the stress. If, when your plant first started wilting, you could still detect moisture in the soil with a "tell" or a finger, it's a pretty sure bet the cause wasn't under-watering. If a plant wilts while the soil is moist, it's usually one of three issues, 1) there is an excessive amount of water in the grow medium, which limits the root system's oxygen supply which in turn limits the plant's ability to efficiently take up and move water to all of its parts, or 2) a high level of dissolved solids (salts) have accumulated in the grow medium and soil solution. This can nullify the plant's ability to move water through its cells' permeable membrane (osmosis). The level of dissolved solids can reach levels so high that water stops moving into cells and begins to be pulled out of cells by the same mechanism that curing salt pulls water from the cells of meat like ham/ bacon/ sausage. When this reversal of water occurs, plasmalemma is torn from cell walls as the water moves out and the cell collapses. The scientific name for this disorder is 'plasmolysis', but commonly referred to as fertilizer burn., or 3) The root system is infected by a pathogen which limits its ability to take up water and nutrients dissolved therein. Did you inspect the roots when you repotted? Did they look healthy with white or tan fleshy tips, or did they smell sour, with many black or slimy roots? Often, fungal infections which cause root rot will create conditions such that when you tug on an affected root, the outer covering slides off and leaves behind the root's ventral core (vascular cylinder). Plants that wilt from over-watering usually perk up at night. This is because small openings in leaves (stomata) close during the dark cycle. This limits water loss through these openings, which allows the plant to rebuild its internal water pressure (turgidity) which relieves wilting to some degree. Is it wise to let the plant stand on the pebble tray? A humidity tray can be 'somewhat' helpful in that it slows evaporative water loss from the plant to the air surrounding it, which tends to increase the the plant's internal water pressure (turgidity) which helps to counter the tendency to wilt. Southern California is not the easiest place to grow bigleaf hydrangeas. But it can be done. My sister lived in Laguna Beach for years and she had great hydrangeas but they were in pretty much all day dappled shade. Plenty of shade and plenty of water will prevent the browning of any flowers prematurely. One of the issues you will have to contend with is the lack of a proper period of dormancy. These are not evergreen shrubs and they need a down time to recharge themselves and the very mild or even warm winter temps you experience interfere with that. Lack of sufficient dormancy will affect flowering and eventually the health of the plant overall. You can induce a "forced" dormancy of sorts by removing any remaining foliage in late fall and not allowing the shrub to flower until after the spring equinox.
