I remodeled and replaced the tub/shower with a beautiful walk in shower that follows the footprint of the original tub. There are no problems with the size at all. There are differing opinions regarding a built in bench. I had one done in mine and it is one of the best parts of my remodel as I use it almost every time I use the shower. It is sleek looking and the "seat" was done with the a remnant of the marble slab I used for the counter. I also used a portion of the slab for the curb. I had to use a shower "seat" prior to my remodel and in my opinion based on use there is simply no comparison. The bench is always there. In order to have a seat that is as stable and large enough to be functional, you need a fairly large one which takes up a lot of space. It also needs to be cleaned around and is always there in the shower - where do you put it when you don't want it in the shower. I have no idea why people don't want one built when the shower is done as it is functional and doesn't cause any issues. Plenty of room left in the shower to shower comfortable. The reason why there might be an issue with a curbless shower is because they require a very specific form of construction because there is no curb to stop water from getting onto the rest of the bathroom floor. So you need an especially skilled tradesperson AND  it has to be done within the constraints of what your current bathroom floor is like in terms of being able to slope it properly. All of this will cost more than a "regular" shower and a "regular" tile walk in shower with nice finishes is quite costly - or at least mine was because of the materials and skilled labor needed to do it right. Therefor the question is why you want a curbless shower? Is it just for aesthetics or do you want it for functional reasons because you want to "roll" into it or are contemplating aging in place and worrying about stepping over a curb. In my experience almost no "senior" or someone with mobility issue  needs a wheel chair and therefore needs a curbless shower. Seniors and others with mobility issues generally can function with a curb especially since you can make one that is lower and less deep than others and they can be managed quite well especially if you have an appropriate grab bar at the entry point to steady the person. I remodeled wanting to age in place and specifically got rid of the tub for functional as well as aesthetic reasons but do have a curb. If at some point I can't manage a curb for whatever reason, I would probably have some time of assistance for bathing anyway. 🤷🏼‍♀️ My father died when he was 99 and it was only in the last two years of his life that he had that kind of help for safety and he still managed a curb

Before you spend a lot of money to build a "simulated" heavy timber structure that could not exist in the real world, think about what you're simulating. Real sloping timbers supporting a horizontal timber would not be stable so there would be a hidden part to the structure. The simplest structure would be a traditional "Raised Tie" heavy timber truss (shown below) where horizntal and sloping ceilings have been installed at the tops of the timber members. Of course the top of the truss doesn't need to be built but this approach allows you to detail the connections of the members in a more convincing manner: the horiontal tie would butt into the sloping member.  You might even simulate a mortise & tenon joint.

If someone is going to mix up a medium for their pot, a little bit of clay-based soil is a lovely addition. However, it needs to be done carefully. There was a time when soil was added to other stuff to give a good potting medium for container-grown plants in nurseries. A mix might have contained peat moss, course sand, a percentage of clay-based soil and whatever else was around and easily had at the time. But times change, fashion changes, marketing looms big sometimes (especially when lots of people have high disposable income) and so recipes change. I can well imagine that your Aloe vera was happy in your concoction. I think you must have made a nice mix. Just re-reading your post. This statement: but the impression on handling it is that the sand content is high makes me realise that you did not make the mix yourself. I presume you bought some different mixes to try out. There are so many variables in a pot containing a medium (height of pot compared to its width, plastic pot compared to unglazed terracotta, size of sand used, amount of sand etc etc) that it's very hard to make any quick response.

@tete_a_tete A gardener mixed this soil for me years ago based on my direction.   I have forgotten the formula, but it was roughly 30% native clay loam soil, 50% sand, and 20% "something else I do not remember".   When the soil is dry, you can easily sink your hands into it, so it has no hardening tendency.   The "feel" of the soil matches my memory of a soil that was substantially sandy loam soil. I have spent a lot of time studying and experimenting with container soils.  A container soil purist would never use any clay at all because the particle sizes are too small.   So it is a real discovery to me to find specific genera of plants - such as Aloe and Sempervivum - that seem to thrive in container soils that have a small amount of clay loam soil.

This involves two steps: 1. Install a drain pan on the floor of the cabinet under the sink with a drain. This catches most spilled water and directs it harmlessly down the drain before it gets to the floor. The problem with most drain pans, however, is they are designed for industrial use and may not exactly fit your cabinet. So, what we do is tile the inside of the cabinet over a waterproof barrier such as Schluter's Kerdi cloth (don't worry if you don't know what that is, your contractor does). With the drain, this takes care of the problem. 2. Second, install a shutoff valve that detects water leaks and automatically shuts off the water. You can get valves that shut the water off at the sink (two will be required, one for hot and one for cold) or a whole-house valve that protects against leaks anywhere in the house. These sensible precautions are something we regularly do to protect kitchens against flooding, and will, in your case, protect your new floor from all but the most unlikely water problems.

Good luck finding someone. In my experience having someone who is local is critical for all kinds of reasons and especially so for kitchens and bathroons. A good designer wants to "inhabit" the actual space in order to get a true sense of the space and the light. I did a gut remodel and after everything had been moved out she came and just sat in the rooms for awhile. I am focusing on what seems to be relatively trivial matters but the sheer number of decisions that have to be made is overwhelming and I was very happy that certain decisions were being made by a professional. My designer was also indispensable as a defacto "project manager" as I don't have the background of knowledge to truly judge construction. Also a local designer will have resources in terms of all kinds of stuff - for my project there were the  "to the trade" sources so that we did a few visits to the Pacific Design Center. She also had artisans - cabinet makers; wall paper hangers; upholsters; custom furniture builders; regular "to the trade" vendors - and even with her designer markup the net price to me was generally lower than what I would have spent - and the expertise was *priceless*. I think remote can work if one is just looking for help in terms of furniture placement or whatever but I think for the kind of remodel of kitchens and bathrooms which OP is planning you really need a talented and experience designer who can be onsite.

"The only inspection a seller may need to pay for is a one that is required for certificate of occupancy to allow the sale of the house." Mike, this must vary regionally. In my state, for single family residences, a certificate of occupancy is only required at the completion of construction, before the structure is first occupied. Buyers often want a "home inspection" (here that's customarily at the buyer's expense) but the quality and usefulness of those cover a very wide range from useful to useless and most points in-between. Customary practices also get thrown out the window in hot markets. Sellers often take the approach "Here's the house, here's how it is. Your question depends on the State, county and even city you're looking to buy a house in, and if you're paying cash or have a lender (mortgage). States differ what is required or disclosed selling a house from everything to almost nothing.  Alabama for example is a "buyer beware" state and only requires a mold disclosure if known, everything else is the buyers responsibility to determine.  In Minnesota the state has no laws requiring an inspection but many counties and cities do. But (and a big but)  most lenders do require an inspection to verify septic conditions and will not make a loan on a house with a bad septic system. I don't believe you can force a seller to pay for anything, you can only ask in your offer. if a seller likes your offer he/she will pay the couple hundred for an inspection.  If you want a house with a septic system you'd be foolish not to pay to inspect the system before risking a replacement cost of $15K-$30 to replace a failed system.

If you are going to plant offspring (cuttings) from that mother plant then I would assume 4-5' width dimensions at some point (contact this person to double-check the width and ask the person how old & wide the plant is in case her plant is still growing wider still). Like Gardengal48 suggested, that 4-5' width would limit you to three plants tops although people make hedges by planting the shrubs closer. If you are planning to purchase mophead plants to grow then I would look for plants from the Cityline Series or the Let's Dace Series. These are very compact cultivars that sometimes have 2-3' dimensions. The Let's Dance Series includes rebloomer mopheads. The blue/purple color of mophead blooms is affected by the availability of aluminum in the soil as well as by the acidity of your garden soil so it is possible to get different colors when you plant a cutting in a different location. So in my alkaline soils, the blooms are a shade of pink but in other relatives' homes in very acidic soils, their blooms are blue. I would normally have to regularly amend my soil with aluminum sulfate to try and get either purple or blue blooms. Identifying specific cultivars of hydrangea macrophylla mopheads may be very difficult as many of the blooms of one cultivar resemble those of other cultivars "too much". The care is usually the same though.

I am far from a floor expert, but... whether or not you can change the direction of the floor depends on your subfloor.  Flooring needs to run perpendicular to joists on most floors.  You can stiffen the floor from above or below to change that, but you shouldn't assume you can change direction. My opinion on your questions... 1.  It depends on your subfloor. 2.  I would consider different tones if you are going to change the wood species.  You generally want to avoid any chance of it looking like you were trying to match and failed. 3.  If you are going to match, match as much as you can.  If you are not going to match, make it distinctively different. 4.  Many engineered products can look good next to hardwood, but you are going to have to spend extra.  So unless there is a compelling reason not to, stick with hardwood. Having said this.  It is your house and my answers may not work so great for you.

that makes sense. what is the risk if having a 2 ton difference in size? is there a risk our evaporator coil might freeze? IMHO the biggest risk you face is lack of proper oil return to the compressor, as the coil is bigger... the oil that runs thru the system has a larger area to pool. Freezing of the coil, just because it's larger or smaller? uh- no. To freeze there has to be some other reason beside that. Typically an AC evap coil is going to run around 40F with some designs in the mid 40's to low 50's. At those temps it's impossible to freeze unless there is some other problem, running with clogged filter, in operable blower motor, improper refrigerant charge, clogged or restricted meter device or running the system with no load and ambient temps 55F or lower outside *(without the proper controls to do so). What's the manufacturer of your system? Is your system working? If it is -- I wouldn't worry about it until it does. They all break. Worry about the things you can control, like changing filters regularly, system maintenance checks performed by licensed tenured techs if you can find one. Some companies will lay into you for a wide variety of reasons because they are looking for reasons to get you to decide you need a new one, or some reason to do an expensive repair you  likely do not need. What's the reason you've been talking to people about this? Is the system working or not? Provide a picture of your e-coil data plate info with model / serial number clearly visible. I'll tell you what it is. -------- In terms of dehumidifying a larger than necessary e-coil for a hvac system will hold water, that water can be reintroduced back into the home as the humidity it tried to expel. This is typically a design issue. With all that being said it was a verbal rule not to go any higher than 1 ton difference from that of the out door condenser, that was 20 years ago when each coil design was seperate and coils were smaller then in physical size all of them. In the search for higher government mandated efficiency requirements I've seen larger differences than that 1 ton. Not typically 2 tons though. *However it should be noted that some manufacturers 4 ton / 5 ton e-coils are interchangeable... meaning that if you have a 4 ton system, the E-coil is the same as a 5 ton e-coil. If larger coils were known to freeze, would a mfg do this? uh-no. The mfg's are after your e-coil money... selling you a 5 ton coil when what you really need is 4 ton? LOL. yeah it's all about money. It's cheaper for the Mfg to make just one coil for two different configs than 2 separate ones. Eventually the waters here could get even murkier due to a wide variety of problems coming to a hot town near you. 2023 is the year, for some it might not be felt until 2025. It's coming, you've been warned. ;-) So a 3 ton condenser paired with one of those e-coils? If that is the case? It's not going to mean much, unless the condenser is 2 ton paired with a 4 ton/ 5 ton e-coil. There can be a number of undesirable effects caused having an oversized evaporator and would basically be the same problems you have with an undersized condenser. The amount of heat absorbed by the evaporator would be more than the condenser could remove at times and some of the gas wouldn't condense to a liquid in the condenser.  So the condenser isn't big enough to provide enough subcooling and some liquid is prone to saturation in the liquid line just from absorbing heat through the copper tube and into gas. This  will cause poor oil circulation, poor expansion valve operation, lower efficiency, excessive power consumption and can ruin your system. Thanks for the cartoon break, Ray.  And now, back to our regularly scheduled program... The OP asked "What are the potential risks (or benefits) to having an oversized evaporater coil?" The capacities of your evaporator and condenser coils should be matched.  A higher capacity evaporator coil will operate at higher temperature.  That will increase run time (it will take longer to cool the space) and decrease dehumidification.  That's a decrease in efficiency--not an increase.

"evaporator and condenser coils should be matched"  Matched how Tim?  The old saying size doesn't matter but how it's used, also applies to A/C coils.  The 5 ton Evaporator coil can easily be used with a 3 ton condensing unit by adding a 6" long "liquid to suction heat exchanger" to control flash gas and oil migration and tweak the TVX. Capacities of the two coils have nothing to do with working together, it's how the refrigerant cycle is controlled and the refrigerant properties.  A typical refrigerator has an evaporator 2 to 3 times the capacity of the condenser coil, and a walk in cooler or freezer have evaporators 4 + the size the condenser size, it's how the refrigerant is controlled. Wondering if the evaporator coil can freeze up?  If the installer raised the Blower speed to 1500 to 2000 Cfm's the answer is NO way ever.  If the install set the blower speed at 1200 Cfm's for a 3 ton coil, it would depend on how well he tweaked the TVX valve to set superheat, but highly doubtful it would.  If the TVX was set rich, on a mild day with above average humidity, maybe.

>>  If you're asking if the stated depth of a cabinet includes the doors/drawer fronts, the answer is no. Kitchen cabinet depths only account for the cabinet box.  Doors & drawer fronts add about another inch. So, a 24" deep cabinet is 26" when counting box + doors/drawer fronts. Knobs/pulls add another 1" to 2", depending on your hardware. Counter overhangs extend around 1.5" beyond the cabinet boxes. >>  If you're asking if you should include doors/drawer fronts when determining the depth of a cabinet, the answer is yes.  In fact, you should also include the counter overhang if it has a counter. It depends on how small the yard is and what kind tropical fruit you plant. No, you are not completely weird and yes, some travelers would be adventurous enough to pick your fruit. Mango is a seasonal fruit on a generally huge tree and has a short harvest season for guests. May/June if I recall correctly. Avocado does not ripen on the tree. It has to be picked to ripen, so a long harvest season. The avocado 'Gwen' is a dwarf almost weeping avocado tree with very nice fruit. Lemon and lime can also be picked over a long period. Orange/grapefruit and the like are more seasonal. Citrus in general is susceptible to countless insects and diseases and may need spraying. Lemon and lime seem the most resistant to pestilence. Papaya is an easy year round fruit that starts producing the first year. There is no such thing as a Banana Palm in my world. There are bananas and there are palms. Bananas trees die after they set fruit and you have a potentially huge, depending on variety, water filled tree trunk to get rid of after the bunch is harvested. New trees sprout from the base. And bananas don't come in nice six packs. They come in 50+lb, 3'-4' long bunches with 100 bananas that all ripen at once. Jaboticaba, Plinia cauliflora - the botanical name seems to be in flux - is a large shrub with really yummy Lychee like purple fruits. All of them are going to need ample water. Choose your fruits wisely for the space you have and the maintenance that goes with them.

That I can tell, you have been working on another new kitchen layout in the same house for over 2 1/2 years begun right after finishing your full kitchen remodel. I've commented on some in the past and have been a bystander of more threads popping up here and there. Each time there is something completely different. First, re-conforming your recent cabinets in a new layout to new cabinets. Going from full-on separate kosher to kosher-lite. Open sitting area off the kitchen to fully walled off Dining. Pantry and remodel of stairs and bedroom to none. Then back and forth on each decision. It seems you have design paralyzation. Part of the reason is you are bogged down by too many tiny details and pretty renderings. You have jumped straight into the very specifics and too many variables to solve. You need to step back and look at the macro level; not the micro level. When you start there you can get a good overall concept, set your budget, and refine your program requirements. Then from a simplistic solution that works, delve your way into the details. The other reason that entered my mind is that you are dreaming and just enjoy putting all your free time into playing with plans and 3D software. I hope that is not the case with so many people offering their free time to help over the years. I do have the suspicion that no matter a final design and even after construction, you will want to change something or second guess your previous decisions. The best bet is to hire an architect and kitchen designer. They will force you to make decisions, or make them in good faith for you when lacking. If this is going to actually come to fruition, they will get you there sooner.

Council approval requirements can vary for every state and council in Australia. So contact YOUR council. Contact your councils planning and building permit department, and before you do that go online and look at YOUR council regulations.  This will help in understanding the conversation with the council planning person.    Council approvals are necessary for any structure on your property.  You can buy all the sunroom building products, but if you have not received council approval, you can not erect that structure. As a bonsai practitioner, I've done full repots (includes bare-rooting, root pruning, and a change of medium) for several thousands of plants over the years. Included were good number of succulents and herbaceous perennials. I can say with the utmost certainty that root congestion can rob a plant of 100% of its growth potential, severely limit its level of vitality and its ability to defend itself from pathogens, and severely detract from its eye appeal. Re the part about growth rate, the plant might even be going backward in terms of true growth, which is measured by the increase of the weight of the plant's dry mass. Since plants are organisms which turn to shedding as a way to cope with a disparity in the amount of energy used during respiration vs the amount of food produced during photosynthesis, even while they are extending, it might not be true growth (if at the same time we see extension they are shedding more dry mass than they are putting on). BTW - the "growth spurt" you'll see after you repot isn't a "spurt" at all. It's just the plant realizing a greater % of the growth potential it had all along. Observing the change in growth rate serves as a good way to get a sense of how limiting the root congestion was. Well, it's sunny/cold/calm out, so I'm going out to play with the birds. The house and garden not being square is the least of your worries, easy enough to deal with, maybe even some potential to do something that looks interesting, or to tuck a useful service zone in behind the garden bed. But there are other questions that need to be included in the decisions. Do you want a lawn? Are you keeping the lawn, and if you are then how much do you need, which gives some idea of how much space you have left for the garden beds. Are you keeping the drive-through, do you need to keep that space clear. How much gardening do you want to do to maintain it, keeping in mind there is no such thing as a maintenance-free landscaping, but there are choices you can make which increase or decrease work required. Do you like straight lines or curves, which is personal taste. Which direction, any easements, how tall do the plantings need to be to provide the privacy. A sketch would be useful, and a list of what you want to achieve, clothesline, bbq, etc?

Here is roughly what you've got in terms of the windows themselves except I lost the vent in the erasing. What style is the house overall?  In general the options have included: 1. Top of the window or slightly above, to the floor. In this case I would only do fixed panels on the end. 2. Ceiling to floor. Also would only do panels on the end. 3. Top of window to sill. These would also have to cover part of the window because if they go to the sill you don't want the width to extend past the sill. These you could open and close. 4. Top of window to top of chair rail. These could be wider so they did not cover part of the window since they would be "anchored" by the chair rail. These you could open and close. The current orthodoxy is that only the first one is correct, and there is something or other wrong with the other options, mostly that it is old fashioned or dated, but I think that depends on the style of the curtain you want,  what the style of the furniture is where it is going to be in front of the window, whether you want them to open and close or not and things like that. Both conventional (vented) and unvented, conditioned attics have been well, exhaustively, evaluated by building science researchers beginning in the 1990's.  A simple google search can provide at least half a day's reading materials.  You can, of course, substitute YouTube videos for peer-reviewed research at your peril. Conventional (vented) and unvented, conditioned attics are appropriate in hot- dry climates.  If you go the unvented, conditioned route, there are a variety of construction methods--not all of which require the use of spray foam. If you need the attic for storage of temperature-sensitive stuff, a conditioned attic provides the benefit of additional conditioned storage (generally the attic will be within 10 F of the conditioned living area temperature.)  If you're doing everything you can to fireproof your home, eliminating attic vents mitigates the risk of embers entering your home.  If you're looking for energy savings in a hot-dry climate, the incremental cost for an unvented, conditioned attic isn't likely to pay back in a reasonable timeframe compared with proper duct sealing and insulation of ducts in an unconditioned attic.

They ruined your waterproofing system. The holes that you see in the block are there to allow the water/moisture to bypass the block and get behind the dimpled membrane and from there diverted under the slab into a drain channel or pipe. By removing that now everything will be draining onto the surface. I see things like this on many occasions and it makes me wonder all the time if someone who does the work doesn't know what something is, why not ask before taking any action. That said, I hope they have insurance or are willing to pay for it, because now you need a new drain channel installed on top of the floor and seal it on top and bottom and run it to the sump pump something like a Drytrack channel. Here is an example to give you an idea.   Good luck

Thanks for your reply @GN Builders L.L.C. With the kind of system that we have, is there a drain that's been installed below the cement? Or is the drain simply the thin channel that's been cut into the cement around perimeter of the floor? It looks like the cement would have to be broken up around edge of the floor to remove and replace what's left of the system. Do you agree?

Yes if it was installed after the slab was in place the floor would be cut (hard to tell from the image if it was or not because of the leftover glue from an old flooring that was removed I assume). If this perimeter membrane was installed before the slab was poured there could be a drainpipe under there connected to the pump... If not it just drains under the slab, but if that's the case there should be 4" of stone with plastic under the slab and water will find its way to the pump, because if not your slab will be constantly wet.

This is pretty much the system you have:   The part you are missing is the plastic covering the wall - which helps direct water/moisture coming anywhere through the entire wall down to the interior perimeter drain, not just from the holes drilled through the bottom row of block. It will be harder to insert it having the dimple board cut off, but 'should' still be able to happen. Typically when you drill that many holes on the bottom row of block, you install an on-slab gutter system like GN shows. Then water can run on top the slab around to the new sump pit. When you choose the expensive version of tearing out the slab and installing a french drain and this dimpled board system, that usually means you have more intense underslab water and leaky walls.

His rep asked what I was doing and told him I'm selling the Option to buy the property with an expiration date, but would deduct the 2% from the full price if he really did buy the property.  The guy pulled out because of me and I still believe he was a swindler wanting to market the properties to other developers in the years to come.  It took a while to get the others to understand how close they came to never being able to sell their own property without a huge legal battle.

It looks like flaking stucco/plaster, possibly from heat exposure over a long time. There would be no reason to apply asbestos in that manner to a wall like that.  However, no one can identify asbestos-containing material by looking at a photo or by simple visual inspection: the only reliable way is to take a small sample to a certified asbestos lab and have them examine it by microscopy.  Your local or state environmental agency should have a list of accredited labs and the analysis should cost under $100.

Grout may shed a few particles here or there after the installation, but if it is significant flaking, flaking can be too from too much water used during installation and/or cleanup. Excess water can also cause color variations within the wall. Flaking can also be from using unsanded grout in too wide a joint. Without the bulk filler, the grout shrinks as it cures, and that can cause micro cracks and flaking. I don't see that happening on your walls though. It may seem crazy, but you may actually want to look at whites/offwhites from the red color family ... right now, I suspect you're seeing pink because you are seeing the contrast from the yellow color family walls and the counter. Lightbulbs will generally either lean yellow or blue, though evenually can get to an orangey light, though the bigger factor may be how much of the spectrum, you're getting. Lower end bulbs won't give true colors; look for bulbs with a high CRI (color rendering index) value to give you truer colors. The true tell of whether it's your lightbulbs or the environment (surrounding colors) is whether your perception of the colors changes between lightbulb light and natural light. If it doesn't look right in natural (window) light, then lightbulbs alone won't fix it, unless you have the lights on all the time.

You should always take multiple cuttings, whatever your plans, in order to cover failures. You could plant them in a clump or singly. They'll look bushier in a clump earlier but in the long run there will be no difference in the shape of the bush. Clumps are sharing space, light and nutrients, so each individual will be reduced in vigour. Singles get it all to themselves. If you plant a single rooted cutting and give it sufficient space and light it will produce a branched shrub, if that is its natural growth habit. You could take the top off the cutting, forcing it to branch earlier, but ultimately an unpruned cutting will achieve the same end. (This applies to single specimen shrubs, not hedges, and only if there is enough space and light.) How long it will take to produce a shrub you consider 'pretty' depends on the traits of the particular cultivar and the environment but you're looking at a few years to achieve a reasonable size. At first you'll have a low mounding plant. 'Full grown' never really happens as shrubs keep producing new growth. Very old species Loropetalums can become small trees.

Agreed with the previous comment: You likely need to sand the entire thing, using a consistent final grit everywhere, and begin again when temperatures are above 50 (ideally even warmer than that). It's possible to match stains, but if your stain is coming off of the entire piece, I think you're better off starting over. You didn't mention what type/brand of stain or solvent(s) you used. I'd guess you used either a gel stain or a wiping stain if it's still coming off. If that's the case, next time you stain, wipe off all excess with a clean rag before the stain dries. (Stains and types of stains are very different - then add in different types/hardness of wood and results vary a lot.) In the meantime, if you absolutely cannot wait for warmer weather and do not have warm space to do this, I'd suggest cutting a piece of plywood (sacrificial) and covering it with contact paper. Alternatively, get a cheap piece of prefab formica. Good luck!

You need warmth to have the products perform as they were designed. You need to sand down the entire surface to a level where the sanding scratches aren't going tp be visible when stained and finished. Do this project when everything is correct to allow a successfully finished product. Until then you can get some 6 mil plastic to tape over the surface. Home Depot will have some. List for us the stain you're using, please.

I just noticed that you sanded at 80 grit to get the glue off. If/when you sand the entire thing, sand up to at least 150 grit - everywhere - if not higher. And don't jump too far from one grit to another. Always increase by 50% of the number or less, e.g., from 80 to 120, and then to 150. Sanding different parts with different grits (and/or not completely sanding at each grit) will cause the stain to "take" very differently.

Are you planning on painting the existing trim and cabinets?  Whites often don't play well together, so matching existing is often easier than picking a new white. If you want a light neutral that contrasts with your white you will still want to consider the trim and cabinet colors and the undertones. Your sofa looks violet gray next to your current wall color, so that is going to be a driving force.  Greige (green gray/ green beige) may look a bit dingy with the sofa and taupe (violet gray/ pink beige) may go lilac on your walls next to your flooring. In your case, where you have both the yellow/gray flooring and the violet gray sofa I would start with getting a bunch of neutral color swatches and try to figure out what you like with your sofa and your flooring. It is sometimes easier to find the color family that works best by looking at mid toned colors.  You can then choose a lighter version of the color. Maria Killam lists some examples of colors in different families that may get you started.   She didn't always pick my favorites from each family, but it is a decent variety and will guide you to the right color space.. Repeat, if you just used standard Jumbo slabs, the seams will NOT have bookmatched vein matching. The veining is produced randomly in standard quartz, and random physically cannot  “match”. Upgrading to the much more expensive Cambria bookmatched pattern is the ONLY way that you get the waterfall seam patterns to sorta match at cuts from *different* slabs. Otherwise, for ”perfect” waterfall matching, an island has to be *small enough* that both waterfall ends come out of the *same exact slab*. Or, you get the standard, ”close, but no cigar” matching of random patterned slabs.

Okay, Round 2... the lattice should be dark brown to match the steps and recede from view if you intend to keep it. As Ken said, it would look best to remove it and screen that area with evergreen shrubs. Deer have only stopped by for an occasional nibble so far... if you plant a deer salad bar buffet they are likely to make your garden a regular hang out. Choose as many deer resistant plants as possible. Since you want roses, try to select highly deer resistant plants as your other choices. Which shrubs to choose? You need a local designer to guide that choice. The landscaping that you're seeing in your neighborhood includes cheapo Home Depot quality plants, probably because your neighbors all DIYed it.  Please do not use barberries, burning bush or butterfly bush because they are terribly invasive in the mid Atlantic and northeast and also because you need reliable evergreens. Boxwood is subject to blight so "no" to that one also. Nandinas look rough after a cold winter and take a long time to releaf so those are questionable for you as well. Yew are deer candy so those are out of consideration. Hollies will be nibbled if the deer pressure is very high but you're placing them close to the house so include hollies. Junipers are a good choice for you. PJM rhodies are a possible if you like the bloom color.  Mountain laurel, mahonia and pieris are possibles (I don't know your location but the crape is doing well so it can't be too cold). How wide should your borders be? Your current borders are so narrow that you can't see the plants when looking out your windows without craning your neck. You want a landscape that looks great from inside the house (winter!) as well as outside. Ideally you will have a mix of shrubs and perennials rather than a thick line of shrubs (say "no" to soldiers in a row). If you create seven foot or nine foot borders now, they will look silly until the plants grow in but ultimately that's where you're likely to end up. I prefer to do all the sod removal at once then fill the empty space with annuals for several years. Your local designer will have their own strategy.

There is no such thing as Medical grade stainless.  304 is for general use in the austenitic (non magnetic) 300 series of stainless.  Surgical stainless is usually 316 or 316L grade but there is no designated medical grade .  304 and 308Lis usually used in the food industry when food is in direct contact with the metal.  All pot and pans are in the 300 family of stainless.  (take a magnet when shopping for stainless cook wear to see if you're getting screwed.) A refrigerator that is magnetic uses metal from the Ferritic 400 series of stainless and are usually 409 or 430 grade and cheaper.  If you find a domestic retail refrigerator which isn't magnetic it's 300 series stainless, expensive and unnecessary. I've used enough 300 series stainless to fabricate food processing equipment in the food industry and know a thing or two about the stuff.

OK, I think I understand.  The existing inside (wood?) window frame is not flush with the cement board, it sticks out a bit.  Thus the tiles on the walls abutting the window have to slant out a bit to cover the edge of the window frame trim. This would be a problem with or without the Schluter.  The window frame trim really needs to be flush with the cement board.  So I'd either (1) pull out the trim, slice it down to be flush and re-install it, or (2) put in new pieces of trim that extend farther into the shower, so that the tiles can butt their cut edges up to it, no Schluter needed.  I t hink #2 is the better aesthetic choice. And btw, I'd use PVC boards, not wood, and make sure the 2x4 framing behind the trim is waterproofed.

There's more than one way to skin a cat and more than one way to approach a whole-house remodeling project. The traditional approach of hiring an architect, developing detailed plans and specifications, and then putting the completed plans out to bid isn't likely to be productive if you're in an area where demand for professional remodelers exceeds the supply.   That's the case in our market and I believe it is typical across most of the U.S. at the moment.  Plus, that approach doesn't provide any real-world cost information until after the plans have been completed and paid for.   Often, the prices are an unpleasant surprise when compared with the budget which puts the project into re-design mode. I recommend you assemble a team that will collaborate with you beginning in the design phase and continue through construction as needed.  That team should include an architect or experienced residential designer, your remodeler, and their various trade partners.  Your remodeler and his/her team should produce and refine cost estimates throughout the design process to avoid an unpleasant surprise at the end.   Here's a link to an article which describes the process as applied to the design and construction of an energy-efficient home: https://www.finehomebuilding.com/2014/05/14/a-better-approach-to-designbuild

Hi, you can't just apply a £2k/m2 rate, particularly with small jobs like this. The extra depth may not necessarially increase proportionately at the average rate if you keep within the span limits of the floor and roof elements (ie don't need a lot more additional foundations or structure, for example).   Also, it may not be as simple as 'getting a box frame steel in place'.  Big steels have big loads that of course only go down at the ends - your existing walls may not be able to take these higher loads so you can end up having to re-build these parts and/or make new foundations to take it.  This can all be time consuming, disruptive and complicated to install so the extra costs aren't just in the 'bit of steel'. If you have a builder in mind an early discussion about 2 options might help inform this. My point is that you need to consider the detail and therefore likely costs and consequences of what the engineering will be so that you can make a valued judgement on whether it is worth it or not. You might well come back to the steel being the right answer but at least then you'll know that.

I've built two homes, one from 1000 miles away and one around the corner. Both were positive experiences for me. I was also a realtor for ten years specializing in new builds (I was hired by the builder that built our home.) A few suggestions. One would be to look at home plans online to see if there are any existing ones that appeal to you and could be tweaked (cheaper than starting from scratch.) We liked the classic look of Don Gardener plans and ended up using one, but that was in 2005 and much may have changed. My neigbors built a custom home using an architect by planning out exactly what they wanted inside (open floor plan, # of bedrooms, mudroom, etc) and then having the architect put a cover on it, so to speak. Ask your builder if he is going to charge you for every change. Production home builders will kill you with change costs. My builders did not, but our changes were easy to do (again, plan and communicate about everything.) You will have a budget for everything (rugs, lighting, painting, fixtures, hollow doors vs solid...) and will go over budget in most things unless your taste is fairly generic. We based the purchase price on  a slightly lower budget and paid out of pocket for going over. For us, we didn't want to mortgage expensive chandeliers or faucets. Or higher quality rugs, more can lighting, etc. My biggest advice would be to choose all your materials, colors, finishes early in the process. Trust me, by the end of the build, when your builder is asking for backsplashes or paint colors, you will be so over it. Pay attention to the materials list. Note which kind of windows are being used. Same with number of can lighting, fans, etc.  Don't sign off on cheap stuff. Your base price should include quality windows, lumber, etc. If your builder uses builder grade windows and cabinets, find a different builder. Ask if a finished driveway is part of it (vs. roughted out and ready for paving). That cost was a surprise to us. Ask about landscaping. Does it include sod? A sprayed on lawn is all weeds. Most importantly go with the best builder you can afford. Ask realtors for recommendations. A good builder should be able to close on time (barring hurricanes and such). Use a builder who is part of the community and will be around for the punch list (there will always be a punch list.) Our builder was as honest as the day is long and helped with any issues we had for as long as we were there. (seven years.)  Once you find your builder and start building, let him do his job. Lastly, show us your plans! We love this stuff!

The reason for using a stem with a fading bloom is that new growth that has *just* flowered is at the right stage of maturity to make a viable cutting. You don't want to make a cutting of material that is either too young, or too mature, or your chances of it rooting are greatly lessened. The fading bloom is just a good indicator or ripeness of the wood immediately below, nothing else. It's a good way for beginners to learn what makes a good cutting. Once you are familiar with the best stage of growth from which to make a cutting, you can use wood from non-blooming wood that has reached the optimum stage of ripeness, from anywhere on the bush.

Not only that, but there are buffering effects. Weak acids and bases do not respond linearly to the addition of more acid or base. Most relevant to soil systems is the carbonate-bicarbonate equilibrium. Carbonate can exist in the form of insoluble carbonate salts like calcium carbonate, or dissolved carbonate and bicarbonate. And there's atmospheric CO2 as well.  The ratio between carbonate and bicarbonate in solution (in soil pore water) will depend on the pH.  But if you start adding acid or base, the pH of a carbonate system will not even change linearly. It has flat and steep places along the way. If you are creating something like the 5-1-1 mix that comes so frequently recommended for a multitude of container growing situations, peat plays a very small role....as it should :-) And the pH of peat is pretty variable, ranging from 3.0 to 4.5 so a strict formulaic application is not going to be all that helpful. The inclusion of the lime initially is to buffer the immediate acidity created by the use of the bark and the peat in the mix so that it does not shock newly potted plants that may not be accustomed to extremes. But the lime leaches out over time anyway and the media will approximate a more moderate level of acidity. The need for frequent fertilization negates any nutrient issues that might be impacted by a pH is that is slightly too high or too low. I am a big proponent of the 5-1-1, which I have used for many years as I find it ideal for just about any container planting situation. But instead of peat, I use a similar volume of a high quality potting mix (also heavy on the bark and very light on the peat) which is already pH buffered and I have never added any additional lime. I don't even own any lime :-) Granted, most of what I am growing are acid lovers or the vast majority of plants that prefer an acidic soil but I have never encountered any issues by omitting the lime altogether. btw, the recipe for the 5-1-1 suggests 1 Tbsp of dolomitic lime for every gallon of blended mix. westes, I have to admire your inquiring mind for wanting to nail down all the details involved with these soil issues. But I do think you tend to overwork them :-) Most plants have a high degree of flexibility and precision is just not necessary. Do you have a background in engineering?

It could very well be lack of water. Rhodies need plenty of water in late summer to fall when they set flower buds for the coming year. Lack of water at that time will result in flower buds not fully developing or aborting. Since the OP lives where there are few if any serious freezes, that is not the issue. Neither is excessive acidity - almost impossible to generate in a potted media and rhodies prefer and will tolerate a high level of acidity anyway. btw, fall blooming can be very common here and it does NOT affect the normal flowering cycle to any significant degree. Also not sure of the qualifications of the growers that suggested rock phosphate and boron but I would ignore them.  Per the American Rhododendron Society: "The popular perception that rhododendron and azalea flowering is enhanced by phosphorus is incorrect." For containerized rhodies, an all purpose fertilizer, preferably one formulated for acid loving plants, once or twice a season is sufficient. They require very little. For rhodies planted in the ground, if the soil pH is sufficiently acidic, you may never need to fertilize these plants! There are massive 50+ y.o. rhodies in my garden that I doubt have ever been fertilized. They bloom heavily and like clockwork.

In a raised bed, what are the reasons that you might prefer using bark over garden waste compost? Not all OM is created equal. In large part, it depends on whether or not the compost is finished. Unfinished compost can be expected to immobilize nitrogen (N). which often leads to the grower applying toxic levels of what nutrients are in fertilizers other than N, and structural changes related to a decrease in the size of soil particles. Conifer bark is rich in lignin and suberin, naturally occurring bipolymers that contribute to resistance of the breakdown of media particles, which limits N immobilization and breakdown of the particles. Hardwood bark generally does not contain as much of these bipolymers and breaks down faster, contributing to N immobilization. Hardwood bark is also related to pH spikes that occur during the breakdown of cellulose and other compounds that readily decay.   A handful of what is in my raised beds. It started as a mixture of bark/ sand, Turface, reed/ sedge peat. The image was taken about 10 years after the beds were made. My contributions to the contents of the beds over the years has been limited to only the media removed from the roots of plants during repotting sessions, which is based almost entirely on equal measures of conifer bark/ Turface/ granite or cherrystone. The medium remains so friable that I can plunge my hand into the soil to a depth of more than 6" with little resistance, yet it retains plenty of air, and moisture except during prolonged spells of hot/ dry/ windy summer weather when I might need to water every 4-5 days. A general rule is a raised bed needn't contain any more than 10-15% OM, and OM that breaks down slowly should be preferred. I would guess that the OM content of the soil currently in my RBs is in excess of 50%, and I'm extremely happy with how productive it is and has been. Al

"I fail to understand why an architect would frown on having a client come to them with ideas." While I don't encourage clients to come to me with a floor plan, it happens all the time, whether a canned internet plan, something drawn out on graph paper or a SketchUp model. And if they already have that I don't say "Don't show me that!", I take a look at it but probably unknown to the person is I'm looking at it differently than the way they are probably looking at it. I'm looking at it as more of a general diagram of adjacencies and desired relationships as opposed to, as you wrote "The dining room looks small, and we will confirm layout of kitchen to make sure all appliances fit." . Really a sort of bubble diagram if you know what those are. That way I'm leaving open in my mind the potential for possibilities that the owner hasn't considered. And typically we end up with something different than the floor plan they brought in my door. But back to your quote above.....coming in with an exact floor plan is a little bit of a slippery slope because the owner may be overly committed to it "But we've spent MONTHS on this!", etc. which is ok but then they don't need me and I'll refer them to a permit drafter because any good architect's job is to look at alternatives. A good architect, when given the chance, will provide a design that can give a client everything they want, but often in ways completely unexpected. But for that to happen it takes a critical element necessary on the part of the client in every successful project and that element is trust and some of the things you wrote above maybe indicates a closed mind to different possibilities and alternatives but I'm only speculating. Often during our initial meeting, the client will reveal their ability or inability to trust others. If I feel the element of trust is not there they will likely be referred to a permit drafter. A creative person should explore other approaches with you in the spirit of "That's great but have you thought of this.......". But for that to be carried forward successfully it takes a trusting client to not only allow the architect to expand on alternative ideas but to objectively look at other approaches in a collaborative effort with the architect. And that's an intangible that all successful projects are born out of. Just be ready to expect any preconceived ideas to be questioned if you do in fact go with a creative partner. They may turn out to be perfectly valid but at least they've been evaluated against alternates as any good architect should do. Finally, regarding preconceived ideas, I've quoted on this board before these two quotes by two creative people..... Henry Ford observed "If I had asked people what they wanted they would have told me "A faster horse". And Steve Jobs mused “A lot of times, people don't know what they want until you show it to them. Everyone wanted an iPhone when they first appeared, but no one could have described what they wanted before seeing one". So put trust in your architect to carry you through the process in the spirit of Mr. Ford and Mr. Jobs and you'll have a home that is the very best. And speaking of the best, here's wishing you the best of luck with your project. Exciting times!

Being from Vermont we never had cornbread stuffing, but I do make it, just not on holidays, cuz, you know, tradition. My stuffing is a lot like my grandmother’s, but I use more veggies and herbs, and she used sausage, which I don’t care for, so don’t use. Saute a head of celery (it’s a head, right?) cut into 1/4” slices and 2 large onions cut similarly in butter and olive oil until soft and translucent. For the last couple of minutes of sauteeing add a large bunch of chopped flat leaf parsley, at least 12 chopped sage leaves, at least 12 sprigs of chopped fresh thyme and two of those wasteful plastic herb packages of chopped fresh summer savory. Let cool. Meanwhile, toast 3 loaves of best quality, dense, chewy (no wonder bread) white, sourdough or wheat bread. I use a mix of all, plus assorted bread leftovers that end up in the freezer. When cooled, tear toasted bread into 1-2” pieces, dump sauteed herbs and veggies into the bowl with the bread and mix well with your hands. Add about 2 cups of homemade or best quality chicken or veggie broth and a cup or so of whole milk, half and half, cream or oat milk and mix together with your hands until it’s uniformly moist, almost spongy, adding more liquid as needed. Taste and salt and pepper to taste, sometimes I add walnuts and that’s also tasty. Butter a large casserole dish and smush the stuffing down well (it compresses nicely) and bake at 300-350 for an hour +-. I would like to give this rubber tree some attention. At a glance, it's clear the plant wants much more light than it's getting. This plant starts life in the forest understory, striving to reach the canopy where it can soak up its share of tropical sun. Only then will it begin to realize the lion's share of the potential it was endowed with by Mother Nature. Question 1: Every time I water (which is not often) it drops a leaf - typically on that right branch (which is why its so leggy) What is the common cause of this? First, there is no direct relationship between a watering session and the loss of 1 leaf, as in one watering = 1 lost leaf. If it seems so, it's a coincidence. There are several common potential causes of shedding, in no particular order, are, Over/under-watering, root congestion (rootbound), low fertility - particularly a deficiency of nitrogen, a radicle change in light from more to less, sudden chill. Zeroing in on the most likely cause is often a process of elimination. If your plant has never wilted from lack of water. shedding isn't being caused by under-watering. If your plant has ever wilted while the soil was still conspicuously moist the shedding could easily be related to over-watering. If you haven't fertilized in a long time, it could be a result of one or more nutritional deficiencies, if you fertilize regularly, you still might have nutritional issues depending on what you actually fertilized with and your watering habits. Leaf loss could easily be related to low light levels, given we recently got beyond the shortest day of the year (21 Dec, if you live in the N Hemisphere). You probably have some idea if sudden chill/cold drafts are a part of the equation. Have you inspected the roots to asses their condition? Tight roots can sap almost 100% of your plant's growth potential, limit its level of vitality severely, cause it to look rather forlorn and cause leaf shedding to boot. question(s) 2: How should I prune and propagate the branch to the right? If you're thinking doing either now, you shouldn't ..... if you're looking at things from the perspective of what's best for the plant and/or what will provide the best results. Each leaf is a food factory where photosynthesis takes place and the plants true food, sugar/glucose, is made. Removing all leaves from the stem/branch now pretty much ensures a super long recovery and a very unenthusiastic response to the pruning. Also, whether or not a cutting strikes (roots) depends in very large part on how much stored energy the propagule has. Weak cuttings are the least likely to prove successful. Even layering the plant now would take an inordinately long time. It would be much better if you planned ahead and did all your work in June, again that's if you live in the N Hemisphere. I'd put the plant outdoors as soon as temps are reliably above 55* and shoot for doing the pruning, a repot, and starting the cuttings around Father's Day. You'll get a much more enthusiastic response and recovery time should take only a small fraction of the time it would take if you do it now. Ecclesiastes 3:1 "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." If I cut, say, 12" from the soil, will it produce new growth from that cut? You can cut anywhere on the stem - as low as you want. Then I'd trim the majority of that stem and propagate the top? That will work. What would you do with that branch? I wouldn't follow the same path you're on. I would use all 3 trunks. The one on the left, with the most foliage, would be cut back .... maybe to the leaf that is 'touched' by the bottom right corner of the picture frame in the image. The one on the right would be cut back so it's about 2/3 of the ht of the left branch, and the short trunk would be cut back to 1/2-2/3 the ht of the right branch. If your intent is to REALLY chop the plant back hard, or you're set on a 2-trunk composition, forget what I said about 3 trunks. Al

I am a fabricator.  When we bid a job in quartzite the processing time in the fab shop is roughly three times the hours a typical stone requires.  Additionally, quartzite consumes the diamond tooling at a much higher rate that typical stone.  It is highly unlikely a 70 sq. ft. job can be done with a single slab so that is probably the difference.  If your stone is purchased specifically for your job and not from the fabricators inventory then your job has a high waste factor.  Expecting the fabricator to charge you only for the portion of the 2nd slab used on your job is unreasonable because the remnant cannot be assumed to be used on another job in the same stone as there is no guarantee it will match.  The remnant will probably be sold but the fabricator doesn't get full slab pricing on a remnant, even one of quartzite.  This is why it is highly advantageous for the customer to use a fabricator that has a substantial inventory as the partial slabs, even of quartzite, can be returned to inventory to be used on the next job in that stone.

I really like 'cake' gingerbread, and I make gingerbread cookies for the holidays every year. I use a recipe from an old cookbook my mom got in the 50s called  'Cooking For Christmas'. Everything is stirred together in 1 bowl, easy peasy. I often use part honey or maple syrup, since I prefer organic and the only organic molasses I can find is very dark - too dark to use all by itself. I like to use fresh grated ginger too. I think it has a lot more flavor than the powdered kind. The cookies come out pretty crisp, but once they're iced, they get softer. I need to get my cooky doughs made, actually, but I've been holding off because I have a cold and don't want to spread the joy. Here's the recipe: Gingerbread Men from 'Cooking for Christmas', 1950 1/2 c. sugar 1/2 c. shortening (butter) 1 unbeaten egg 3/4 c. molasses (1/2 cup honey, 1/4 cup molasses) 1 tsp. soda 1 tsp. cinnamon 1 tsp. cloves 1 tsp. salt 2 tsp. ginger (1 Tbs. finely grated fresh) 2 tsp. vinegar 3-3 1/2 c. flour Combine all the ingredients except the flour & stir until thoroughly mixed. Add enough flour to make a fairly stiff dough. Divide into 2-3 parts to make rolling out easier. Wrap in waxed paper & chill in the refrigerator overnight. Roll out quite thin & cut into shapes. Bake on parchment @ 375F - 8-10 minutes. Decorate as desired. I make a white icing with cream and powdered sugar and a bit of vanilla, and pipe thin lines to decorate, rather than a solid layer over the whole cooky. Or I simply sprinkle with coarse sugar before baking. I've never built anything out of gingerbread, but I imagine this recipe would work, since the results are very sturdy. Ann Reardon has some good tutorials for building gingerbread. She uses melted white chocolate instead of royal icing to stick things together, IIRC.

I've never known a builder to supply kitchen appliances. You're thinking of the 25% contractor markup as an extra but if the allowance amount had been accurately estimated, that cost would already be in the allowance. The real problem is 25% is very high and might be inflated above the builder's normal OH&P % but it might also be due to the local market .... something to deal with up front when first interviewing contractors. Another problem is who the builder buys from; you'll never know the subcontractor or supplier's markup and often there is no competitive pricing. This process is unique to homebuilding; a commercial project would require competitive sub contractor/supplier bids for allowances similar to a Cost P;us contract. At any rate, pick out as much as possible now or supply it yourself and avoid allowances. Also, you should be carrying a healthy contingnecy in your budget.  Its not possible to predict the final cost of a building.

Your heating in Kansas was probably natural gas, where as your heat now is electric strip resistance heat, one of the most expensive forms of heat. If that comment is true as I suspect of course your heating costs will be more now. The other is difference in utility rates what you pay per KWH in Kansas vs what you pay in MS. A 5 KW heat strip will pull roughly 20 amps. You have 10 so that's in the realm of 40 amps just for the heat strips. A run of the mill AC might be in the realm of 15-20amps (outside condenser). So under those circumstances it's not hard to pay more for heat than you do cooling.  You're pulling more than double the power when you run the heat.

@margretg2 This is true that the majority of shaker kitchen doors have a solid timber frame, if its painted than its usually an ash frame, but the centre panel is an oak or ash veneer. This is because the panel is thinner and if it was a solid timber it could be prone to movement so being a veneered mdf or chipboard means a more stable door. Neptune use a hardwood ply for their centre panels (according to their brochure-also in their brochure they say that they've moved some of their production to a purpose built facility in China) Other factors to look for in a quality shaker frame is along the tenon joints, a cheaper door has a V groove along the joint as this masks any assembly defects and any hairline cracks due to movement that may appear over time. A smooth tenon joint is completely flat/smooth and can be reinforced with dowels to help prevent any later movement. Also consider with timber is how the log is cut. There's 3 main ways timber is cut for furniture. The cheapest timber cut is plainsawn and has the cathedral arch characteristics and is just slices along the length of the log, this is more prone to movement/splitting (but is used with walnut to display the natural woodgrain). Quarter sawn (traditional and modern cut) is a more expensive way to cut logs but is ideal for oak giving a straight grain and is used for quality furniture especially if its to be lacquered. Finally there's rift sawn which is the most expensive cut and characterized for its clean sleek lines.

We went to Panama first, and stayed in the old town. We stayed in a very cool hotel on a town square. The building had been a department store in the 1930s. Rang in the new year (literally) with beautiful church bells. Unfortunately they also rang every 15 minutes starting at 6am, haha. The canal was very interesting. The new city is a huge, sprawling snazzy skyline. The old city is still mid-gentrification, shall we say, but had some superb dining. Did a fun bike ride on an 8 mile causeway with great views. Also took a longboat trip into the countryside to visit with an indigenous tribe. We then flew to Medellin. Very large sprawling city in a beautiful valley surrounded by the Andes mountains. Jungly-vegetation even in the downtown. Cool/hip upscale shopping and dining.Our first hotel choice was not quite to our liking (all three rooms looked onto cinderblock walls!) but we found an excellent alternate easily. Very interesting tour of the "Comuna 13", which I guess one could call a gentrifying shantytown built in the side of a hill, covered with graffiti, or murals, depending on your POV. The neighborhood is so steep it is the equivalent of a 28 story building. Outdoor escalators and cable cars were added to better integrate with central Medellin. Botero park has 24  of his famous sculptures; go after lunch or you won't be hungry anymore, LOL. We took one day trip to a flower farm and another day trip to a whimsically painted mountain village. On the way to the village we had a tour and lunch at a coffee plantation.  On both trips we ate lunch in their homes and got to meet the families, which was so nice. On to Cartagena, where we had a wonderful private villa in the old town, with a courtyard pool. The President of Colombia was staying across the street  the whole time we were there, so our road was closed off (very nice!). The city's architecture and greenery and churches and squares could not be more charming, and again, a very hip, upscale dining and shopping scene. We took a daytrip on a boat to snorkel in the Rosarios Park. We also took private salsa lessons as a family, which was a hoot. As always, so glad to be home. I was so craving toast! PS Thanks to Jojo for recommending a tour co in the area. I don't usually use one, but in this case I wanted a relationship with a local co. in case we ran into any COVID issues. It was also a good idea because English was not that common, and of the 5 of of us, only 1 knows Spanish. She was great, Jojo.  My family is like "wait, what? where did you hear about this person again? huh?" LOL

On the first day of Seal training, McRaven and 150 other students stood at attention. The main instructor offered some initial words: “Today is the first day of Seal training. For the next six months you will undergo the toughest course of instruction in the United States military.” Apprehension was visible on the faces of the new trainees. The instructor also added, “You will be tested like no time in your life,” and that, “Most of you will not make it through. I will see to that.” In full view of the new “tadpoles” was a brass bell hanging in the large asphalt courtyard. The instructor explained that to escape all the misery, “All you have to do to quit is ring this bell three times.” “Ring the bell and you wont have to get up early. Ring the bell and you wont have to do the long runs, the cold swims, or the obstacle course. Ring the bell and you can avoid all this pain.” He also had another message: “If you quit, you will regret it for the rest of your life. Quitting never makes anything easier.” Out of all the lessons that McRaven learned in Seal training, he said that this message was the most important. Life is hard and there are forces that will try to break us down, but if we stand tall and strong against the odds, then life will be what we make of it, and we have the power to make it great. No matter what happens, never, ever, ring the bell!

I post the below all the time. Anything in bold is what is not working with your house plans. The best houses orient the public rooms towards the south for the best passive solar heating and cooling The best houses are L, U, T, H, or I shaped. The best houses are only one to two rooms deep. And covered lanai, porches, garages, etc count as rooms in this case. The best houses make sure kitchens have natural light, meaning windows so one doesn't have to have lighting 24/7 to use the kitchen. (And no, dining areas with windows 10' or more from the kitchen will not allow for natural light.) The best houses make sure all public rooms and bedrooms have windows on at least two walls. The best houses do not if possible put mechanical rooms, pantries or closets on outside walls The best houses keep public and private spaces separate. The best houses do not have you walk through the work zone of the kitchen to bring laundry to the laundry room. The best houses do not have the mudroom go through any of the work zones of the kitchen. The best houses do not use the kitchen as a hallway to any other rooms. The best houses do not put toilets or toilet rooms up against bedroom walls or dining areas. The best houses do not have walk in closets too small to stand inside. The best houses have an organizing “spine” so it’s easy to determine how to get from room to room in the house and what makes sense. If you have not already read Sarah Susanka's book, The Not So Big House, I highly recommend it no matter what size house you are building. And, I disagree about the value of an architect. You're afraid to spend $50,000+ for one, but a talented architect in the long run will save you that and more in terms of how the house works, lives and all the things you DO NOT know about building a house. Unless of course your background is in design. In reality, you can't afford NOT to hire a person of design talent. I know this info is hard to hear especially when you worked so hard on your plans. However it's like falling in love with the wrong man. If you marry him, your life will not be easier but instead you'll always be making accomodations for him.

Hello Jennifer, Engineered wood flooring is much more stable with moisture changes due to the plywood core and the thinner layer of hardwood on the top.  However it will still move in response to moisture changes, just at a slower rate.  https://www.woodco.com/news/what-you-need-to-know-before-buying-an-engineered-wood-floor/ We have installers in dry climates like Arizona that no longer install engineered but rather go with a solid plank.  This is because the low humidity levels was causing the wood to shrink, but with the stable plywood core, the wear layer of hardwood was shrinking at a different rate than the plywood and causing splitting issues. Unfortunately, the long-hailed performance attributes of cedar shake have disappeared along with old-growth trees. If it's what you really want, go into it with your eyes open. Cedar shingles, whether roofing or siding, take regular maintenance to maximize their lifespan, eventually becoming brittle. Be aware that the color will change continuously over time. How quickly the decay occurs will depend on climate and many other factors. Direct sun will dry them out somewhat faster, but constant dampness and strong freeze/thaw cycles are also harmful. Wood has low resistance to fire, insects, and other issues so insurance rates can be high. Unless you live in an area where it is a common or required material, it can be harder to sell a home with wood shingles. If you love the look, but not the downsides, consider a synthetic shingle, like DaVinci (one of our favorites for roofing) or even fiber-cement like James Hardie. As to color, it comes down to personal preference, filtered through any local or HOA regulations.

"...any ideas on cost to switch regular indoor outlets to gfci?" Yes. A gfci receptacle costs $12-$15. You turn off  the breaker to the existing receptacle, disconnect the wires, and reconnect them to the gfci receptacle. It has the same connections as a regular receptacle. The technology is built in to the gfci receptacle, and there is nothing special or complicated about it. If you have a screwdriver,  you should be able to do this. A lot of people offering land contracts are not going to offer a promissory note and mortgage over a land contract. Land contracts can be a great tool to transfer property when there is significant risk of non-payment.  For a seller the big difference is that land contracts don't require a foreclosure, but instead require a forfeiture.  Forfeitures are much cheaper and typically don't require an auction, so they allow a seller to take a risk on someone and have little exposure if that risk doesn't pan out.  You spend a few thousand on an attorney, go to court and remove the other person's ownership interest, no seizure of property, no sheriff's auction, no massive attorney fees. Some states have straight forfeitures, no matter how much you have paid or how much the property is worth, you simply forfeit your ownership interest in the property.  Many states have a limit to the amount of paid in equity that can be forfeited.  For example, my state caps the loss at the greater of 20% of paid in equity or the attorney fees in a forfeiture.  Few states allow for recovery of appreciated or improved equity, so anything you built on the land is usually forfeit. The problem with land contracts is that the tools that help limit their risk for sellers also enable exploitation by those preying on the less fortunate.  In my experience land contracts only turn out favorable when there is an existing relationship.  A family member helping out another family member, or in my case, a landlord letting a long-term renter buy the house they have been renting.  Rarely have I seen fair and legitimate land contracts from typical arms length transactions.  When I see the words land contract, I assume some sort of exploitation. In any case, someone offering a land contract might not want to carry a mortgage, especially with rates this low.

Your rights and responsibilities are set forth by the contract and your state's statutes. We often see land contracts that only transfer equitable interest, that is the standard for land only in my area.  So in my area, building a house on a land contract parcel is usually just about as easy as building a house on any parcel of land that you don't own. ETA: let me be clear, no one can answer your question.  There are certain things that your state probably mandates, but other than that land contracts can contain a wide variety of provisions.  I have seen cancellable land contracts, where the seller can pay out the equity and reclaim the land.  I have seen land contracts that transfer ownership immediately and put in a buyback provision.  An attorney in your area can probably get you a contract that will work for you if that is what you want.

You don't say what you're making or exactly what kind of marks need to be done. In factories, there are tiny snips in the fabric at the seam allowances and tiny holes drilled into the fabric about one-quarter inch (I think) short of the end of the dart.  I poke holes with an awl sometimes, always in the seam allowance. Sometimes I put a large glass headed pin in to mark something, and press it with an iron and steam and use the impression the head made for my mark. (Works okay on solid fabric, not so great on prints.) You could pin it and mark the pin head with chalk, too. Sometimes I bite the bullet and use tailor's tacks. I agree about the tracing paper. It isn't what it used to be. It didn't always wash out, either. But *both* sides of the fabric? No, it should only be used on the *wrong* side of the fabric.

If you need drapes, then I would use a fabric that has more fluid drape and less stiffness and mount the rod at the ceiling. Silk is beautiful but make sure it has a lot of drape but I think silk is too formal with the fabrics you've selected. Linen might work but it's really to do with how the fabric hangs rather than what it's made of.

The question is a bit odd. There is no distinct point where a coating is no longer a paint and if you are trying to make that distinction then cabinets haven't really been painted for a long time... like in the last 100 years.  Technically a paint is purely decorative and a coating is protective, but that is a ridiculous distinction. As to the question you asked... It is a bit complicated.  Conversion varnish is just a lacquer with solid contents high enough that it needs a stronger acid to catalyze.  So they replaced nitrocellulose with Xylene (which is basically synthetic formaldehyde).  Any paint that is marketed as a non-xylene (or equivalent) conversion varnish is not really conversion varnish... it is just marketing, however, it can still be a good coating. In America, in order to get Xylene emissions to acceptable levels we bind the Xylene molecules to slow down their release, this means that cabinets off-gas for much longer but at lower levels overall.  In Europe, binding the Xylene was not allowed and so European companies began developing alternatives. That alternative, 2k polyurethanes, are now pushing conversion varnish out of the U.S. market as they are not only better for you, they are also a better product.  Today, most companies are switching to 2k poly's and so no... everyone doesn't use conversion varnish. --- There are many products you can get a brush stroke in, including conversion varnishes and 2k poly's.  The coatings can look plasticky or not depending on your preference and the particular product.
