System will be heat pump/gas furnace combo. This is also called a dual fuel system. It is more expensive than a gas furnace and AC only system. The primary advantage of a dual fuel system is being able to switch to furnace or heat pump heating depending on the cost of gas or electricity. If you post the gas and electric rates a calculation can be done to determine which fuel is cheaper with today's prices. Seattle has mild winters and summers. I am not sure if you really need to spend the money on a dual fuel fully variable or modulating HVAC system. The list you provided is very nice but they are going to be expensive.

How much heat and how much flexibility you need depends on many things, but I trust an honest load calc will be prepared. How well insulated your old house is or isn't how tight it is or isn't., etc. I'd thought the Greenspeed-type heat pumps were for places where frequent sub-freezing temps were common. I suspect your money will be better spent with a more conventional, less expensive heat pump (performance wise) and a gas furnace for a boost. The gas furnace can also help recovery from overnight setbacks if that's something you prefer, as many do. A heat pump can struggle to recover from more than a few degrees of setback. I'm a fellow homeowner though I've bought two completely new systems for my two homes in the last 4 years. You're looking at top brands, that was something I preferred too. Recognize they have different lines (and different tags) that can affect price and, to a lesser extent, features. I wound up getting Bryant equipment in both places - the same as Carrier, same models, slightly lower cost. In the old days, like GM making Cadillac vs Chevrolet. Beyond that, the good advice I got was that the name on the workers shirts means more than the names on the equipment. Meaning - choose the contractor by reputation and recommendations and pay less attention to the equipment they provide. You're buying a service as much as hardware and a top contractor can make a system out of lower quality equipment perform well, where a lower quality contractor can take top equipment and make a mess of it. Good luck.

1. Does anyone have experience with any of these systems, or know of any reason to go with one brand over another (specifically with respect to this type of system). Of these major brands you list, some may limit the variable nature of which these systems are capable of. Not sure if they still do this or not, but the Carrier models of the recent past limited their models to 5 speeds. Things change with time, so these models may no longer be made. The other is proprietary controls. Some you can use older controls at a cost to performance as in most cases using older controls will turn the machine into a two speed machine. None of these brands AFAIK or can prove make the parts "namely the compressor" -- that drive these units. Nearly every part that makes the machine run are made in other countries and at best are merely "assembled" in the US. If the pandemic has taught me anything... assembled in the USA is NOT the same thing as "made in the USA". Whether you buy a fully variable speed AC (Inverter) or not, these things are the same for lesser models. 2. In particular, does anyone have experience with the proprietary thermostats that you use with each? This is my biggest reservation. You need to use the communicating thermostat that goes with the system, and I am concerned about that kind of proprietary tech from a company that isn't in that business. There are all sorts of reviews that the thermostats are incredibly buggy, updating constantly, and the tech is clunky. Why nearly all major brands chose to take this approach to control their upper end variable (inverter) systems I believe is partly to cut out the nests, and ecobees of the world. But with that comes trouble. Namely expense and as you suggest buggy kinds of problems. There is another brand of Inverter that doesn't do it this way. All you need is a simple 24 volt signal and the "smarts" is in the outdoor condenser. (Bosch) Another brand that has gotten away from proprietary thermostats is Amana. However the Amana will require the Amana furnace paired for their inverter as the furnace contains the communicating functions to communicate with the outdoor inverter. Communicating is buggy for similar problems that make your internet connection go down. Because they use thermostat wire connecting parts and pieces of the system to the "network" that runs or tells the AC system "what to do". So any connection problem or interference can cause intermittent "communication problems". The Bosch Inverter solves those problems completely. As it's doesn't rely on communicating the way the big box boys chose to do it. The problem? Bosch is a disruption type technology. There is risk when competing with goliaths in the industry, for fear they squash you like a bug. The manufacturer or "owner if you will" of Bosch tech, doesn't make the unit they designed. They went out hired a manufacturer to make it so it's German engineered and made in China. Currently Bosch are back ordered here and have been for months... but you may find the same thing when dealing with major names as many of these parts made to make these systems come from place like China and elsewhere. 3. There seems to be a lot of advice that the installation/installer matters more than the system in many ways. Installation matters. In the realm of variable speed AC systems / heat pumps (Inverter driven) -- This equipment is expensive, requires a good amount of knowledge above that of installing a traditional single or two speed machine. In the communicating realm of machines one must also know what causes networks to go down and be able to fix those problems in addition to everything else we must know. Some HVAC companies that don't get into these Inverter driven or "proprietary controlled" things are more likely to try and talk you out of it. They are also dangerous --- touch the wrong thing the right way and you could become a krispy creme. While one could argue a simple single speed system is also dangerous. ----------------------------- I chose the Bosch Inverter for my own home in Katy, Texas in October of 2019. I don't regret that choice yet. Reasons: cut my electric bill in half. Does a much better job dehumidifying. In a more mild climate like Seattle... I believe this choice has more to do with electricity costs and better over all comfort. Many parts on the west coast pay a higher utility rate so these machines can pay for themselves over time and use.

Jason, From years of experience with most varieties of Holly I suggest you do the following. Select and tag the young trees you wish to move. This is the perfect time of year for the next step before the snow falls. Using a transplanting shovel, root prune around each young plant about 12 " from the trunk. Make those cuts straight down....do not try to lift the trees in any manner. Next spring, early March, begin the transplanting project which is pretty standard. Plan to dig and replant each little tree one at a time, placing the dug root ball on a section of burlap or old blanket. At this point I like to have a strong-back companion and together we will walk the tree to its new location gently, decide how large a hole to dig and settle it in firmly. I do not like to   leave them sitting in a deep, concave water collecting area, especially if you have clay soil. Everything in moderation. If all the leaves fall off, don't give up. Wait and observe the green buds that may form close to the trunk. If this happens prune just ahead of those buds and the tree will recover and grow normally.

This water, 'perched water', is extremely limiting whenever it is present in a medium. Water is best held inside of media particles with open pores - bark, Turface, calcined DE, ....., on the surface of all particles, and at the interface where soil particles contact each other, leaving the large spaces between the particles filled with air. A critical aspect of the formulation when there is a wide size gradient between the particles, is that there should NOT be enough fine material to fill all the spaces between particles larger than .100" (1/10"), which is the size at which a medium is incapable of holding perched water. Nah, the porcelain is definitely cracked through there. Unfortunately, this is a fairly common problem on electric ovens with the heating element under the floor (which is most high end ovens these days). The heat is very intense and can exacerbate the effect of any corrosive foods etc. that might fall on the bottom. With this type of oven, it's always a good idea to use a cookie sheet or whatever to protect the bottom from corrosive spills, and if one does happen, wipe it up ASAP (as soon as the oven cools down) and especially before running self clean (ideally keeping the number of self clean cycles to a minimum to minimize heat stress on the bottom). Whether you get it fixed is up to you. You would want to wipe the oven to make sure there aren't remaining flecks of porcelain that could be blown by the convection fan (food safety!), and that it isn't chipping further. Watch out for your fingers, porcelain shards can be sharp! Since the protective porcelain is missing in those cracks, if something corrosive is spilled on that area in the future, it could be a long term problem in terms of the oven bottom rusting out. To get it fixed, either call an appliance servicer who works on Thermador (if you can't find one on the internet I'm sure Thermador would be happy to help you find one in your area by calling them) or post your model number here so we can lookup parts if you want to give a go at replacing the bottom yourself (this isn't possible on all models, but it looks like it might be on yours).

"Filler panels should match door finish?" It depends on the cabinet style. Full overlay cabinets have doors that cover the frames completely; partial overlay cabinets have doors that sit over the frames but don't cover them completely; and inset cabinets have doors that sit flush with the frames. With partial overlay or inset, the filler is just part of the frame. With a full overlay, if the filler doesn't come up to the level of the door, it would be the only part at frame level. That's not necessarily a problem, but if one wanted everything flush, similarto the look of inset, one could add trim pieces to the fillers in order to bring them up to the level of the doors.

Some more info:I’m in zone 10a, Southern California.  I hand water at the base of the plant when there’s been no rain (there usually isn’t any rain here, especially the last few years). This is an own root rose, planted in this big ceramic pot when I got it over a year ago, so this is only its second year with me. I didn’t prune in January like I do for my other roses because it’s so young, but I did defoliate the plant completely and spray copper and dormant oil in January to help control for fungus and insects that may have overwintered. I fertilized with osmocote in early February, and I give it a weak liquid organic fertilizer every few weeks as a supplement — fish emulsion and/or liquid seaweed. I gave everything, including this plant, a drink of alfalfa tea over a month ago. One plant got a little chlorosis directly after, but not this one, don’t know if it’s related. The LoS in the same soil mix I make for my other roses in pots — a mix of dr. earth and lots of perlite and some other stuff — and the mulch on top is a mint compost I buy in bulk from heirloom roses and have used to great effect on my other roses in pots for years. I haven’t repotted since it first went in the pot over a year ago. I cleared the old compost and topped up with a bit more soil, then gave it new compost about two months ago when I did the other dormant season routines. The area it lives in is a gated portion of my driveway, full sun with east and south exposure, and I’m on a corner lot so there are no nearby neighbors and nobody has access to walk up to it. The other roses in nearby pots are doing great and show no sign of damage or disease (knock on wood) so I don’t think it’s spray coming from anywhere nearby. I don’t think it’s aged leaves — all the leaves on the plant are very young, having emerged in the last few months since I defoliated in January. The plant currently has rosebuds set — probably ten or so. Until I noticed these leaves the plant was doing fantastic. There were a few other diseased/damaged leaflets that fell off on their own, I picked them out of the mulch and threw them away. I’ve battled aphids with a hose and ladybugs I bring home from the garden store, but so far haven’t had to use sprays. Nothing about it has changed recently aside from the weather — we’ve had a run of cold snaps and heat waves here but it never dips below frost. For instance one weekend in February it hit 90F, the next weekend the lows were back in the low 40s. Winds when the weather changes here are hot and dry and gusty (The “Santa Anas” as they’re called if you live down here too). It’s possible I overwatered? I usually only water when the soil is dry, and then I water until the water trickles out the bottom of the pot. It’s on pot feet for maximum drainage. Normally in winter that means I water a couple times a week, but we did have a few heat waves where I had to water every couple days. Thank you all for your time and thought!

text: RMV seems to be the most likely explanation for the yellowed leaves.  Spring weather triggers RMV symptoms, and it is definitely the correct season now.  Also, Austin's have come already infected with the virus in the past.  There have been RMV infected roses sold by Austin, and if my memory is correct, no redress was forthcoming from Austin to satisfactorily compensate purchasers of  those infected (defective product), roses back then. The standard procedure rose gardeners take when a RMV is discovered is to continue giving the infected bush good care, and to disinfect pruning tools used on the bush immediately  after each and every pruning the bush gets. This keeps the virus from spreading to healthy roses. The second possibility is over watering, which causes root rot and subsequent yellowing of the oldest leaves on the bush's stems before they drop off.   Accidental over watering is especially  easy to do when a rose, or any plant, is container grown. The natural  potting soil layer of perched water that's present toward the bottom of the container of all plant growing containers, can easily be made too moisture retentive if over watered.  Correct the over watering, and new roots should make a comeback where they died in the perched water growing medium layer. However, if the potting medium is too moisture retentive in the first place, the perched water layer will be very hard to manage properly, and root rot, leading to yellowing of the bush's oldest leaves followed by them dropping off, can be a chronic issue. Moses

Source: https://agrilifeextension.tamu.edu/library/landscaping/mosaic-virus-of-roses/ "Rose mosaic virus and most other rose viruses are not spread by insects or pruning tools. They infect roses through budding, grafting, or rooting cuttings from infected plants." What's "possible" is commonly limited by the amount of money you'd like to spend. First things first ... to have a bathroom, you need both a soilpipe (drain) and water supply pipes. The drains must be connected to your main one, which from your floorplan looks like it is at the back of the house, in or near the current bathroom. So wherever you place the bathroom/ensuite, the drains must run from there. The water supply ... there's a "cupboard" marked upstairs. Is that empty or does it actually contain a hot water cylinder and/or the boiler ? In the kitchen, where is the sink ? I can basically think of two options (sizes of components not "true" only indicative for placement):   One is a (really) small ensuite, given you'd have to take the drains to the rear, most likely for the rear bedroom. The space indicated there would re-use the existing cupboard; if that contains a hot water cylinder and/or boiler, this choice would mean you'd have to replace the heating system first (to a mains-fed combi boiler then to be located downstairs). You'd probably need a pocket door as this space is only about ~0.8m x 2m internally, and a door swinging inwards would take too much space. The downpipe would go through the ceiling into the kitchen below and probably be boxed in along the left side of the room all the way to the rear. Second is a "normal" bathroom, around 1.5m wide and 3m long. For this the pipework could be laid outside, on the rear of the house. It'd fit a 700mm x 1700mm bath. You'd use a normal door. Neither would, in the simplest case, have a window. You therefore would need to provision for a fan / extractor. For the centrally-located, probably straight up through the main roof, in the rear, just through the wall. Or, for the rear, have a new opening made and a window fitted (my recommend if you go for this, it makes a difference in so many ways). It all depends what your situation is wrt. to existing pipework, and what preferences are. Talk to a planner / bathroom installer ?

Paul, kudos for keeping it alive in a challenging climate!  It sounds like it’s mature enough but lacking the long period of optimal conditions to bloom. Repot into a larger pot now, too.  Switch to a balanced slow-release fertilizer.  9-58-8 is not for flowering trees like plumerias, but annuals like petunias. My recommendation would be to have an HVAC company come out and take a look at it while it goes through its’ cycle. Some issues can only be found and repaired with specialized tools. Also, getting a maintenance done on it would be a good idea. (Checking gas pressures, clearing condensate lines, checking components are within proper voltage, amps, ohms, etc, cleaning burners, making sure flue has no blockages, proper airflow, etc). sometimes the burner will do it's initial ignition (small orange flame) and then extinguishes itself with a kind of huffing sound instead of lighting up fully (blue flame) for proper heating. I noticed the gas line is connected copper tubing. This is not good if the furnace is using natural gas. The gas line should the same black pipe as the elbow in the picture. The pipe should have a drip leg to catch any debris. The fact the burner is having problems could be a sign of debris getting into the gas valve orifice. You should have a licensed plumber fix this and the piping to the hot water heater. Have you inspected the exhaust flue for blockages? Did any of the techs suggest replacing the pressure switch? The condensation theory is plausible. But if it were a condensation drainage problem then I would think it would happen even with short heating cycles and more frequently. The only way to solve intermittent problems is to be able to reproduce them when the HVAC tech is present. If you can figure out hot to make the furnace reliably fail then you have a chance of solving the problem.

Thanks for the response. All the electrics and gas pressures were all fine when checked by the previous technicians. No apparent blockages in air flow or condensate lines that could be found. The error code is listed in the manual as "Pressure Switch Failed to Close or Opened on Heat Demand". So pretty vague. There's lots of things that can cause a pressure switch to fail to operate properly. Next thing to try is a new pressure switch I suppose. But I can't shake the feeling that the pressure switch isn't the problem since sometimes it works just fine.

It’s possible that the pressure switch could be failing, but in the long run you may be just be replacing parts that don’t need to be replaced. It is possible to bypass the pressure switch and see if the furnace operates normally but that is not a task that should be performed by the average homeowner without knowledge of the furnace or electricity. I would refer back to my previous recommendation to have an HVAC company perform troubleshooting/maintenence on your furncace and do not let them leave without cycling heat several times. If it fails after that, document and call the company back. Make sure to get a breakdown of any and all work done.

I just experienced a similar situation where I couldn't pinpoint the exact pest I was dealing with, as I mistakenly didn't segregate a new succulent before repotting and putting it out front with all my other plants. I had webbing on some, others had issues closer to the root, ect. I researched extensively and was so frustrated that I finally just decided to do everything I could think of to fix my plants because I was so devastated. By the end, I ended up doing several different things to about 25 succulents of various kinds and sizes. First, I sprayed all of my plants with a dawn/ water solution as well as sprinkling with Diatomaceous Earth when they were dry. When it was clear that this wasn't enough for maybe 18 of the plants, I took them out of their pots, cut away any rotting areas, including roots, stems, and leaves. Then I sprayed them down with rubbing alcohol, really saturating them and wiping off the leaves and stems. I used a clean paper towel for at least each plant, usually multiple as to not spread any pest or possible disease. I also kept any healthy leaves and stem pieces that may have fallen off during this process to propagate later. I placed each plant on a paper towel on a cart, mainly because I have cats, and wheeled it into a sunny room where they couldn't get to them. I checked daily for weeks to make sure I didn't see new webbing, pests, black spots, or signs of further rotting. I misted roots with water occasionally. At the same time, I began dumping the soil out of the pots (sadly because everyone received my fresh soil mix a few months before this happened) and I sanitized the pots. I slowly began repotting each plant and kept them all away from each other until I was sure everyone was healthy, which of course ended up coinciding with having to bring them in for winter. The process took months, and quite a few of my plants decreased in size from having to cut away so much of them, but I ended up only losing one whole plant with this ordeal. I'm impatiently awaiting for more consistent warmer weather to see my plants thriving and growing again!

I just had my AC replaced with a 5 ton 16 SEER unit but did not replace the 15 yr old furnace. If you don't have a matched furnace then you really don't know what the actually SEER rating. Mostly likely it is less than 16 SEER. Was the previous condenser also a 5 ton size? If not then then there is a good chance your duct work is undersized and you are not getting 5 tons of cooling. The 2000 CFM or 400 CFM per ton is a guideline. It is possible to have less and not have the coil freeze. What is more important is the actual air flow. I assume the installer set the blower speed to the maximum setting of 1800 CFM and did not actually measure the air flow. If he did I am confident it would be less. Flexible duct work is inexpensive. It should have been replaced if there was any concern about reusing it. I assume it was reused to save installation costs.

Sounds like 1800CFM is the maximum setting on your furnace, not necessarily what the true CFM is.  So you're probably stuck with it if you keep the existing furnace.  However, 400CFM/ton is a starting point - plenty of systems use 350CFM/ton, particularly if dehumidification is a priority. I hope they didn't up-size your AC condenser from 4 ton to 5 ton (?) and they should not have re-used old flex duct.

Could this air flow rate potentially cause freezing of the evaporator coil?  Thanks for your feedback.

If the actual air flow is 1680 CFM then you are only getting the effect of 4 tons of cooling. It is rare a residential house has the duct work to handle the air flow for a 5 ton condenser. Sacramento can get very hot so it is difficult to say what the heat load is for your 2487 sq. foot house. The fact that is only 17 years old would suggest it has better insulation than the average house. This is the reason I always suggest doing a load calculation and measuring the duct work when replacing HVAC equipment. If your coil did not freeze with the old 5 ton condenser then it will probably not freeze with the new one. I believe your climate is very dry so that will help. You will have to monitor the situation when the temperature is in the 90s.

What is specified in your contract? I did a gut remodel and everything was specified but expenses were allocated differently. For example for items that were totally within the control of my GC he paid for those completely per the line item in the contract. He had given my a very specific bid based on the specific plans I had sent to GC's for their estimates and that was attached to the contract. An example would have been all of the subflooring for my wood floors and all labor costs. Other items were an allowance because there might have been something unpredictable that came up like all the electrical work. Again this was based on very specific plans so it minimized surprises. Anything above and beyond the scope was discussed - i.e. it turned out that I needed a new electrical panel which would not have been known originally. The shower doors and mirrors were an allowance - again this would have covered installation based on the specifications in my plan but I decided I wanted Showerguard so this was an additional change order which I paid for. In terms of timing I paid 10% on signing and then 50% when work was started on a phase of the project and then about 40% on satisfactory completion which accounted for the 10% payable on final completion of the entire project. By the time we were into the project both my GC and I (and my designer aka project manager) had a great deal of trust and respect for each other and so it became a little less formal.

It's oedema, a physiological disorder. Something I wrote about it: Oedema (aka edema) is a physiological disorder that can affect all terrestrial plants. It occurs when the plant takes up more water than it can rid itself of via the process of transpiration. The word itself means 'swelling', which is usually the first symptom, and comes in the form of pale blisters or water-filled bumps on foliage. Under a variety of circumstances/cultural conditions, a plant's internal water pressure (turgidity) can become so high that some leaf cells rupture and leak their contents into inter-cellular spaces in leaf tissue, creating wet or weepy areas. Symptoms vary by plant, but as the malady progresses, areas of the leaf turn yellow, brown, brown with reddish overtones or even black, with older damage appearing as corky/ scaly/ ridged patches, or wart/gall-like bumpy growth. Symptoms are seen more frequently in plants that are fleshy, are usually more pronounced on the underside of leaves, and older/lower leaves are more likely to be affected than younger/upper leaves. Oedema is most common in houseplants during the winter/early spring months, is driven primarily by excessive water retention in the soil, and can be intensified via several additional cultural influences. Cool temperatures, high humidity levels, low light conditions, or partial defoliation can individually or collectively act to intensify the problem, as can anything else that slows transpiration. Nutritional deficiencies of Ca and Mg are also known contributors to the malady. Some things that can help you prevent oedema: * Increase light levels and temperature * Monitor water needs carefully – avoid over-watering. I'd heartily recommend a soil with drainage so sharp (fast) that when you to water to beyond the saturation point you needn't worry about prolonged periods of soil saturation wrecking root health/function. Your soil choice should be a key that unlocks the solutions to many potential problems. * Avoid misting or getting water on foliage. It slows transpiration and increases turgidity. * Water as soon as you get up in the AM. When stomata close in preparation for the dark cycle, turgidity builds. If you water early in the day, it gives the plant an opportunity to remove (for its own needs) some of the excess water in the soil. * Put a fan in the room or otherwise increase air flow/circulation. Avoid over-crowding your plants. Al

Illinois is a low use market for AC, typically 3 months of fairly regular use is about it. 15 years old is an average when it comes to AC equipment replacements. ( I use to live there over 20 years ago) The obvious problem is if this machine is R22 Freon. Just because it's Carrier, doesn't necessarily mean it's the newer R410a... even if it is R410a... the same will be happening to it as is R22 Freon. At best a few more years, the more liberal run the state probably less. Here in Texas this fun begins in 2025... currently the new equipment with the new refrigerant isn't available just yet. (R454b OR R32) Ultimately when this AC machine fails (breaks down) the question your daughter will have to face is that if it's worth it to put money into this machine as opposed to buying new. When it does break down it also comes down to what is it that is wrong. Many times (not always) it's a lower cost repair like a fan motor, starting components, maintenance type things. If it starts leaking Freon, whether it's R22 or R410a doesn't matter all that much... refrigerant leaks are expensive regardless and in most cases equipment replacement is often times required to fix those leaks. That said... Circa 2021: you could fix a refrigerant leak by replacing the indoor coil and that new coil *could be* leaking again in as few as 3 years or less. (regardless of the name on the box) In my 27 year career, there has always been refrigerant leaks. It's nothing new. Larger companies I worked for in the past bought refrigerant by the pallet. I can nearly guarantee you that nothing has changed in that regard. The short answer: It depends what is wrong with it, when you find out it has failed. Not to mention how honest the tech is that you called. I service the Katy, Texas area.

"The AC part of the HVAC system is a 2005 Carrier. Should that be of concern?" How the indoor environment of a home is controlled is always a concern.  The HVAC system's compressor or air handler may be circa 2005, but the ductwork, insulation, distribution, etc. are likely to be a lot older and may not be well designed or installed properly.  If those need major work, consider the additional costs along with that to replace the equipment. For the record, Carrier started using R-410a in 1996.  You can check the nameplate on the equipment to be sure, but there's a pretty good chance a system manufactured in 2005 utilizes R-410a refrigerant (Carrier labeled it "PURON")

For the record, Carrier started using R-410a in 1996. Yeah, but adoption was slow due to cost. After the proposed cut off in 2010 manufacturer's started shipping R22 Freon condensers dry to circumvent the phase out. Carrier was the lone mfg, that fought that battle and mostly lost until about 2014 or so when the industry finally realized to move on from R22. If you can read the equipment sticker still if it's not faded it will tell you what type of refrigerant it uses. The other way would be to call HVAC service as there are ways to figure it out other than the equipment sticker.

Better to be forewarned than to be disappointed later. Yes, it is true that most geothermal heat pumps will be a bit noisier due to the compressor being within the envelope with the house. However, most people have geothermal heat pumps with the compressors within the house. If noise levels could not be mitigated most geo owners would not have them; it is not a ‘Red Flag’. This is a mature technology that has been around for quite some time now and has only gotten better and quieter. Today you have a choice of geothermal heat pumps that might be either 2-speed or variable speed which means they will be even quieter than single stage heat pumps of 10 or 15 years ago. There should be no noise coming from the borehole pipes. The ground loop fluid circulators or flow centre as they are called should be completely silent unless you’re barely inches away from them. Our geothermal heat pump, which does not even have a sound blanket over the compressor is quiet enough that we can leave the door open to our mechanical room while watching TV just adjacent to it. Today’s geothermal heat pumps with everything variable, compressor fan and load centre pumps can be extremely quiet particularly when operating at reduced capacity, achieving the highest efficiency attainable by any active HVAC system. I personally would go for it. Probably the best form of solar renewable energy per square foot available. You might be able to heat and cool your entire home with a footprint of just one square foot. I recently had two discs just wrapped in plastic wrap that were supposed to be overnight and got pushed three days.  It was 100% white whole wheat.  I've only previously used red, which has a different texture than white flour.  I think it was the long stint in the fridge, however, that made this crust so tender and flaky.  Probably the bran absorbed a lot more of the water, but the dough was still plenty moist, and there were still plenty of visible butter globs.  And that's the thing.  You want the butter to remain more or less intact for the most part because a lot of flaky comes from the water in the butter globs steaming and pushing apart the flour.  It worked out so well, I'm planning to do it on purpose for Christmas.  Air tight is really important, especially for the flavor.  You don't want the butter going rancid or the dough picking up odors.   Given that, though, the only considerations are whether the texture changes in a bad way from the components marrying, and whether you introduced bacteria or mold in the making.  Otherwise, there's nothing in there that should spoil very fast.

It does not matter if this was accidental damage or a way of fixing a problem.  What you need to learn is whether the hole goes through to the waterproofing layer or not.  There should be waterproofing of some kind under the shower tile on the floor and the walls (several different ways of doing that).  If the waterproofing layer has been penetrated, you likely have to redo the entire shower. I would not call the seller.  If they did not disclose this hole, and if your state has a seller’s disclosure form requirement, you should have the form.  If you don’t know if there is such a form required in your state, you can either google it or call YOUR realtor (not the seller’s realtor) and ask about it.  I would not talk to the realtor about the problem, just ask if there is such a disclosure form and tell them that you can’t find it in the closing paperwork.  You may be going after the seller for some restitution, so you want to keep quiet about the problem until you know if you are going to sue.  Traditionally, both realtors represent the sale of the house.  That means they might discuss things if you tell your realtor, then word can get back to the seller.  “Buyer’s agent” was becoming more common when I last bought a house 15 years ago, but unless you signed something that said the realtor working for you could not disclose information you gave them, I would not count on privacy of information.  You may be able to get some money back in small claims court if you don’t want to hire a lawyer.  Check out what your law says about failure to disclose (if you have that requirement in your state) and how disputes are handled.

You've heard the term, winterize, but maybe are not aware how it works.  You apply a strong nitrogen fertilizer after the grass has fully stopped growing.  Usually this is in late November.  You wait until the grass has turned off, but the roots are not frozen.  Then when you  apply the nitrogen, the roots can take it up and store if for the winter.  In the spring the roots will be fully charged as the temps rise.  Fully charged means that you do NOT need to add more fertilizer at this time.  Even with no winterizing, the roots work with the soil microbes to recharge.  The difference would be that with no winterizing it might take a week or so longer for the grass to awaken.  In either case the grass roots have enough stored nutrients to power through the entire spring.  That means you do not need to fertilize early.  Yes, I realize this advice flies in the face of all the people trying to sell you more fertilizer (than you need), but it works just fine if you don't do anything until May (warmer grasses) or late May (cooler grasses).  The stores are packed with fertilizers and the airwaves are filled with people selling fertilizer, but NOW IS NOT THE TIME to apply.  Save it for Memorial Day.  Even if you do apply now, you will need it again in late May for the summer heat.  Don't waste the time or money now. The 4 or 5-step programs are a way to sell products so the company owners can make their boat payments all year long.  You are correct to challenge the need for them.  But having said that I can outline some steps that the lawn forum communities have come up with over the past couple of decades.  You can call them steps or not - potato/potahto. That is 5 steps if you want to think of it that way; however, you have many options of what you are applying and what not.  What you are not applying is any insecticide.  Not only to most lawns not need it, most soils will suffer terribly from unneeded applications of insecticide.  Microscopic insects comprise a large fraction of the soil microbes which keep your soil healthy.  If you apply insecticide, as is included in the Scott's summer application, you are going to change the balance of fungi, bacteria, and microarthropods (teensy insects) in the soil.  The soil microbe populations will eventually rebalance, but why do the damage in the first place??  Most lawns don't have a problem.  In my own (anecdotal) experience of 55 years of lawn keeping, I have never needed an insecticidd.  And I might say that the advertising you see in the summer will lead you to believe your lawn is suffering from grubs, army worms, spiders, ants, or some other bug, but it almost never is.  If you believe you have an insect problem, please write to a forum to ask.  There are simple tests you can do to verify a problem and then make an informed decision about which products to use and how to use them.

There is a difference between the nominal width and dressed width of lumber milled into anything including wood clapboard siding. 8" siding material will dress out at 7 1/8" +/- depending on the mill.  Courses of horizontal siding are installed with an overlap.  What's left over is called the "exposure" or "reveal" which is a better way to specify siding since it's not subject to any variation from mill to mill.  The particular exposure you select should be depicted the elevations of the architectural plans for your home-- not left for you to make a just-in-time selection during construction. We find that there's no one-size-fits-all siding exposure for all homes.  Our practice is to experiment with different siding exposures in the design phase and choose that looks best for the particular home.

How "zone appropriate" this plant is is up for discussion. If you have not grown it, then just relying on Internet (mis)information is not likely to give you valid or sound data. An established plant may well be able to tolerate a "typical" zone 7 winter. But that tolerance drops significantly for any newly planted Edgeworthia, as they are notoriously slow and somewhat difficult to establish. Since the flower buds develop in summer for the following season, they are subject to cold damage, specially late season cold damage, that will prevent any flowering. And even result in significant stem dieback. I would never attempt to grow Edgeworthia in a zone 7 garden unless in a very sheltered/protected location with some reflected heat. Akebono is also reportedly less tolerant of cold. While there is some ongoing discussion as to the distinction between the two common species under cultivation, Akebono is a cultivar of E. papyrifera, a less robust, less hardy and non-fragrant form of paperbush. The intensely colored forms all tend to be of this species, rather than E chyrsantha, which only offers cream to yellow flowers, but highly fragrant.

I would agree that it's probably not worth the time and effort to save, if you want fruit, a grafted tree, some well draining soil (if you want to go bagged there are some good ones, depending on where you are, but you need to look at what's in it), a good pot, and some lights will get you a lot closer to fruit. If I did want to try to save this, I'd probably treat it like a cutting I was trying to root. Trim off everything dead with a pair of clean scissors wiped down with alcohol to sterilize. Then make some holes in the bottom of a clear plastic cup, fill it with some sterile seedling/cutting soil, moisten it, plant what's left of your tree, then flip a second plastic cup over the top and tape all the way around the rim to seal it. Cut a few vent slits in the top cup, set over a plate to catch any drips and then leave it and wait and see. If it's going to survive, you'll eventually see new growth. If it dies, at least you gave it a chance.

Ok, you do say you're a "newbie"!  Yes, you are!  The finish is "eggshell", not "eggplant".  Oh well, as least you're willing to learn! Will you be painting all these things yourself, or just want to understand what your painter will be doing? Different brands will use the same name - i.e., satin, but it will still vary as to the amount of shine. Flat has zero shine, hides imperfections the best (usually recommended for ceilings).  Hard to clean and can be hard to touch up without it showing. Matte finish is next.  Again, varies from brand to brand, and between the lines of the same brand.  Example:  Benjamin Moore Aura flat has less "shine" vs. Benjamin Moore Scuff X (from their Ultra Spec line).  The TDS sheet will give you a closer idea - it will be listed as "3 degrees at a 60 degree angle/ 5 degrees at an 80 degree angle).  Scuff X matte is somewhat higher, but not noticeable to most people. Satin is next.  It can range from 20 degrees to 35 degrees (+/-).  Then Semi-gloss, then gloss, and some paints have a HIGH gloss.  The higher the gloss, the more imperfections in the surface or the paint itself will show. Personally, I prefer eggshell for my walls, and satin for my trim.  I lean towards all Benjamin Moore products for walls.  Recently used the Scuff X in matte on my walls and the Scuff X Satin for doors and trim.  It's leaves a very nice finish. While flush cuts (removing the branch flush to the trunk or the lower order branch) are inappropriate for trees in the landscape, they are ok for trees that will live out their life in a container, as there is little chance an indoor tree will fail structurally and damage property or people when it fails. There are 2 good ways to approach pruning off dead stubs of trees in containers. First is to cut flush to the trunk. This can be accomplished with a pruning saw, or, there are specialized tools made specifically for pruning flush. These tools, a concave cutter (top) or knob cutter (below) will remove branches and leave a concave depression in the trunk or lower order branch. When callus forms at wound edges and start to cover the wound, it will be least noticeable if a concave cutter was used.    The other method is to allow the short stub to stat on the plant for a year or so. The stub should have any green growth that occurs on it rubbed off, or the stub won't die back to the base. As the rest of the tree continues to grow, you'll see evidence of a branch collar forming around the base of the stub. When you can identify the collar, cut the stub off flush to the distal edge of the collar. This should be used whenever the tree will be planted out, or on trees with thin/smooth bark known to be slow to close wounds. The advantage of leaving the stub until a branch collar forms then cutting flush to the collar lies in the fact it allows the tree to completely compartmentalize the wound to keep any pathogens from spreading to living wood adjacent to the wound. For more on "compartmentalization of decay in trees" and how trees 'wall off' injuries, use the search words CODIT Shigo, or see Wikipedia for CODIT. Wounds heal faster if you can keep the tissue surrounding the wound moist. When the tissue surrounding the wound dries out, it increases the size of the wound, and callus will need to arise from the wound edges and roll over all the dead parts before the wound closes. I often cover all but small wounds with waterproof wood glue immediately. I 'paint' the wound, being careful not to get glue on the living bark surrounding the wound. Some use Vaseline or even Preperation H to cover wounds so they stay moist. They also make cut paste to cover wound of trees destined to live their lives in pots.  In the center is a large wound on a maple tree due to a trunk chop aimed at increasing a future bonsai tree's taper. You'll see how the wound was covered by callus over time:  This particular wound ^^^ was covered with sphagnum moss (not peat) which was kept moist and covered with aluminum foil. The moss significantly speeds up callus formation.    This is the wound after 1 year. Notice how the wound intentionally comes to a 'V' at the bottom, like an upside down tear drop? That helps make the wound less conspicuous when it's closed.  After 2 years ^^^  After 3 years ^^^  Same tree ^^^ - notice other wounds closing and the taper due to the trunk chop.  Summer 2021 ^^^ - still a young bonsai, but it's 'getting there'. Al

@SylviaWW 9a Hot dry SoCal in hot conditions where the sun is brutal, any distance you can put between the physical plant tissues and the hot, reflective, heat-radiating wall surfaces will help. Allowing air circulation behind the roses, between them and the wall will not only help to permit the heat to dissipate, but will also reduce the amount of water stress caused by the hot wall literally cooking the moisture out of the roses. The hotter it is, the more they sweat (transpire) and you can literally force them to contract fungal issues, most notably rust and mildew, from severely water stressing them. Growing grass around them will increase the possibilities of water stress as the turf competes with them for water. The rose feeder roots will grow within the top few inches of soil and that's where the grass roots are. Ideally, there wouldn't have to be lawn around them, only a deep organic mulch to keep the soil moist and cool. But, the reality is, you have to do, what you have to do. Good luck!

I've been there and done this. Twenty five years ago we found an entire kitchen of cabinets from a 1920s mansion for sale for $500. Did this problem start when the water heater was installed?  How old is the house? Somewhere there is a partially clogged supply  line or an interconnect between hot and cold pipes. Good luck tracking this down!My previous house was built in 1931 and had original plumbing.  The shower controls were in two sections. There was a mixer valve to control temperature and then separate on/off controls for the main shower head and the body sprays We had a problem when we went to replace the water heater and couldn't drain the heater after shutting off the cold water supply.  Turned out the shower mixer connected the hot and cold system and water was flowing through the valve; in our case sending warm water to the cold water feed at the bathroom sink.

If this is an electric WH, I'd say only your upper heating element is working, so due to convection, you only have a few gallons of 130degF water at the very top, and the rest of the tank is lukewarm.  The scalding burst from your bathroom sink probably did not last very long, and just happened to draw-off a "slug" of very hot water, right off the top.  Only one heating element is on at a time.  The LOWER element does 90% of the work, heating the WHOLE tank, from the bottom up (convection).  The UPPER element only kicks on WHILE you're using hot water, trying to compensate "on the fly" for the incoming cold water, to let you take a little bit longer shower. Your lower element might be bad from the factory, or just not connected.  Turn your circuit breaker OFF before checking, OR... just exercise your warranty.  ;')

We had mini split system installed in January, had to upgrade our electrical from 100 to 200 amps, 2 condenser units (capable of working in very cold temps in NE), and 6 heads. We paid about $30k for the whole thing, expecting to get $5-7k back in state rebates. We also qualified for a zero interest loan, based on the MA Save program (for a portion of the cost). It’s not cheap to install. We live outside Boston where labor is high. Our monthly heating costs have dropped dramatically since we removed an older steam boiler (quite inefficient) and all the radiators to switch to the mini splits. We are still only a few months in, but expect our annual energy costs to reduce by $1500-2000. A slow ROI, if you look only at the cost of the mini split system. Our boiler was needing replacement within the next few years anyway. We took advantage of the rebates and loan offered in the state. And our house is consistently a comfortable temperature!

Disclaimer: I am not a trained professional weight lifter or trainer. To me it sounds like you need to increase the weights. I do about 5-10 reps, 3 sets. The old way of thinking was that women should do lower weights higher reps but that is no longer the recommendation. We aren't going to bulk up like the hulk so higher weights are good. I lift 5x / week right now (alternating upper and lower body). If squats aren't doing it alone, then add weights to your squats. I always hold added weight with my squats. Try goblet squats too. You can also try squatting side steps. Sometimes I'll do them around my basement one direction and then the other. There's also the good old fashoned wall sit from gym class (keep knees 90 degrees, don't use your hands for support). As for the shoulder, you might have an injury. It's absolutely possible to do minor injury like small tears and still be able to continue exercising with some pain. I'd give it some time to rest and then start in slow with maybe pushups from the knees instead of plank position. You might also need to add in some other shoulder exercises to strengthen surrounding muscles to support injured tissue after you've rested for healing. Soft tissue injuries can be slow to heal and it takes more and more time as we age. I don't do much abs-specific work myself. You might try looking up alternative ab workouts to try something new. There are so many different options out there and if you're not feeling the burn, you probably have plenty of strength for the exercises you're doing there. You may need to try a different type of ab exercise to hit different muscle groups or add some weights to the mix with your current exercises (ankle or hold a dumbell or kettlebell).

The various bases are designed to work with the colors you are mixing.   Lighter colors go into Base 1 which is a white base. You make the decision of what color you want and to achieve that color the person mixing your color will choose the base that is used for that color formula.

I am neutral on the side splash, but since everyone is now talking about the cabs.... If you paint them any of the grey colors you have in the swatches, you will absolutely need to paint your wall color - because the grey and grieges will look very awkward against your creamy wall colors. Cold against cream is not a good look. Wood cabs are definitely trending up, while greys trend out. I think the light color greys you've chosen are not too "grey trend" -- that is, I think they would be charming in your kitchen for some years to come, and i appreciate your desire for a lighter kitchen.  But painted cabs are a lot more trouble than wood cabs (and prone to looking really beaten up within a few years), so given that your wood cabs are having a renaissance right now, i'd be really inclined to try and work with them.  They would look a lot more modern with a less creamy wall color, and some other contemporary upgrades to your kitchen. Lighting, hardware, ditch the wrought iron etc. In short, if you are trying to update your kitchen, I think a wall color update is required either way.  You can keep the walls with your existing wood cabs, but it won't look "current".  But you definitely can't keep the wall color with the light grey cabs. So if you're not planning on painting the walls, definitely don't do the grey cabs.  You could do a light cream cab instead - but still subject to the caveats that it would look more worn than the wood cabs in a few years.

text: Hi Hector, I would recommend that you consult with a structural engineer (we did on our design) to make sure that you take into account such issues as snow load, extreme wind and soil stability.    Structural requirements vary state to state and in some states, building such a structure may require a building permit and approved structural calculations.   Here in California, with our expansive soil type and the potential for earthquakes, additional structural measures had to be taken: deep pier foundations, metal connectors between beams, larger beams and rafter supports.   Best of luck on your project!

adardich, Thank you, the photos show exactly what I wanted to see, so we will get right to work.  dsegel, welcome aboard, it's nice to have the interest in what we are doing.  Jump right in if you have questions, or comments. Gather your supplies first.  I would say two pots, standard orchid pots, clay and slotted if you can find them.  One pot about 4 inches, the other large enough to hold the large plant.  Its difficult to say what size now, because we don't know how much of a root system you will have when you get it out of the pot.   Get enough good quality orchid bark (preferably Fir bark} mix to fill both pots, and I would suggest you invest in maybe  a dozen six, or eight inch galvanized rhizome clips. ( you can cut the long ones to fit the small pot)  You are in central FL, so I'm thinking you will not have too difficult a time finding this material.  Try orchid greenhouses, plant shops, or the ever open internet.   Lets make sure I'm correct in this,  As I see it, the bloom spike is coming from the side of the Keiki, and is not a branch of the old bloom spike that sprouted the Keiki.  If this is a correct assessment, my suggestion is to remove the keiki, and then remove the old bloom spike by cutting it an inch or so from where it exits the big plant.   Leaving about two inches or so of the old bloom spike attached to the Keiki might be a good idea (reason in a minute).   Remember, a sterile razor, clean cut straight across the old bloom spike. Now, your little Keiki has an extra part that you normally do not have to be concerned with when planting a Keiki.  That's the bloom spike.  I would suggest soaking the roots of the keiki in room temp. water, overnight, before you try planting it.  Fill your small pot heaping full of mix, and empty  it into a pan of water.  Mix the bark and water until the bark is soaked, and pour out the remaining water.  Fill the pot about half full of mix.  Take your little Keiki and very slowly and gently try to bend the roots so they will go into the pot with the Keiki standing up as straight as possible.  It does not have to stand up straight...Phals. grow in the jungles attached to trees and rocks, with the plant facing down so standing water will drain out of the crown to prevent rot.  Nature does that.  Your plant, over time will also do that also, no matter how you put it in the pot.  Nature does that.  Remember, your plant has an extra part, so while you are doing all this other stuff, pay attention to what is going on with that bloom spike.  You are not going to get an award winning display of blooms from this bloom spike anyway, but lets try to not damage that spike too much,  so we can get a look at the blooms.  The bloom spike can really point in any direction at this time.  You can lay it over the rim of the pot, tilt the plant so it points up a bit, the goal here is to get as many of the roots into the pot as you can, in almost any direction you can, and have the bloom spike waving in the breeze.  Nature will take care of the rest.  When you get the little plant placed in the pot to your satisfaction, hold it in place and begin to fill the pot with mix.  When the pot is filled with mix, place the rhizome (cut to length) clips around the plant.  I would try to get one of the clips over the top of the 2 inch section of old bloom spike you left attached to the Keiki.  That makes an excellent handle to hold the little plant steady while its roots grow in. When the potting is complete, water the pot thoroughly, and put it in a shaded location,and let it dry thoroughly.  That is dry until it begins to look a bit limp.  Then water it again, and dry it again.  Do two or three cycles of this before you gradually start working it into its regular growing location.  Running the plant dry for a while, allows the roots to heal, and the plant to be thirsty enough to want to send roots out to find moisture. Enough school for one night.  I'll be watching for any posts announcing you have completed this project, or have questions, and then we will go to work on the big plant. Have fun. Bill

I have a handicapped accessible shower floor that is 37 3/4 x 63 inches with a shallow trench drain at the point where it connects to the room floor.  I put a second shower floor system outside of the shower, sloped to a drain.  It consists of a set of sloped floor foam forms, drain, and uncoupling membrane by Kerdi.  I am so glad that I put in the floor drain!  In three years I have flooded the bathroom about three or four times with overflow from the shower drain.  Twice were due to having a ridiculous amount of hair shedding during  a shower, slowing the 4” square drain in the trench drain.  Once may be due to not using my shower heads one at a time.  Too much water for it to handle. My shower floor is solid surface (similar to Corian) and the manufacturer even designed in a 1/2 inch high dam that directs the water to the 4” drain.  My trench is only 1/2 inch deep, due to it being part of the shower floor pan and not a metal drain that hangs down below the floor surface.  I am sure that contributes to my need for my floor drain.  You must make sure that your drain system can handle all the water you are giving it!  Listen to the professionals who posted above.

Unless you are doing a project that triggers a whole-house code review you don't have to do anything to bring old work up to current codes. If you have to bring it up to the current code it's going to need to be bigger in all dimensions, which will be a challening remodel to have it look good. Making it taller is probably fairly easy with bigger plinth blocks under the side pillars, but making it wide enough to get the requisite side clearances (12" iirc) requires a potentially ugly splice. I'd think about cutting it in half and adding an element in the middle that looks intentional rather than like a mistake. Then you will have to deal with the now-exposed brick/wallboard border, which can probably best be done by tiling over both the brick and whatever is under the current mantle. "How common is it to get chips around the sink from washing dishes?" This has everything to do with sink edge profile selection and little to do with material or mount style. The larger and more round the edge at the sink, the less likely chipping will occur. All our sink replacement jobs get a 3/8" radius. Show me a pencil edge at a sink and I'll show you a chip factory no matter the material. "Are we safer to get an overmount to avoid them?" This is a poor reason to get a top mount sink. You want a slight positive sink reveal. Negative reveals are crud hiders and expose the bottom edge of the stone to potential chipping. A flush reveal creates an elongated silicone joint line that frays and becomes ugly and unsanitary. A slight positive reveal protects the stone bottom and makes a tight maintainance-free joint between the stone borrom and the sink flange that never turns black/brown from leaking when strapped in place. I guess first, I should mention that I live about 100 ft from a wetland buffer, so that definitely changes the humidity profile in my house. (I can't keep garlic or onions more than a week or two before I have a full blown plant complete with roots sitting on my counter, and my orchids grow aerial roots like crazy and I have one that's been trying to climb our accent wall). I do grow in an organic soilless potting mix that contains bark fines, bark, pumice, and a few other ingredients which include bone meal and bat guano. I can look at the bag, next time I can get to it, as I spent a considerable amount of time going to local nurseries and reading soil mixes until I found one with a profile I liked. I have noticed that mixes that contain bat guano just result in much better growth. My plants are all potted in unglazed terra cotta, though I do this because with the humidity, even a well draining mix just won't dry in plastic. I know somewhere drier plastic can be a help. I use a mix of lights, daylight style LEDs all day during the winter from about 5 AM to 9PM, and then I use the west/southwest window in spring/summer once the days are about the same. The temperature in that room really varies as the heating doesn't really work in that part of the house, so it drops 10-15 degrees every night and can get cold in winter. The coldest I've measured was 45 degrees on a day when temps outside dropped into the single digits. None of my plants were too happy that day. In the summer I still have the 10 degree drop, but temps in the room have gotten above 89 before on really hot days. Usually when it gets that hot, I pull the blinds and use lights as I've noticed my kumquats just seem to resent too much heat. Their room averages about 68-70 during the day year round except for the odd extreme. I give them the occasional dusting of kelp meal for micros and feed them with a chicken manure/feather meal bagged fertilizer mix twice a year. Other than that they never move from where they live other than to be rotated for light. I do keep all my plants elevated over extra large humidity trays filled with lava rock and just let the drainage water evaporate on its own. Hope it helps! Just some of what I've learned in my climate that's given me some pretty good results.

This is just in case...  When the theoretical power of the burner is increased, the size of the burner is increased.  This is sometimes a bad thing - the heat from the flames may miss the pan altogether if the burner is turned all the way up or, in the case of dual ring burners, the wee center section turns up and down in proportion to the outer ring and the center of a large pan stays relatively cold.  Specifically, for a dual ring burner used with a wok, there will be more btus at the top of the wok than at the bottom - which isn't what you'd expect to happen. Some of this you can affect with pan mechanics - heavier pans, larger pans, etc.  But sometimes nothing will help.  It is somewhat from the sealed burners and somewhat because the "standard" for sealed gas burners just isn't very good.  It will vary by maker. The other thing to be careful about is whether your favorite cookware on the center ring will cause all of the other burners to become unusable. I have no experience with any of these cooktops, but really try to see one working if that's at all possible.  Cause cussing out sealed burners is not a hobby anyone else needs to have.

Hens and chicks typically refers to Sempervivum tectorum (and a few other S. species). These are incredible tough and hardy garden succulents and do not necessarily appreciate being grown indoors. What individuals are advising here is the best/correct building techniques.  You must decide risks you will take and time/budget constraints for yourself. To begin, concrete is porous. Therefore your best approach is to prevent moisture/condensation AT the foundation.  This is the caution from @worthy where the fiberglass will absorb moisture and it cannot pass thru into the basement.  Long term you will likely have mold and musty odor behind  the drywall. At minimum kraft backed fiberglass should replace what is installed.  Best would be remove the studs, place XPS foamboard against the foundation, tape the seams then reframe the walls.  Doing this will provide the best long-term build and greatest comfort. Plan to keep humidity at 45% or less.  Have return air and heat vents installed appropriately.  Plan electricity and other utilities to be installed before drywall. Good luck.

If asked I would always recommend triples for someone who is in climate zone 6 or higher. Whether dual or triple pane making sure that it's a good window with a good glass package that is installed correctly is much more important than the number of lites. I live in northwestern Wisconsin (a few miles from Minnesota border) where 17-19F is considered to be a reasonably comfortable high temperature for several months of the year. I do have triples and I wouldn't consider changing that if I were considering ever building again. For someone in climate zone 5 triples are likely to offer a bit of a comfort upgrade over duals but probably not much in the way of significant ROI if that is a priority. Whether triples are darker than duals depends mostly on the coating(s) used and to a lesser extent on the width of sash/frame since sash/frame is included in VLT calculations for the entire window package. A dual pane glass-only package using Cardinal's LoE-240 (picking on Cardinal since something like 65-70% of all residential coatings come from them), has a visible light transmittance of 40% whereas a triple with two separate LoE-180 coated lites will have a VLT of 70%. Even using LoE-366 with LoE-180 in a triple pane IGU make-up results in glass-only VLT of 57%, 17 percentage points higher than the dual pane. Examples are all for glass-only IGU configuration using 1/8" lites. Thicker glass will result in lower VLT numbers, roughly 3 percentage points lower when using 1/4" glass in place of 1/8" for example.

There have been comments in this forum that induction is induction is induction. Or that it might make financial sense to buy two of the less expensive cooktops so that when the inevitable failure happens, you can simply replace the broken one with the backup for less than the cost of repair.  Personally, I paid up for a Wolf because of the two year warranty, but now question if I really needed to spend so much for an induction cooktop that doesn't offer anything radically different than a less expensive brand.  I'm really happy with the Wolf, but perhaps I would have been just as happy with a GE. The differences between the brands are how the controls operate, placement of controls, knobs vs. touch controls, burner size and placement, burner wattages, power sharing between burners, individual timers, wi fi connection, & bridge features. I don't care for the largest burner being in the center, like in some of  the Frigidaires.  That crowds the cooktop if, say, you put a big boiling pasta pot there but you need to make a pasta sauce or veggies.  Some prefer the smallest, weakest burner in the back; I like it in the front where I can keep an eye on temperamental sauces or custards that need constant stirring & careful temperature control.  A bridge feature is very nice not only for breakfasts & grilled sandwiches, but for making gravy in a roasting pan. Some love having individual timers, I don't need them. So do your research & think about what works best for your needs. I hope you'll be as surprised & delighted by how nice induction cooking is as I was!

"Your furnace is 16 years old and has been working year round (cooling as well as heating)." No. The OP's air handler has been operating in heating and cooling modes for 16 years.  A furnace creates and moves hot air.  It operates in heating mode, but not in air conditioning mode.  An air conditioner operates only in air conditioning mode, not in heating mode.  The OP's air handler may be replaced along with the air conditioner evaporator coil, but not necessarily.  The existing furnace unit doesn't have to be replaced, provided it's compatible with the replacement air handler. " A two stage furnace would only make sense if you need it to operate a 2 stage AC condenser." Heating and air conditioning systems are designed for heating and air conditioning loads, respectively.  A single-stage furnace might be paired with a two-stage air conditioner and a two-stage furnace might be paired with a single stage air conditioner depending on the climate zone, the home's construction, and the owner's objectives.

An air handler? is an electric furnace and evap coil with heat strips or in some cases a heat pump that is capable of heating as well as air conditioning. Heat strips when paired with a heat pump are considered emergency heat or second stage heat when conditions warrant their use. Some air handlers are heat only, they contain no evap coil -- just a heat kit with resistance heat strips. A heating and air conditioning system for our climate (zone 4) typically consists of three components:  an air handler (which some people refer to as a fan-coil unit,) a compressor (either a heat pump or air conditioner) and a gas furnace.   The term "furnace" used in this context means a gas-fired heater.   In milder climates, electric strip heaters might be used in lieu of a gas furnace or as back up heaters for a heat pump.  They are separate components which need to be selected by the system designer to work together as a system (both heating and cooling loads are calculated when designing of a system.)   If your climate requires a heating-only system, the term "furnace" would mean an air handler paired with a gas-fired heater and sold as an integrated unit.  That's not what the OP described as their heating and air conditioning system. If you'd like to consult another source with regard to what an air handler (fan-coil) unit is, you can look to Carrier Corp. for an explanation: " A fan coil is an indoor unit of a heating and cooling system. It controls your home environment by moving air inside your home and can also affect your indoor humidity. As a complement to your air conditioner or heat pump, our variable-speed fan coil units can give you premium comfort and energy-saving performance. With an optional electric heat strip, a fan coil can also provide heat to your home if you live in milder climates." https://www.carrier.com/residential/en/us/products/fan-coils/# Because they are separate components in a heating and air conditioning system (each is ordered on a separate line item of our order and shipped in a different box,) any of them can be replaced without the need to replace all of the components.  That's the point of making the distinction between "furnace" and "air handler."  With proper maintenance, a furnace (i.e., a gas-fired heater) will typically outlast the air conditioner by a good number of years.  The OP's question is whether it makes sense to replace their furnace at the same time they replace their air conditioner.  They have the option to do either.

For technical reasons that are clearly way above and over the head of the builder... it would be counter productive to pair an "air handler or fan-coil unit" to a gas fired heater (furnace). If you try to pair the above with a fan coil too (pictured below)? --- you've got big problems. (The blower in the furnace is in the way of air flow.)   Technical reasons why: Fan coil or air handler either one will require 240v to operate. A gas furnace will require 120v to operate. Katy, I haven't sown your particular parsley, but a couple of things... Storage dry in the fridge is only storage, not stratifying.  To stratify, seeds must be moist with that moisture having breached the seed coat,  reached the embryo.  Once moistened, they cannot dry completely out again or the embryo will die. If you want to stratify your seeds in the refrigerator, that temp is fine.  Very very few seeds actually need to freeze and this isn't one of them.  Letting moisture penetrate the seed coat then plunging abruptly into a freezer can damage many seeds and its not helpful, they don't begin to germinate until kept somewhat less cold.  40F is plenty chilly for almost everything. I see suggestions for sowing flat leafed several places,  with suggestions to soak overnight then sow, or sow outdoors just a little before last frost, to just plain sow.  Stratifying in your fridge won't hurt them and just may help.  You can put them in a tiny zip lock with a bit of moist sterile sand or moist vermiculite, then when ready to sow, sow the contents of the bag....sand or vermiculite,  seeds and all.

Ventilation, the "V" in HVAC, is getting more attention in building codes as concerns about indoor air quality increase.  Code revision is a slow process; codes generally lag best practices by a number of years.  The 2018 International Residential Code requires a bath vent fan in each bathroom with an exhaust rate of 50 cfm intermittent or 20 cfm continuous.  It doesn't take into account the size of the bathroom or number of fixtures.  So, while a 50 cfm intermittent rate meets the minimum standard, explaining to your spouse that your bath vent fan meets code when there's mildew growing on the ceiling isn't likely to end there. I'd look to the Home Ventilation Institute (HVI) guidelines or the most recent version of ASHRAE Standard 62.2 for better guidance on bathroom ventilation until the codes reflect current best practices.

There are 14 nutrients essential to normal growth that plants absorb through the root pathway, and the fertilizer you are using has only 3 of those nutrients, which makes it inappropriate for use on containerized plants w/o additional supplements, which complicates nutritional supplementation, so let's look for an approach that's easier and offers the grower the most control over what the plant gets (in terms of nutrition) and when it gets is. First, though, I'll explain why the older leaves are turning yellow. Some of the nutrients are mobile in the plant. That is to say they can be moved from place to place. The mobile nutrients are nitrogen, phosphorous, potassium, and magnesium. The rest of the 14 are either immobile or largely immobile in the plant. When there is a deficiency of any of the nutrients considered to be mobile, the plant will rob them from older leaves or leaves which are not pulling their weight when it comes to producing food for the plant. The plant then uses the 'cannibalized' nutrients to fuel new extension growth by providing the nutritional building blocks the plant needs to make the vines/branches grow longer and and the leaves that appear as they extend. Suggested fix: * Purchase a container of Foliage-Pro 9-3-6. It contains ALL nutrients essential to normal growth, in a favorable ratio, making it a complete form of nutrition in a single container. * The next time your plant needs water, flush the soil thoroughly by slowly pouring a volume of room temp water through the soil. The volume should be equal to at least 10x the volume of the pot it's in. This will flush out any accumulation of salts and reset the EC/TDS (fertility level) to near 0. * Snap off the collection saucer so the plant can drain. Tipping the pot will make a big difference in how much excess water will drain from the soil.  Compare image B to A above to see how much more water exits the pot when you tip it after a thorough watering. * When the pot has stopped draining, right the pot and fertilize with a production strength dose of Foliage-Pro 9-3-6 until water is exiting the drain hole(s) again, then tip the pot again.  * Flush the soil each time you water (so at least 20% of the total volume of water it takes to wet the soil exits the drain  hole) and fertilize about every 4th or 5th time you water. To keep track of how many times you've watered your plant, drop a marble/ button/ bottle cap ...... into the pot at each watering. When you're about to drop the 4th or 5th item in the pot, fertigate (fertilize + irrigate). The plant should not sit in the effluent that exits the drain hole. Flushing the soil purposely flushes salts from the soil. Allowing the plant to sit in the effluent allows the salts removed from the soil a pathway back into the soil, undoing your efforts. HI, Weedy, A recommendation for an alternative to the LP Smart Side panels would require more information about the specific application and climate zone.  Do you need a single panel for an architectural feature or is it cladding for an entire home?  You noted the need for a waterproof material.  Smart Side is an engineered wood product.  It's not waterproof.  PVC is waterproof, but it's not as dimensionally stable as wood or an engineered wood product like Smart Side and a panel will cost around 10X what the Smart Side panels cost.  If your application is exterior cladding using panels, you might consider the panels offered by James Hardie. For the record, I'm not a fan of Smart Side products.  I don't have a problem with the "side" just the use of the term "smart" in conjunction with it.  Joe Lstiburek of Building Science Corporation referred to OSB as the "SPAM of wood products."  In my opinion, Smart Side products are an attempt to elevate a wood SPAM analog to a level where it doesn't belong.

Not 10x the cost of Smartside but PVC sheet stock is running about 3x the cost. On a small scale, PVC would be the preferred material over Smartside and Hardie. I think Boral also makes a similar product. Check the box stores for LP products, ours have LP sheets in stock.

I use 3/4" x 4' x 8' Azek smooth PVC as material for cornice stop and shapes and sometimes for small area panels--but I typically use Hardie panel for panels.
