"Ficus" covers a lot of territory. There are more than a thousand species of Ficus, and that doesn't include the myriad of cultivars of the more popular species. Ficus benjamina alone has several dozen cultivars of the species plant, all varying from the species plant from a little to a lot. I have several trees of a cultivar of F benjamina which naturally has leaves around 1/10 the size of the species plant. The name of that plant, with binomial and cultivar, is Ficus benjamina "Too Little". Since I'm not familiar with the species name 'regina', I was looking around only to find the same tag (and the name 'regina') on at least 3 different species of Ficus (F audrey, F alii, and F benjamina). That leads me to think 'regina' is not the plant's species; rather, it probably has something to do with trying to lead people to their operation (exclusively) in order to purchase the plant. Your plant looks very much like F elastica, but I can't be sure because there is nothing in the images that allows us to get a good sense of the size of the leaves. "Why is my plant dying?" The broad answer is, all plants die because they are being subjected to cultural conditions they are not genetically programmed to tolerate. Somewhere within the range of conditions they are programmed to tolerate (wet to dry, hot to cold, humid to arid, et cetera) you'll find a sweet spot such that, if we're providing all conditions in 'the sweet spot', the plant will realize as much of its genetic potential as possible. Asking the plant to tolerate conditions at the extremes of what it's programmed to tolerate causes stress which causes the plant's systems to wobble out of balance, the price for which is lost potential in terms of growth, vitality (health), appearance, and where applicable, yields. stress unchecked leads to strain. Strain causes the plant to use more energy than it can produce, an unsustainable condition that always leads to death of the organism unless the cause of stress/strain is eliminated. That's how it works, but there isn't enough information in your post to determine why the plant seems to be in fairly serious decline. "I have moved it into the spare which gets more light and is warmer. have i made the right decision?" Unless the conditions where it was before the move were favorable, it was certainly a good decision. There are soo many potential causes of leaf shedding that we can't nail anything down w/o more info; however, the first suspect for plants that were growing in a spot which was too cool and dark would be over-watering, and the symptoms are consistent with those presented. I suggest you start by monitoring moisture levels at the bottom of the bot by using a "tell" to "tell" you when it's time to water. See "Using a Tell" below. If you're determined to work toward learning how to keep cultural conditions in your plants' 'sweet spot', This Overview of Good Growing Practices should be very helpful. For more specific advice re long term care of Ficus in containers, what I share in this piece focused specifically on the Ficus genus, Long Term Care of Ficus in Containers, will help you avoid all the common pitfalls you're likely to encounter as you work toward a higher level of proficiency. I have 30 - 40 Ficus trees I've cared for for around 40 years, covering 12-15 different species, and I've learned much about the entire genus along the way. If you have questions you think I can answer, or concerns you'd like me to weigh in on, I'll be following the thread. Also, you really do need to put together some kind of regimen aimed at providing supplemental nutrition (fertilizing) if you don't already have that in place. It's an essential part of the care of virtually all containerized plants for any grower looking for average or better results. Nutrients are the building blocks plants use to grow and provide elements necessary if they are to keep their systems orderly. Ask if you have interest .... Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

When I started using gritty mix, having learned about it here years ago, I started with what appeared to be a "standard" or accepted formula.  As I recall, that included bark, and I removed bark after about a year.  By experimentation, I got that narrowed down to what worked for me -- 1 part each Turface, pumice, and poultry grit.  I still use that simply blend today, about 5-6 years later. BUT -- I also vary mixes and have plants in "gritty" mix that DOES NOT include Turface. Turface holds a lot of water -- a lot.  In a non-porous pot, I found that even though the mix drained, the plant still stayed wet longer than I wanted.  Now, I will put plants in pumice only.  Pumice DOES hold water, especially in plastic or ceramic pots. I used Manna Pro poultry mix and sometimes throw a handful of that in as well.  I haven't used cat litter, but I would follow Rina's advice above if you want to try.  My personal belief is that gritty mix becomes a personal experimentation highly dependent on your plants, your location, your pots and your results. Don't be afraid to experiment.

As robinswfl said...experiment & customize to your conditions. My most used mix contains lots of sifted perlite & grit (approx. equal amounts) + small amount of soil or cocopeat (usually 15-25% of total) . Pumice is great, but not easy to get for me & bit pricey - so I use perlite.

The single stage Preferred series is marketed as a variable speed furnace. That is a deceiving label in my opinion. It is really a multi-speed furnace. Yes Jasmine hello , i  thought about 20years ago my epiphyllums also had virus , i even was advised to throw them away which i did with some of them at least.  i even thought fungus rust and fusarium etc . after much thought it occurred to me that it only started after i started to  fertilze  and it  also occurred at the end of the season after the feeds? . The epiphyllum experts book i mentioned led me to ponder the disorder related to too much feed particulary nitrogen and  and later i discovered from  some cacti and succulent  experiments carried out  by  an expert , the conclusions were that feeding  cacti at even normal and high levels  damaged and harmed the plants and that  cacti definately dont like even half strength fertilizers  ! I stopped the feeding and flushed all my epiphllums in the sink  . new growth was clean, even in  the badly infected (virused) plants they where the ones i didnt have the heart to throw away . your epiphyllum oxypetalum  naturally lives in leaf litter in trees so they are used to very low nutrient  levels  and the rain flushes the roots . Epiphllums need very low feeding and are ok till you start feeding them like an ordinary houseplant . sometimes even the amount of feed in the compost you buy is too much. (adding pumice and perlite etc  makes the compost weaker, as well  as adding drainage and air etc). i have found   that not feeding (at least at first  ) is the way to go .then 1/4 even 1/8 next season  and only if  needed . and flush plain water a few times when outside in the  summer . there is nothing you can do about the affected parts  but i sincerely hope  you hold off the feed and flush  you see, watering  with little runoff causes a build up and concentration of undesirable substances slowly , even if not feeding . however i can see its a big plant so dont worry about flushing    just  now . just think about what you said , you said you didnt or cant remember feeding the two years previous but you did last seaon and the problem only occurred in the Autumn after the feeding . i think your epiphyllums new growth will be fine . by the way viruses of course exist in epiphyllums but it often looks different more like a mottling like the epi on the table in the video  but it can also look similar.  so in honesty i cant and wont rule out a virus . i just thought i would let you know it might not be  .and there is hope for  your epiphyllum by simply not feeding yet, then at a low level  and flushing the pot when you conveniently can  .

Rule-of-thumb on bladder air pressure is 2 psi below switch cut-in pressure. This turns on the pump before the tank is empty, keeping you from experiencing an annoying loss in pressure and water as the pump comes up to pressure. To adjust the pressure switch, look inside the protective cover. Most switches have instructions there. I would adjust the pressure switch first, then bring the bladder pressure up to spec. A manufacturer will offer several operating ranges for pump switches, the switches are identical with only the spring setting as the difference between them; I like well systems operating in the 40-60 psi range.

Broad tips for choosing a paint: 1) If you can, prime first, before choosing a color. The existing wall color will reflect onto you paint samples, and also the way you perceive a color is affected by the color that surrounds it (lots of optical illusions play on this). 2) Rather than painting sample colors directly on walls, paint large samples on foam board that you can move around the room. If you can't prime first, it's important to leave a white border around the sample color so that your perception of the color isn't "colored" by being next to the green of your walls. 3) Maybe you are past this stage already, but before I get to the large sample stage, I start with lots and lots of small paint chips that I move around the room and look at at different times of day. I pare them down at each viewing. It helps me weed out the clear losers before investing the money and effort in large samples. 4) Paint colors will look different on different walls and at different times of day. They just will. Figure out what you can live with. What room is it most important look best? What time of day? Or would you rather have it look pretty good everywhere/all the time but not ever "Wow, that's amazing!"

You need to understand that color is 3 dimensional, hue is only one part of the equation. The 90 degree hue at low chroma levels and light luminosity is just slightly orange (ish) yellow. See below where it is shown next to a neutral gray (upper left corner).    Yellow is unique in that we don't see dark yellow (think about powder blue and navy).  Now picture powder yellow and try to picture a yellow that would be comparable to navy.   It goes to gold and then to brown.  As we desaturate yellow it goes to olive green. You also need to understand that because the human brain ingests so much information we group the information coming into our brain and we automatically compare colors. Painting samples on your wall means that you are seeing the color in comparison to whatever color is currently on the wall. I suspect that you have a lot of greens in your space in addition to the green in the kitchen and possibly have a bit of green undertone in the wall color that you are painting over. I have the opposite problem as you do with Edgecomb Gray  - it is far too yellow/green  (looks like an old yellowed tooth).   I have a lot of pinks, reds, purples including a large pink brick fireplace wall. The center blocks below are all Edgecomb Gray.    Can you see why it turns yellow for me and fleshy orange for you?   To test the colors you really need to be looking at the colors without the influence of your current wall color.   Prime the wall white or use large white poster board behind the samples.   Look at the colors next to all colors that are going to stay.  (Flooring, trim, furniture). Edgecomb Gray will always have just the slightest orange tinge.  It will probably never look good with your colors. Do you like how light/dark it appears (LRV or Luminosity)? If so you want to try some colors with similar luminosity and chroma, but increase the hue. Here are some I have in my file:   My sister has a home with a lot of green undertones and if I were pulling colors for her home I would start with SW Sedate Gray, BM Hazy Skies and BM Paris Rain. Keep track of the LCH codes and note what you like/don't like. Best of luck - let us know how things work out.

In an area like MN (I'm next door in WI), you are going to want to familiarize yourself with thermal and structural performance ratings given the harsh conditions. Thermally you will want: -a low U value (preferably triple pane sub .20), -Somewhat balance SHGC (unless your home is designed to take advantage of passive solar gain), -High Condensation resistance (60's-70's), Structurally you will want: - a low air infiltration rating (under .05, but lower the better) - a high DP (structural) rating. Minimum DP50 IMO, but there are products that get 60, 70, 80 even as double hungs. There are windows that will fit those numbers in various materials (vinyl, fiberglass, etc), although they generally aren't the "household name" brands. Softlite, Okna, Sunrise, Polaris, are a handful of vinyl products that do, then there are a couple Canadian fiberglass lines that do as well, Inline being one that comes to mind.

I'm not going to recommend any particular plants. I don't know what type of soil you have or its pH. Your local nursery personnel know your local conditions and are better able to make recommendations. Right now you should search for internet articles on plants that fit your needs. You won't be able to plant until spring. Save articles and photos of things you like. Look for plants hardy to one zone colder than yours to make sure they make it through an unusually cold spell. You can clear out unwanted plants over winter. However, I'm leery of using a skid steer to clear a planting area around trees. The majority of any tree's roots are in the top 3' of soil. Damage to the roots is damage to the tree. English and similar ivies can be extremely persistent. They have deep roots and any bit left behind can resprout. Dig out what you can, but expect to have to come back and remove sprouts repeatedly to get rid of the plant. Some of your existing shrubs might be rejuvenated by cutting them back. General pruning either calls for all branches to be cut back by 1/3, or 1/3 of the oldest branches are cut back to ground level. Some shrubs can be cut back hard, but you need to look up each species for specific information. Shrubs are relatively low maintenance, and broadleaf and coniferous evergreens provide more winter interest than deciduous plants. Still, consider using shrubs with colorful or interesting winter stems, or fruit. The word "dwarf" only means smaller than the species, so pay attention to the expected mature size and spread listed on plants tags. Don't put a plant that will grow to 36" wide closer than 18" to a wall, fence or path. New shrubs will be small; the largest usually comes in a #3 pot. Don't place them too close together. It's best to fill in around them with annuals or low perennial ground covers. Don't over mulch. The main reason for mulch is to protect soil from rain. Large rain drops can hit the ground at 20 mph and splash soil particles up to 5' away. But mulch placed against the base of plants can lead to fungal disease. As plants grow they provide their own mulch in leaves. I think it best to apply a layer of compost around established plants than to continue to use mulch. A specimen shrub can stand on its own, but when adding colorful plants it is best to repeat them across the entire yard. Instead of pulling out all the boxwood across the front, perhaps you could just replace the two flanking the steps with a smaller shrub. That will visually expand your entry, and you can always replace the others later. I agree with getting rid of the shutters. None of your shutters look wide enough to actually cover the windows if they were operational. Those on the side are ridiculously small. Consider painting the window trim a contrasting color there.

Are the seams still visible through the paint?  If so, here's my method, though it does not seem to be very popular on GardenWeb, it has never failed me and It has been much easier for me than using a steamer. Most wallpaper I have seen are made of two layers; the top decorative layer made of vinyl or higher grade paper, and the backer layer which is porous and will absorb water very easily. Starting at a corner or one of the seams, at the top or bottom of the wall, gently pry off the top layer with your nail or the tip of a knife, to separate the two layers.  The top layer should peel right off like the skin off a banana. Once the second layer of paper is exposed, fill a spray bottle with lukewarm water and a dash of dish soap.  Spray the paper until it is saturated, and keep it saturated.  After about 10 minutes, take a putty knife and start scraping.  If the walls were properly prepped, the paper should peel right off with minimal effort. Skip the gizmos that scuffs or cuts the top layer, I find that because they only partially pierce the top layer, they only marginally help water penetrate down to the bottom layer. Once the wallpaper is removed, the key is to remove ALL the glue from the walls.  If you can get someone to wash the walls with soap and water as you go before they have a chance to dry, that's the best situation.  Then rinse with clear water, changing your rag often, and you should be ready to prime and paint, or apply new wallpaper.

If rotated clockwise, she's golden ....... a quarter turn counter clockwise will cause the plant to fall out of the pot.  If it doesn't become more symmetrical after you start rotating it, when you next repot you can change the planting angle. Also, this isn't a good time to be pruning a lot of foliage from your plant, but come Jun (if you live in the N hemisphere), you can snip off the stems that contribute to the lack of symmetry. Just FYI, many endeavors which require an artistic bone or two make much use of triangulation because the triangular silhouette looks most natural. Arranging rocks or trees as eye candy in the landscape use a great deal of scalene (3 sides of different lengths) triangulation in their designs. Bonsai, kusamono, shitakusa, bonsai, and other originally eastern arts which make use of arranged plants rely heavily on the triangular silhouette of not only the plant, but how they are arranged in relation to other plant's/ objects.  Al

And bear in mind your plant, Thaumatophyllum bipinnatifidum, is a vine, not a shrub or tree. It’s always  going to be a bit floppy. It’s looking for a tree to climb. The stems in your picture are actually leaf petioles. Pruning them off will not improve the structure of your plant since they cannot branch.

Hi, Lindsey, Most homes operate at slight negative pressure due to a combination of HVAC system issues and stack effect.   Duct work seams should be sealed with mastic designed for that purpose, but even meticulously installed HVAC ducts will leak.  A leaky return duct can indeed pull moisture, odors, and soil gases from the crawl space and the air handler will dutifully distribute them throughout the home.   Duct leakage can be tested (and quantified) with a duct blaster test. Most HVAC replacement work and most crawl space encapsulation work are performed without the benefit of permits or inspections.  And the majority of both are performed by individuals who don't know anything about basic building science principles, in my experience. It may not make sense at first, but a sealed, conditioned crawl space actually requires mechanical ventilation in order to comply with the building code. I'm betting your crawl space doesn't have any ventilation-- which would otherwise dilute the concentration of soil gases and odors-- or has a return opening from the crawl space which is the non-sensical of the two code-prescribed methods to ventilate a conditioned crawl space. The International Residential Code (IRC,) which forms the core of most statewide building codes, requires ventilation of "unvented" crawl spaces at a rate of 1 cfm/ 50 sq. ft. of floor area--which is not a lot.  The prescriptive methods to achieve that are listed in section R408.3 of the code.  Of the two prescribed methods, I recommend continuous mechanical exhaust.  I've found that the other prescribed method--supplying air from the HVAC supply can create localized conditions which favor growth of mold and mildew. Some of the earliest work evaluating methods to construct conditioned crawl spaces was performed by John Tooley in your home state of NC.    I believe he's retired now, but  he worked for Advanced Energy in Raleigh.  I suggest you give them a call.

None of the above.  What you are seeing now are some winter annuals and not the summer annuals that the product would be expecting.  The time to spray herbicide is April 15th, tax day.  Mid April give the spring and summer weeds time to germinate and mature somewhat.  Actively growing weeds die better than dormant weeds.  The next time to use herbicide is September 15th.  Do that only if you have some spots that need it. Your best line of defense against weeds is proper watering.  Deep and infrequent is the mantra for watering.  Deep means 1 inch all at one time.  Frequency depends on the air temperatures.  With temps below 70 you should water deeply once a month unless you get rain.  With temps between 70 and 80 you should water once every 3 weeks.  With temps between 80 and 90 you should water deeply once every 2 weeks.  With temps in the 90s you should water once per week.  With temps above 100 you can water once every 5 days.  Where I live in Texas I can usually go 10 days to 2 weeks in the heat of summer (high 90s).  There are other factors like sun/shade, clouds, wind, soil type, grass type, humidity, and others I've forgot.  The main one is air temp, so go with that as your primary indicator.  Why do this?  Because weed seeds need continual moisture to germinate and take root.  If you are watering a little bit every day, that is perfect conditions for germinating weed seeds.  Of course Mother Nature often gets in the way of deep and infrequent watering plans, so you'll have to adjust.  If you get a week of rain in May, you're going to have a week problem in the summer.  Crabgrass loves a week of rain in May.

I want to use the white 52 as trim. Does it pull any undertones with these colors? Not sure what pull any undertones means exactly. But we know that White 52 belongs to the Green-Yellow hue family. It's very low in Chroma (colorfulness) and it has a Value of 9.26 which is the brightness that you'd expect with a color of white. Low Chroma, high Value colors of white from the Green-Yellow hue family like White 52 are often perceived as "just white" and appear neutral under a range of light sources and in various contexts. Eider White and Repose Gray have more Chroma and are darker than White 52; you'll get a nice pop of contrast. In terms of the colors relate with White 52, they're next to each other on the color wheel. Which means they go together. Not that that matters all that much because colors of white from the front half of the green yellow hue family typically go with everything because of their neutral appearance.

Planning Policies rather frequently concern themselves with "the look of the streetscape" and focus rather strongly on the "Outside" - what materials extensions are built in, window types / sizes / placement, style and shape of roofs and so on. Speaking pointedly, out of sight out of mind, what one can't see from the street concerns the planners little. In any case, most planning departments offer a "free consultation", a chat with a planning officer on the phone for half an hour about planning / the plans you're hoping to submit. Check with your local planning department whether they offer this service. You can ask them open questions, "what level of detail do we need to provide in the application for materials, finishes, windows, doors, sizing, ...", "what do our local planning policies suggest we should do for external finishes", "how can we obscure views from large upper-storey windows so that we're not overlooked / we're not overlooking", or "what kind of changes, should site conditions require it, can we make after without invalidating the planning permit once given". It's usually better to ask thus openly than to "request" (I.e. don't tell them "on our listed building we intend to use bright flourescent pink window frames on a huge 3m x 4m glazed wall for the front dormer with protruding balcony that you're hopefully going to approve ... is that ok ?", if you know what I mean).

A bad/weak heating element can sometimes have a similar effect on electric models.  Preheat may run both the bake and broil element to speed up the heating process.  The bake element is the primary heat source after preheating is done.  Some ovens may run the broil element at lower wattage for some upper radiant browning heat, which may not be sufficient alone to maintain the target temperature.  A control board could also be the fault, not powering the bake element.  Proper troubleshooting is required to confirm what's the cause ... checking resistances on the element and voltages on the wire terminals, etc.  Call a servicer if you're not up to handling it.

While you're working on the shower, definitely upgrade to a handheld shower -- that single plain shower head isn't "enough".  In addition to showering, you'll love that it makes cleaning the shower easier. What's "behind" the shower head?  Could you steal from that space and enlarge the shower? Leave the toilet where it is Yeah, this seems to be a non-issue, and moving a toilet is real money. update  the vanity and mirrors I note you have NO drawers at the vanity; I'd make that a priority ... with duplicate sinks and no drawers, your counters will always be cluttered with products.  I'd rather have a single sink flanked by a stack of drawers for each spouse. You might consider deep medicine cabinets for more storage.  If you can't get in enough storage, perhaps you could place a nice cabinet just outside the door for linens and extra toiletries. In this small space, I'd keep the BIG mirror ... but give it a frame.  With this room's lack of lighting and small dimensions, broken up mirrors, though trendy right now, would not be your friend. Was  initially thinking of making that a linen closet but now thinking maybe  turning it into a makeup/seated vanity area. You need storage somewhere -- I wouldn't see a seated spot as a priority.  Personally, since the bathroom is so dark, do you have a spot in the bedroom where you could put a vanity table? Also, current the door is  only 24 inches wide.  Opening that up to 36 and using a pocket door. Yeah, we had a 24" door to the bathroom in our old house, and I always wondered WHY?  Well, I know the answer:  a smaller door allowed space for a triple dresser in the bedroom.  Fortunately, we never had any problem with it -- my grandmother could even get in with her walker.  Still, not something I would've chosen. Pocket doors, wonderful for doors that stay open most of the time (like a pantry or mudroom), are a poor choice for a bathroom.  They're harder to open/close, and when they break (not if they break), you'll probably need to hire a pro. You definitely have a door problem ... the shower and the entry door are too close together, and they crowd a person at the sink.  Consider doing the most simple thing of all:  a bigger door that swings towards the bedroom instead of into the small bathroom space.  My previous bathroom (yeah, the 24" door) swung out, and it wasn't a negative in any way. Suggestions: -  Lighting is key to this project.  I'd vote for something sparkle-y.  This bathroom has no personality at the moment, and really pretty lighting takes up no more space than builder-basic. - Depending upon how much you're looking to spend on this reno, how about opening up a stained glass /leaded glass window between the bathroom and the bedroom?  It'd bring some natural light into the bathroom.  You could do a small window above the tub OR something larger that'd span a greater width.  I'm thinking of a short-wide window that wouldn't impede short furniture in the bedroom. - Hardware is another area where you can bring in some personality -- again, with none on your vanity, the bathroom looks "unfinished". - While we're talking hardware, those builder-basic faucets at the sinks aren't doing the room any favors.  Choose a wide-set (easier to clean) with some personality. - You need some color on the walls -- I'd say keep it light but don't go neutral.  Again, this room has no personality at the moment. - Get one loooooong bathrug that'll serve the whole room.  Maybe one of those Rug-ables that can be washed. - With those doors crowded around the shower, where will your towels hang? - The wall above the toilet and tub is awfully large and dull -- need some artwork.  A train rack above the toilet, which could hold towels, would look good. - Think about where a hamper could go.

the mutations are usually inherently weaker ... and to get them a bit more vigor.. they are grafted onto more vibrant understock ... any tissue color away from green is weaker in the sense that it doesnt photosynthesize as green would .... and when your talking about a plant that might be a foot or 2 big in 10 yeas.. if half your tissue is white.. or yellow.. then one reason you have a reduced annual growth rate .. is because of such ... when you back up to the a species ... you can .. well the growers can ... root seedlings of the common species in bulk.. by the hundreds or thousands .. to use as grafting material for the odd balls ... and if it took ten years to get that foot or two big ... you arent going to have a lot of material you can graft .. it might be 10 or 20 years before the plant can come to market .... ken

Limiting to 2 tablespoons of detergent is not a hard-fast rule.  Depends on a myriad of factors including water hardness, soil level, load size, amount of water (a deep-fill Bulky cycle will reasonably take more detergent than a low-HE fill level cycle). Ammonia, detergent of any type, and Biz powder surely can be combined, but DO NOT put the powder into a detergent dispenser with any liquids.  Put the powder product(s) directly into the tub and liquids in the dispenser. Dosing sudsy ammonia (vs. non-sudsy) can be tricky because of the sudsing factor, which is less controllable than detergent sudsing.  Biz can also promote some sudsing.  Biz can be used alone, it has some function as a detergent, I've done that a couple times on pillows or items that need a blast of stain treatment.  Not unusual that I use 4 tablespoons of Biz plus detergent for a super-grungy load, or more Biz than that for a Biz-only blast treatment. I find that a temp of 120°F to 125°F and up does the trick for me on pillow cases darkened from sweaty/oily hair. I don't have any down-filled items ... but I washed a friend's down comforter a couple times.  The last time, several years ago (before she died), I blasted it with oxy-bleach (I hadn't yet rediscovered Biz at the time) and HOT water, twice.  It came out white.  I thought it was a cream color, had never seen it white.  She said it was originally white.  She was a heavy smoker ...

Neem oil is too lightweight to be considered an effective dormant spray. I would avoid vegetable based oils for that reason. They wash off easily with rain and lack enough viscosity to get into all the surface nooks and crannies where overwintering insect eggs hide. Go instead for a superior weight petroleum based oil. They also contain emulsifiers to enhance mixing with water or other pesticides (like copper and sulfur) for a full dormant spray regime. While a dormant spray will help to control both insect and disease issues, it does not necessarily eliminate them. Save the Neem for later season use if you need it. btw, copper and sulfur are best applied during dormancy as they can create a phytotoxic issue when plants are in bud or leaf.

Spray while tree is still fully dormant....before bud swell. But not if the temp drops below 40F for 24 hours or more. And you also want to avoid wind and rain. Whatever petroleum based hort oil you can access should work fine. Bonide makes an 'all-season' oil that works for dormant spraying but is lightweight enough to use during the growing season.

Cost is determined by amount of involvement needed and location. 10-30 % of a project can be some rough numbers for the required pre planning and studies that your location may require. You live in a location with serious oversight and  will need lots of red tape resolved in order to do anythng.  You need an involved design build type of solution. That may be hiring the architect first to create the project design, in consultation with the engineer and a recommended and chosen builder. Or it may be a design build firm. The difference in approach to hiring the design separately from the build is the control that you retain over the process, and to a certain degree, the results. A design build generally designs the easier path to build, which of course will be the less expensive path. But they may discount presenting you options up front as being too expensive, or the wrong approach. They curate their design approach, based on their strong suits. A design first, with  builder consult input generally explores broader options and ideas up front before mutually deciding on a design path. Sometimes those ideas can be more expensive, but sometimes they are less. It gives you more control over the final chosen path, because the ideas presented will not be just about the strengths of the team to implement. For instance, an engineered retaining wall might be on the table, and a design build firm might not even present an idea that had poured concrete walls covered with thin brick, because they don’t have a good masonry contact in their team. They suggest the big kids building block type walls, because its the easier route for them. But even though the costs are maybe 20% apart, the design build results are mainstream, and not that attractive, compared to a stucco or bricked concrete wall. And you wouldnt even know about a different alternative, because it wouldnt have been presented to you.

You don't have a furnace. You have a high efficiency gas fired combinational condensing boiler. Now I understand why running the hot water heater causes a noticeable amount of exhaust. Here is the Phantom Combinational Installation Manual. It has diagrams of various ways the air intake and exhaust can be piped out the side of the house and up through the roof. This is a an expensive boiler. Hopefully it was sized and installed properly. The grey PVC pipe in your picture is the the exhaust, the white one is the air intake. The installer took the easiest path and went straight back to the exterior wall. It might be possible to add a 90 degree elbow and turn the pipe to the right when looking from the inside. The pipe could run along the way and exist the house further away from the window. You will have to determine if there is a spot which is far enough from a window. The other limitation is the pipe has to be sloped 1/4 per foot towards the boiler. That means if the add an 8 foot section of pipe the overall rise of the pipe on the section has to be at least 2 inches. This will limit how far you can move the exhaust opening. I think this will be much easier than trying to go up through the roof. The other thing is potentially a problem with the current intake and exhaust is they are too close to the ground if a snow fall blocks either opening the boiler will shut down and you will have no heat or hot water. Both these pipes should be extended upward above the highest anticipated snow accumulation.

You have hot water heat. I'm guessing it provides the domestic hot water also. You do not have a reasonable option of replacing it with electric. The cost of replacing the entire heating system with an air-air heat pump would be huge and the operating costs of electric resistance boiler would be many times your current heating / water heating costs. Solar PV wouldn't offset that either. Venting for condensing gas appliances (all gas appliances, really) is not anything you can get "creative" with. Improper venting can lead to carbon monoxide poisoning and death. It must be done according to manufacture's instructions. You may not substitute vent pipe materials, you may not exceed the length, add more elbows, etc. It may be possible to run the PVC pipe inside an unused masonry chimney chase - for example - but you can not simply connect to an unused flue. Most code for venting calls for 12" from the vent to the bottom or side of the window on a direct vent appliance. Your installation appears to meet this code. Your code may be different - and I obviously can't measure from your photo. It's possible that you could extend the vent horizontally some feet to get a greater distance from the window. Ideally this would be done inside the basement and then exit the new location - again keeping in mind all of the requirements for slope, elbows, etc. The air intake would not need to be moved. If you do similar research on "is the earth flat?" or "will the covid vaccine make me magnetic" you will likewise be rewarded. "The natural gas has been used to its fullest potential and all that's left is toxic compounds... " is simply nonsense. Natural gas is primarily methane. The most common exhaust compounds are water vapor and carbon dioxide - neither are toxic. Indeed there are some toxic compounds - such as carbon monoxide. There are also small amounts of other chemicals such as oxides of sulfur, nitrogen, etc.  I'm not suggesting that significant exposure to exhaust gas is healthy - but your "...all that's left is toxic compounds" statement is grossly incorrect and suggests you are not evaluating any of this factually. I think the fact that you can see the water vapor now is intensifying the fear that you have created with your "research". Before you go further down the rabbit hole with the venting - do a more thorough examination of the allergies. You say you are experiencing this in the winter, with the windows closed! This most certainly isn't the outside gas appliance vent. Even so, my guess is that you will never be satisfied with the sidewall venting at this point - no matter what anyone says. With all of your internet research, you failed to find the manual online for that boiler. Assuming that this is the correct installation manual for your boiler (you need to verify) you will find all of the venting instructions including the instructions for venting through a roof. Find a qualified contactor to do that work according to the manufacturer's instructions. These instructions are not unique - they are pretty similar to the venting instructions for other condensing furnaces and water heaters I've seen. As a homeowner, you can be excused for not knowing about venting condensing gas appliances. It's not excusable for the professionals who have given you seriously wrong information. You did not hire a qualified contractor. 13 QUESTIONS TO FIND THE RIGHT TILE INSTALLER Qualified tile contractors have the verifiable experience and use proper methods and materials. But how do you know your contractor is qualified? We have surveyed homeowners, designers, contractors and other construction industry experts to compile a list of questions every homeowner should ask an installer before starting a project. To help ensure the tile contractor you hire is the right fit, start with these 13 questions: 1.  Are you licensed in your area? Verify. Some states do not require tile contractors to be licensed. 2. How many years have you/your team been working exclusively as tile installers? It takes many years to become proficient as a dedicated, qualified tile professional. Five years or more would be an expected minimum. 3. How were you trained? Do you participate in on-going professional training from organizations and/or manufacturers, and specifically what? Tile installers who have completed an apprenticeship under a Qualified Tile Installer/Organization and participate in industry training are generally more likely to follow standards and industry recommendations and stay current with products, materials, and industry updates. 4. Tell me about your favorite tile installation project and why. What project(s) were challenging for you and what did you do to overcome those challenges? Get to know the tile professional as part of your project team. Do they take pride in their work? If you have a General Contractor (GC) or Designer who is hiring the tile installer, it may make sense to request meeting with the GC/Designer and tile installer in advance of the installation to plan and answer your questions. 5. Do you have a company website or social media pages with photos of your work? Professionals will have a public presence that is available to consumers so you can review their work and customer reviews. Lack of a traceable, legitimate, and experienced business should be a deterrent to hiring. 6. Can I speak with recent customers and view photos of those projects? Qualified, experienced tile contractors will have a history of satisfied clients that are happy to recommend them and share their experience. 7. Are you familiar with the TCNA Handbook and ANSI Standards? Does your work follow these industry recommendations? The TCNA Handbook coupled with the ANSI Standards are the industry recognized guidelines for the installation of tile for a wide range of applications. A qualified tile professional installer will be familiar with and know how to specify and use these reference tools. 8. Do you have successful experience working with the type of tile I plan to use? There are different methods, materials and considerations when planning and installing various tile products such as ceramic, porcelain, large format tile, handmade tile, mosaics, natural stone or glass. Verify their experience and training with the tile product you have chosen for your project. 9. What manufacturer’s products do you use and do you comply with manufacturer instructions? There are many manufacturers of quality tile setting materials. Most perform well with use of approved methods and adherence to manufacturer specifications. Most qualified tile installers will be well versed on the methods and systems they prefer and should be able to answer your questions about their process and materials and associated warranties. 10. If wet areas (showers/baths) are to be included in the work performed, what approved system/methods will you use to assure a long-lasting installation? Tile installations in wet areas require some very important preparation to avoid leaks and unwanted moisture problems. Unapproved methods, and the use of materials inappropriate for this application can contribute to a very costly and unwanted result that too often requires complete removal and replacement by a qualified professional. A quality installation should last decades or longer. 11. Do you have liability insurance, and if you have employees, are they covered with Worker’s Compensation Insurance? Make sure you can verify appropriate insurance coverage. 12. Do you belong to professional organizations like NTCA (National Tile Contractor’s Association)? Industry involvement is one indication of a tile installation company’s commitment to their craft. It gives them access to education, technical information, and other resources to assist them in professionally serving you. 13.  Are you a Certified Tile Installer (Ceramic Tile Education Foundation, CTI) or do you have Certified Tile Installers on your team? The certification of tile installers is an important step forward for the consumer and is “one” indication of professionalism. The industry has established a process to certify tile installers. Certification identifies an installer as being a dedicated and knowledgeable professional whose competence in installing tile has been verified to meet specific tile industry standards.

It seems like the best place to start is the rootzone, and the 3 areas that need examination are the grow medium + your watering habits + how you fertilize and with what. First though, clay pots offer plants a better opportunity to realize a greater measure of their genetic potential when measured against plastic pots or other pots with walls made of materials that are not gas permeable. This, because they offer significantly better gas exchange between gasses in the rhizosphere and the air surrounding the pot. Where applicable, the increased amount of evaporative cooling they offer also makes them passive root coolers when pots are exposed to direct sun or high ambient temps. The increase in evaporative water loss is a major contribution to decreasing the interval that perched water remains in grow media, limiting root function and health. Any patina of dissolved solids which occur on the outer wall of the pot are not in the soil solution, so are not available for uptake, and represent no threat to the plant. These dissolved solids pull water outward from the grow medium by the same mechanism curing salts 'pull' moisture from ham/ bacon/ sausage. What medium have you chosen as home for your plants' roots? What do you use as a fertilizer and how/ how often do you use it? Are you using any other products like tonics, insecticides, sprayed-on topical products of any kind? How do you make the determination it's time to water? BTW - I agree with Rhizo in that the solution is not going to improve if you add more P than the plant is capable of using. That scenario has no potential to be beneficial, only potential to be limiting. Excess P in the soil solution limits uptake of several nutrients (called an antagonistic deficiency), namely potassium, calcium, iron, copper, and zinc, some of which cause chlorosis. Also, the idea that nitrogen is "for foliage", P is "for roots", and K is for the plant's well being (often remembered by the phrase (up, down, all around) is misleading to the point of being pernicious. All 12 nutrients plants absorb by the root pathway are essential to the normal growth of every plant organ; and, you'll find that tissue analysis reveals very little deviation in the % of nutrients in the various organs of any individual plant. IOW, the leaves, roots, and stems that make up plant A will all have roughly the same level of nutrients in all 3 types of tissue. As it applies to conventional container culture, you would do yourself a favor if you can resist being drawn into the trap of dosing your plants with compounds aimed specifically at providing one or only a few nutrients. One of the major goals of fertilizing containerized plants is to make sure ALL essential nutrients are in the medium and available for uptake, at a ratio that mimics the ratio at which the nutrients are used, as closely as possible. That cannot be achieved by hobby growers who tend toward adding a little of this or that nutrient or tonic because they heard somewhere that more than necessary could somehow benefit the plant. Fertilizing Containerized Plants How Much P is Enough? Al

Ontario building codes does reference different grades of lumber for different building applications with the exception to Trusses.  In this case it's refers to loads and deflection minimums and references to ATSM standards used for certification. I would take this as to say no grade is specified in code for trusses but will be determined by engineered design to meet minimum requirements in the code through ATSM standards.  So they could make the trusses out of pop sickle sticks if engineered to meet the minimum requirement of the code through ATSM testing standards. So it doesn't matter if they use MSR or grade 2 and why the two truss companies use different grades.  Both will have the desired outcome when engineered and both acceptable to use, so it could be just based on the preference of the material the two companies elect to use.  One grade over the other may not be compatible with their software design program or truss jigs and could be just be a matter of economics to support both grades of lumber to build the trusses.

Roof trusses are not covered in the OBC because they are proprietary to each supplier. It's the same for floor trusses. The permit office or Inspector have no jurisdiction in this area. They have to accept the drawings/calculations provided by the manufacturer because the manufacturer takes all the liability for the performance of those components. Ooh, new garden beds, that’s exciting!! :) Here are my top plants with long blooming periods: 1- Echinacea: if they do well in your area, look for long blooming varieties.  I've planted 6-7 varieties, and so far my favorite is Bright Star.  It blooms for 2 months! 2- Penstemon: I have 2 varieties that are equally gorgeous: Dakota Burgundy and Onyx and Pearls.  Dakota Burgundy was planted 3 years ago.  They are long blooming, the bloom stalks and foliage are beautiful as well.  And when the snow melts, the foliage still looks fresh! 3- Nepeta: I have 4 varieties, my favorite one (by far) is Dropmore.  It looks good in fall even after a hard frost. 4- Delphiniums: if you don't mind staking them, they're a lovely addition.  They bloom for a long time and if you cut them back, you'll get more blooms, even with our short summers! 5- Tall phlox: they’re beautiful and they smell great! :) 6- Achillea: I love these.  I’ve had Terracotta for a few years and I added 2 more varieties in 2021.  They were still blooming at the end of September. 7- Veronicas: I planted White Wands 3 years ago and love it.  It does bloom again if you cut them after the first blooms are done. 8- Coreopsis Moonbeam: love the soft yellow, and it blooms much earlier than my other varieties. And here’s my list of top plants for striking blooms that reliably come back: 1- Darwin tulips: if you’re in a deer-free area, you gotta try these.  I planted the first ones 7-8 years ago, and they’ve always come back.  I read that they must be planted deeply, which I did.  Nothing beats tulips after a long winter. 2- Peonies: itohs and herbaceous.  They are new to my garden, except for Bowl of Beauty, but one of Canada's largest grower is very close to where I live, they grow both itohs and herbaceous so you'll be ok. 3- Iris: Bearded and Siberian.  My favorite Siberian is Pink Parfait, it has a longer bloom period than my other siberian.  It's too hard to pick a favorite tall bearded, but Don't Stop Believing was a show-stopper. 4- Clematis: I can never get them to look as good as what other people post online (mine look sparse in comparison), but still, the blooms are amazing.  I go mostly for type 3 clematis, the ones that bloom on new wood. Type 2 are ok, but since they die back to the ground, they never get very tall (max 7 feet). 5- Daylilies: this one is a no-brainer for cold zones.  I know many people don’t like them, but maybe it’s the ditch orange daylily that they think of?  The foliage stays fresh until late fall here.  One of my favorites is an old one, Siloam Double Classic. 6- Lilies: I’m just getting started with lilies.  I’ve had Apricot Fudge reliably come back for 5 years, and I’m now looking to add a lot more varieties in 2022. 7- Leucanthemums: I’ve planted a few varieties over the years, they’ve always come back. 8- Liatris: they were among the first perennials I planted.  Their bloom period is not super long, but they look SO good with echinaceas! I think that's all I can think of.  There are other plants/shrubs that I really like but they are recent addition in my garden so I won't recommend them until they've been in the ground for a few years. Hope this helps!!

I am assuming the 44" opening is cased with drywall. It is not a problem to leave drywall behind a framed infill or something. However, keep in mind: - On the outside flush face, you will have to remove at least the cornerbead and if you leave the drywall jambs you may have to cut back the jamb face if it sticks out to interfere with the new sheet butting flush in the same plane (strike side of door). - On the head, the drywall should probably be removed. A door is rough framed at about 82 1/2" high, but you don't know what they framed it at. So they might have dropped the drywall casing down to match a height of an adjacent door frame head, and you need the whole 82 1/2" for a new door. - On the inside of the closet, I suppose using 2x4 instead of 2x6 saves you from ripping a jamb extension. Leave the cornerbead or remove it, just depends on what's there, how it's finished, and how much drywall you plan on removing. - It sounds like you are new at DIY, it might be good to try out the drywall installation and finishing yourself. The rough-in frame will be 32" wide, so that leaves a 12" wide piece of drywall on the front and back to fill in. That is not a lot to hire a drywall + finisher to do for you, and a handyman probably has no more skill than you in finishing. So use it as learning. The hardest part for you I bet will probably be getting a sheet of drywall home.

The term "invasive" only applies to introduced species that outcompete native species. The American Beech is native. At worst it is an aggressive spreader. That being said, I understand your concern. Lawn grass is said not to grow well under Beech trees, so planting them near the ravine makes sense. HERE is an article. One final thought, even forest plants do better with more light. Too many people have lost too much in this pandemic. My dad got it in summer 2020 in India and was hospitalized for a couple of weeks. Their healthy albeit older next-door neighbor died. Yet they traveled by train unvaccinated.... Eventually, they got vaccinated of their own accord and us kids learnt that sometimes it is what it is. Long story short, it is easy to label people anti-vaxers but often things are complicated and human psychology is unfathomable. text: You didn't say how high your hedge needs to be.  Are deer a problem? How's the drainage? No for Prunus caroliniana. It is a tree and can get damaged in winter. But there may be other Prunus such as Skip laurel, provided they get enough moisture. It can get 8 to 15 feet. Prunus laurocerasus 'Otto Luyken' works for many years. Doesn't get much over 4 or 5 feet. But can eventually get white scale and die out. Euonymus is great provided your area is fenced from deer. Golden euonymus, Silver King euonymus, etc. Wax myrtle may work, but can defoliate in really cold winters. Also, snow loads can break them up, which is discouraging, but deer don't like them. You might consider Viburnum pragense. It's a bit course, but with shaping looks fairly good. Takes regular maintenance. Stays evergreen. It's tough and deer don't care for it.  Leaves droop in coldest weather. Then there are all the hollies, such as I cornuta 'Burford', 'Needlepoint', 'Carissa', I. cornuta Rotundifolia, Ilex crenata and all it's cultivars, the Blue hollies and all their cultivars.

An ice barrier is required to be installed from the edge of eave to a point 24" inside the exterior wall line. Since the roll is 36" wide, usually a roofer will lay just one row and stop no matter the eave length. Another row might be beneficial and more exact to code, but since the self-stick ice barrier is very difficult to get off in the future, it is typically not installed all the way up to ridge. And there usually aren't roof leaks in the blank field of a roof; they mostly occur at penetrations and transitions, so the ice barrier over the entire roof plane may not help in any leak prevention anyway. Though it is good to put in valleys if you have them. The rest of the underlayment can be the tried-and-true felt, or you can choose a synthetic product (that feels like Tyvek).

Hood system requirements follow from the characteristics of cooking plumes, mainly their diameter, divergence as they rise, volumetric flow rate, and their velocity.  The requirements somewhat vary with the design of the hood -- particularly the volume under the baffles that I will call the reservoir -- with horizontal baffle residential hoods representing one end of the configuration spectrum, and high pitched baffles within a commercial hood representing the other end.  Pitched baffles seen in some residential hoods, such as Wolf Pro hoods, are an intermediate case that is closer to the horizontal configuration than the high commercial configuration. We start with the hood entry area.  It should be large enough to encompass any plume from any burner and pan.  Generally, a hood width of 6 inches beyond the range width is considered adequate for residential cooking.  More refinement can be made from plume types and their divergence angles from the locus of potential pan areas, but for this message these details will be left unstated.  So we get 48 + 6 inches as a desired width. Front to back depth should be a deep as available from residential units, although one can get custom/bespoke designs of almost any configuration.  Assume that the hood aperture is 24 inches within a 27-inch hood (see Wolf Pro hood details).  This hood, then, has an entry aperture area of 4.5 x 2 = 9 square feet and should be adequate up to 36 inches above the pans.  (Note that I am working with a wall hood here and not an insert into a cabinet like structure.  What is available for such applications may not meet what is desirable in hood entry aperture sizing.) We need the airflow to be sufficient to deal with entraining the plumes into the baffle flow.  Worst case, this could be calculated from potential plume sizes and velocities, but given that residential hoods with low reservoir volumes cannot average plumes across the entire baffle space, some approximations are needed to achieve adequacy.  The one I like that is derived, in a sense, from the Greenheck method (https://www.tagengineering.ca/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/KVSApplDesign_catalog.pdf) is to assume that the baffle gap area is half the aperture area, and that the effective plume velocity can be 3 ft/s (peaks to 1.2 m/s have been observed).  This leads to a need for 180 ft/min in the baffle gaps, or 90 ft/min across the aperture.  No one here building to that standard has yet complained about inadequate flow, so we will go with 90 ft/min. 90 ft/min x 9 sq. ft. is 810 CFM.  That is the desired actual flow rate at full blower power.  Blowers are rated for free air (zero static pressure) performance, and this will need to be about 1.5 times the requirement to make up for (at a minimum) baffle pressure loss. In this case, the result is a 1200 CFM blower. Poor MUA pressure balance may lead to a higher requirement. An internal blower will not be quiet at this level.  An external blower just outside the mounting wall will be barely quieter, unless an even more powerful motor is used at reduced power.  Best quieting with standard residential components is a roof blower with a large enough duct and an intermediate silencer.  Note that internal blowers are limited by the space available, while external blowers can grow larger, but compatibility with hood controls could be an issue.  Roof vs. in-line in the attic is a matter of many small details I don't have time to address. In common residential applications the level of grease deposit on ducting and external motor parts is relatively low, and what grease there is tends to rancidify and turn to varnish.  If grease is deposited on a roof, UV sunlight will likely decompose it.  A shaded wall mount might show grease on the wall that isn't decomposed, and which will need occasional cleaning.  Commercial applications require grease capture at the blower, in addition to at the baffles. In general, I would expect that you would only need to clean the hood baffle assemblies (usually in a dishwasher) and wipe out the hood interior. I can't price different configurations.  I use a roof blower. MUA in households is considerably more painful to deal with than in commercial spaces.  There is the issue of yet more ducting, location of diffuser(s) to supply the air, possible additional blower and control system, filtering, and heating.  If you search here on 'MUA" and 'kaseki' you should find a lot of messages dealing with different aspects of this that you can generalize from, or, if you find an impediment, ask about a specific issue. There are aspects of this quest that I can't answer for you.  In particular, you will be working in a trade space that includes cost and aesthetics.  High performance and good looks will not be compatible with low cost.  You have to find the balance that best fits your circumstances.

text: The question comes down to - how long do I need to leave it on to mimic sunlight? Sunlight, with the sun straight overhead, is 100,000 lumens/square meter. The sun usually isn't straight overhead, so the sunlight we really get is more like 40,000 lumens/meter. Your Grossyland 2000W light (it's really not 2000W, but rather 2000W incandescent-equivalent, or 400 real electrical watts ) puts out something like  35,000 lumens. So, shining on one square meter (which is somewhat larger than the lamp itself), is something like the average sun. One foot above the plants, the 20x20 inch lamp is probably lighting up maybe two square meters. So  you're illuminating that area with about one half of average sunlight. That being the case, it you want to shoot for the equivalent of 8 hours of average sunlight per day, you could probably leave your lamp on for twice that per day. Of course, we always have cloudy days, so you really aren't going to get 8 hours of average sunlight anyway.

It's often referred to as a museum reveal-- its usually done with a Z bead profile, or some people create with with two layers of drywall, or some finish material set against the framing, and then covered with the drywall layer with some sort of bead at the reveal. It's an expensive tricky detail to do right, the floors have to be dead flat or the bead needs tobe adjusted all along to maintain the width. And, then, if you are not careful you will hit the bottom with a vacuum cleaner or whatever you use to clean the floor and it's not as sturdy as a baseboard. I hand this with wood paneling in my last place and I also had to go around and clean it with a cloth wrapped around my finger because insects would make cocoons in the crevice, things like that. A slightly sturdier but just as tricky to execute is flush or recessed baseboard. EZYJamb makes this product. I don't want to discourage you from doing it, if that's what you want, but it's more expensive to execute (lots more, speaking from personal experience) and harder to maintain. But very handsome in a modern setting.

Replacing a bearing beam in the basement is a huge expense. New posts, footings, maybe replacing it entirely, and in this scheme multiple beams. And then framing around the new stair requiring new joists and girders. All requires removal of MEP. Simply work with the existing structure. You're going to see the hole if you don't do it correctly. But, if you want to try it, strip and sand off the old finish first. Get a good wood filler in the same color of the wood. (Birch is what you have) Break off a little piece of toothpick and shove it in the hole, tape off the back side of the hole and fill w/the colored wood filler.  the pick gives the filler something to bite on to. Make sure to get enough in there or else you'll end up w/a divot. try and scrape off all the excess around the hole.    let it dry.  get a 100-150 grit paper and sand it smooth.  finish w/a 220 grit.  use your fingers to go over it.  they'll tell you if it's perfectly smooth. (when you remove those doors, make sure you mark them so they go back in the same place.  After 60 years, they hang a certain way and if you mix them up, they won't look right) Even if you end up painting, you'll still want to do a good job filling the hole so it won't show through.  There are diff wood fillers.  you want something that is stainable/and can sand.  I've used this brand and some others.   Give the cabs a final sanding w/220 (no higher) and apply a wood conditioner before applying the stain.  Use something like Varathane or General finishes. There is nothing in worm castings in the way of nutrition that can't be found in fertilizer, and not only is there no chance it will improve a container mediums structure, as it's fine texture will be detrimental to any medium that is appropriate for conventional container growing. How detrimental is directly related to how much is used. About mycorrhizae - A) Pots generally offer inhospitable conditions that aren't conducive to the long-term survival of fungi that are capable of forming symbiotic relationships with plants they share the pot with. Populations  of beneficial fungi tend toward boom/bust at best. E.g., when I repot in early spring or occasionally in late fall, or when I check roots in  winter by tipping the plant out of the pot to examine roots, the pots  are generally well-populated with of hyphae of a variety of fungi. Once  summer temps and sunshine (sunlight striking the pot and creating heat) come into play, the fungi seem to vanish until temps cool again. I can't  imagine that indoor conditions would be any better. Almost all the  temperate plants I grow are passively inoculated by beneficial fungi spores which arrive on the wind, and the fungi proliferate under influence of cool/cold temps, but I've  never seen the fungi or evidence thereof in a planting that has been growing indoors. B) All else equal, plants in pots that DO form relationships with beneficial fungi do not need a root system as large as plants that do not form the relationships. Plants are very economical, so if they don't need a larger root system they will not grow it. This means that if something occurs suddenly that reduces the population of fungal pals (like application of a fungicide or other  product not appreciated by the fungal friendlies, the root system very  suddenly becomes much too small to support the top of the plant, which  can cause serious consequences. This is the primary reason I choose not to court growth of friendly fungi in pots. At least for the way I grow,  their cultural wants are well beyond what I'm willing to do to try to keep them thriving. I'm growing plants, not fungi. Be very careful about holding great expectations for products claiming to contain live mycorrhizae. It takes very little heat to kill packaged/living fungi. Some products will contain some live fungi and some none. Some will contain fungi that are unable to live in or adapt to the cultural conditions under which we expect them to prove beneficial. As a variation on the theme "if you build it, they will come", if we establish a container planting and the conditions in the container are conducive to establishment of beneficial fungi, they will arrive and establish quickly w/o our help. 1) Since retaining wall blocks are seldom, if ever, used in house construction, this is certainly a landscaping question. 2) The blocks are most definitely backwards. The rounded side is the face and the crease showing is the interlocking feature that should be against the soil. The blocks should also fit snuggly together around the curve so that there are no obvious gaps showing on the face of the wall. Any gaps will be in the back  to form the arc and are then filled by the soil. 3) If the standard 6" height, this is barely a retaining wall at all and more of just a tallish edging system. Don't try to over-engineer it. A 2-4 inch gravel base trench is fine but the first course should be at least half way below grade. If the finished height is less than 24", the wall really doesn't require anything more than to be back filled, but if it makes you feel better you can backfill immediately behind the wall with more gravel before filling in with soil. If the interlocking features are addressed properly, that wall is not going anywhere with the modest soil weight behind it.

Most homeowners aren't willing to pay for completely fixed walls but the imperfections should be fixed where practical.  A good painter will walk through the job with you before giving you a price so he can decide how much prep work you are expecting. Some homeowners are extremely particular and willing to pay for the prep work while others only want the worst damage spots touched and just want to see color on their walls. When we did the house I live in, my partner took a high output LED worklight held at a slight angle to the wall and checked for spots where the light reflected differently.  Most jobs don't get this level of prep work and mine didn't get that much attention in secondary spaces. Short answer: hard to say. You'd have to buy a quart/gallon, have it mixed, let it dry and look at it. Long answer: Paint colors (surface colors in general) don't have undertones. Undertones is a theory hatched into existence on the internet; it's based on subjective opinion and speculation. In other words, undertones are just someone's subjective opinion of what a paint color looks like to them under whatever light source there is and in whatever random context. Undertones aren't facts. One can say a paint color has any undertone they want to. The science behind a paint color formula is fact. Most importantly it's repeatable. Which is why they can mix gallons of a color over and over in different store locations and the result is a color that matches an original paint chip. When that formula is altered, the result is a new color. That new color **might** have similar attributes hue, value, chroma, LRV as the color you started with. It might not. Because it's factually new formula for a new color. What 25% lighter means is open to interpretation. 25% of what is the question. 25% versions of a color can vary greatly from store to store or even tinter to tinter. Again, won't know until it's mixed, dried, measured and compared to the color you started with.

If you do seeding in the spring, you are almost guaranteed to get crabgrass instead of real grass.  The real grass seeded in the spring will not have time to develop deep hardy roots before the summer heat hits, and so it comes in thin and dies quickly.  Further, crabgrass, Mother Nature's bare soil filler, loves the daily watering it gets from people trying to start lawns in the spring.  Crabgrass is a summer annual plant designed by Nature to sprout in the spring and thrive in the summer.  There is such a thing as frost seeding where you seed now(ish) and let Nature take Her course with germination in the late winter or early spring.  It's not the preferred method, but every month from now on your chances of success diminish. As for shade, you should be overseeding with a shade tolerant variety of fescue to help with that.  Weeds, if you use herbicide, should be sprayed in mid April after they have become established.  You can help yourself out by not watering more frequently than once every month to 3 weeks until late April, then every 2 weeks changing to every week in the heat of summer.  Always water 1 inch at a time when you do.  Check that with tuna or cat food cans placed around the yard when you water.  One inch probably takes longer than you think.  Dog pee should not be a problem if you have a healthy soil.  You can improve the soil's health by using organic fertilizer at least once a year.  Late spring seems to be good for that.  In the mean time, if you suspect you have dog pee spots, drop a handful of table sugar on the spot to help the soil microbes to repopulate.  Sugar is not exactly fertilizer, but it is food for the bacteria which process the urine.  The bacteria turn the urine into plant food, so sugar is more like a stimulant.

The yellowing foliage is not symptomatic of chill injury, which involves leakage of phenolic compounds from cells into intracellular spaces (spaces between cells), after which the affected part of leaves very quickly turn dark and limp. In order frequency beginning with the most common potential causes, chlorotic leaves as shown are most often caused by * over or under-watering, * natural senescence (aging), * any of: poor nutrition - especially a deficiency of nitrogen, root congestion, soil compaction * a high level of dissolved solids (salts) in the grow medium. W/o knowing more about your watering/ fertilizing habits and an idea of whether or not the medium you're using is working for you instead of against you, it's difficult to tell with any certainty which of the list is the likely cause. Where you currently live, is the supply plumbing routed through an ionic exchange water softening system (uses salt)? EVERY plant grown in a pot is stressed. The idea someone should wait for 3 months before finally deciding to become proactive and address stressful cultural influences doesn't make sense. If we keep doing what we're doing, we'll get more of what we've already got. The appropriate approach is to immediately try to identify the cause and eliminate that source of stress to the greatest degree we think is appropriate. Our green thumbs are earned not by leaving the plant to its own devices and hoping Mother Nature sorts things out favorably, but by being ever vigilant and proactive. Mother Nature always sides with the hidden flaw. I've put together this Overview of Good Growing Practices so growers struggling with plants in decline or in need of help can compare their care regimen to proven practices. As you read through it, you'll likely find areas that can be improved. Being proactive doesn't necessarily mean you have to act immediately. Being proactive works best when you have a care regimen planned so as to take advantage of the part of the growth cycle when the plant is strongest and make allowances for when the plant is weakest. A fast-draining and well-aerated medium, good watering/ fertilizing habits, regularly repotting plants so roots have room to run, and keeping other cultural influences like temps, light levels, relative humidity in the plant's sweet spot. I can't emphasize enough how much influence our choice of grow medium has on our ability to offer our plants the best opportunity to realize as much of their genetic potential as possible. The largest step forward we'll likely ever take as a container gardeners is gaining an understanding how to control the amount of air and water a grow medium can hold. I am a US patent attorney. All patent rights are country specific. If there is no granted patent in the US the innovator cannot enforce some other country's patent here. Pending patent (applications) are not enforceable until they are granted at which point limited damages may be claimed for the period when the application was pending and infringement occurred. As a home gardener I would generally only worry about granted US patents. The best place to look for them is here using key words: US Patent Full-Text Database Boolean Search (uspto.gov) If you have a specific query I would be happy to help. Trademarks are also country specific although it is a bit more complicated. There are commonlaw trademark rights that accrue from use even if they are not formally registered. most arthritis drugs for dogs including rimadyl and previcox are processed through the kidneys and liver.    long term use can lead to issues that are very, very difficult to manage when it comes to organ function. this old gal is 8.5 and started showing significant issues with arthritis in her hips and spine several months ago.    the vet put her on daily previcox at the time.    she had pre-op blood work done in november prior to having her left eye removed (glaucoma).   her kidney values and liver enzymes were elevated, most likely due to the previcox.    normally, i would have postponed the surgery but it was necessary as the IOP in her bad eye was extremely high and was causing her a lot of pain.   thankfully, she sailed through it and is completely recovered. since having to discontinue the previcox, i put her on galliprant as this drug is not filtered through any organs.    she's doing great on it and after the addition of a liver supplement and switching her to a renal support diet, her follow up blood work several weeks ago was perfect.
