It is a bit difficult to answer your question as there are different versions of conversion varnish and lacquer. Any true conversion varnish is going to have Xylene and it should definitely not be sprayed in your home.  Really, it should not be used on consumer goods.  In the U.S. manufacturers bind the xylene molecules to reach permissible levels, this makes the Xylene offgas less but for longer periods of time.  In Europe that is not allowed thus conversion varnish is not allowed. Having said that, there are some water based products that are marketed as conversion varnish but don't have Xylene.  These products are not as durable as true conversion varnish. Pre-cat and post-cat lacquers are bright and durable but will yellow over time (a fairly short time).  CAB acrylic lacquers resist yellowing but are not quite as durable.  Lacquers are not exactly good to breath, but much better than CV. BM Advance is not really a cabinet coating.  It is a great product for trimwork, but isn't the best product for cabinets. There are many durable products that can be sprayed in the home.  Two part polyurethane is a good product and safe once it cures.  Envirolak is a company with several good products.  There are many other products that are durable and good.

I added some veneer to chest of drawers once. It was an inexpensive unfinished wood 3 drawer that had unfinished edge that showed the raw plywood edge. Once it's that bad repair is probably not a sensible option. Instead do what a higher quality maker would have done in the first place on such a wear surface, laminate a piece of matching solid lumber onto the edge 1/4 to 1/2 inch thick. A desk edge is no place for veneer on particle board.

It seems to me that you can either have a conventional boiler that heats water and pumps it around radiators, or a warm air system or some sort of electrical heat source in every room.    (Assuming an ASHP is not practical and installing a wet underfloor heating system is too disruptive and oil is undesirable). When I looked at this I concluded that if I were starting from scratch I would have chosen a warm air system which seems to be the heating of choice in colder countries like Canada and in Scandinavia.  Warm air heating does seem to work faster than radiators and modern advances in filters mean it’s no longer associated with dust or allergens as it was in the 70s.   You also free up wall space although the ducting will need consideration. Whether or not you decide on radiators or hot air the thing to consider next is the fuel source.   It seems to me that with gas price rises the gap between gas and the more expensive electricity is narrowing. It does however seem that more powerful gas boilers are available than electric ones and the water flow rates are better so if you choose a combi then you can get a good flow rate for your morning shower.    You might still conclude you prefer electric boilers (apparently they last longer and don’t need the regular servicing of a gas boiler).  If you go the electric route then you might decide on more than one boiler, a tank of hot water rather than heating it on demand and thermostats in each room make it more efficient. Whatever you decide- best of luck

Thoughts on tile: - You're using an awful lot of similar tiles.  I'd like to see something solid /near-solid to break up what will end up being an awful lot of same-same-same.  To go with these tiles, gray makes sense.  Where to put it?  Maybe on the countertops?  Not the floor; the floor is much too large to go with a gray ... not in a room without natural light.  Gray on the shower floor would look good. Now some thoughts on the layout: - Look at your door swings:  You want to reverse your bathroom entry door so you enter and are "oriented towards" the room /not running into a wall /walking around the door to enter.  Similarly, you probably want the linen closet door to open towards the main room. - Are those 33" bathroom sinks?   A 33" sink in the kitchen is a great idea, but why in the world would you want something that large for the bathroom?  And why would you ever want a duplicate of that large sink?  Look at a yardstick and ask yourself whether this is really where you want to splurge. - Next to those massive sinks, you have 15" drawers.  Note that the sides /hardware will eat up 3-4", so you'll have 11-12" actual drawer space at the sink.  This isn't bad storage, but it's also not exactly generous, especially given the size of this bathroom ... I'd cut those sinks down /go with a standard 18-22" sink and allow yourself more at-sink storage. - You have roughly 8'x8' empty space in the middle of this room.  Why?  You could literally put a king-sized bed in this bathroom.  This is a lot to tile, and it serves no purpose.  Unless you're planning to bring in a bathroom seating area or exercise equipment or MMA fights, this large empty space will feel cold, especially since you don't have a window in this bathroom.  Think again about how this large empty space with all your working-parts floating around the edge will look in reality. - Yet with all this empty space, your shower is modest in size.  I had a shower that exact size in my old house, and while it was perfectly serviceable, it was not luxurious.  I can't see going with a modest shower and all that empty space. - Your shower head should be on the other end of the shower enclosure ... but keep your controls by the door (so you can turn on the shower without walking in).  With the shower head on the left side, you'll be able to step into the shower without being directly in the water stream.  Having your shower head "back up to" a closet is a wise choice ... it means that a plumber could access your shower's internal workings by cutting through your closet drywall /not your expensive shower tile.  I have an access panel in my linen closet that allows access to plumbing.  Because plumbing will one day break, that's future-proofing. - Where will you hang your shower towels? - I always dislike toilets-in-closets, especially since this one is stealing the only window in the whole large bathroom.  And yours is minimal in size.  36" wide feels narrow, even to a small person like me.  It's like using a bathroom stall in a store, and you have no storage by the toilet ... no space for extra toilet paper or medical needs you may develop as you age.  Even if you want a toilet-in-a-closet, why would you make it minimal in size, while you have all this empty space in the middle of the room? - If you lose the linen closet, you could enlarge the shower ... it's also going to cause an odd viewpoint as you enter the room. You have a mallet cutting with an adventitious root, and what you have created is a viable solution, even if not the best. I'll describe what I would do, then offer an alternate because I'm guessing you would have enough faith (in what I recount) to do what I first describe. I would first cut the leaf across the veins so it has 1/4-1/3 its current surface area. Then, I would reduce the length of the adventitious root (with a very sharp tool) so the node from which the leaf and adventitious root emanates can be situated atop of the grow medium. I would then use moist sphagnum moss (not peat moss)  to cover the node, then cover the top of the moist medium with a piece of Saran Wrap or its equal. Reducing the surface of the leaf alleviates the demand that the roots work well enough to keep the entire leaf hydrated. It also reduces the potentiality of the entire propagule collapsing by way of the leaf being shed if roots are unable to keep abreast of water requirements. Situating the mallet end of the cutting ensures a direct connection from de novo (newly formed) roots to the propagule's existing vasculature. Alternately: I would secure a deeper pot, one that allows the mallet end of the cutting to rest atop of the grow medium. A quart milk carton of waxed cardboard or plastic could be pressed into handy service - don't forget to add a drain hole. Fill the bottom 1/3 of the container with about 2" of the medium shown in your image. Then add an inch or so of a mix of 3:1, perlite to peat, peat being the larger fraction. Situate the end of the adventitious root into the container so when you fill the remainder of the container with a 2:1 mix of Perlite, the mallet end rests on the soil. Cover with moist sphagnum moss (see image above) or simply cover the top of the container with plastic wrap or aluminum foil. Should you chose this alternate method, it would still be a good Idea to reduce the surface area of the leaf for insurance. Al

I am not an attorney. However, here’s my reading of this: Mechanic’s liens were intended to protect workers from not getting paid for their work. They are enforceable against the property owner because the property owner benefitted from their work. For that reason, you are obligated to make sure that the contractors have been paid for the work they have done up to the point of the GC’S death. The subs contracts were with the GC. He is dead. Assuming there is no legal entity (a corporation) surviving the GC, any claims for work not yet done is the responsibility of the GC’s estate.You are NOT obligated to fulfill the terms of the contract for the GC. The contracts are not enforceable against you. You are only obligated to make sure that the subs were paid for the work that was actually done. You are not liable for any penalties, late fees, the balance of the contract, termination clauses, etc. You may be liable for reasonable collection fees if you don’t deal with some of this. At this point your job (with the new GC and attorney) is to determine how much work was completed by each sub and what is owed to them. There are a couple of ways to determine this, but looking at written contracts and progress billing would be where I would start. Percentage of completion is where I’d go next. If, for example, an electrical sub has a $20k written contract and that’s within “normal and customary” range for a job this size and the contract states 50% at rough in – for example- and rough-in is complete, I’d honor those terms. There are some trades where the costs are front-loaded, and some where the costs come at the end of the contract – so percent completion can be tricky… this is where your GC is very helpful. Also, the GC can help determine what is usual and customary. Ultimately, determining a fair amount for the work that’s actually been done and not paid needs to be a mutual agreement and everybody will take a haircut. The subs who will come out best will be the ones who have well documented contracts and progress billing, come to an agreement on what is owed to them at this point, and agree to finish the job based on a new contract with the new GC. Payment for work done under the previous GC is contingent on them agreeing to not file a lien for work done under previous GC. You don’t have the benefit of seeing the GC’s payment records, so a sub could BS you about not being paid. You can caution them that if it comes to light that they lied, you will come after them. You really want your attorney to get out ahead of this to avoid liens being filed. Again, I think that making a good faith effort to promptly clean up the mess will work very much in your favor in the event that subs decide to do an end-run around the settlement process and make an unreasonable claim and lien.

$29,000 doesn't sound bad if the contractor is including all the materials and fixtures to completion. A lot of noise about liens, but did you have a contract with dead GC?  If so there must be a notification in the contract stating "Subcontractors or materials suppliers may file a lien against the property upon which the work is being done if they are not paid for their contribution" or words to this effect.  This would be the pre-lien notice for the contractor and subcontractors.  Without a pre-lien in a notice the contractor and subcontractors lose the right to file a mechanics lien against real estate property. If the subcontractor's right to file a lean notice isn't in the GC's contract they must notify you within 45 days after work begins or material delivered to job site of a pre-lien notice to have the right to file a lien, did you receive any?.  One point to make is even if the subcontractor gives proper pre-lien notice, that once the General contractor is paid in full the subcontractors will then lose the right to file a lien. You did not mention the state you are building in as others have asked, but the lien notification process above is for Minnesota.  The 120 day period mentioned is a time limit AFTER the work is completed which they can file a lien. The lawyer will give the details for your state so take your papers with you.  I'm kind of thinking the Subcontractors have lost the rights to file a lien and the plumber/HVAC guy is willing to cut the price and trying to scare you. Who paid for the building materials?  Good chance the suppliers will be coming after you next if the GC didn't pay them.

"We're running into the frustration that everything we see is only remote dimmable (with included remote) for color temperature and dimming  functions." If you choose a fixture that allows you to dim the light and control the color temperature, then you will have to use the supplied remote because, I believe, there's no standard dimmer switch that controls both these values. Instead, choose a dimmable fixture whose color temperature is fixed. Then you'll be able to control the fixture with an off-the-shelf wall dimmer. Examples: Note that there are several types of dimmers including TRIAC and ELV and that different fixtures require different dimmer types. Always check the requirements of any fixture you're considering. Note also that ELV dimmers are more expensive than TRIAC dimmers. The Vega Minor happens to work with both TRIAC and ELV dimmers and the its webpage lists supported dimmers. The Lunedi requires a TRIAC dimmer.

"My question is, how is the one part peat better than the removed small particles of bark?" That's a valid question and I don't have the answer. Might be worth an experiment :-) ZM, acidifying with vinegar water is a pretty common practice for those who like to grow acid loving plants but whose irrigation water is alkaline. It's a pretty dilute solution - a tablespoon of table vinegar to a gallon of water - and is harmless. Vinegar can act as a herbicide but it needs to be of a much higher concentration (even undiluted table vinegar is only marginally effective), must be sprayed directly on the foliage and it must be applied with direct sunlight to generate the phytotoxic reaction that kills the plant. Or at least the foliage - roots are rarely damaged.

Luna Tonks, The flue pipe you show is not a combustion pipe. That is a flue pipe. Combustion air is not drawn from a flue pipe it is drawn from fresh air around the appliance, in this case that air is drawn from the attic which is why the attic space around the plenum that sticks up into the attic is open. If gas furnaces do not have proper combustion air this results in incomplete combustion and produces large amounts of CO or carbon monoxide. Gas furnaces are not a DIY appliance. There are safety concerns to be considered. Do not attempt to seal that cavity up from the attic, it is there for a reason. If you want a more efficient way to heat your home, consult a professionally licensed Texas HVAC contractor in your area. I service the Katy, Texas area.

The last time I rebuilt the stair/walkway I removed the paving bricks, about an inch of sand and then varying amounts of crushed stone until I came to what seemed to be undisturbed clay soil. I live in central Massachusetts. The entire yard has a varying slope. Depending on where along the way I was working I dug down from 4 inches to around a foot to reach the soil. I did not put any type of fabric on the clay although I tamped it aggressively with a 30# tamper. I did not remove the PT timbers, but worked on each horizontal section at a time. On the tamped soil, I threw in 2" of asphalted crushed stone that a local landscape supply yard recommended. I tamped each layer of this mix thoroughly before adding another, to fill up to about 3" below the tops of the timbers. I screeded the leftover sand to the level of the bottom of the pavers, laid them tight and swept fine sand into the cracks. The surrounding timbers appeared to be in good shape with little rot so I felt comfortable working to them.

I think the problem is your base is failing.  You have issues with base depth and base lining preparation. Let's talk about base depth.   At a high level, the common wisdom is that a paver patio should use a base that is four to six inches deep.   A driveway is typically done with a base that is eight to 12 inches.   I had another thread here recently where I was trying to cheat on those rules down to two inches, and your case is a great example of why my question was misguided.   I think a properly prepared base that is a *minimum* of six inches will solve your problem. Let's talk about base lining.   I know this is hard to believe, but rocks sink into clay over time.   If I were to put some rocks on top of clay soil that is exposed to water, and if I were able to do time-lapse photography where each frame was one month of time, what you would see in those videos is rocks slowly sinking into the clay, almost creating the illusion that the clay is a soft mud when of course it is rock hard.   What happens when you have a thin base and no liner on the bottom is that parts of your base sink into the mud.  This asymmetry creates sections of the base that collapse.  Eventually, the pavers collapse in or distort away from level. Let's assume you want six inches of base material.   On top of that six inches, there will be one inch of sand.   The pavers go on top of that.   So plan the excavation depth using those numbers, with your goal being to get the tops of the pavers where you want them.   It will be a lot of digging, and you might want to hire someone to do that.   Excavate one ditch and implement it and install and test that before investing in excavating the rest.   Or hire a pro to do it all for you. Once you have excavated the ditch - let's say it is eight to nine inches deep - you need to line the base with landscape fabric.   NEVER use plastic.  That will block water drainage out of the base.  You want to use a landscape fabric that will pass water but block the clay and stone sides from mixing.  The cloth helps to spread out the load as well, so any "sinking" into the clay will take place across a broader area and be less likely to cause paver failure. Assuming you want a six-inch base, you put no more than four inches of base material and then tamper that completely   Then two more inches and tamper again.    Then you can place one inch of bedding sand, and your pavers go on that.   The final tamper of the pavers is important because it forces the bedding sand between the pavers. 95% of contractors use as a base material 3/4 crushed rock that includes small sizes down to fines.  It compacts well but does not drain very fast.   I prefer the "open-graded base" method that Unilock uses.  You can research that on Youtube and the Unilock website, then post a separate question about it here.

'Citrus are sun and HEAT lovers., so too with the Yucca.' That's a bit overstated :-) Some citrus can grow outside here but most remain indoors for most if not all of the year and so never get much heat or sun, yet manage to thrive AND produce fruit! Same with yucca. Some varieties are hardy down to zone 3 so easily tolerant of below freezing temperatures and also very adaptable to less than full sun conditions. There are also many hardy or borderline hardy palms that would thrive in these conditions. There seems to be some misapprehension that a north facing conservatory will somehow not provide adequate lighting. Since a conservatory typically includes 2 or more glass walls AND a glass roof, there is generally plenty of light available. Unless there is some obstacle or structure nearby shading it. And since conservatories are attached to heated structures, there is generally plenty of ambient radiated heat to keep things comfortable even in the dead of winter.

@James Eddy Woodworks By the way, in a pure "open-graded base" solution, the top layer is not sand, but instead 3/8" crushed stone with irregular surfaces.  Technically, you should put a geogrid between the 3/4" crushed stone layer and the 3/8" crushed stone, to prevent the 3/8" stone from moving down into the 3/4" layer.   Some videos show ways to use that extra geogrid layer to lay down cement at the edges of the paver patio and prevent movement of the pavers outward.

I'm not sure there's a perfectly responsible answer to this because of the drought; however, fescue is definitely NOT an answer.  The reason you have bare spots in the fescue is that once a fescue plant is damaged enough, it dies and does not come back.  It takes periodic overseeding, often annually (in the late summer), to keep fescue looking really nice.  If you lived in El Segundo or one of the foggy morning beachfront cities, you might get away with fescue.  Lake Arrowhead would work for fescue because of the summer cool temps, but you are down in the relatively dry heat. The only warm season grass that will work in the shade is St Augustine.  It can take a lot of shade and still look nice.  It does well in full sun and becomes very dense, but shade is fine.  Rather than recommend some variety that you cannot get locally, I'd suggest you call some of the nurseries around to see what they carry.  See if you can find a nursery where the local landscapers buy.  We have one in San Antonio where you can buy individual pieces of St Augustine sod for $1.75, whereas the price is $2.99 at HD and Lowes.  Furthermore the nursery sells 14 pallets per day while HD and Lowes sells maybe 5 pallets per week.  So the nursery sod is guaranteed fresh and the box stores is guaranteed diseased.  Once you get the grass, it must be installed the same day to keep if from overnighting under other grass and getting the disease. Unlike fescue, St Augustine goes dormant in the winter when the temps drop below freezing.  It returns in March.  Some people overseed with 'winter rye' to keep something green all year, but I always advise against that.  The winter rye provides enough shade on the dormant St Aug in the spring that awakening is delayed by 4-6 weeks.  After a delayed awakening the grass seems to struggle the rest of the season. Mow St Aug at the mower's highest setting all the time.  In the shade there is never a reason to scalp it down.  In full sun, after many years, you might want to scalp it in the summer to reduce the density.  I like to mow mine every 2 weeks to keep it tall.  Tall St Augustine tends to prevent weeds and other grasses from growing.

A test kit should be a container and instructions for mailing it to a lab. It's really just a sample collection and shipping kit. Assuming the lab is a good one - and they should be certified for asbestos work, ask them if it's not clear - the results should be accurate. If all you'll be testing is the popcorn ceiling, no real need to have a professional come out and charge you a lot of money. If there is no local lab, a test kit should be fine.

A reliable test needs to be done by a certified asbestos testing lab.  Your state or local pollution control organization should have a list of accredited labs.  You bring or send a small sample to the test lab and they perform a special kind of microscopic inspection to examine for fibers that are characteristic of asbestos.   It should also not be very expensive: a reasonable price to expect would be no more than $100.

Also, it's very important to hang onto those test results and file them in their own folder that stays with the house if/when you move. You think you'll remember in 10 years, but you won't, and it will also save future homeowners a hassle and expense. Not to mention that when you sell, you can tell them definitively whether it's ACM or not.

I use the cold start method in the Instant Pot, and the result is delicious.  Going to post a lengthy one to show my method.  I have made it so many times now, ask any questions and I will answer to the best of my ability. My Cold Start Yogurt Method Unbelievably easy. And making your own yogurt is so much cheaper than buying already prepared yogurt. I get all the ingredients from Walmart. You don’t have to use the heavy whipping cream. I like it because, to me, it seems to make the yogurt thicker than if you don’t use it. Just my opinion. AS 1 bottle Fairlife brand milk in the red bottle* 1 – 2 Tablespoons fresh, unopened, plain Chobani Greek yogurt I always use 2 T. 1 cup heavy whipping cream (you can omit the cream) Pour the whipping cream into the IP stainless steel insert and add the 2 T Chobani yogurt. Whisk until it is very well mixed together, whisk fairly easily, you don’t want to get a lot of air into the mixture. Pour in the bottle of Fairlife and whisk together well. For the IP 6 quart Duo, select YOGURT Normal (press the YOGURT button repeatedly until Normal displays). Press the +/- to set incubation time to 12 hours. Then press Start. The IP will beep and start counting up. When it is finished, the IP will beep and display YOGT. I do it right before bed. The longer it incubates the tarter and thicker the yogurt. You don’t have to put the IP lid on but I do. You can just use a lid that will fit or sit a dinner plate on top. The reason is that for the yogurt setting no pressure builds up. I just prefer using the IP lid. In the morning do not stir the yogurt or do anything to it, it will not set up correctly if you do. Take the inner pot out and put in refrigerator with a paper towel on top of the pot to absorb condensation and the IP glass lid or a dinner plate put on top. Chill all day. Again, Do not stir, this breaks down the yogurt. Only scoop. Use an ice cream scoop or spoon to scoop out the yogurt and put into jars. You don’t have to put into jars; you can just leave the IP insert in the refrigerator and scoop out as you need or you can scoop into another container, but be gentle so the yogurt continues to be set. This was so very nice and thick. And tastes great. The addition of the heavy cream really helped to thicken it up. I use the yogurt in the place of sour cream, so don’t make a sweetened yogurt. If I want sweetened, I scoop out about a 6-oz serving and add some honey or preserves or granola or Nutella, fresh fruit, or brown sugar, jam, fruit spreads by Smucker’s, apple butter; anything you want and/or a combination of items. To their individual servings, some people like to add cinnamon, white sugar, some 1 T dry instant pudding mix, Jell-O powder, nutmeg, almonds or any kind of nut, coconut, etc. I have even added peanut butter and jelly to a serving - it was really quite tasty. If you want to make a sweet yogurt from the beginning, you can add one of the following to the above mixture before incubating: If adding one of these, use full two heaping tablespoons of yogurt as your starter. 1 14-oz can sweetened condensed milk (you can use the whole can or half of it) 1 16-oz Natural Bliss creamer (vanilla or sweet cream are my favorites) ONLY USE THIS BRAND OF CREAMER, OTHER BRANDS DON’T HAVE WHAT IS NECESSARY TO MAKE YOGURT. OR 1/2 14-oz can sweetened condensed milk and 8-oz Natural Bliss creamer and 1 tblsp of vanilla I purchased these yogurt cups to make yogurt in in the IP: https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B017Z060Z6/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o01_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1 So, the way I incubate the yogurt now is a bit different from the instructions above. This is what I do. Pour the whipping cream into an old Tupperware Mix-N-Store Bowl/Pitcher (I like to use this because it is not as heavy as the large glass measuring bowls/pitchers). Add 2 T Chobani yogurt. Whisk until it is very well mixed together, whisk fairly easily, you don’t want to get a lot of air into the mixture. Pour in the bottle of Fairlife and whisk together well. I put the cups into the racks before filling the cups. Then carefully pour into each individual yogurt cup. I do this in the sink, so if there are any spills, they are easy to clean up. Put the lids on the cups. Add 1 – 1 1/2 cups water to the inner pot of the IP. Then lower one of the racks into the inner pot and then lower the other and place on top of the other rack. Put the lid on the IP. For the IP 6 quart Duo, select YOGURT Normal (press the YOGURT button repeatedly until Normal displays). Press the +/- to set incubation time to 8 hours. Then press Start. The IP will beep and start counting up. When it is finished, the IP will beep and display YOGT. I do it right before bed. The longer it incubates the tarter and thicker the yogurt. You don’t have to put the IP lid on but I do. You can just use a lid that will fit or sit a dinner plate on top. The reason is that for the yogurt setting no pressure builds up. I just prefer using the IP lid. In the morning, take the racks and cups out of the IP and put in refrigerator to chill all day.              This is a great website for cold start yogurt making; I believe Frieda is the originator of the method. https://www.friedalovesbread.com/2017/06/easy-cold-start-yogurt-no-boil-method.html Frieda Franchina You can use as little as 4 cups of milk directly in the liner, which is a half batch of my yogurt recipe. Yogurt keeps for at least 2-3 weeks and if you make plain yogurt, you can use it as subs for mayo or sour cream in many recipes. I make a half batch which comes out to about five servings. In my Cold Start yogurt recipe & FAQ, I indicate that ultra pasteurized or shelf stable milks can be used. This includes powdered, canned ...and boxed milks. This is great news for those who live in remote areas that have a hard time accessing fresh milk.

Even with the recessed lighting and fan light already there, you may want to add a floor lamp and a table lamp or two.  Try using different lighting combinations to see which ones work better together in the evening and move them around as needed.  I would add matching drapes on the triple window and single window in a quiet-colored pattern which goes with your upholstered pieces.  Add additional art where wall space allows.  Don’t add too many pillows.  A rug four feet wider and four feet longer than the dining table allows additional color. My mom went through the rebate program with approved contractor's.  She called three different contractors one kept cancelling. Your friend is pulling your leg :-) But maybe not intentionally. First, soil temperatures are quite slow to react to changes in ambient air temperatures. They will retain their level of heat for days, not just overnight. At most you could expect a drop of a degree or two. Second, enclosed/contained potting soils exposed to all day sun and heat can sometimes heat up more than you expect. If air temp is 85, the soil could be as much as 10-15 degrees warmer. In which case, even a drop of a degree or two overnight is of no consequence. (ps. the air also tends to be very still at night, so very little "air flow" to be concerned about.) You might try adding some 'loam' to your raised beds. Yes I know there may be a weight issue in your situation... My experience is that highly organic (lots of organic matter like composts) soils in raised beds can easily get hydrophobic when using drip irrigation - the areas which are not getting wet grow over time as the newly dry soil areas are not able to wick moisture as before. The soil down a foot may be fine but the surface 6" is not retaining moisture unless it is right next to  drip emitter. This makes it hard to get transplants started... Really hot weather just makes the problem much worse. Reducing the OM content has largely solved this problem for me. the same thing happens in Large pots if you don't have a lot of emitters... Photos of your current space would help. We're getting close to the end of a complete gut remodel of a condo kitchen close to the same size as yours except ours is a bit smaller (ours is 9 x 13). Although ours is a different set-up, I had many of the same complaints you have. Ours is a U configuration (as in your new plan) set up with sink, range and fridge on the same walls as your plan. And, there are just two of us. After MUCH deliberation we went with a plan that has super susans in both corners (love them a lot and so glad we went with that option). Our sink is in the same spot as yours, but the dishwasher is to the right of the sink, and that helps to really open up the range corner.  (In the past, both of us were trying to crowd into that one corner by the range to cook and load/unload dishwasher.) We have an interior kitchen with no natural light at all. We did lots of can lighting AND we opened up two large, 5' wide by 3 high "window" pass throughs (one on the sink wall and one on the fridge wall.) Be prepared for the fact that, even if you can get to the adjustors -- there may not be sufficient adjustment room to allow adding a threshold. Why are you trying to add a threshold at this point? Have you remodeled and it's necessary to hide where two floors meet, or what? I had an issue in a bathroom re-tile where the floor was going to be raised enough to interfere with the travel of a pocket door.  I knew there wasn't enough adjustment to raise it high enough, so it had to be trimmed. Instead of removing the complex molding to remove the door, I opted to trim the bottom of the door in place. I put tape across the bottom of the door on both sides to minimize splintering, butted a 7/8" spacer against the bottom of the door, put a fine-tooth blade in my oscillating multitool, and made repeated plunge cuts across the bottom of the door using the spacer as a straight line guide. I only went halfway through the door on the first side; then I did the same using the spacer on the other side to make sure I had a straight line there.  It was a little scary, but it worked great in the end. If you have a multitool and the skill to use it accurately, this might be a solution.

I think solid lumber would be much stronger than plywood in this application-- in plywood half the grain is running the wrong direction. I'd save this by cutting a tight fitting mortise-- a square hole-- in the end of the stretcher where it broke off, probably 4" deep then make a new "slip" tenon that would be glued into the mortise and function just as the old one did. It's a bit awkward to do that in the end of a long board, but not too bad. I'd drill out most of the waste using a small forstner bit in a hand drill then square up and fit the sides with a mortise chisel. This is not a situation where you want to rely on either glue or mechanical fasteners. A well-fitted wood joint will be pretty much as strong as the original. (The original tenon looks slightly under-sized to me, i'd have made it a tad bigger.)

Hi, Maria. Severe root congestion causes what is often called "the poodle or pompon look" the most conspicuous symptoms of which are concentrations of foliage immediately proximal to vine apical meristems/ apices, which are found at branch/ vine/ runner ends, and the function of which is to generate extension growth. Included as additional visual clues, would be markedly slowed extension growth, shorter and shorter internodes as the root congestion progresses, and diminishment of that glow of vitality we all strive to achieve. It doesn't matter much how faithful one might be about trying to keep up with the plant's nutritional and moisture needs as they will not prevent or alleviate the limitations levied by tight roots. There are 2 ways to relieve the stress of tight roots. The most common is by potting up, which I'm sure you're familiar with. It consists of lifting the root/soil mass from pot A and situating it in a somewhat larger bot B, then filling around the bottom and perimeter of the root mass with fresh soil. This is a half measure and provides only a little improvement in vitality, growth rate, and possibly appearance. The reason I identify potting up as a half measure is because it ensures the stress of congested roots remains as a limiting factor interminably, or at least until a pair of human hands gets into the root mass to correct the congestion and the wayward roots it causes. A full repot, OTOH, consists of (usually) bare-rooting the plant, pruning the roots with a focus on removing the largest of roots not attached to the base of the root-to-shoot transition zone and other 'problem' roots (encircling/ girdling/ crossing/ damaged/ j-hooked roots, or roots growing straight up/ down, and roots growing back toward the center of the root mass. A full repot frees up space which fine roots, the ones that do all of the plant's heavy lifting, can colonize, and works to ensure all roots get their share of moisture and nutrients. My experience with mandavilla is limited to a few plants grown as individual specimens and a few included in mixed plantings. Those plants I over-wintered were kept quite dry on the floor of a cool basement in low light. I very quickly learned that if I was to expect the plants to perform well year after year, they would need to be repotted every spring (hibiscus, too). A plant with a badly congested root system is much like a runner with a degenerative muscle or nerve disease in the feet or lower legs. No matter how much Gatorade (s)he drinks or supplemental nutrition bars (s)he eats, the disease is going to limit performance - same with a plant and root congestion. A healthy root system is a prerequisite to any hope for a healthy plant. A normal part of Mandeville's morphology are the preformed root primordia at every node, which places them among the easiest of plants to root. I wouldn't use water to root cuttings as the roots which form in water are structured much differently that roots that form in a solid medium. Water roots are filled with an airy substance (aerenchyma) which allows oxygen essential to root function to diffuse through the specialized root tissue from plant parts above the water line. This can be a problem in transitioning from a liquid to a solid medium because roots which form in water are very brittle, so they break easily, and they are inefficient at absorbing water from a solid medium, so they often die while transitioning between media types. This represents wasted energy because the propagule, now in a solid medium, is often asked to generate a second set of roots when most of its energy reserves will have been spent on the first roots to form, so at a minimum, it increases the likelihood of propagule collapse due to low energy reserves. Too, rooting a cutting is a race to determine whether or not roots can form and make connection with the propagules existing vasculature before fungal or bacterial, or even abiotic pathogens clog the plumbing and make the connection impossible. Anything that increases the time it takes for that connection to occur increases the probability of failure. Al

The images look fine. Good job. The necrotic areas on the leaves shown is likely caused by over-watering. How do you determine when it's time to water? Are you familiar with using a "tell" to "tell" you when it's time to water? When you water, are you making sure the entire soil column is getting moistened and at least 20% of the water applied at each watering exits the drain hole? I ask that because salts from tapwater and fertilizer salts can accumulate in the soil to the point where it makes it difficult for water to move into individual cells. It is essential that the level of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil solution is lower than the level of dissolved solids in water within cells if water is to move through the cells membrane. When the level of salts is too high, it limits water movement into cells, and can even pull water out of cells by the same mechanism curing salts pulls water out of meats like bacon, ham, salami, ..... . This causes plasma to be torn from cell walls as the cells collapse, killing the cells. The technical term for this physiological disorder is called plasmolysis, but it's commonly called fertilizer burn. The above is not to say I think it is fertilizer burn, only some watering habits and a high level of dissolved solids in the soil solution can work in concert to limit the plant's ability to move water efficiently to all parts of the plant. Over-watering causes the same symptoms as under-watering; this, because under-watering limits the soil's oxygen supply, which in turn limits the roots ability to do its job of taking up and moving water to all the plant's organs. Even when the roots are awash in a sea of plenty, the plant's chemical messengers can be "fooled" into informing the plant it is in a drought situation. To tell whether of not your plant needs repotting, lift the plant from the pot. If the root/soil mass comes out of the pot as an intact mass, it's time to repot when it's next most appropriate, which would be in the 2 weeks before the summer solstice in most parts of the Northern Hemisphere. What are you fertilizing with/ how often? Al

Over-watering is much more common than under-watering, but allowing the medium to go completely dry might mean you need to water sooner. Try watering when you can barely detect moisture on the tip of the tell, and make sure you're wetting the entire soil column and flushing the soil as you water. You might want to consider going to 1.5 - 2.0 tsp FP 9-3-6 per gallon and fertilizing every 5th time you water in the winter and every 3rd or 4th in the summer. To keep track of what plant needs to be fertilized at any given point in time, drop a marble/ button/ cement block in the pot each time you water. Questions: Field pine is not a biological term. Forest have many different pine trees. What type of pine tree is it. @krnuttle, that's an excellent question, but I'm afraid that I don't know the answer. These trees are very common here, and all that I've ever heard them called are "field pine". These typically grow very tall, and the lower limbs die off and look ugly unless you trim it. Upper limbs have a tendency to break off, too, which can be pretty dangerous underneath. They attract ants, and it's not uncommon to find them completely eaten away on the inside. A few years ago I cut one down that was green and healthy looking at the top, only to find out that the entire inside was gone and it was nothing but bark! When it fell, literally millions of black ants came pouring out! They're also covered in creosote, which makes them popular kindling for fires because it's very flammable. So with all of that, these are good trees to have in the woods as an evergreen and help prevent erosion, but definitely not something you want up close to your house. I had one very large one in my back yard when I moved here. It was pretty cool looking, but one evening there was a storm and we heard a huge WHAM and the whole house shook!!! Like, pictures fell off the walls kind of shake. I thought an airplane had crashed! But no, the tree had fallen over, and luckily fell away from the house. With it fallen over, I could easily see that the root system was relatively shallow. That's what scared me with these other trees that are closer to the house than I would like... all it takes is one good storm, ya know?

Pre-wiring for a home theater is not extremely difficult, but one does need to be educated regarding the hardware and you should have a plan to work with before jumping in with the physical wiring, etc. Read through various 'how to' sites and learn the details of the hardware before going at it. I used this site's design software to locate my front and side speakers locations based on my room size and seating locations: https://www.audioadvice.com/home-theater-design We will have 3 front speakers (L, Ctr, & R) and 4 ceiling speakers (mid L & R, and Rear L & R) and a sub-woofer (L Ctr), all are pre-mounted to be behind drywall with only the grills showing once complete. RCA plugs are mainly relegated to signal-level applications with amplified power typically using binding posts. My theater will have an electronics closet behind it with the digital receiver, DVD player and amplifiers there on shelving. If needed, I will use an infrared repeater system to communicate from the family room with the hidden electronics. The electronics will connect to the speakers through the On-Q connection box below. Ceiling and wall speakers have their own (hidden) insulated plywood enclosure, so speaker connections are the mfr binding posts on each unit as well. Wall mount speaker binding post connections are available if you go that route.

We are going through the same decision process right now and I have been going back and forth on whether to do a dual fuel or all gas since we are also getting a single electric                                              oven.  It seems to make sense to do both, and as a bonus you save a little on the range being all gas. As for brands we are considering Thermador, Wolf, Monogram, and possibly Bluestar. We priced out a package with Mongram and Thermador, which have some nice incentives if you buy a couple other appliances from them (essentially you get a free dishwasher, microwave, or a credit).

I wouldn't by just based on the package they are offering. Quite frequently, appliance manufacturers have one type of appliance that they are really good at, and the rest is only OK; or it is bought from a different manufacturer and has a new label slapped on. Wolf and Bluestar both make great gas ranges. Get a Wolf, if you want to stay a little more mainstream and need more of a "polished" product (and absolutely do not get their electric ovens!). Get a Bluestar, if you want raw performance and uncompromising ruggedness. In many ways, it's Julia Child's Garland range with minor upgrades to bring it up-to-date with modern standards. We love ours. Wouldn't want to trade it for anything else. But it does take a little more effort to set it up initially (pay a good installer to do that for you), and the strict focus on form-follows-function is something that not everybody wants. As for wall ovens, I can't say enough good things about the Miele CSO. It's a game changer. The speed oven, is less of a unique appliance. We bought it, because we like that it uses space efficiently, by having an oven and a microwave in the same unit. And I still stand by that decision. It also turns out to be both a good convection oven and a good microwave in its own right; but the speed function is not particularly important to us -- and we knew that from the beginning.

Wolf is one of several manufacturers that have not yet solved the decades long problem with the enamel coating in their ovens failing over time. Anecdotally, the information in the Houzz forum suggests that this is primarily a problem with electric ovens. So, I would stay clear of electric ovens that have this type of coating, unless you like eating shards of glass. Gas ovens appear to be fine from what data I have seen people report on Houzz. And Miele's CSO and speed ovens (but not their regular ovens) are also OK, as their oven liners are made from stainless steel. So, getting a Wolf or BlueStar gas range or range top is good. Getting the Miele specialty ovens is good. But getting any electric convection oven is potentially problematic. Wolf is a very mainstream brand. They also own SubZero, and their refrigerators are unrivaled. Customer service is generally considered to be very good. And their gas ranges are "fine". But I am not super impressed by their burner design which does leave some cold spots, changes flame pattern with power output (i.e. flares outward), and is harder to keep clean than Bluestar's open burner design. That's not to say that Wolf doesn't make good ranges. I just don't feel they are as good as can be. And as an opinionated hobby cook who takes this hobby very seriously, I would feel let down. On the other hand, Bluestar is a very no-frills design. It's designed like a tank. The open burners are super easy to keep clean, once you build up some protective seasoning on the cast iron. The power output is super even and predictable. Cooking in a wok is pure joy with the built-in wok ring. It regulates very evenly to lower levels -- assuming the installer did their job right. And if things go wrong, all you need is basic household tools to service it. Anybody can do that without needing to buy specialty parts. It's all industry-standard components. The oven is extremely spacious. It holds full-size cookie sheets, or two half-sheets side-by-side. I don't need this very often, but when I do it's very convenient. The downside is that the huge oven cavity takes forever to preheat (at least 20min, better 40min). That's why I love pairing with my small Miele ovens. They preheat within a few minutes and 90% of the time, the smaller capacity of the 24" models is exactly right, even when cooking large and elaborate meals. Once pre-heated, though, the Bluestar oven is extremely even and predictable. I love cooking and baking with it. It is very boring, and that's a good thing in an appliance. Also, Bluestar ovens have amazing broiler elements. This is the closest you can come to a commercial salamander in a home setting. We use it almost daily. Great for making toast, searing vegetables or meat, ... Even my 9 year old loves using it. The downside with Bluestar is the fact that it is a much smaller company. While any technician that has seen a commercial range should be able to service it, that might very well be what you have to do. Their service network is smaller and outside of major markets it really depends on how good your local providers are. Their customer service has been mixed over the years. Personally, I have always had great luck. We completely reconfigured our range when we remodelled and bought a bunch of replacement parts (higher feet, different back guard, color change, ...). Customer service was extremely reasonable in accommodating our requests. But others here on Houzz haven't always had the same luck. So, just keep that in mind; you might sometimes have to be the squeaky wheel. If you have questions about the Miele oven(s), let me know. I love the combination that we have, but I realize this isn't cheap and not everybody is as passionate about their hobby.

The Miele CSO is noticeably smaller than "normal" American ovens. But I find that actually works really well. It preheats so super quickly. And since I do have access to a large oven in my range, I never find the smaller capacity to be a limitation. In fact, steam helps with distributing heat very evenly and you can pack things very tightly in the oven. The CSO has both very precise control over temperature and over humidity. This means, I can use it for sous-vide cooking. I can use it to proof yeast dough (it does a wonderful job with that!). It can boil eggs very precisely. If you have a particular firmness that you want, you can perfectly reproduce it every single time. And it works amazingly well for blanching vegetables. Steam cooking asparagus is a game changer. Yes, of course, I can blanch it in a pot of boiling water. But with my CSO it's completely hands-off; so, I can focus on other tasks at the same time. And I can set it to be perfectly cooked while still nicely crisp. Softening cabbage for cabbage rolls is always a big mess when using a pot of water, but it becomes much more manageable in my CSO. And if I cook for a large group of people, the CSO is the best way to make insane amounts of boiled potatoes or rice. I have cooked a multi-course meal for more than 100 people (before the pandemic), and the CSO made that so much easier to manage. Oh, and it makes the world's best Kaiserschmarrn! The kids love how I can make the most fluffy and delicious Austrian pancakes. Heck, it even makes for a great impromptu warming drawer. Steam is just another parameter that you can control. You don't have to use it every time, but it's great when it's always right at your fingertips. Doesn't take long to figure out what it does, but it helps if you spend a little time reading up and understanding the concept. Steam holds a lot more heat energy than dry air. So, it can work really well for heating things evenly. You can use it at low temperatures (where you'll see condensation) or at high temperatures. Doing so means that your food will be done much faster. You'll be very confused with your time management the first few times, when you discover that meat cooks so much faster. But if you want to crisp things up, you probably want to switch to dryer heat. For baking, you initially keep humidity high, to allow the starches to gelatinize. This gives bread dough the ability to rise dramatically (aka "oven spring"). Later, you set the crumb in place by forming a crisp crust. That requires drying out the outside of the bread. I personally think you get a better deal with the RNB. The Platinum has a "weird" oven heating element. It supposedly addresses the problem with taking a long time to preheat. But it comes at the cost of having more hot air focused in a few spots close to the back of the oven. Personally, I'd rather deal with the longer preheat in exchange for a perfectly evenly heated oven. It really just requires you to plan ahead. And on days when I didn't do that, the CSO is up to temp within 5 to 10 minutes. So, I always have options. I understand the market pressures that made Bluestar come up with the PowR oven. But I just wished they had a more flexible built-to-order system that allowed you to opt out of this feature. The extra BTU for the improved burners on the Platinum can be nice though. It certainly makes a difference when cooking in a wok. The RNB is already infinitely better than most competing models, but you can never have too much power when stir frying and searing. Fortunately, it is relatively easy to replace one of the RNB burners for a Platinum burner after the fact. Bluestar will throw a hissy fit, if you ask them to do this, as they desperately try to differentiate their product lines. But with a little effort, you can find the required parts online and switch them out yourself. It's really easy to do and should cost about $200. Maybe, if you ask really politely, your dealer will even do this for you (they are not supposed to, but some dealers just go the extra mile for their customers). We felt, we really only needed this for one of the burners. High power is needed in relatively few and short periods during cooking, and the difference between 22kBTU and 25kBTU is only just over 10%. So, it doesn't make much of difference, but sometimes, every little bit helps. I find that the Bluestar burners regulate to low temperatures much better than pretty much any other gas range (only some, but far from all, induction ranges do this even better). This of course requires the installer to have adjusted the shutters and the low set point correctly. And that depends a little on the gas mix that you get from the city and on the altitude that you are operating at. So, make sure your installer checks this. If they don't, it is something you can do yourself. Bluestar has YouTube videos showing you how to. But you really shouldn't need to; this is a job for the installer. I believe the vast majority of complaints about Bluestar ranges are a direct result of the installer failing to do a proper job with the checklist. Either because they didn't calibrate everything correctly, or because there was damage in transport that nobody wanted to take responsibility for. We felt that even the 22kBTU burner simmers pretty well, and the 15kBTU burners that we have in the back work wonderfully for simmering. So, we ended up removing the dedicated simmer burner and replaced it with another 15kBTU. Having an extra 15kBTU was more important to us. This works great 90% of the time, unless you really need very low temperatures for an extended amount of time. And in those cases, I find that simmering on the cooktop is actually the wrong technique. Do what restaurants do; move the pot into the oven. Ovens do a much better job at providing very even and precisely controlled amounts of heat. This is one of the reasons why I feel you can never have too many ovens. We really like having the gas range, the CSO and the speed oven; and in extreme cases, I have had to co-opt the gas BBQ on the patio as another oven. Four ovens are such a luxury to have when managing a complex multi-course menu. Knowing how and when to use ovens has improved my game so much. It took a bit of a learning curve, but it was well worth the effort. The oven door hinges were a genuine problem with earlier models. Our range was bought at a time, when this was an issue. It is now over 10 years old. We reached out to Bluestar when the door started seizing up after several (8?) years. It was well outside of the regular warranty period by that point. They offered to sell us a current model door at a heavy discount, and they even gave us the option to change the color -- that conveniently coincided with our kitchen remodel. We picked a black door to match the stainless&black look of the Miele ovens. The old door just lifts out and the new one drops in. Very happy with how this worked out. Presumably, in the new model, this particular problem has now been fixed. I found Bluestar's customer service fine to work with. They are not outstanding, but they are also not bad. But it sometimes does require a few follow-up calls. We have had to call them a few times over the years, as I had made changes to the range for the remodel, and as we bought a floor model as a gift for a friend's cabin; and that floor model turned out to have a bunch of missing and broken parts.

Google the installation instructions for your tub, manufacturers will have them documented. There are differences depending on the tub material and the height and shape of the flange. Kohler says if you have a cast iron tub the wallboard should come up to the top of the tub rim/flange leaving a 1/16" gap. Then the tile goes over that and is held back from the deck of the tub by 1/16" gap which is  filled with silicone. Today many installers span the junction between the tub rim and the wallboard with a waterproof membrane and something like Kerdifix or mesh tape and a topical membrane speced to span gaps. Your picture looks like the gap is greater than 1/16" and I'm not sure the tub is cast iron. If you have an acrylic tub with a tall, thin flange then the wall board goes over the flange, but must not go down to the deck of the tub, and a bead of silicone is applied between the end of the wallboard and the flange. Then the tile goes on and must end below the wallboard and have a 1/16" gap down to the tub deck which again gets a bead of silicone.

So, do you need this much parking? If so, consider building a 2 vehicle carport on the left side of the paved area near your house to shelter your own vehicles. There may be set back limits as to how close to the edge of your property any building can be. If you don't want all this paving, you will have to have it removed. Paving is a layer of asphalt or concrete above a layer of gravel, over hard packed earth. It's a big job to remove the paving and gravel, then bring in new soil to fill in the hole. Plus, you have to make sure there aren't any water or gas lines under the paving that could be damaged during the project. It's a big job. A less expensive option might be container gardens using galvanized water tanks with drain holes punched across the bottom, or retaining wall blocks lined with landscape fabric to keep soil in place. Most plants don't need more than 2 feet of soil depth, and you can place these on top of the paving. Choose sun loving perennials like daylily, coneflower, salvia, shasta daisy or black-eyed susan. Repeat these plants in the timber bounded bed with the shrubs. Plant a low growing shrub along the edge of the pavement and across the front of your yard against the sidewalk to highlight your lawn. I used Ilex crenata, cv. Brass Buttons, but you can choose any small shrub as a border. Just check the tag for the expected mature height and width. If a plant is expected to grow 36" wide, don't plant it closer than 18" to a pathway or wall. Every plant will be small when you first get it, so fill in between with annuals for the first several years if you want a lusher look.  Do the projects in stages. Start with a raised bed. Fill it with soil. Then plant perennial and annual flowers this coming spring. If your winters are harsh, you can use dwarf evergreen shrubs to keep some green in the raised bed and other garden areas. Dwarf only means smaller than the species, so again pay attention to the expected mature size on tags. If your winters are milder you can use hardy winter annuals such as pansies, and ornamental kale. Snapdragons and sweet William can also grow through winter and flower in early spring.

Aphids and mites can be controlled and in many cases eradicated by spritzing at 4-day intervals with a 2:1 mixture of water (2 parts) and 70% rubbing alcohol (1 part).  Set the spritzer to fine mist and mist the entire plant, making sure to wet the underside of the leaves and all nooks/crannies - especially the crotch formed by the leaves and the branch/stem they're attached to. Distilled water or water from a dehumidifier, air conditioner, or water that's been routed through a reverse osmosis filtration system is best because it leaves no residue on the plant's surfaces. In many cases, you'll miss seeing mites unless you use magnification. I have this 5X device w/light, and it works great. Al

Are you a proponent of the 2-stage then in the sense that it would run presumably at the lower speed compared to full blast/single stage and therefore have a significant enough cost savings? The main benefit of 2-Stage equipment is comfort. There is some operating costs savings but not enough to justify the added cost. If the furnace is running in the low stage, the run time is longer and the amount of fuel used is about the same as running in the high stage. There will be less short cycling and less blasts of air. I think 2-stage equipment is worth the extra money. Buying over sized 2-stage equipment with the idea that it will not be problem because it will run in the low stage most of the time is a waste of money and energy in my opinion.

there is not such thing as a soft, hard or intermediate quartzite.  quartzite either is or isn't. Quartztite is made up of quartz. (over 95%)  If you get a place that says, "oh there is some marble in it, but it's quartzite", they're lying. The slabs labeled as Macaubas are usually a quartzite.  The Fantasy Macaubas is one of them.  This is from my own stone place  (I believe the price on this was $2300 a slab)    In no way would I mix this with a black or gray leathered granite!  that sounds horrible! Too many diff patterns. If you want to do a solid gray quartz on the perimeter, that would be fine.  I did it w/my own kitchen (but I have a marble on my island).  I used Silestone Eternal in a suede finish  This is another White Macaubas, Vein Cut.  Sea Pearl is a true quartzite and has soft blues and greens.  If you want a blue, look at Ocean Blue quartzite.  This one you would have to test.  some have it labeled as marble.  or, Ijen Blue  quartzite may be difficult to fabricate (it is harder than granite) so make sure you have a top quality fabricator. Quartzite will not etch, but the lighter ones can stain.  Always use a sealer. To test if your slab is a true quartzite, try the glass test,  the lemon/acid test, or the stain test.  Glass is softer than quartzite or granite, but it's harder than marble.  is you take a piece of marble and run it over glass, the marble will turn to powder.  If you take a piece of quartzite and do it, it will scratch the glass.  vice versa. take a shard of glass and try to scratch the ragged end of the slab.  what happens?  does it scratch it?  then the slab is probably calcite (marble)

The US actually has a split phase system that provides 240V to the house. This is well within the specs of European appliances. The only other difference is 50Hz vs 60Hz line frequency, but that is very unlikely to matter for these type of appliances. So, other than requiring an electrician to change out the type of plug, there is no technical reason why this appliance couldn't be connected. People import non-US appliances all the time and use them without issue. The bigger concern is non-technical. Non-US appliances sometimes have different dimensions, as they are based on metric units, whereas the US measures everything in inches. Things tend to be close, but its not always a perfect match and requires minor tweaks to the cabinets. Importing from abroad can be painful, especially at a time when shipping routes are disrupted. I am still waiting for a shipment that should have happened two years ago, but the vendor has the hardest time securing space in a container. Also, import duties are a big hassle to deal with; not impossible and not even necessarily expensive, but just annoying from a paperwork point of view. Your building inspector might take issue with the appliance not having been UL tested. That doesn't mean it's unsafe; if anything, European testing requirements tend to be more stringent. But paperwork matters. That also could theoretically make it impossible to get a home owner's insurance policy, although in practice that risk appears overblown. And finally, warranty service is going to be a bit of a pain, as you'll have to ship parts back and forth. None of these things are insurmountable. It can absolutely be the correct answer. This question does come up with some regularity. People do buy direct from Europe or take appliances with them when they relocate internationally, and they generally are very happy with their decision. But this only works, if you fully understand what you are getting into and why the trade-offs are worth it. It generally makes sense, if you need an unusual appliances that you wouldn't be able to get otherwise. It is less clear whether it makes sense just to safe money, a the savings aren't always as much as you'd think.

At what phase of life are you, Tartuso?  If you are switching to a walk-in shower for aging in place, my advice will differ from if you are starting a family.  If you want a full height linen closet in the bathroom, you can have one. You can order an 18” wide cabinet that is as deep as your counter and put it on the toilet end.  It will partially block the view of the toilet, which many people on this forum find objectionable.  Or, you can put it next to the wall by the door, before your vanity.  Many cabinetry companies make such linen towers to match their vanities.  Figure out what style of cabinetry you want.  Even wall-hung floating vanities can be found with matching linen towers that also hang. This is your opportunity to think of what other things you might want in the bathroom.  A heated towel rack on the wall across from the shower?  A towel heater appliance that sits on the floor and plugs into the wall?  A plant?  A towel ladder?  You will need to redo electrical probably to bring it up to code, with outlets every 4 ft along the vanity.  So how about putting one next to the toilet for a bidet seat with warm water wash and air dry functions?  You can move the outlet near the entrance at the same time. Do you want more towel racks to give places for towels to dry?  Hooks for towels, instead (and robes)?  USB slots in some of the outlets?  Dimmers on some lights?  Lights in the new shower (I love mine!)?  Plan all of this in advance so that you can know just what needs to be done. As for your shower, who will build it?  What waterproofing system will go under the tile - or will you use an acrylic or solid surface instead of tile?  Those need to be decided before hiring the contractor.  If using tile, ask the contractors you contact what waterproofing system they use before you meet with them for an interview, and read up on how that system works so that you can intelligently discuss it with them.  Be sure to write into the contract that the shower will be built using XYZ waterproofing system, installed according to the manufacturer’s instructions.  If not using tile, be sure you know what the manufacturer of your shower gives as instructions for installation and discuss that in the contractor interviews, then have in the contract that the shower will be installed according to the shower manufacturer’s instructions.  If you are doing a wheelchair-accessible shower, we need to talk about drains.  I did a floor drain outside of mine, and am very glad I did!  If you want to see my bathroom, do a search in this forum for “ADA Reveal.” If you are preparing for aging in place, be sure to specify shower grab bars and have the contractor install 2 x 6 boards between the studs so that they can be installed now, or later.  One vertical bar coming into the shower and at least one horizontal grab bar.  If you will have a hand-held shower head, too, consider giving it a bar that is also a grab bar.  If a walker may be in your future, it might be good to put the vanity closer to the toilet, leaving 30” open near the door.  That gives you space to set your walker to the side as you swing the door open.

There is a good chance that the refrigeration coils are frozen solid and the auto-defrost just can't keep up with it. That would manifest in exactly this type of symptom. Maybe, you accidentally didn't close the door all the way one day? You need to find where the coils are (not the hot ones on the back of the unit, but the cold ones on the inside). They are often behind some protective panel that can be removed if you are determined to find the fasteners. Then either turn off the appliance until all the ice has melted completely (this can take a surprisingly long time), or use a hair dryer to accelerate the process. It's a bit messy, as you'll have water dripping all over the place. So, make sure you have rags and/or sponges ready to mop everything up. The reason why I tell you to remove the cover for the coils is that you have to make sure they are completely free of ice, and with the cover in place there really is no good way to reliably tell that. So, you might only do a half-assed job and a few days later you are exactly back to where you were before. I don't know anything about your specific model, but I have learned that there often are very instructive videos on Youtube showing you how to service your own appliances. So, that's where I would start. Defrosting manually is tedious, but honestly that's the best-case scenario. In the worst case, your insulation is water logged and/or frozen solid. If that happened, there really is nothing you can do. That fridge is beyond repair. Alternatively, the thermostat, the compressor, or the fan between fridge and freezer cabinet is broken. Those parts can in principle be repaired. But you probably have to call a service technician and it might cost more than buying a new appliance. If you are good with DIY, these would all be things you could investigate yourself. If you at least knew which part is defective, that could inform your decision on whether to call for service or save up for a replacement.

Unfortunately, planting a fruit tree from a seed is not going to get you the same sort of tree as the fruit the seed came from. It will produce a peach, but it will not be an Indian Free. It could be similar (but not exact) or it could (and most likely will) look and taste nothing like Indian Free. All named forms of fruit trees can only be reproduce by asexual (non-seed) propagation - cuttings and grafting. That is the only assurance of getting the same fruit. There are fruit specialty nurseries that carry this tree but they are either sold out for the season or it is too late to ship bareroot stock. You would be better off preordering the tree in late summer or early fall for winter 2023 delivery.

Before applying anything, industrial vacuum clean the floor, and wash with a mop and bucket. This is to remove all the concrete dust that would of accumulated. If your walls are plastered brick, you don’t need skirting boards. If your walls are timber studs covered in gyprock, then wait until your floors are dealt with before installing skirting boards. If skirting boards are included in your build, then ask the builder to provide, but not install.

Systems that are based on Clack or Fleck control valves are very reliable. Fleck based systems are available over the internet whereas Clack has prohibited internet sales. For that reason, Fleck based systems tend to be less expensive and more common. If what you are trying to do is remove hardness, you don't need $5,000 worth of equipment. Water softening is a commodity business. There's no "special sauce" that makes water "more soft". Buy a SOFTENER - not a conditioner or anything like that. If you can get one that uses a Clack or Fleck valve - that's good. I've often talked about $600-700 Fleck based softeners on Amazon (softener only, no install, sizing, etc). It has lost about 1/3 of its leaves and continues to drop about 3-8 leaves per day.First, there IS a possibility you're care regimen is not to blame for the leaf loss. Schefflera, like many houseplants, respond to a decrease in light levels by shedding foliage. The mechanism by which this occurs is technical, but I'll describe it if you like. When a plant is raised in full sun or under light shade cloth, then shipped to a wholesaler or its point of sale, then arrives in a home, the light level is only fraction of what the leaves are conditioned to, and they would be perfectly conditioned to the amount of light they were getting when they were maturing. While leaves are somewhat adaptable to changing light conditions, few can directly transition from very bright light to light levels in a home that doesn't have a LOT of sun exposure. For the record, leaves are better at adapting ti an increase in photo load than a decrease. So, given the fact the plant is rather new, and it often takes a month or more for symptoms resultant of a light reduction to be made manifest in the symptom of leaf shedding, what you see just might be an inevitable result of the change. By inevitable, I mean that no amount of 'conditioning' the leaves gradually to a dimmer environment could have made a difference. Some changes in light levels are simply beyond what the plant is genetically programmed to deal with, no matter how gradually the change occurs. It has had lots of new growth the entire time I've had it, but the new leaves are drooping. A drooping appearance in newly emerging leaves is a normal part of the plant's morphology. Schefflera is particularly affected by Ca deficiencies due to over-watering, even when there is an ample supply of Ca in the grow medium. Growing things proficiently can be very easy if you get the basics right. The main areas where growers get into trouble are soil choice, light levels, watering issues, and fertility, the first 3 are pretty much equally important, but fertilizing is an essential part of all container grower's care regimen, so ask about that if you like. This short piece about Overview of Good Growing Practices will help you avoid all the most common pitfalls every grower faces at some point on their journey to a green thumb, if it's put into practical application. Questions/ concerns?  Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so.
