You don't say where the noise is coming from. I have heard that LVP flooring even with underlayment can still be noisy. Without underlayment LVP will definitely be noisy. The fix is to cover the floor with rugs. You will want a large rug (at least 9x12 for the living/family room. However, that still leaves walkways between such areas uncovered. A wide runner or several smaller size rugs could work to cover walkways. Unfortunately, most runners are seldom wider than 31" and a pathway is better with a rug closer to 42" wide. Still, any rug with a proper pad beneath will control LVP noise. Here is a Houzz Article on sizing/placing rugs. If noise comes from outside, the usual fix is to cover windows with heavy drapery which also makes the room dark. But, there are Window Inserts that can diminish outside noise.

Ideally, the hood should be 6” wider than the cooktop, so in your case, 42” wide.  Don’t know why the salesperson said 39”.  However, in a smaller kitchen, a homeowner may not want to forego the upper cabinet space, and stays with a 36” wide hood, so it depends on your setup.  If you have the space, a 42” hood not only has better capture area, it looks better too. I would actually be more concerned with:  (A) the depth of the hood front-to-back.  Many of the less expensive hoods are less than 20” deep.  That means your front burners won’t be covered, and you’ve spent all that money not to have the front burners covered.  (B) the size of the duct that goes from the hood to the outside.  It needs to have an 8” or 10” diameter depending on the hood.  Smaller duct than that and you will get more noise and less exhaust.  People don’t pay attention to their duct size and then complain how noisy their hood is.

Get out your coat and boots :-) NOW is the ideal time! I just noticed the development of fat buds on many of mine and that signals to me that pruning time has arrived!! And pruning does produce significant benefits. Hard pruning for any type 2's or 3's for their first few season does encourage additional stemming, resulting in a stronger and more floriferous plant and less vulnerable to damage (or wilt). And type 3's or those that bloom on the current season's growth need that hard pruning each season to a) keep size in check; b) keep flowers at a visible height; and c) keep the vine tidy and free of dead stems and foliage. The only time I veer away from this timing is with type 1 clems or the so-called 'no-prune' varieties. These often need to be cut back to control size and that is best done immediately after flowering.

Your location isn't as important as the specific cultivar. generally speaking, clematis that bloom off current season growth should be pruned early spring to encourage a lot of new growth which will produce a lot of blooms. Those that bloom off old growth, should be pruned soon after blooming to produce a lot of old growth for the next year. Those that bloom off new and old are treated the same as those that bloom off old growth. The problem is there are officially 3 distinct types of clematis. In reality, the lines can be blurred. Some may be type 2 in most applications, but type 3 in your garden. You have to observe how they grow in your garden before deciding how to prune. Another issue is clematis aren't always what you think you have. They're mislabeled and/or what one vendor thinks is A, is actually B. There are so many cultivars that look alike, but grow differently.

Having grown far too many different clematis over the years (a previous garden had more than 60!), I have simplified pruning to those vines that get pruned and those that do not. And those that get pruned annually ALL get treated the same......a hard prune down to the second set of buds or somewhere around 12-18". With the length and mildness of the PNW growing season for clems, this treatment has almost no impact on the flowering of group 2 clems except to delay the initial bloom cycle slightly. erasmus, that recommendation to prune back group 3's to around 6-12" (or the second set of buds) has been in practice for well over a hundred years with excellent results. I'd be interested to know why your book suggests pruning to the ground. It offers NO benefit to the vine other than perhaps stimulating multiple stems from the root crown but also does not allow the stems to enlarge and become sufficiently woody.

What species of juniper is it? They're not all created equal insofar as their ability to tolerate low temperatures. If it's J chinensis/ Shimpaku or J procumbens, J rigida, J horizontalis, leave it outdoors during cold snaps. If temps are to be below 25*, make sure it's resting directly on the ground or on the floor of an unheated garage where rising geothermal heat will help keep its feet warmer than ambient air temps. Leaving it on the ground and covering it temporarily with a box or tub is also an option. If you have some dry leaves, it would be good to provide mulch enough to cover the pot all the way to the lowest foliage. You needn't worry about the foliage, only the roots. You could also situate it on the ground or in a window well on the north side of a heated building and mulch the pot. I left several J procumbens and J chinensis "Shimpaku" on the grow benches through last year's winter and all awoke with no discernible reason to think they were worse for the exposure, even though they suffered through almost 2 weeks of temps in double digits below ) at night and single digit daily highs. These were just free plants in nursery cans given to me by a friend who owns a nursery and I had no time invested in them.  I'm not recommending that type of treatment as a habit as I understand that root damage from chill occurs incrementally. IOW, the finest roots are first to succumb and as temps continue to fall, thicker roots also fall victim to the chill. I can't be more specific about killing lows because it varies so much by species. Al

I used to raise waterlilies in mud bottomed ponds.    Crawfish love to eat the new shoots that waterlillies put out in the springtime.   Plus, if I bought a new waterlily and put it in a pond where there were crawfish, overnight, they would cut all the pads off.   However, if a waterlily was established and growing, the crawfish would pretty much leave it alone. I had a couple of ponds that were 8' deep, but the ones I raised waterlililes in were about waist deep.   Every spring I would pump out the water in the ponds that I raised waterlilies in, and pick out all the crawfish.   I would get about a 5 gallon bucket from two ponds.    I boiled them.   I don't do like real cajuns and eat the "fat" out of the head.   I threw the heads away.   I made etouffee, and added the peeled crawfish tails to it.   Etouffee has a distinctive orange-ish color, from the crawfish fat, but even without the heads, the etouffee had the distinctive color and flavor. I am not crazy about crawfish...just to eat boiled, like in the above picture.   I was married for many years to a commercial fisherman, and we ate shrimp.  Easier to peel and tastier than crawfish, in my opinion.   Some people make etouffee with shrimp, but it lacks the color and taste of that made with crawfish...so that is my preference for eating crawfish.    When I peeled the crawfish, it is easy to remove the mud vein along their back,  like you do with shrimp.  Actually, easier, in the you lift up a little flap of meat and can easily remove the vein. By the time crawfish got re-established in the pond, the waterlilies were big, and they would leave them alone. After I removed the crawfish and re-filled the pond and planted waterlilies, I would pump down the water a few feet in one of my deeper ponds, where I had some big koi.   Then re-fill it.   This was usually done the very first of March.   The fresh water would stimulate the koi to spawn, plus a certain temperature that they liked.   I then transferred the eggs to a lily pond and the eggs would hatch and the baby koi would grow there. The advantage in a modulating / variable speed system is the ability to ramp up and down as needed the split second it's needed. The difference? waiting 20 mins from a timed standpoint if the 24v signal remains active to ramp up. IMO, you lose alot of the benefits of the machine doing such things. The choices in modulation in standard or legacy mode on this machine are decided by suction pressure on this machine. So if they got the communication aspect wrong... how big of a leap is it to suspect refrigerant charge probably isn't right either? It's very easy to over charge these kinds of systems. If the system is running in communication mode, how much more input does the machine have? It likely has humidity reading built into t-stat, temperature inside, temperature outside, refrigerant pressures and so on. All this info is passed to all equipment in communication mode... to make run decisions from in a split second. Typically variable speed has the advantage of ramping up and down via 1% steps. Manufacturers that put all their eggs into communication based systems break this chain if any one piece of the equipment suffers communication problems. They put fallbacks in there as a way to avoid the system becoming a paper weight. Personally I don't recommend any wi-fi type controls for a number of reasons I won't get into here. If you need to control a HVAC system remotely there are better options to do so than via wi-fi. Communicating systems are "hard wired" to communicate between the various pieces of equipment & the thermostat in most cases. You may well be over-watering. If you have a 10" deep pot, when the top 2" of the grow medium feels dry to the touch, the bottom 6" of the soil column could easily be 100% saturated. The commonly offered advice to water when the top inch or two of the soil feels dry is fine if the pot is 5" deep or less, but serves as little more than a recipe for over-watering in deeper pots. What's important is what moisture levels are at the bottom of the pot. To monitor for moisture deep in the pot, I suggest you use a homemade "tell" made from a wood dowel rod (any hardware or big box store like Lowes, Home Depot, Menards. If you water your plant when the dowel comes out only slightly moist, you'll avoid stress associated with both over and under-watering. Water meters, the inexpensive ones, don't measure moisture levels. They measure electrical conductivity, and as such they are notoriously unreliable. Using a "tell" would serve you much better. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

No, that is not a quality job. How did you choose the tiler?  Why did you separate out the materials and build tasks? Most  professional tile installers would never take on a job that did that. They must control the entire process from the studs out, as well as the materials selections, in order to produce a quality result. Or to warranty anything. A typical tile install where they control nothing, and relybon someone else’s prep, would not receive any workmanship warranty, if you could find someone to accept those conditions. Frankly, it is  is a red flag if they would take the job as outlined.

Clarification on your use of the word "metal" - if you are referring to light gauge framing (e.g. steel studs), then there is no reason to do that and you won't find a contractor to build it for you. If you are referring to a red iron steel structure, then that is for larger than a 2 car garage. No reason to do that either unless you have a 40x50 garage or something. Also it probably wouldn't blend in with anything if you have that concern. As far as modular, I don't know of a garage that is built modularly. That means it is pre-built in a factory and trailered in 12' widths to the site. There is panelized, where wall panels lengths are pre-built, trailered, then craned in to place. None of that seems viable for a 2 car garage. Go with stick built wood framing and trusses.

There is a lack of info given, and maybe some misinformation, on what you have to do. A good assumption is the basement was finished without permits. Often, a second full kitchen is not allowed in a single family house under most zoning classifications. Basements need 1 egress - meaning a way to exit the house walking while standing up. This is accomplished by walking up the stairs and exiting the front door. If you intend to close off access to the basement as a separate rental from upstairs, then you need to add a door to the basement. Any sleeping rooms require an emergency escape and rescue window - meaning a large opening to crawl out of, or for emergency personnel to come into the room, when the egress route is blocked. Now there are some exceptions to this requirement, but noting how it was probably not permitted initially and changing occupancy from storage to a habitable unit means you will need windows in both bedrooms. There are also some light and ventilation requirements for living spaces. Again, there are exceptions to this requirement, but typically providing the right mechanical ventilation to get around adding windows is more complicated and doesn't lead to a well-received living space that has no windows.

There are plenty of egress wells that allow lots of light, and most can have a plexiglass cover to keep water out.  It all depends on the space available on that part of the house.               As you can see, if you must use a precast well, you can get a cover, but if you have a deeper footprint available, you can do more natural foundation drainage.

I think you can go with any motif you want. I would be careful with too much of one type of foreign motif, you don't want to look like an ethnic restaurant. Or like Cost Plus World Market. I say this as someone who has collected a lot on my travels and collects a lot in general. You need to be judicious in what you choose, and if you have a lot of things, then use your closets (even under the beds if you have to) and rotate your lovelies. And by the way, there are only 20 tigers left in Tibet, and as per my earlier comment, that marvelous wallpaper doesn't have to be interpreted as Tibet unless you want it to be. As for how you use it, I would not use it to paper a whole wall. You could cut large panels of it on either side of the four windows and frame those panels in large black frames, maybe two inches. Then inside those wallpaper panels mount black brackets on which you display objets of beauty and interest. Not things so huge that they obscure the wallpaper of course. Treat them like the scrolls on the back wall of a tokonoma. It could be a beautifully formed glass vase with a few stems of greenery or flowers (odd numbers) or lucky bamboo (which is really dracaena sanderiana.) You can find second -hand Simon Pearce or Steuben, etc in charity shops and online for a very reasonable price with only minor etching on the inside base which won't be seen anyway as the stems will obscure it. You can display architectural artifacts, (no clocks!) fossils, taxidermy, sculpture, ethnic handiworks, candlesticks, plates, etc. My favorite of course would be a purple shoe with crimson sole and crimson lining curled at the toe :)

Get the radiator size that is right for the room and then move the pipes accordingly. Old radiators had to be wide to heat the room but many newer more efficient radiators take up less space. I post this list all the time. Anything in bold is not great and needs work. First which way is north? The best houses orient the public rooms towards the south for the best passive solar heating and cooling The best houses are L, U, T, H, or I shaped. The best houses are only one to two rooms deep. And covered lanai, porches, garages, etc count as rooms in this case. The best houses make sure kitchens have natural light, meaning windows so one doesn't have to have lighting 24/7 to use the kitchen. (And no, dining areas with windows 10' or more from the kitchen will not allow for natural light.) The best houses make sure all public rooms and bedrooms have windows on at least two walls. The best houses do not if possible put mechanical rooms, pantries or closets on outside walls The best houses keep public and private spaces separate. (A master through the living room is not keeping private spaces separate.) The best houses do not have you walk through the work zone of the kitchen to bring laundry to the laundry room. The best houses do not have the mudroom go through any of the work zones of the kitchen. The best houses do not use the kitchen as a hallway to any other rooms. The best houses do not put toilets or toilet rooms up against bedroom walls, living rooms or dining areas. The best houses do not have walk in closets too small to stand inside. The best houses have an organizing “spine” so it’s easy to determine how to get from room to room in the house and what makes sense.

With 3/4" hardwood over a solid 3/4" subfloor, there is no reason to add a <1/4" underlayment. If you have problems with waviness or unlevelness that will just transmit through any underlayment less than 1/2" thick anyway. Fix the 10% of your subfloor right. text: Roseraie de L' Hay- for a tall bush, 4'-5'.  Best flower formed larger blooming Hybrid Rugosa there is, IMHO.  Few to no hips,  consequently it's a v.g. rebloomer. These are my 3 favorite Hybrid Rugosas. Grow tested about 30 different Hybrid Rugosa varities....some were real dogs! Never spray anything onto Hybrid Rugosa foliage.  That includes Neem oil, insecticidal soap, foliar spray fertilizer, or foliar spray fungicide.  The foliage will burn and drop. Some hot dry summers, spider mites can be a problem with Hybrid Rugosas.  Just let nature take it's course since spraying is not an option both from your veggie garden standpoint, and the foliage damage inevitability if sprayed.  A soil drench miticide will work for mites, but not near veggies. Hydrangea Little Lime, at 3-4', or even Hydrangea Bobo, at 2-3', may be better heights outside your vegetable garden fence.  H. Gypsum board has been prohibited since the 2006 code revision as a tile backer board in wet areas like showers. Meaning you can't bond tile directly to the gypsum board. Doesn't matter if it is plain ole gypsum board or moisture resistant gypsum board. There are surface applied membranes (Kerdi for example) where the manufacturer of Kerdi allows Kerdi to be applied directly to gypsum board. Now it's fine that Schluter allows it, but even after all these years there are still some AHJs that don't allow it. When using a surface applied membrane (liquid or sheet) often the safest approach...and the most sensible...is to apply the SAM over cement board. Liquid membranes need to be applied to a specific minimum thickness for them to be able to provide waterproofing to the substrate behind it. Will they use a mil thickness gauge? Or guess? As Mark mentioned in the previous post, ask your builder what the construction/waterproofing sequence will be for the shower. Also for the shower floor. If using something like an Oatey membrane, code requires the floor membrane itself to be sloped to the drain. It's a code violation to install the membrane flat on the subfloor and simply install sloped mud and tile on top of the flat membrane. Don't forget to ask about the shower ceiling. If you're paying for it, don't forget you're the Big Boss. Everyone works for you.

I'm not convinced that the frame is fake painted wood grain, versus quarter sawn oak. (I'm looking at a small screen and I really can't tell if the pale lines in the second photo are quarter-sawn oak "rays" vs. paint trying to look like quarter-sawn oak rays.) Either way, you'd need to sand the frame and possibly the doors. I suspect that the difference between the doors and frame is due to a few things: different "cuts" of wood (e.g., if the door rails and stiles are rift-sawn oak and the frame is quarter sawn, or even painted as you suspect); different species of wood, which could have resulted in the doors darkening more than the frame; or different finishes on the doors and frame, possibly from a previous attempt to refinish. To do it right, I'd recommend sanding and refinishing all of it - not just the frame. But if you do that, you would indeed have a good chance of getting a better (though perhaps not perfect) match. A bigger question I would ask is whether the doors and drawers are functional and sturdy enough to stand up to however you expect to use them. Make sure the face frame and doors are all solid and that their elements have not separated from each other. Good luck, and please share your finished results if you decide to take this on! You need mature plants to gather propagation material from. A mature plant of 'Marcella Boccella' can take up to 5 years to grow from a new start (band). Some cultivars can take as little as one year to become usable for propagation, some may take a decade. What Kim says is true: don't continuously harvest cuttings from small plants or you will starve and kill them, and the resulting plants from weak cuttings may never become saleable plants. Realistically, you need to be thinking in terms of a 3-5 year timeline to get to a point where you're ready to roll and actually have a reliable volume of plants available. Or, you could find a wholesale nursery that propagates the varieties you want, who produces flats of rooted cuttings in trays of 32 or 72 which you can pot up and grow for a few months to make a saleable plant. Greenheart Farms used to offer that service. No idea if they still do. (It appears they do: https://www.greenheartfarms.com/files/General%20Availability%2003-21-22%20All%20Brokers.pdf)

When the blower used with a hood is remote from the hood, whether in-line in the duct path or outdoors on roof or wall, and there is enough length and diameter to fit it, then a silencer can be added that will remove almost all blade tip turbulence noise generated by the blower.  Such silencers look like truck mufflers and are available from Fantech.  Baffle noise, duct noise on the hood side of the silencer, and any flow transition induced noises are not affected, but these tend to not dominate the noise as the blade tip turbulence does. So whenever feasible, use remote blowers with large hoods needing high flow rates to achieve the needed air velocity at the baffles. If your hood is, say four feet by two feet in entry area, then I recommend 8 sq. ft. x 90 ft./s = 720 CFM actual flow, which will require a 1000 - 1200 CFM rated blower.  You will also need a make-up air system. While induction cooking lacks the added gas combustion products in the cooking plume, the cooking plume still expands as it rises.  This is the rationale for wider and deeper hoods than have been historically used in kitchens.  But best is the enemy of good enough, and good enough depends on configuration of cabinets, burners/hobs used for grease and moisture laden cooking effluent -- middle or boundary, cross drafts, and other effects. There are a lot of ways to transport grease into the air without frying or searing, so frying rarity may not be a good reason for not going wider.  It is more of an architectural issue in already existing kitchens than a "we don't need it because ..." issue.  Wider does have various increased costs associated with it, but I won't belabor this paragraph touching on them.  Please review the many hood and make-up air related threads on this forum for perspective and references. This forum is littered from more than a decade ago with commentaries supporting induction and, conversely, gas.  Induction wins on safety, ease of cooktop surface cleaning, low heat warming (chocolate is not just for breakfast anymore) and other cooking that can make use of its wide "dynamic range" (full power to minimum power), less heat in the kitchen in summer, and other factors I've forgotten.  Safety includes no gas risk, and lower surface temperatures than with other electrical or gas cooking approaches. Negatives are no roasting of peppers over the burner, need for inductive base pots and pans, significantly more electrical power needed at the cooktop or range location, and theoretical and experiential lower long term reliability due to electronic complexity, although this is improving, I think.

"So a 200A service should be OK with an induction cooktop unless a lot of current is already allocated to big power dissipators such as electric heating, a heated driveway, electrically heated high air flow MUA, or a Tesla." Yeah, they may be fine w/ 200 and may not be. It depends on what electric devices they have or will have in the future, how they use them and what their current service entrance is. They can stick an IotaWatt or similar on their service to get an idea of current usage - both peak amp draw and voltage drops (pushing the limit of the service entrance/xformer can cause voltage drops that can quickly damage electronics). It's important to account for seasonal variation though and to understand the limits of their service entrance and how close the new induction will come to stressing it. It's much better that we recognize our plants have rhythms (search Circadian and endogenous rhythm) during which its level of vitality varies significantly, and to work in concert with these rhythms to make life easier for our plants, than it is to act on impulse and not reap the rewards of working with the plant instead of against it. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

BUT our mason ground the existing bricks down so that the surface was smooth, and he repointed where necessary.  We also solved the water coming in from the outside. The hose you poked may have some residue but it's probably not the source of the flow obstruction.  You can clean it with a suitable brush but be careful not to puncture it or dislodge it, otherwise you'll need to disassemble the machine for access to fix that problem. More likely the screens in the machine's inlet valve are clogged from debris in your water supply. Turn off both supply faucets (hot and cold).  Disconnect the hoses from back of the machine ... can do one at a time.  Look into the connection ports to see if the debris screens (that should be in there) are clogged.  Clean the screens as best you can.  A machine of that age probably has wire/mesh screens (pic 1 below) which can be difficult to remove without damaging or deforming them ... so clean them carefully in-place.  A toothbrush or other small brush dipped in a cup of water.  I have a basting/marinade injector syringe (pic 2) that works nicely for squirting water repeatedly at the screens to flush them clear.  Don't puncture or deform the screens, or debris in the future can pass through and jam the valve from closing which leads to flooding. There may also be screens in the hoses at the faucet end.  Usually not but sometimes there are.  It's a good idea to add them if there are none for extra protection.  Screens at the faucets are easier to clean and help avoid the need to clean the screens in the valves.  You can disconnect the hoses from the faucets to check and clean them if necessary.  And add screens there if you wish, you can get them at plumbing or home supply stores (pic 3), they take the place of the rubber washers without screens.  (Don't add screens into the supply hoses at the machine end.)

text: Do you have super long arms???  How do you expect to get the middle of your island countertop CLEAN???  REALLY CLEAN... Maybe you should consider instead, a 78" long by 42" wide island.  If you are looking to make the other side into seating area for breakfast nook alternative, the extra 6" will provide more overhand to push chairs mostly in, and provide more eating area for plates and cups!  You will be able to clean the center of your island as well, and save money on your solid surface countertop as well!  An island that is too large becomes an "albatross" in the kitchen, that is what I call something that is awkwardly sized, and somewhat design killing in aesthetics.  In life, many, many times, larger is just not better, and is rarely efficient!  Think about traffic flow, you will tire eventually of having extra long paces to get around your super large island.  In showrooms they look fabulous, but in life... not so much.  they can make a room feel too small even when made too large.  You literally only need a 24"x20-24" prep area per person that is cooking or prepping meals!  I can remember my mother working relatively efficiently in an L-shaped kitchen that had a cleared 24" wide by 20" deep prep area in her kitchen... and she was Italian, and a fabulous cook, who often experimented with a multitude of foreign dishes, she was a before the times, "Foodie" ;o).  Big kitchens and 100's of gadgets don't make you a better cook, but they will make you a confused, financially broken, time consumed clean freak... who orders out more than they cook, because too many options and too much space can be...  overwhelming and a pain to keep clean and free of dust!  I have a big kitchen, it was here when I moved here... I have been mindfully considering reducing it's size and taking much of that space and turning it into a butler's pantry or food pantry with additional small appliance storage space for crock pots, griddles, food processors (I rarely use), and ultimately reducing the cost of my kitchen update, because I will have less cabinetry, (maybe even some additional windows for natural light), and a smaller work surface... with enough room for 3 people to comfortably prep food for holiday meals, or family dinners...  a family who loves each other, cooks with each other!  Instead of focusing on competing with "the Jones" think about what is really important to you, and incorporate THAT into you new kitchen.  Have fun and be original, be you, when you pick your final finishes!  And I hope you find everything your looking for in this new Post COVID era of minimal options for materials.  Good luck! Oh and one more thing...  unless you really need a bigger pantry, don't increase the size, you'll be bumping into it constantly as you make the turn into that area of the kitchen, and the additional cabinet next to the dishwasher will result in the same problem, but you could put a floor to ceiling bookshelf to display collective items in upper shelves and COOKBOOKS in the accessible shelves below!  To help you be adventurous in your cooking endeavors with your family.  Maybe with the new cookbooks you can make a new family tradition of cooking something new on Sundays for a special family dinner weekly. I saw the sketch with the table up against the island... this will again, impede in your pathway to the sliding door.  You would be better to put a small family kitchen table in front of the windows & if you like cottage or vintage styled homes, you could build a bench seat in front of the windows for the kids, as long as the windows are raised high enough to give clearance for a bench back support and some throw pillows. Making the garden work for dogs was a prime issue here - when we moved here in 1999 we had a Golden, followed by a Lhasa Apso, and now a miniature poodle....  Plus we dog sit a lot and have experience with a lot of breeds (e.g. Airedales, border collies, Lab and Lab x Australian Shepherd, Australian terrier, Springer Spaniel, malamute, Bouvier, Briard, Boston terrier, and others....)  It's important to pay attention to the dog's needs and wants and accommodate those in the garden!  All dogs want to patrol their territory, so a path that largely follows the boundary of the space is desirable - otherwise they will make their own!   Most dogs will literally 'take the path of least resistance' so having planned paths through beds helps keep them from wandering through the plantings at random :-)  Before we laid out most of the paths, we watched the dogs to see what their normal route was and, as much as possible, put the paths there :-)  Kids also tend to like and follow paths through the garden beds :-)  So, watch where your dog goes and see what that tells you about what it needs in the garden :-)   If there are wet places in the garden, they need fixing - add drainage or redirect the waterflow or plant appropriate plants that will make use of the water and ideally provide support with their roots.  We have several places like that here, most of which have been improved over time by various means.  The picture below is from 2014 when the paths in 'the wet corner' area were in bad shape so DH and a nephew added 'crusher run' gravel that was then covered in pine bark mulch to make it disappear!  The low iron fence at the edge in the picture was there to keep the Golden we had back in the early years here out of this area after she, in the first year here, regularly came back covered in mud!  She could have easily stepped over the fence but it was sufficient to tell her that this was a no-go area!  One important thing we did here was shape the spaces - particularly the little grass that remains! - so that it makes the space have impact regardless of the season.  If that space is kept reasonably neat, the whole garden looks organized even if it is a bit messy (e.g. needs some weeding or pruning etc.!) I'm not aware of a truly optimal recirculation system, although I'm sure that theoretically some complex of filters could be arranged to nearly perfectly remove effluent from the captured cooking plumes.  On the basis of reports here, the Vent-a-Hood ARS seems to be satisfactory, if not optimal (in the sense of effluent removal without regard to cost).  Broan/Best have recirculating products, but no reports have been posted here. In general, you want a hood that overlaps the cooking plumes, which requires overlapping the cooktop, and sufficient velocity into the baffle space to ensure containment of the plumes by entraining them into the air moving into the baffle slots. Ejection outside is the best means of further filtering.  (For gentle, low plume velocity cooking, mesh filtering can work (with outside ducting) but still requires a larger than cooktop hood.) So, if you didn't already have a hood, then you could go through the simple process I've outlined dozens of times to establish hood size, desired CFM, rated CFM, etc.  Then, try to find a recirculating hood that accomplishes that and also performs decent filtering of odor, grease, and other effluent.  I don't think the consensus here supports recirculating gas cooktop plumes due to the difficulty of removing all the harmful trace compounds in the combustion products.  Induction cooktop filtering might be OK.  Opening windows to dilute any contaminants escaping the filtering is also useful, except in highly polluted cities. In any case, there are many factors that mitigate against striving for optimality of performance, including cost, space, and aesthetics, so I'm not going to be fanatically strict about what YOU should do.

What temperature are you setting on the thermostat? How are measuring the indoor humidity and how accurate is your measuring device? The AC can only lower the humidity when it is running. If the temperature is set at 76 the AC will have less run time then it were set at 74. A humidity level of 60-65% at 75 degrees should be fine. If you want lower humidity you can will need a dehumidifier. In your location it makes sense to buy a better machine and not the low cost type sold at the big box stores.

Relative humidity levels of 60% or more are typically required to support growth of mold and mildew.  And the relative humidity needs to be at or above that level for a sufficiently long time for mold spores to germinate and become established.   Once established, however, mold and mildew can grow at relative humidity levels as low as 50%  I suggest 50% R.H. as a target maximum indoor relative humidity, but you can find recommended maximum relative humidity levels as high as 60%  The lower the target the higher the margin of safety. A properly-sized air conditioner will remove moisture as it cools the air in your home and reduce relative humidity.   In so called "shoulder seasons," where neither air conditioning nor heating is required, relative humidity control generally requires a dehumidifier. With respect to operating bath fans, range hoods, etc. to deal with point sources of moisture, keep in mind that the volume of air exhausted needs to be replaced with an equivalent volume of outside (unconditioned) air.  That can raise the indoor relative humidity.

We had no issues with indoor humidity during the hottest months of the season (RH inside maintained at 45%) but now as we are “in between” seasons in Florida - where outdoor temps are 60-80 degrees, our indoor humidity can be 60-65%. This is a common problem for areas in which there is higher humidity. Humidity is independant of temperature. So this isn't anything unusual for a high humid type climate. You can run your AC at a lower setting when it's not as hot. Most run of the mill AC's are not recommended to run below 55F outside temp as damage will likely result with out the addition of controls to operate as such. The trade off is that you will need to adjust to a cooler inside temperature than what you are accustomed to during the summer months. As the machines run based on temperature not humidity. Some HVAC systems that have humidity set points are limited in a tight band off the temperature setting. So you still have to adjust temperature setpoints for such systems. Short cycling: when it's cooler out the AC system (most of them) are designed to lower temp. They are either on or off. So due to this there is little dehumidification from them unless you force them to run by dropping indoor temps further to force that additional run time. 2 speed AC's: you get some better dehumidification with these... but 1st speed is typically 70% of total capacity of the machine so in off season use they are still over-sized in terms of trying to dehumidify the home. Enter the Inverter AC or variable speed AC; The ability to run in 1% increments up and down some systems could have upwards of 50 different speed levels or more. These machines still run off temperature, some may have dehumidify functions built into them -- but as mentioned above dehumidify functions are often tied to a temperature band off temperature set points. The advantage to inverter AC is better dehumidification due to the nature of how it runs. Also it will pay for itself over time because you're only ever using the amount of cooling you need in 1% increments up and down. (some manufacturer's units may not perform as mentioned here due to configuration, design, etc) Add a dehumidifier; sure this is one option but costs will go up. The cost to operate it, the cost to maintain it, the cost to repair it and eventually replace it... it's another system to maintain. Running a dehumidifier alone blows warm dehumidified air. Some people who are more heat sensitive than others won't like this mode of operation in that you're burning energy to dehumidify then need to burn more to run AC to drop the temperature. Some areas of the country a stand alone dehumidifier is the better choice but it's a very small market in my opinion. If you like it warmer inside with less humidity then this choice might be the better one. Me personally I like it a bit chilly. I ran my Bosch Inverter last night... seeing record temps here in Katy, Texas with highs in the 80's. Humidity is always a problem here short of a few weeks here and there.

"Humidity is independant (sic) of temperature." The terms "humidity" and "relative humidity" are often used interchangeably, but they are not the same.  Absolute humidity is the mass of moisture per unit volume of moist air and is independent of temperature.  Relative humidity is a comparison--expressed as a percent-- of the amount of moisture in the air with the maximum amount (saturation) that it could hold at that temperature.  It is temperature dependent. When we're talking about indoor conditions--whether design or actual--we're referring to relative humidity which is temperature dependent.  With respect to occupant comfort, 35% - 55% +/- 5% relative humidity is generally considered a comfortable range, albeit influenced by a number of other variables (e.g., temperature, air flow, clothing) as well. Depending on the specifics of the OP's system, they can consider retrofitting it to extend run times or adding a dehumidifier or both.  If the equipment is nearing the end of its useful life, replacing it with a system that offers more turndown would enhance control of relative humidity.  I live in coastal Virginia which is a mixed-humid climate zone.  I've found the addition of dehumidifiers to be an appropriate solution for controlling indoor relative humidity during shoulder seasons for most applications in our area.  I have one on each level in my home.

Relative humidity, which is what is usually measured, is dependent on temperature. Providing the relative humidity amount without a temperature does provide the amount of moisture in the air. Different part numbers mean different parts no matter where you purchase them.  The same part numbers mean the same parts no matter where you purchase them. There is no Delta faucet that you can purchase at a plumbing supplier that you can't purchase at Lowe's or Home Depot, but I am not sure about other big box stores. --- I have put this myth to bed so many times now.  No audit firm on the planet would issue an unqualified audit letter (which the SEC requires) for a company that has two different costs for the same part.  The idea is patently ridiculous.  Moreover, that is not how manufacturers really reduce costs.  Any faucet manufacturer is going to do an Activities Based Cost analysis and be more concerned about line change-over, handling, and warehousing costs. Generally, in manufacturing quality increases over time but parts may feel cheaper.  This happens because when products are first developed process problems and tolerance issues are addressed by using higher quality materials, as tolerances and processes get refined cheaper materials become just as reliable. --- In short, plumbers may not be manufacturing experts.

"Those on the shelf are specially built *exclusive* models with lesser specs." It would be more correct to say that exclusive lines are typically reskins of existing durable product lines.  Rather than different products with lower specs. As I mentioned above, as a line ages it becomes cheaper for the exact same quality,  some of this is because the processes get refined and some is because of treatment of marginal manufacturing overhead. Much of the manufacturing costs for something like faucets is overhead.  The more parts you order, ship, handle, warehouse, etc. the higher your costs are.  One of the biggest costs in manufacturing is changeover, which is the process of shutting down production of one item, unloading the line, changing all your machinery over to the new line, reloading the line, and restarting production.  So it often makes more sense to just change the housing of the faucet rather than all the parts. This is what companies who make things like faucets do, they spend a lot of money to perfect the process of changing just a few small things, like the housing, to speed up efficiency.

Leaf chlorosis (yellowing) could be increasing for a number of reasons. The main suspects would be over or under-watering, severe root congestion, a high level of dissolved solids (salts) in the grow medium, low fertility - in particular a deficiency of nitrogen, and soil compaction. The degree to which the neem/soap solution was harmful depends on what "soap" you used. Not likely a problem if you used a soap based on long-chain fatty acids of potassium, but very likely if you used any of the numerous dish soaps or other cleaning products on the market. These surfactants strip leaves of their cuticular wax (the leaves'  water-proofing), which increases water loss through leaves and provides easy access for biotic pathogens. All you really need to keep miters under control is a quart-size spritzer filled with 1 part 0f 70% rubbing alcohol to 2 parts water. Spritz every 4 days, covering all plant surfaces, and your mite issue will soon be a memory. The statement "..... since  the plant has  been watered at most once a week and not abundantly .....", "not abundantly" tells us you haven't been watering to beyond the point of total soil saturation, so you're flushing accumulating salts from the soil as you water. If you cannot do that w/o paying an over-watering tax in the form of poor root function or health, the medium you are using is inappropriate. This doesn't necessarily mean a change is necessary, but it should be addressed in such a way that the amount of excess water a medium can hold is reduced to levels that allow you to water correctly. We can talk about that if you like. Yes, you should lift the plant from the pot and inspect the roots. Look for slimy or dark (colored) roots or roots that when pulled on, the outer root covering slips off leaving the root cortex. Also, roots should smell like a handful of moist, freshly-dug earth. If roots smell sour or you can detect the odor of H2S (hydrogen sulfide/ rotten egg gas), you have a fungal infection of one of the several damping off diseases. The plant should not sit in the effluent which exits the drain holes after watering.  Water over the sink, let the pot drain, then tip it to a 45* angle and watch how much additional water exits the pot. Compare images A and B below to see how well this trick works.   Ballast (see image D) is also a very good way of reducing how much excess water a pot can hold. I'll wait to see what questions you have before I say more. Al

While I'm not saying the neem mixture is at fault for the condition of the plant, I am saying that most dish soaps have somewhere between 12 and 20 phytotoxic (poison to plants) ingredients, including the dyes and perfumes, and the best surfactants to use to help emulsify neem oil are commercially prepared insecticidal soaps. Too, all neem products are not created equal. Extraction methods which make use of steam, or formaldehyde/ other solvents, can significantly reduce the efficacy of the active ingredient neem oil contains, azadirachtin. The best choice is pure, cold-pressed neem oil, and it's best stored refrigerated until used. It should also be used in acidified water as it undergoes a process called alkaline hydrolysis when pH is above neutral. You didn't mention how much water went into the emulsion, so there is no way to gauge the severity of damage the dish soap might have caused. You expressed concern about whether your plant is particularly sensitive to neem oil. A few plants ARE, but more are sensitive to the vehicle (water is the vehicle by which cleaning chemicals are delivered in a car wash) that contains the neem oil or the emulsifier if it's inappropriate. "I only used this  neem mix for 4 days ...." Four successive days? If 'yes', that could easily cause problems. Al

"I did some math" "What needs to be factored in is:" You are missing some factors: the function and mood of a space and the level of house. You are designing a home, not a floor of an office building. "Rule of thumb" equations figuring lumens (thus size of lumenaire and spacing) can only follow the establishment of a concept of the lighting. For instance, you are caught up on an equation for a general, sustained amount of lumens in a bedroom. That is not typically how you use a bedroom. At the end of a night, when you enter the room, you can use the switch by the door for overhead cans, but that may not be the type of light that will relax you. You may only want that light highlighting a bay window; or an accent wall; you may just want a soft eye-level light next to the bed (table lamps); you may not want a recessed light pointing at your pillow as you lay your head down and hold the book over your face. Or, you have a perimeter soffit or tray ceiling, so you want small accent cans to highlight that feature and design lines, combined with switched table lamps. So you determine a concept for lighting that you want by space function and layout (including furniture), then find fixtures that fit that concept. Your concern with the cost should also be addressed with this concept. There is a big difference between basic painted baffle 3", 4", or 6" lights; 2" box trims; hidden trims; gimbal/eye/adjustable housing accents; baffle finish; etc that may change a bit with house level, finishes, how it's constructed, and your lighting concept. If you prioritize the lighting design as much as you might the veining of your marble countertops, then final cost is a secondary decision. If the lighting design is just a way to keep you from bumping your knee in the dark, then cost may be the primary decision. I will say though that in a typical contempory home, a general grid of light providing a uniform lighting level sometimes fits the design concept of open and flowing rooms. The ceiling "grid" of lumenaires becomes another design element. But, you have to design around that for areas requiring fine tuning like kitchen work counters and islands.

Remember that once you embed a trimless recessed lights in joint compound you won't be able to change them. Your lighting plan and the fixtures you choose better be right! In contrast, if you install housings, you can experiment with different types of fixtures, bulbs, etc. later. After installing 4" recessed cans in my living room ceiling I bought and tested several integrated recessed lights from Halo, Juno, and Nicor none of which I liked. I switched to Juno trims with PAR20 bulbs and then tested at least four bulbs before finding one of those I liked. Finally, I changed the dimmers to support the bulbs.

I always start by planning my overall / whole home color palette. Each of us have colors that we love, those colors that make our heart sing.   We pick them out of the crowd when looking at art, clothing, pillows or bedding and they call to us "buy me".    Mine are purple and blue greens with touches of wine reds.   Since my walls are a backdrop for my art and furniture and décor the next thing I look for is the color family for my neutrals. When looking for the neutral you have to consider the things that must stay.   For me, since I am doing new flooring throughout most of the home, and I am renovating kitchens and baths - there were only 3 items that were staying - my foyer floor and my pink brick wall and my teak furniture. I forgot to add my teak in the pictures below when I created them. (after I had picked my neutral) Most wood tones work with most neutrals, but there are exceptions - Yellow pine will not look good with pink beige, taupe or violet gray. You may also need to consider your upholstered furniture, cabinet colors, countertops, backsplash or other items in your 'colors that must stay'. top left - taupe top right - pink beige bottom left - violet gray bottom right - orange beige  Top left - blue gray top right - yellow beige bottom left - green gray / greige bottom right green beige  I prefer the taupe shades with my things and it works with my pink brick.    Someone else may have liked the violet gray  or even the blue gray, but I don't think anyone would pick the orange, yellow or green beige. Once you pick your neutral then pick a white that looks good with your neutral. Now you can use that color palette to pick the colors and finishes for each room and know that the colors will flow from one room to the next and feel coordinated.   You won't get boxed into something because you picked colors or finishes for one room that don't work with your overall color palette.

Beyond VaH repelling me with their "Magic Lung" claims,* duly parroted by the sales force, I came to realize that the best residential hood (defined as one that fits below an 8-foot ceiling) is one that is least deviant from commercial hood practices.  This includes having baffle filters. Wolf answers their phone.  Their telephone contact connected me with one of their engineers who provided me with fan curves for several of their blowers, which are (were) manufactured by NuTone.  Fan curves are essential for performance estimation, and at the time (2007) pretty rare except in the aerospace industry. As to relative performance of VaH hoods in the noise category, I think @clinresga provided measured data in a thread here back around 2010.  There may be differences with modern VaH hoods. Others here have commented on cleaning difficulty; some recent comments suggest that this may have been somewhat improved in the past decade. VaH have also leaked some fan curve data.  What these show is that their squirrel cage blowers appear to be more sensitive than radial centrifugal blowers in flow vs. pressure loss.  VaH may now make more conventional hoods, I have no need to investigate them unless a specific question arises. In any case, I wanted an outside (roof) blower.  This moves a source of noise away from the hood and allows a Fantech silencer to occupy some of the duct length.  Blower noise is significantly reduced.  Remote blower operation can also allow in-line axial blowers, where they might have merit, and optionally roof-mounted commercial up-blast blowers that can be sized to run very quietly if oversized for the purpose. ---- *VaH like to claim that their x CFM blower(s) is/are equivalent to 1.5x standard blowers (that might fit in the same hood).  All they are really saying is that because they don't use baffles for grease extraction, they save on that pressure loss.  But there are other pressure losses that affect overall flow rate.  These include duct length, duct transitions, vent caps, and most significantly, how well the MUA brings the kitchen pressure close to the outside pressure.  So the achieved flow depends on the fan curve and the resistance curve of the entire hood and MUA systems. Note that blower rated CFM is a free air (zero static pressure) value and bears little resemblance to the actual CFM obtained in a system.  VaH CFM is (I hope) that of the blower(s) and hood combined, but not counting any other factor.

I grew up with a central vacuum system and had one installed in my current home when it was built 9 years ago.  I'm not an expert but did a lot of research over the years so here's my take on your questions. 1) Best Brands - My parents built a big, brick house (Home Alone house) back in the late 80's and their builder put in a Nutone unit as many other homes in the neighborhood had.  It worked fine but sometime around 2000 the motor unit burned out and my parents replaced it with a MD Silentmaster unit.  Both are bagged units but only needed to be emptied a few times each year.  In my current home, our builder put in a Vacuflo copycat filtered cyclonic unit with the Dirt Devil label.   It was very powerful and very loud.  Emptying the bagless canister was disgusting and dog hair and dust would coat the pleated filter so with each emptying you had to remove the filter and bang it against the ground.  There would just be a giant dust cloud.  I'm not sad that the motor died within three years. We replaced it with a bagged MD central vac unit like my parents.  It's much quieter, very powerful and so easy to change the bags when needed.  I will never go back to a bagless central vac system. 2) Installation Considerations - Both my parents and myself had our builders put the system in so we didn't provide too much input.  I did get to pick the general location of the inlets but not the exact placement. There are a couple of inlets I would have preferred to be in a different spot based on furniture placement. For instance, the one in our family room is on the wall behind our couch.  Granted, our couch floats in the big room so it's not blocked but just would prefer it be on a different wall.  We have regular inlets for use with an electric hose as well as vacpans to sweep up small messes without needing the hose.  About a year or two into owning this house I had an installer put in a "Hide a Hose" inlet on the main level of our home.  If I were building again, I would only install the Hide a Hose inlets.  I am not a fan of dragging around the long hose and wrapping it up when I'm done as you do with a traditional system.  They now make battery-powered electric heads for hide a hose which work just as well as a normal powerhead.  We also made sure to have an inlet in the garage so that we can clean our cars and garage floors.  If I were to do it again, I'd have two.  One in the front of the garage by the driveway and one on the unit as it is now. 3) Maintenance & care - The bagged units are virtually maintenance free.  In the last six years I haven't done anything with the MD unit besides change the bag. Overall, I think I will always have a central vac in the homes I live in.  However, I don't think that they are for everyone.  If you're someone like me who uses the hose attachments a lot for dusting, cleaning dog hair off the couch, etc. then they're a great option.  But if you just want something to quickly do your floors then a regular vacuum might make more sense.  My parents are in their 70s and never really use their central vac anymore.  They no longer have kids or pets in the house so they get by with a Riccar upright and Dyson cordless.  I also have a Dyson cordless and self-emptying Roomba that get a lot of use.

I always find it helpful to understand the color that is currently on the walls to determine what I want next. If you look below Monroe Bisque has an LRV of 61  (Column M). The other numbers I am showing below are the LCH (columns XYZ) L - luminosity - again light or dark - the higher the number the lighter the color C - Chroma - how colorful or gray the color appears.  (Monroe Bisque has a chroma of 17 - colorful enough that it borders on color vs neutral.  Balboa Mist and Collingwood are at the other end of the neutral spectrum with a Chroma of 5.   Pure Gray/Black/White will have a chroma of 0. H - Hue - the actual core color.  All of the colors you picked are near yellow (~90)  Revere Pewter has a hue over 90, so it is bit more green than the others.  Smokey Taupe has a hue of 83, so it is going a bit oranger than yellow.   Because it also has a low chroma it is likely to flash pink or purple.   Have you looked at Natural Linen. Welcome to the Kitchens Forum Dallastx1984! To be able to give you useful advice, we need more information.  We need measurements of the space(s) as well information about you & your family and how you plan to use the space(s). For our purposes, square feet isn't very useful.  What we need is a fully-measured layout of the space.  If that is not the layout of the entire floor the Kitchen is on, then we also need that sketch. From the "New to Kitchens?  Read Me First!" thread: By "fully-measured", we mean a layout with the widths of each wall/window/door/doorway and the distances between each wall/window/door/doorway labeled. See a sample below. If something cannot be moved or changed, label it precisely on your layout (see post in sample) and tell us why it cannot be moved/changed -- we may have some ideas for you. The sketch of the entire floor lets us see how the Kitchen relates to the rest of the home. It doesn't have to be to-scale, but it should accurately show how the rooms relate to each other and should include all interior & exterior doors. In addition, it will help us see how traffic flows in, around, and through the Kitchen. Label the front entry and family entry. The family entry is usually a garage or side entry, but it might not be. It's helpful to know which door you use to bring in groceries. Regardless of how you draw it up (by hand, computer, etc.), please be sure all measurements are labeled. (Note: Computer generated layouts often lack key measurements and, sometimes, measure to/from things like the middle of a wall or the middle of a window. Neither are useful. Measure each item and the distances between each item.) Other questions...

It is a concern.  two potential reasons is the plaster has come loose from the wood lathes or the ceiling joists are sagging. Climb up a ladder and tap on the plaster where the sag is in the ceiling.  If it sounds hollow it's coming loose from the lath and will eventually fall.  If it sounds solid it would be sagging ceiling joists.  Tap on the walls to see what a solid sound would be, then on the edges of the ceiling with no sag, the sound should be the same.  Now go to the sag to compare and check the sound. No easy fix for either situation but loose plaster can be fixed without removing it but I won't describe how until loose plaster is confirmed. the crack on the wall above the door is common from settling.  To fix it tale a 5 way and scrape out about a 3/16" of plaster, coat with drywall mud, sand, recoat, sand again and then paint.

It has been stated that the  average homeowner has their hardwood flooring sanded and refinished  every 15-20 years. Just to reiterate to others commenting, this panel is in another room, accessed from the other room on the other side of a shared wall. "If you add another wall, plywood to isolate shower valve from electric panel and ice n water shield the plywood wood this pass code?" So I looked up NEC 110.26 for your code discussion (Canada you're on your own), but as always your inspector will be the one with final say. Code all addresses the front of the panel, not behind it. Closest to apply is: NEC 110.26(e)(1)(a) dedicated electrical space: "The space equal to the width and depth of the equipment and extending from the floor to a height of 1.8 m (6 ft) above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower, shall be dedicated to the electrical installation. No piping, ducts, leak protection apparatus, or other equipment foreign to the electrical installation shall be located in this zone."   This drawing is actually representative of what you will be doing - building a sistered wall to house your mixing valve and shower head stub that would be clearly outside of the panel footprint, no interpretation needed like for the existing 2 vanity supply lines that were allowed in the same deep stud bay space. If done this way, I see nothing in code that requires protection on the backside from leakage, etc. (NEC does in fact allow sprinklers over panels, and do not require protection from that water). However, it is common sense that you would want a material for leakage, spray, and moisture (rust) protection sandwiched between these sistered walls. Whether that material is a poly plastic, CBU, or bitumen membrane on ply is up to you and your inspector. Personally I'd go with something that doesn't stink and doesn't mind moisture, because you won't ever be able to replace it.

Picture of the opening? If this is a normal closet door situation with a walk-through-able door, you want standard butt door hinges.  Butt hinges are available in several different finishes to match door hardware.  Butt hinges can be changed out if you later want to change hardware finishes, usually with minimal effort. The Blum type Euro concealed hinge is not designed for this application.  Starting with doors are inset into a frame...normal application for Euro hinges is for cabinet doors that overlay the box or frame.  Euro hinges are designed for cabinetry with the expected almost furniture like close tolerances.  Euro hinges have limited degrees of opening swing.  And Euro hinges protrude into the space & be a potential clothes grabber, skin scraper...(except for the compact hinges which definitely are not suitable for a closet door). There is a photo on this forum from a few weeks back.  Documenting how an attempt to use concealed Euro hinges on a pass thru door had gone wrong.  Consensus was 'wrong hinges for the application'. Lastly, standard butt hinges for doors will last generations; changing them is not difficult.  Zero guess work getting a replacement if you want a new finish.  Vs using a complex hinging that will last, at best, a few years in a situation the hinge was not designed for and present challenges in obtaining the correct replacement.

Unless you want to keep growing it in a container, no reason not to plant it in the ground. Paniculatas are extremely hardy and do well here in the PNW. In our climate, they thrive in full sun but would appreciate a good soaking periodically during our dry summers. More shade will produce less flowering. Since Little Lime blooms on new growth, you can prune as desired before May. Personally, I would only remove any very thin side branching and maybe any tall, leggy stems that appear out of proportion (I don't see any in the photo). This cultivar is bred to be compact. If planting in the ground with any decent soil, no fertilizing should be required although, mulching annually with compost never goes amiss :-) If you DO want to keep this in container, come back for further suggestions. Container growing has very different challenges than do inground plantings.

My experience has been that my heavier, higher-quality pans (cast iron, my monster 12 in demeyere skillet) are less buzzy/more quiet than the lighter, generally less expensive ones (the Calphalons and my cheapy one from Target "sing" at times). Capture area (hood intake aperture area) should overlap the expanding cooking plumes.  Assume at least 10 degrees from vertical for all points across the top area of all likely pots and pans to be used on any or the hobs, and add some for burner flames if applicable.  This implies that the capture area has to grow with height, and doesn't account for plume deviations due to cross drafts and human motion turbulence. Capture areas smaller than this will likely miss capturing effluent and the effluent will spread into the house where it either condenses on walls and fabrics, or is eventually removed from air replacement. Numerous threads here discuss sizing the hood, sizing the flow rate to assure that even if the plumes are captured they don't reflect out of the hood, sizing the duct for best balance between grease collection due to impingement and grease collection due to condensation, blower rated CFM to achieve desired CFM, and make-up air (MUA). Quieting of the hood system can be achieved using a remote blower and intermediate silencer such as Fantech makes. A 6-inch duct should be limited to 400 CFM, so a 600 CFM rated blower might be appropriate given typical pressure losses and blower fan curves.  10 x 4 duct, from a pressure loss point of view is equivalent to 5.7-inch round duct. (IRC Table M1506.2). For a given blower restricted by duct size, it is probably better to use a larger hood and miss out on some extreme cooking capture due to insufficient CFM, then to miss out full plume capture on all cooking due to insufficient area to overlap the plumes.

MDF will sag or "creep" over time more than solid wood when a load is placed on it, especially a continuous load. I have MDF shelves that I have to flip over every so often, and they don't span very far. You are assuming that bunk beds would be engineered the same way as shelves, I submit that is not a safe assumption.   However, all wood species and sheet goods will sag under load when horizontal.  We could get into the reasons for this, but they are largely immaterial here, there are several calculators available to calculate the sag. To make an MDF bed, you typically use MDF torsion boxes, which will not sag under load.  They remove most of the problems with MDF and will outperform poplar.

OP says "bunk beds". You span that heavy torsion box 75" and have someone sleep on it 8 hours a day and I guarantee it will sag. My MDF torsion box for my CNC router spans 96" with several hundred pounds on it for days at a time (the CNC gantry assembly itself rests towards the middle of the table and has to weigh 100 lbs) and it is dead flat after several years of continuous use.  Even 1/50th of an inch from dead flat would cause serious problems for the CNC router.  So not only will I take that bet, there will be a line of several thousand people behind me with money in hand ready to take that bet. This is well settled, most cabinet shops use MDF torsion boxes for dead flat assembly surfaces.

Yes, leave the stems alone for a few weeks. Some roses take 4 wks to root, and some can take 3 mos or more. Depends on the variety and the temperature. I've been rooting florist roses the last two yrs with pretty good success. But I find myself getting impatient and checking them too often!!  I don't pull them up to check if they're callousing tho. They have to be left alone for at least 4 wks. The more you handle them, the more chance of failure. Also, be sure whatever soil medium you use is tamped very tightly around the stem. If the stems are too loose they won't root easily. If however you see that brown rot coming up the stem out of the soil medium, remove it and toss it. I have found that when it turns brown, even cutting above there is worthless. Once it starts turning brown it's done for! I have never had one end up rooting when I cut it off. One suggestion... add some cinnamon to your rooting powder. If you're using a liquid one, then sprinkle some cinnamon over the wet end, or keep a small container of it to dip it in. It helps to deter the brown rot. Not always, but I've found it does help! Good luck! It's lots of fun, but you do have to be patient!
