"It takes a while" is too vague to help us decide how appropriate the grow medium is/isn't. I suggest you start using a "tell" to "tell" you when it's time to water. See "Tell" below. The all-important question is 'what to do to save it'. The answer to that, though broad, is, examine the cultural influences under which the plant grows. At least one, maybe more are asking the plant to deal with conditions it's not genetically programmed to deal with. This Overview should help you decide what needs tweaking. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

A hip would be the type of roof shape. Valleys in roofs are usually created from the footprint of the building. A simple rectangle footprint could have no valley. A simple 'L' footprint could have 1 valley. An 'H' footprint could have 4 valleys, or none at all. If you are concerned with the look of many nested gables, porticos, dormers, and so forth, those can illustrate the footprint or be added to the simplest of roof shapes with nothing to do with the footprint. I've never treated any insect on rhododendron or azaleas.  It seems like when I have a plant with lacebugs or whatever it goes away after a year or two.  Oh wait...I lied!  I treated root weevils with nematodes and it seems to have worked.  https://www.gardenweb.com/discussions/3872626/has-anyone-successfully-treated-root-weevils-with-nematodes But generally speaking I feel like in an ecologically balanced garden, these issues work themselves out.  The exceptions are 1) I treated adelgids with neonics years (2008?) ago to save my hemlocks.  Just needed one treatment.  Hemlocks are now gone...were not part of the long term plan for the garden regardless  2) treated root rot sensitive rhododendrons with antifungals (really, anti watermoulds) to experiment with growing them here.  They can, and then die without it.  Experiment concluded!  Although there are a handful of varieties that capture the excitement of the high elevation Himalayan rhododendrons in plants hybridized for root rot resistance ('24 Karat'), the better long term solution is to graft them onto resistant rootstocks.  This is, for example, how I am keeping the excellent variety 'Ruby Hart' alive.  It has the very alpine R. forrestii in its parentage and would therefore definitely die on its own roots around here.  Alas, our dunderheaded 'horticultural industrial complex' seems very resistant to this practice with a very few exceptions like Abies cultivars on Abies firma (grafting for root rot resistance).  And it's not like those are easy to find! Oh I forgot: 3) I tried to save one of my ashes with an injectable neonic, but it was too late.  I didn't really want the tree long term, I just wasn't ready for it to die yet LOL. Obviously in the case of EAB and adelgids, with a foreign invasive there's no 'ecological balance' to be restored.  Although the funny thing about adelgids is I'm near a site where a biological control was released by the USDA & state of MD, and the neonic I used in 2008 or 2009 would probably no longer be having an effect. As a former caregiver, I understand your frustration.  But, no two disabilities are the same.  Disabled means many different  problems that require different solutions.  People on Houzz are always, myself included, trying to have people look ahead to possible situations that will require accommodations.  I always tell people when they build or remodel to install blocking between the studs even if they aren’t going to install grab bars for several years.  We urge new builds to include first floor bathrooms for future problems.  But a hip replacement and a permanent quadriplegic require quite different solutions.  Spinal stenosis is not the same as ski accident.  Disability can range from my arthritis in my hands to the total dependency on a ventilator for my family member.  The changes I made in my kitchen are totally useless to “Bryan” who can’t sit up, feed himself, or breathe without help. Not even hospitals have the same bathroom setups in every room, choosing instead to design the ortho floor differently than the neurological wing.  Please don’t be hard on strangers who perhaps could help with your specific needs if you would only ask.

I don't believe that you have to spend a fortune just because a space will be used by someone with disabilities. If you look at a bathroom, you still have tile floors, tiled shower walls, faucets, a toilet, etc. The placement of these items and how they are designed are the critical points. Adding grab bars where needed, doing a zero entry shower, lower the shower controls and handheld on a slide bar, do a shower curtain or pivoting shield instead of sliding glass doors, doing a top and sink that a wheel chair can fit under, lower or tilting mirror. These are readily available and easy to spec out. For a person who requires greater assistance ( ie tracks in the ceiling so someone can moved from their bed into the bathroom and that sort of help ) , will be more difficult and yes more expensive. But those bathrooms can look great as well. I try to design beautiful spaces for all my customers no matter what hurdles they may have. Everyone deserves a great space.

Two very different colors. Urbane Bronze is a dark Yellow. Where it 'lives' on the color wheel is over near the Yellow-Red hue family - this is where the perception of brown/brownish will come from - that is if it actually shows up as brownish. "Brown" is commonly a classification of dark orange. If it sat squarely in the Yellow-Red (orange) hue family there'd be no question you were gonna get brown. However, Urbane Bronze can also show up as greenish - because it is factually a dark Yellow, not dark orange. As we decrease the Chroma (colorfulness) in a Yellow hue family color, it gets cooler in temperature and that's where the green can come from. It all depends on the light and context as far as how it will actually show up. Which is why it's always best to test. Overtones and hue family are just as relevant to dark, low Chroma colors as they are to lighter and neutral colors. So, this is a great question. Iron Ore belongs to the Green-Yellow hue family. Light, mid tone and darker colors from the GY hue family are often perceived as being the most neutral. Meaning no discernible hue bias. Iron Ore will - likely - show up for most people as an off-black or very dark grayed charcoal. Nothing brownish about it. And despite technically belonging to a hue family that carries "green" in its name, Iron Ore is less likely to show moments of green than Urbane Bronze. Because of its hue family - AND - because it has a chunk less Chroma (colorfulness) Which also means Iron Ore is the more neutral in this comparison. We know all this because we have the factual numeric hue, value, chroma notations as a framework and can apply it for predicting how colors can actually show up in different light sources, in different contexts for different sets of eyeballs.

If your ceiling is not level - and almost all ceilings are not level so yours probably isn’t - the crown is used to make up for the ceiling’s unevenness.  The cabinet crown is not just for decoration; it is scribed to meet the ceiling even when the ceiling height is uneven across the kitchen. Typically crowns are 3 pieces, even when 3” thick.  My own cabinet crown is 3” and is made up of 3 pieces.  The top & bottom of the 3 pieces do not change in size throughout the kitchen’s crown molding.  The middle is the "filler" piece that varies in height, scribed to the ceiling’s height. By varying this filler piece's height, you accommodate the different ceiling heights without noticeably affecting the appearance of the crown. Any contractor with experience knows how to do this.  It is Cabinets 101.  I advise you to question your potential contractors on this. If they show any hesitancy about scribing the middle piece of the crown to the height of the ceiling, find another contractor.  Even apprentices learn about this within a few months of starting.  But unfortunately we have seen posts on this forum about contractors who are ignorant and claim there should be space between the crown and the ceiling because the ceiling is uneven.  They are the inexperienced ones who should not be in charge of a kitchen renovation.

I have the red/purple/green Vermont Slate in my foyer and cleaned it, sealed it myself.  The biggest improvement came from recoloring the grout. I fixed any areas that had missing grout, then cleaned again. I used a paint brush and applied Grout Release to the slate - careful not to get in on the grout, then applied Polyblend® Grout Renew 381 Bright White (2 coats) over the grout.  I found using a toothbrush was the easiest way to apply and scrub it in where needed and not get too much on the tile. When the grout was all done I cleaned again with the Aqua Mix Concentrated Stone and Tile Cleaner. Then sealed with TileLab SurfaceGard  Sealer  (not shiny) https://www.custombuildingproducts.com/products/tilelab-surfacegard-sealer

My 2 cents... Sometimes I really love the advice to see an attorney, sometimes I don't.  You really have to decide for yourself when it is worth it.  As @Joseph Corlett, LLC noted it is a standard contract with a standard liability limitation clause.  Moreover, they are unlikely to change it unless you represent a once in a lifetime job for them and there is a 95% chance that the next reputable company uses substantially the same contract.  Assuming this not a 5,000 square foot garage where you house your collection of vintage Ferraris, your choices are likely accept the contract or decide to not epoxy your garage floor. However, as an internet stranger who is not your attorney let me say that courts have generally limited the enforceability of these clauses.  You can disclaim the results, so it is fine for the company to say, "we will give it a shot but we can't guarantee it will look great."  You can also generally disclaim any damage that was noted, so they can say "we can try it but it may damage X, and we will not be responsible for X if it is damaged."  However, courts frown on them limiting liability from their negligence. These clauses serve two useful purposes.  (1) They get consumers to accept smaller settlements as they believe that is all they can get, and (2) they usually require an attorney to overcome and that keeps down the frivolous claims. Good luck.

First, cost has a very specific legal definition in contracts.  It is the amount of money paid by the contractor after all discounts and rebates.  So, by definition, a contractor must pass along his discounts on materials and can't charge a mark-up other than his builder's percentage. If you purchase materials instead of the builder he will typically add his percentage to what you paid for that purchase.  However, contractors often choose not to add their percentage to appliances because...  the contractor assumes responsibility for proper installation and proper working order for anything there is a builder's percentage on.  In other words if your range isn't working properly he has to solve that problem.  He can still go through the appliance company to do that but because that is more trouble than it is worth major appliances are often excluded. Typically, the builder's percentage will not get added to employees of the contractor.  Cost is only for amounts paid to an outside vendor.  However, a contractor has some leeway to modify various terms in the contract.

Not to make light of your situation, but the facts as presented could be used as part of a first year contracts exam 😂 It appears that your contractor did not realize that the exact specifications of your door - the size and wanting operational side lights - would cost more money because the manufacturer needed to manufacture them in a certain manner which was more expensive. Most probably the contractor did not realize this until he actually placed the order with those specifications. At which point - presumably - he came back to you and indicated that the cost to purchase the door from the manufacturer was higher than he thought it would be. This is different than a contractor who is actually building the door raising the charges after the contract. My doors aren't that elaborate but they were custom made by my GC when I remodeled. Since he built them and installed them he shouldn't be able to claim a "mistake" if he couldn't do it as cheaply as he thought. Same analysis for my cabinets which were also custom and which might be differ if the GC was ordering cabinets from a manufacturer with custom modifications without knowing that these would be much more costly. Under these circumstances I don't think you would be able to "hold" him to the original quote because there was arguably "no meeting of the minds" and a "basic" mistake during the formation of the contract. If you want the doors I would probably determine exactly what the increased charge is and then negotiate so that you only pay the actual increase charged by the manufacturer with no GC fee charged on that amount. Otherwise the GC is going to return your deposit and you will just have to search for another GC and wind up paying the same if not more for the doors you want and have to deal with delays and aggrevation. Personally it wouldn't be worth it to kill the deal rather than attempt to negotiate something that is fair to both you and the GC.

Shakes are naturally delaminated wood fibers. When raw it is not visible. But, when the raw wood comes in contact with water such as during water popping process or a water base finish application.  The fibers will work it's way apart from each other. The thinner part will usually curl up like paper just like  your image. To repair, you can apply high strength super glue specified for the use with wood underneath and press it in place. After it cures, spot sand, stain and finish. In some cases, board replacement needs to be done. It can be prevented by making a quick inspection after water popping. Spot repairs can be made before moving ahead with staining process.

linear drain one pro is no cutting of tiles to fit round drain. If you are starting from scratch, the floor angles can be simplified to slant to the linear drain at the edge of the shower. A round drain near the center requires slanting the floor to the drain from all sides of the shower. A linear shower drain is basically an enhanced method for drainage that offers a seamless and minimalist look to your shower, or to any shower, for that matter. To get this installed, the shower floor just needs to be sloped in one direction towards the drain as opposed to center drains which need to be sloped evenly from all 4 corners of the shower area. cons - Water containment is an issue. Unlike regular showers where there’s a curb to keep the water in, this isn’t the case with a linear shower drain as it’s just open but sloped. If the drain isn’t installed properly, you might end up having water all over and that’s not a good experience. Another major problem of a linear shower drain is that it performs unpredictably. They are too much of a hassle to clean and they clog up easily as opposed to center drains which go straight down to the main drainage system.

The two kinds of gas fireplaces you described are "ventless" and "direct vent". A ventless gas fireplace allows the byproducts of combustion to enter the room. The "direct vent" gas fireplace is a closed heating appliance where air is drawn into the firebox through the outer part of a double-walled vent pipe and the byproducts of combustion exit to the outside through the inner part.  The vent pipe termination can be at the roof or through a side wall higher than the fireplace.  The warm air around the firebox is blown into the room in normal operation. For the ventless fireplace the odor of gas would most likely be from a poorly adjusted burner.  For the direct vent fireplace the odor of gas might be from a leak in the gas line. Its also possible you are sensitive to the odor of hot painted metal from either unit but what is most likely making you sick is odorless carbon monoxide from the ventless unit but that should only occur with the direct vent unit if there were a leak in the closed system.  The CO level should be checked by a plumber with a sensitive detector.  If its a serious problem the CO detector in the house should be sounding off.

Aloe is a tough plant and thrives on benign neglect. I see some minor damage but nothing life threatening. It looks pretty good, and I wouldn't do much to it. Next time you have a burn or something, cut off the worst looking leaf and use the gel from it. Water it only when it's completely dried out ... if the dirt is still moist, don't water it yet ... not sure? stick your finger down in to check. Ours get light enough to fall over and suffer no harm from the dehydration of their medium. One of our aloes actually fell out of its dirt; we stuffed it back in when we noticed after a while, and it was fine. We had another that got abandonned in the basement for a year, and it was fine, too. The fastest way to kill an aloe plant? Overlove it.

My personal experience with NAS is good. However, what I've learned over the last 30 years of native seed is don't give up, especially with perennials which can take several years to germinate. Texas wildflowers come up in late fall, overwinter as ground-hugging rosettes, and don't put out top growth until it begins to warm in the spring. Some species require winter cold before germinating in spring. I have had better germination with rain than with irrigation. Flowering and seed-set are done by the end of June for most. It is possible to plant in early spring and still get flowers. Grass is better for drainage areas than wildflowers. Most grass seed is planted in early spring. For the area in the foreground you might prefer a short species such as buffalo grass. Indian grass is mid-height until it sends up showy seed heads. Two of my favorites: Lindheimer muhly is a medium size evergreen grass, and bushy bluestem definitely prefers drainage areas. Evergreen grasses should never be cut back, but most native grasses don't do well when mowed. Dead foliage can be cut away in spring as new growth begins to show, but it's not necessary. Sedge is a grass-like plant. It's seed heads look like burrs but they are and remain soft. Frogfruit is a low, spreading plant with tiny blooms that loves full sun and poor soil. The more diversity in native planting the better.

If you're saying the water you're using for irrigating plants has been routed through an ionic exchange softening system that uses salt as the exchange medium, you need to find another source of water for the plants because water from ionic water softening systems undoubtedly contain phytotoxic (toxic to plants) levels of Na and Cl (sodium and chloride). That has little or nothing to do with the water's pH (acidity/ alkalinity). Also, I can't get a sense of how large/small the plant and container it's in are, but it would be best to start monitoring moisture levels deep in the pot with a wooden "tell" you can make yourself. See more about using a "tell" below. Have you been fertilizing regularly? Supplementing your plants nutrition is an essential part of the care regimen, so just ask for guidance if you think you/ your plants would benefit from it. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

What lars said 1000X. People who muse about oddities in English often haven't learned another language in depth. As lars mentions, many languages are like English in having some degree of expressions/idiomatic uses or irregularities that don't translate literally or follow consistent patterns. Compound words in German can be broken down but often are not immediately recognizable. Case declensions in German (and Russian and other languages) are very difficult for people whose mother tongues don't have case declension forms. English and Romance languages are examples. One of many oddities (from an English language perspective) in French - to say "I miss him" is not a sentence in the first person form, it's in the third person. The subject of the sentence is He, not I. Literally translated would be "he is lacking from me". For a pronunciation treat, tell me how you would think to pronounce Reims, the center of the Champagne district. If you don't speak French, I doubt you'll get it right. There are many pronunciation landmines in English for learners where a word may appear to be a homonym to another but in fact is pronounced differently or is pronounced differently from how spelled. That exists in other languages too. It's fair to say that spelling, pronunciation, word usage, and grammar can be unpredictable, irregular and even random. But it's that way in many other languages as well as English.

In the 1930s cabinets fully pivoted away from Shaker to slab doors. Sometimes these were inset doors but I found at least one example of what look like full overlay doors. Pastels were on the rise (lots of green, yellow, and pink). Tile counters were still the most common, but laminate counters were the hot new technology. 4x4 tiles were king (3x6 subways were so 1910s, and 6x6 didn't start rising in popularity until after WWII). I'm not suggesting you do a fully historically accurate kitchen. White cabinets would be more broadly acceptable than pastels. I would probably choose slab over Shaker for historical accuracy. I like 4x4 tiles and put them in my kitchen (1910 house); I'm not sure how the masses regard them (they were pretty unpopular when everything was "subway, subway, subway"). I don't think brass was very popular in the 30s, so maybe chrome hardware? Or polished nickel? Black shows up in historic photos, too. You might want to look at Streamline Moderne style; it's a subcategory of Art Deco that was popular in the 30s. Or Art Deco more broadly. I love Art Deco hardware. Laminate and tile counters are both probably a non-starter for a high-end rental, but granite and the currently-popular marble-look quartzes are not going to serve a historically accurate "feel." You could do a solid-ish quartz or solid surface. As far as not having any luck with succulents, if you follow these guidelines, you should have great luck: THE POT Use pots with holes in the bottom.  Don't put a plant with a small root ball in an oversized pot.  That won't make it grow big.  Plastic, glazed or terracotta pots are good. THE MIX Your potting mix should be commercial cactus and succulent mix combined 50/50 with perlite or pumice, all from your nursery.  The usual nursery potting mixes hold too much water for succulents because succulents hold plenty of water in their leaves and need a fast draining mix. LIGHT Succulents like lots of light, some need direct sun.  If they don't get enough light, they will "reach" and get what is called "etiolated," all stretched out and not looking as they should. WATER Water only when the plant is dry, and if you are not sure, insert a wooden skewer at least halfway into the mix and wait a while.  If the skewer is damp when you remove it, don't water.  If you are unsure whether your plant needs water or not, wait a week or so.  It' won't die, but if you overwater, it can die.  Whenl you water, take the plant to the sink or outside and water until it comes out the hole.  Allow to drain thoroughly and not sit in a saucer in drained water. Hope this helps.  Good luck. Greenheck recommends that a gas char broiler be provided with 185 ft/min updraft at the hood entry aperture for commercial hoods. Here's a hint I've shared before concerning using Overdrive from libraries as a source for ebooks (including in Kindle versions) and audiobooks: In my state, there's a program that provides state funding to help support local libraries. A quid pro quo for libraries that accept this support (and most do) is that they're required to issue free library cards to applicants who live in-state but not in their library's territory. Especially since the pandemic started but also before, online card applications are often possible, it's not necessary to physically visit a library in a distant location. n. I believe there are many states and library districts around the US that also allow cards to be issued to those who would otherwise be considered "non-residents". Sometimes for a small fee but often for free. Why does this matter? Overdrive's available inventory includes, by its own description, millions of titles. Libraries as Overdrive customers choose which titles will be made available to its patrons, and how many simultaneous use "copies" of each it procures. Even for libraries of large cities, any one library's "collection" of Overdrive titles will be a very small subset of what's available. Which books are chosen, how many copies are available, and how long a wait list can be, depend on the decisions made by each library and each is often very different. Having a card for more than one library provides more variety and sometimes quicker access to popular titles. Just a few months ago, I found a library of a small city in an urban area that has a fantastic Overdrive collection and apparently very few patrons. Several book titles that interested me, NY Times best sellers, had waiting lines many months long at other libraries but were immediately available to check out. I applied for and got the card online, no need to appear in person. You didn't hear it from me but keen Overdrive users can benefit from sharing library card numbers with friends that live in other locations and in other library districts.

You do have to take into consideration movement in timber floors but this can be greatly reduced by remedial work on the subfloor and the correct floor build-up. The green wire on the transformer is just a ground wire connected to the case of the transformer.   if the new transformer doesn't have a green wire, look for a screw terminal on it that may be painted green (NOT one of the two on the front which are the output terminals). Actually looking at the pics on ebay, there is a silver screw where the B&W wires come out of the transformer.  This is almost certainly for connecting a ground wire. The two front terminals on the transformer are the 'secondary' or output winding of the transformer. They are electrically equal (as opposed to the input wires where black is hot and white is neutral). LOAD means to hook up your chime to those terminals. Doesn't really matter which way. NEC is Natl Electrical Code. I'm not sure why that is there but it doesn't indicate that the terminal next to it is different from the other terminal. I assume one of the red wires goes to the button to break the circuit (and then to the chime) and the other goes directly to the chime. I don't know what to tell you about the Google Nest chime, there should be instructions with it.

As for your longer window, NEC states: "Minimum height above countertop to receptacle: 15" Many inspectors will then allow you to overrule the every 48" rule under a window because you don't HAVE 15" of wall above your countertop along the window, especially older inspectors who are used to approving kitchens for many years where you didn't have to put them under windows. They'll actually let you put the receptacles under the cabinets sometimes as an exception or not at all. This is really up to the inspector. Also: if you get permission from one inspector he/she better be the same one that comes when you are done. If your inspector demands them, there are pop-up external outlets that mount to the face of the wall and can pop up when you need them, and require no box space in the wall. https://www.houzz.com/discussions/4179111/wall-of-windows-behind-kitchen-sink-how-do-you-meet-nec-code I'll tell you that many, many inspectors just simply ignore missing outlets under windows that come right down to the countertop over sinks. The two story house would probably be lower cost to build.  I’ll use a 2,000 sq ft house to illustrate. With a ranch, you will need a 2,000 sq ft basement (materials plus excavation) plus a roof over 2,000 sq ft of ceiling.  With a two-story house, you’ll need 1,000 sq ft of basement (materials plus excavation) plus a roof over 1,000 sq ft of ceiling. A two-story house *may* also cost less to heat. In general, a compact house will be more energy efficient than a sprawling house. If you want to save on energy costs, stay away from cantelever floors or unusual bump-outs and keep the design compact. And spend extra on insulation and air sealing that is more than code minimum. It’s much easier and cheaper to do while the house is being constructed than to try to retrofit later.

Any single family house only needs 1 egress door, meaning a way to exit the house walking while standing up. That is historically the front door. All the rooms, whether on a 2nd floor, attic, or in the basement, use this same door. So to exit the basement in an emergency, this is accomplished by walking up the inside stairs to get to the front door. If you ever intended to close off access to the basement from inside, say as a separate rental from upstairs, then the basement would need to retain it's own exterior basement door. Separately from egress, a basement requires 1 emergency escape and rescue opening, meaning a large opening to walk or crawl out of, or for emergency personnel to come into the space, when the interior stair route is blocked. Note that this opening can be either a door or a window. Any sleeping room in the basement must have this emergency escape and rescue opening placed within the room's footprint. There is a distinction between the terms "egress" and "emergency escape and rescue opening," as there are different requirements associated with each. There are some minor exceptions to these basement requirements, but from your goals it doesn't look like any would apply. I have not experienced a jurisdiction amending code to require an exterior basement stair, but I see many firemen build their own houses with them. They create their own construction and maintenance issues, and I suspect that is why yours are so deteriorated.

You need to "check two boxes" when researching if your plant will produce blue blooms in a new garden: your soil must have naturally occurring aluminum in appropriate quantities and the soil must be acidic (soil pH much less than 7.0) so the aluminum will not chemically mix with other minerals and become impossible or difficult to absorb through the roots. Get a soil pH test kit to confirm if your soil pH is adequate. Kits are available at most plant nurseries although availability may be questionable during the winter season. Acidifying the soil with garden sulfur or aluminum sulfate may be required in order to produce blues or purples in alkaline soils (soil pH above 7.0). Follow the instructions on the package and observe the change as new blooms open (blooms that are already open will not change color or will not change the color much; also, normally white blooms will not change color at all). Apply the acidifying product forever per the product directions (every three months or ???) and follow the instructions precisely because (1) if you discontinue applying the product, the soil will have a tendency to slowly revert back to its normally alkaline pH and (2) the tiny, shallow, fibrous root of hydrangea plants could get burned by applying excessive amounts of these sulfur containing products.. If after applying the product for about a year or two does not yield the correct shade of color, proceed to slowly increase the amount applied of the product until you achieve the correct results that you want. A soil pH kit that gives numeric results may be more useful when doing this. Some color changes may slowly occur when a plant is originally planted outside in the garden, as the root system slowly expands from a non-acidic potting soil medium and into an acidic garden soil. Notes: Some rock mulches (like the one in your picture) may be alkaline and hydrangea plantings near cemented areas can also be in alkaline soil as cement leeches lime and lime raises acidic soil pH into alkaline territory. Blooms tend to be pink with alkaline soils (pH above 7.0). Below 7.0, some blooms may turn purple and as the soil pH becomes much more acidic, the blooms turn blue. Also Also, there are some cultivars of hydrangea macrophylla that resist turning blue and turn purple instead at normally acidic levels. There are too many cultivars that produce blue and purple blooms with very few differences so it is hard to identify cultivars. Can you ask the person who provided you with the cuttings?

In my opinion, for the most part, yes, most of Crate & Barrel sofas are better quality than Ikea sofas. However, you really need to look at the construction details of the actual piece you are considering. Each one is going to be constructed differently and at least C&B has different manufacturers (some made in the USA and some overseas). For example, I think the Crate & Barrel Axis II collection is pretty solid, mid-cost quality. If you look at the details on their site you'll see details like this. I believe that this particular Crate & Barrel sofa is made by McCreary Modern(but I'm not 100% positive) and is made in the US (North Carolina). This collection has been sold at Crate & Barrel for a long time and is quite popular. If you're able to sit on one in person, you can determine if you like the comfort. Personally I found it very comfortable: firm and solid feeling but still cushy and comfortable. I do not own one of these, but have seriously considered purchasing one as I am currently seeking sectional options. C&B also offers performance fabrics that describe the content and I bet you can get details on the double rubcount (durability measure). One of the track arm options at Ikea is the KIVIK. (I'm choosing this as an example for comparison because I own one.) These are some of the details from the Ikea site. As I mentioned, I own a KIVIK in leather. When I sat on a fabric version in the store it was in terrible condition and looked cheap and rumpled. The leather looked better, so we opted to upgrade to the leather. The construction very much feels like a particle board or plywood box covered in inexpensive foam and leather. Once it's assembled it looks pretty nice, but the construction quality is obviously more budget than durable. To me the first step is to understand what types of construction are available on upholstery these days and looking into those details on the pieces you are considering. Frame and springs/suspension are going to play a huge part in durability. And finally the fabric quality and durability and the cushion construction are going to be very important. But at the end of the day you have to decide whether budget is more important or durability.

I am not going to iterate @pricklypearcactus 's excellent advice but IKEA and Crate & Barrel are not comparable except both are sofas. When shopping for a sofa you should learn what is involved in the actual construction of a sofa. Also what are you looking for and what is your budget. People with lower budgets will probably do well with IKEA because they offer acceptable quality for the price. Aside from differences in actual construction you are going to have limited style choices and probably your fabric choices will be beige, brown, gray and maybe blue 😂 However no one should buy a sofa without visiting sofas in person because at the very least you want a sofa that is comfortable and different sofas - even of the same "objective" quality will feel differently to different people. Your size - e.g. height will make a difference. Your mobility will make a difference as rising from a low seat without arms becomes more difficult as one ages or if one has older visiters. Depth of seat matters as does height of back. The type of filling and whether you have one seat cushion - pillows etc. will all change how an individual feels in a particular sofa. And of course how do you use the sofa - is this intended to be a sofa for lying down or is it going to be used in a more formal setting where people sit upright. Can you nap on it comfortably? However Crate & Barrel objectively is not necessarily worth the price. The whole category of middle class retail furniture - Crate & Barrel, Pottery Barn, Restoration Hardware has declined in quality from when people bought mid level furniture and it lasted for years. When I was remodeling and decorating I was shocked when my designer told me that these furniture brands had a life expectancy of about 7 to 8 years. I said you mean cheap furniture and she said - no - these kinds of brands. So paying more isn't going to necessarily get you super high quality. There is still furniture being sold that is not intended to be disposable - or semi-disposable if that is the kind of quality you are looking for but that isn’t necessarily Crate & Barrel.

Your cabinets will not be a standard 36" + countertop. Standard is 36" including countertop: 34-1/2" is a standard base cabinet + 1-1/2" countertop material is usual, equalling 36". I doubt there is anything in Kentucky code regarding kitchen countertop height and 36".  This would go against American Disabilities Act Guidelines for Universal Access which sets countertop height at 32"-34". This is not to say that you should not have 36" countertops, which is the standard height, it's just saying that it's doubtful that there is an actual code requirement that is both 1) so specific and (2) contradicts a National guideline.

"My understanding is that the fans that are above and behind the cooktop work better than those that are built into the cooktop (like Jenn-Aire), simply because they are higher up and more likely to pull gasses off  tall pots." This is not the reason for overhead hoods.  Hoods over the cooking zone collect the rising and expanding cooking plume effluent that has high upward momentum.  Typical plumes of this sort result from frying, searing, and wok cooking.  Attempting to divert this flow of often significant plume CFM to the side (for a pop-up) or reversing the momentum to bring the plume to the counter (for a downdraft) is not practical for the apertures and flow rates that these downdraft schemes can implement at non-deafening flow rates.  Side-draft, and to a lesser degree down-draft schemes may work for low velocity plumes such as from slow simmering bacon and capturing vapor from a hot liquid surface. Cooking plumes from gas ranges can reach 1.2 m/s upward velocity.  A modest sized hot cooking* plume could be moving 240 CFM into the hood by itself.  Hood system air flow has to entrain this as well as any other plumes into the baffle filter, while assuring that plume components that hit metal and reflect typically downward are kept from escaping the flow. Also, the hood should overlap the cooking pans at the front as well as at the sides.  The key words for thinking about plume capture and containment are expanding and momentum. *(Hot cooking means at the vapor point of the oil used. If no searing or stir-frying or other significant plume generating cooking is to be performed, then a side-draft system may be adequate.)

"I will make sure to stress this as I look for it." Water softeners all work the same way. They replace hardness ions (calcium and magnesium) with sodium ions from the salt.  Thus, the level of sodium in soft water is = to the amount in the water in the first place + the amount of hardness. No water softener produces more "drinkable" water than another. Soft water is fine for humans. There are some people on a very low sodium diet who are advised not to drink soft water. I have very hard water (24 gpg) and when I drink softened water it tastes fine. That said, small animals and fish may be more sensitive to the slightly elevated sodium levels in the same way fish are to chlorine in municipal tap water. Plumb a faucet in the kitchen with unsoftened water. My cold water in the kitchen is filtered (removes chlorine, taste, odor, and many chemicals) but isn't softened. This is what I use to cook with, water indoor plants, put in the dog bowl. This is a common setup with soft water.

Here are some ideas: 1)  a sheet of regular printer paper against a current white will allow you to see if the white is cool (blue-tinged) or warm (yellow-tinged). At most restaurants, unless the portions are very small, or sometime if it is a very special restaurant, I end up taking about half my food home. I can almost never eat the amount of food I am served. And I have never been in a restaurant, even a fancy one, that did not have containers, (sometimes really fancy ones) to take things home with you. (And the reality is if someone leaves a large portion of  expensive meat or takes one bite of dessert, it's likely that when it goes back to the kitchen someone will cut around the bit you picked at and eat the rest) I was taken care of by a Japanese woman, growing up, and my mother became good friends with this Japanese woman's friend, who also did tailoring, and she often wanted to feed me when I went to get things altered. I learned to take much less than I was going to end up eating the first time around because it was expected I would take at least 4 helpings or she would be extremely disappointed. At home we were not served a lot of things we did not like, (there were a couple things that by mutual agreement between my parents my mom did not cook at home) but we were expected to try everything. Portion sizes were flexible and we were not forced to clean our plates. But we ate what was on the menu for the day, there were no special meals for anybody. When my dad was in his eighties he stopped eating certain things (mostly certain vegetables) and I asked him why because he had always eaten them before, and the answer was that he did not want to set a bad example or promote not liking something just because he didn't. It worked for me, there is very little that I really dislike, I will eat any vegetable under the sun, I am not suspicious of unusual food or the way things are prepared, and no one else in my family is picky in that way either.

When I was a child, we were told to eat everything served, because there were "starving children in China" who would be happy for the food, even if we didn't like or want it.  Once, as a teen, I offered to mail it to them.  On occasion, one of us (siblings) was left at the table until we finished our dinner. There's no question that what we're taught as children affects our relationships as adults - that's not only true for our relationships with other people, but our relationships with other things (food, alcohol, money, etc).  Of course, what we're taught can be unlearned and/or overwritten, but it's there and it's real, and it often takes a lot of work to overcome the challenges our parents left us, whether wittingly or unwittingly.  And a lot of people, whether fat or skinny, still have unhealthy relationships with food.

We were expected to eat what was served for the most part. My dad had very plain taste in food so most of what mom made was palatable to a child. We were allowed to have dislikes (peas and lamb for me) and were not served those foods, but just ate whatever else was being served. I practiced the same with my children, although my husband and I are much more adventurous eaters than my dad was. When the kids were old enough, if they really didn't care for what I was making, they were allowed to make themselves soup and a sandwich but also had to clean up after themselves.

I'm 73 and have the same relationship with food I had when I was 5. I do take a doggy bag at a restaurant for the meat only. I have a dog who enjoys a nice steak even if cold. I have no problem asking for one. Jane

You have some tough decisions to make about your deck or patio first. Start with your space needs (table size, firepit, grill, etc) and how you want to circulate from the house to it. Then design the softscape holistically with the hardscape (e.g. not only so they work in plan layout, but in addition to plantings at the easement line, maybe you want a partial screen or pergola built on a wood deck, or a planter box with some smaller sitting-height plantings with a patio). It looks like there is plenty of height to your first floor. A deck performs ok if it is at 16"-18" or so above grade, which should allow around 8" of air circulation underneath (which when lacking is the downfall of wood decks at grade). It would be good to take advantage of not needing guardrails (verify your AHJ max deck height) because with the basement stair guardrails and fall protection over the stair that would be a lot of visual clutter. The decisions involve where you access it, from the Family Rm only, wrapped around the corner for access only/also from the Mudroom in the same elevation, where it steps down to grade next to the sidewalk/garage, etc. A paver patio looks to have some tricky decisions as well. You never want to raise a patio more than a couple inches above grade anyway (the higher you go, the more expensive and probability of settling), and you have the fireplace bumpout which would hamper that anyway. You would have steps down from the Family Room, so if you don't want railings beyond 2 risers you have to have large landings in this small space. It also does not look like it can be at sidewalk elevation, so you will have a "3-tiered" space - porch, patio, and sidewalk - so plan for more steps and/or retaining walls. Sometimes everyone does not agree on how many chill hours a particular apple variety needs. It might be thought, for example, that one apple might manage to do okay with 500 chill hours, but will really do much better with 700. Some varieties might have more of a defined cutoff than others. Some of this is due to anecdotal observation, which might be a little bit different from different sources. A cherry tree variety that one nursery says is zone 4 and another says is zone 5, might be able to survive in zone 4, but is probably less likely to do as well. It might benefit from being planted in protected locations, or with some insulation wrap around the trunk and main branches. It's not like any tree will do perfectly fine in zone 5 but then be guaranteed to suddenly die in zone 4. Maybe the "zone 4" that tree can survive in is the warmer part of zone 4, not the colder part.

Just from looking this up on the internet, it is not granite.  It is a lava stone with similar properties to granite, but not granite.  Every article I see says that while it is durable, it is very porous, more porous than most granites if not all granites. One article (but there are many that discuss its porosity) says:  "Basaltina is super durable (with a composition comparable to granite) and porous at the same time. This is due to the lava cooling down too fast for the tiny bubbles to evaporate."  Another online article says "Basaltina is a porous material with naturally-occurring holes that may remain unfilled or be factory-filled with resin or cement."  And another article says, "Basaltina is still considered porous: Small, naturally-occurring holes appear in its surface because of how rapidly lava cools...As a countertop material, Basaltina needs to be sealed (sometimes extensively) to make it resistant to staining—and any oily spills should be wiped up as quickly as you can. Just as marble would, a Basaltina surface will eventually show off some signs of use—but if you're opting for a natural material with a rich look to it, like this, that's part of the fun of living with it." From the extensive mentions of Basaltina's porosity, it appears that your experience living with it will be similar to a kitchen that has marble counters.  The counters will need to be sealed frequently, and its porosity is just part of its makeup and cannot be changed, just mitigated by sealant.  You will have patina on this counter.

I don't know exactly why your plants died, but it could be because they got too cold while outdoors. Gourds are a warm weather plant and don't like the cold at all. I don't know where you live, but it's way too early to start gourds here. Gourds can't be planted outside until all danger of frost is past and the weather stays warm. What kind of soil did you have your plants in ? The soil in the top pic looks pretty bad. It seems have a lot of salt buildup, and there appears to be a crusty ring of it around the base of the plant. Soil salinity may have had something to do with the death of your plants, but it's more likely they just got too cold. Next time, plant in a well-drained potting mix with no fertilizer and fill the pot almost full. Keep your plants where it's warm all the time until they are ready to be planted outside. When you transplant them try to not disturb their roots, they don't like that. Good luck with your next plants and I hope they grow and thrive !

EWW! First thing to do is remove all the dead leaves and stems as they become agents for disease if not already infected.  Then if there is any life in it, remove it from the oversized pot and pot down to a much smaller pot.  Use a good potting soil for the repot.  If the soil is dry, then lightly (LIGHTLY) water it - do not saturate.  Put it under some kind of humidity dome (a baggie will work but not the best) and put in a well lit area for several hours a day (12 hours is a good number of hours but not necessary either).  Check on it every few days for moisture and fungal diseases.  If all goes well you should start seeing new growth in a couple of weeks or longer.  Remove the humidity dome/cover for a few hours to see how it responds to normal household conditions.  If wilting then it is not ready and needs more time being pampered.  Eventually you should have a beautiful plant that can thrive in your home.  This looks like it was one of the small leaf rexes at one of the big box stores (Home Depot, Lowe's, Walmart) and they can thrive if they get enough light, just enough water to meet their needs, and a little care. Here is one of my Hugh begonias.   Each leaf can be used for creating a new plant.  Here is a small aluminum pan I used to start 20 or so of them in 2016   It certainly stands out in a group of dark leaf begonias in 2014   I combined these mini rexes I bought last year from the big box stores into a 10 inch pot.  This picture was from the 17th of this month.  I have them under T8 cheap fluorescent shop light running 12 hours a day.  This is still in its original container from the big box store.  I bought this one from Walmart and moved it to an 8 inch pot.  The secret is to lightly water so it is not water logged.  It is much easier to add a little water if needed than try to remove water from a waterlogged soil mass.  some I started from leaf wedges last spring in Jiffy pellets and moved up to 3 or 4 inch pots this past fall.  From humidity trays to living in the conditions of a heated basement with cheap shop lights.  I started 21 plants from one very large leaf last spring.  I potted up 15 of those in 3 to 4 inch pots and gave those away at our begonia meeting last fall. Generally the smaller the rootstock the faster the tree will produce it's first fruit.However it's been said that after the first couple years the bigger tree will produce more fruit than the smaller in any one of the following years. Some of the larger rootstocks will not tend to blow down as they root better especially in poor soil like clay, An apple rootstock like MM111 which some call a semi full size will grow as a semi dwarf in colder climates or poorer soils. That one also is said to not need staking in most places. Many sources of trees won't tell you what rootstock you selection is on. One that does is Fedco Trees from Maine who sells to customers in Zones as cold as USDA 3. There are also differences from one rootstock to another in resistance to tree diseases such as fireblight. If your tub leak means that you cannot put off the remodel until you can afford the things that will make the bathroom work for you in the long run, then replace the tub and whatever structural parats that need to be replaced.  When doing that, think ahead to what you would want for shower walls when the time comes to do them.  Some  shower materials (especially tile) require a waterproofed substrate like cement board that is installed correctly and waterproofing is done (either behind it, painted or membrane applied to the front of it, or some specialized waterPROOF board for under showers).    No drywall behind tile.  Other shower walls like solid surface (Swanstone, Corian, Transolid and others) or fiberglass or acrylic wall systems all have their own installation instructions.  You need to decide when the tub is replaced what will eventually go above it and then do the new walls according to the company’s instructions.  Lets say you just put in water-RESISTANT drywall above the tub and later decide to tile.  It would all need to be torn out. While you are inside the walls of the tub and shower area, it is your time to install 2x6 boards between the studs everywhere where a handrail may one day be installed.  At a minimum, plan on a vertical one to hold when climbing into and out of the tub and a horizontal one on the back wall.  If you can only afford to do this much now, then get a scrap piece of sheet vinyl for the floor near the tub and save until you can finish the bathroom.  You need it to be nice looking, you need it to be functional. I have one full bathroom and a half bath at my house.  I started buying items for my bathroom remodel six years before we actually did it.  In my case, my contractor had been here working on our kitchen remodel or the living room fallen-in slab fiasco and was in the basement working when the shower on the main floor dripped down on his head.  He poked around and thought he saw a lot of wet wood that was starting to rot.  So I recaulked the tub.  Because we had been under construction for such a long time, hubby was insisting that we have at least 3 years to live in peace and to save money for a bath remodel.  I started planning and did buy a few things and when the three years were over, my contractor was tied up doing a big commercial job.  It took a few more years for him to be free, by which time I had bought and paid for everthing but the shower.  He got with me to finalize that plan and even talked with the manufacturer about installation before I ordered it.  When he was ready, I pulled that trigger and ordered it, hired help to get our garage contents into a storage unit, and prepared my poor hubby for chaos again.  I had used my computer’s spread sheet to record each item’s brand and model, price, and location in the basement, down to the very shelf they were stored on. You can do the opposite of what I did and do your bathroom in stages.  Get whatever MUST be done due to the leak to get the bathroom in usable shape, with the proper preparations for what will be going over the tub to make a shower.  Don’t pull out the vanity (unless this is where the leak is, and then you can set the bath tub aside for now.)  Same for toilet.  Then save and watch for sales on the items you need to buy.  When you have been able to buy all the supplies for the next area, you can do it if it is DIY.  Otherwise, simply buy things and save for the rest of the remodel and get the contractor back to do it all at once.

As for your tile, go through the boxes and pull out any bad ones or ones whose color you do not like.  Don’t throw any out, you may still need to use some of them.  Then count what you have that are desirable.  Measure what the square footage would be for varous tile layouts.  Add 20% to each of those layout sums.  Then you will have a good idea of what your tile will cover.  Then come back and post a question asking what you need help with and you will get lots of help.

All tankless heaters I've seen (indoor and outdoor) have an electric resistance heater around the heat exchanger that prevents the heat exchanger from freezing as long as power stays on. These are considered "Backup". You don't want to regularly subject your heater to freezing temps. There are two problems: 1. When the power doesn't stay on - like during a storm- there's no freeze protection. 2. It doesn't protect any of the plumbing leading to the heater. It only protects the heat exchanger. Design your setup so that your plumbing isn't exposed to freezing temps - even in much lower than normal situations. Put your heater inside the heated envelope.

True "growth" isn't a measure of how far a branch extends or how many leaves a plant puts on over the course of some arbitrary segment of time. "Growth" is measured by the increase in the weight of your plant's dry mass. That had to be said so I could point to the fact that, even though your plant produces a new leaf from time to time, that series of events does not mean the plant is growing. Plants "grow" when they are able to make more food (plants make their own food, sugar/glucose, during photosynthesis) than they need to keep their systems orderly. Growth, in large part, provides additional storage space for surplus food that occurs when the plant is able to make more food/energy than it needs to keep its systems orderly. It's not unusual, in winter, for houseplants to operate such that they are producing roughly as much energy as they are using. In many cases, they might actually be using more energy than they are ably to create via photosynthesis. As shedding organisms, plants adjust to their inability to provide at least as much energy as they create by shedding parts, most often leaves and roots, but sometimes branches/stems and fruit as well. Usually, what I just described is based on the amount of light a plant receives and whether or not the light load is sufficient; however, the 'grow one - shed one' cycle your plant is currently coping with could also be caused by a nutritional issue. Have you been fertilizing regularly? If not, consider this: the nutrients nitrogen, phosphorous, potassium, and magnesium are considered to be 'mobile' in the plant, with the others being immobile or nearly so under normal conditions. "Mobil in the plant" means the plant can rob nutrients from (usually) older and less efficient leaves in order that it might provide the building blocks/nutrients required to form a new leaf near branch tips. In any case, the cause is a cultural one that occurs because the plant is being asked to operate at near or beyond the limits it was genetically programmed to deal with. This makes improving the limiting cultural issues currently holding the plant back the key to reversing the plant's decline. Unfortunately, you didn't provide much information to go on. My suggestion would be to start by reading this short Overview of Good Growing Practices and ask any questions it brings to mind; or, just start a dialog based on the contrast between what it suggests and what your current habits might be. It's a pretty sure bet you'll collect enough information to make good decisions. Questions so far? Al

Hi, Cory, The problem with learning from experience is that you get the test before you get the lesson.  You got the test-- and, fortunately--before the lesson needed to address how to get rid of mold and mildew, too. Let's start by looking at what's going on. Indoor air contains water vapor which can condense on surfaces if their surface temperature is less than or equal to the dewpoint temperature.  For the conditions you noted (50% relative humidity at 63 F,) the dewpoint temperature is around 53 F or 54 F (tough for my elderly eyes to read the psychrometric chart exactly.)  So we know for condensation to occur that the temperature of some portion of the foundation wall is less than or equal to 53 F or 54 F.  It appears that the band (rim) joist (installed around the perimeter of your open-web trusses) is uninsulated.  The temperature on the inside surface of the band is somewhere between the outdoor and indoor temps, but certainly lower than the dewpoint, so you'll get condensation there which can then run down the plastic sheet on the foundation. Now for the remedy. You'll need to install rigid foam insulation (I like the extruded, not the expanded type) on the foundation wall, preferably bonded to the wall with adhesive, and with the joints taped to prevent any air from getting behind the insulation.  You'll also need to insulate the band joist with closed-cell spray foam insulation to prohibit moist air from getting to the back side of the band and allowing water vapor to condense.    Once you have the spray foam and the rigid insulation installed, you can construct a wood stud wall on the inboard side of the rigid insulation and use batt-type insulation in the cavities.   I suggest you run a dehumidifier in the basement--at the very least during the summer months. Best wishes for a successful outcome.  (I don't service the Katy, TX area.)

The vapor barrier always has to be installed on the warm side of the insulation. And you only want one vapor barrier so you don’t trap moisture. Remove the vapor barrier, batt your stud walls, and install new vapor barrier over the studs. The Kraft paper on paper faced insulation will be the vapor barrier if that is the insulation you have.

Cory, In my experience, spray foam insulation installed in stud cavities will eventually shrink and pull away from the framing--in which case it will allow air to contact the uninsulated basement wall.   I've seen it with both closed-cell and open-cell insulation.  You need a continuous air barrier and continuous insulation.  Extruded polystyrene is the ticket. You might also consider using steel studs or channels in lieu of wood studs--less food for mold if something goes wrong.  I'd also suggest removing the polyethylene sheeting.  The rigid foam will perform the same function if well adhered to the foundation wall and with all joints taped.  With regard to a vapor retarder, the latex paint on the drywall is all the vapor retarder you want.  The wall needs to be able to dry to the interior (conditioned, basement) side.

text: No, scarification is where you weaken the seed coating to encourage germination. That's what I meant. You can do that by physical abrasion, or by biological degradation. The former is fast. The latter is slow. I do the latter routinely with my Malabar spinach seeds that have a firm coat. You plant those, and they will largely not come up at all promptly. Major PIA to scrape them with sandpaper or a knife. So what I do is plant them on New Years Day, LONG before they'll want to germinate. Then, every year, on March 15, they start popping up. By then the firm seed coat has degraded, and the soil temps are nicer. Now, one might say that  parsley seeds just need scarification to germinate, but the study I referenced says that scarification doesn't work for them. So I guess with parsley, it isn't a matter of having them sit in moist soil until the seed coat degrades. They're just slow.

Depends on how you define odd. The oddest thing to me is a person of sound mind that is more concerned about aesthetics than safety. Now that I have smacked the living crap out of you, back to the topic at hand.... There are grab bars that clamp on very securely to the edge of the free-standing tub. My grandmother in her 90's used one very successfully on a daily basis. This was a while ago, I don't remember the brand or model. Do a google search for clamp grab bar bathtub There are many different types, narrow, wide, tall, short. What you choose depends on your tub and the person's needs. If there is a physical therapist involved in the person's care, they might make a recommendation. Some cities have senior citizen care agencies that can help you make a selection that is appropriate for the individual's needs that will also work for the bathtub. Were you aware of the change before or after closing on the house? This question is a bit complicated.  If you became aware of the change after closing, it is possible that you have some recourse available, but it is not an easy or cheap position to argue and very likely isn't worth your time or effort. There is a concept known as promissory estoppel, where a promise or commitment was made by one party and the other party reasonably relied on that promise to take some action.  In your case, the question is going to be, did the original site plan constitute a promise or commitment? Was it presented to you without a disclaimer (e.g. subject to change)?  If so, you can argue that it formed the basis of your acceptance of the house and were damaged by the change (the damages are the easy part). Promissory estoppel is not usually a strong argument, but the particulars of a situation could make it fairly strong.  In reality, it is doubtful that you would recover attorney fees even if you did win, so it is not worth your time pursuing.  The most you are likely to get economically would be a privacy fence or some landscaping. Good luck

The proportions are by volume. I had planned on creating a large batch of the mix to use for various  pottings - is this advisable or should I proportion a mixture for each separate planting? How I approach things: As long as I have everything assembled and the Turface screened. I make several small batches such that the total volume made in any day-long session would be somewhere between 50-100 gallons, and I store them in 32 gallon heavy duty trash containers with wheels and keep an 18 gallon tub with rope handles ready at hand. The gritty mix is very easy to alter so it has more or less water retention. I make the 1:1:1 ratio in large quantities, then alter enough mix to suit an individual plant. While I almost always suggest any alteration should include more Turface MVP and less grit (for added water retention), or more grit and less Turface MVP for less water retention. Adjustments can as easily be made by simply adding a handful or two of one or the other to change water retention. Ideally, the bark fraction should remain at 1/3 of the mix, or less, to ensure the medium's structural integrity over the long term. The beauty in being able to use large particles of Turface MVP or grit to adjust water retention lies in the fact that aeration remains consistent and there is no need to suffer the consequences of relying on perched water to increase water retention. Water is still held on the surface of soil particles, in the internal pores of materials with open internal porosity, and at the interface where soil particles contact each other, leaving spaces between soil particles full of air from top of the soil column to the bottom of the pot. This results in a very healthy environment for roots, 'healthy roots' being an essential prerequisite to a healthy plant. Al

Is it better to have the front door and the frame match in the wood stain You will find different points of view about this. IMO, exterior color serves the purpose of wayfinding. Especially important for a front door; It needs to clearly and quickly signal "this is how you get in the house". Aesthetics matter, of course, but the psychological functionality of color on structure is equally important. There is a hierarchy of color distribution to follow. In other words, certain guidelines to color code the parts of a house. The wood stain works to distinguish the entry from everything else - hierarchy. Consider the idea that pulling the window trim color to the entry throws off that hierarchy. While it might look 'fine', in an unconscious psychological wayfinding kind of way, is it confusing? The flip side to that is painting the side lights white will emphasize the actual door. The sidelights are, in fact, windows too. There isn't a single right answer, it comes down to preference. And you feel like you want the entry to stand out more. So, maybe the pop of white on the sidelights is the right answer for you.

Been in telecommunications for a dozen years. The White/Blue and White/Orange pair from the drop (wires entering on the left side of the NID (phone box)) Should be tied down the the splitter module. Those modules clip into a copper peg on the left back side, which is attached with a bar to every ground point in the whole NID. So if the ground wire running to the lug is tied down to a decent ground and the splitter modules are seated properly and not hanging, everything should be grounded. To answer dennisgli, when lightning hits the buried copper, it blows the splitter modules in two where they seat on the copper lugs on the back side. I have seen the entire NIDs blown off the sides of houses many times. Our equipment takes the hit to save the inside equipment. To answer Rick, I have seen and replaced fried modems that were affected by lightning and I have seen the Ethernets hurt computer network cards, however the modems we're fried from a surge in electrical power, not from the phone line. Even without a ground, the splitter modules in the NID cannot take a large spike in power and blow up if they get a surge. If they are not grounded, they also usually fry the modems inside as well, but I have never seen that circumstance cause any issues other than frying the dsl port on the modem. Usually the modems will still show power, they just don't sync up and give internet anymore.

First, you need an accurate as-built showing more than the actual skylights, show the ridge, headers, window mullions (and double check your sink isn't in front of a mullion), and actual door types. The lighting locations as shown could be better: there is no lighting on the stove/ref wall counters; the ref looks to be crossing under a beam into a flat ceiling area instead of in the vaulted portion so the adjacent counter + opposite wall counter are not lighted (disregarding the 1 undercab light); the lighting over the sink counter competes with the aisle lighting; the bay window probably has a soffit/header so the light placement is not indicative. As far as fixture type, any recessed light on a sloped ceiling that does not angle perpendicular to the floor, will give you more glare. And wafer lights give you glare whether on a sloped or a flat ceiling. Certainly when you look straight up into a light from directly below it, you get glare; but when you are looking across a room at human eye level, your peripheral vision also sees the flush(er) lights (as opposed to ones tucked up into a can with a baffle) - that's the glare. And when the ceiling is sloped, your peripheral vision sees more of the ceiling plane no matter what your view angle, so it has the potential for more glare. Having them tucked up away from the ceiling plane with a baffle reduces the glare, and on sloped ceilings using an adjustable pitch can will direct their light straight down to the surface where you want it, as opposed to borrowing the diffused cone spread for your surface.

The advantage to recessed is using sloped ceiling cans, which will ensure the light faces down. The wafers will just run with the ceiling and effectively light across rather than down. I would use regular cans, with sockets so you can choose the light bulb over built-in LED anything, as they are supposed to last forever but fail. and when they do the next batch may not have the same color tone as the first.
