The purposes of make-up air are mainly these: (a) No air leaves the kitchen via the cooktop hood that isn't replaced; and (b) If air isn't replaced with low pressure loss, the household pressure drops to the point where the hood blower can just keep up with the leakage that exists at that pressure.  In this case one risks back-drafting any household combustion appliances that might take air from the household common air space. This is a safety hazard and is the reason why most code enforcement authorities will require MUA if the hood blower is rated for more than 400 CFM.  Unfortunately, even if the rating is 400 CFM or lower, one is of depending on household leakage, which is an undesirable method of supplying MUA.  Also, for many of the cooktops of interest in this forum, a rated 400 CFM hood system provides too little air flow for complete cooking plume capture and containment. To the OP's question, without a wall behind the cooktop, there is an additional side of the cooking space where hood overlap must extend past the cooktop, just as for island and peninsula applications.  One might want to review the Wolf Design Guide for examples of island hoods vs. wall hoods.  The back and side overlap may force the cooktop farther from the wall line, or make the "view" space wide enough to accommodate the hood width. (If this view space is a cut-out like shape, then possibly a wide and deep enough wall hood could be mounted on it above the "view," but the hood depth will need to be in the 27-inch regime, and the cooktop appropriately placed so that the center of the cooking zones can be centered in the front-to-back dimension of the hood entry aperture.) I have no personal objection to this design, but the increased costs of a larger hood, larger ducting, a larger blower, and a larger sized MUA system need to be considered.  The OP may wish to tour the large number of hood and MUA threads on this forum for improved perspective.  Most locations will need, if not require, heated MUA.

We went with a small builder that sounds similar to your Option 1.  He is a one-man show, has no employees, but he's been building in our area for decades so has established relationships with a trusted group of subcontractors and vendors.  He only uses cost-plus contracts and had us pick out as many items as humanly possible ahead of time in order to create a 20-page detailed cost estimate in order to (hopefully) avoid too many surprises. Our builder is on site every working day and supervises all the subcontractors himself.  He even does some of the carpentry work and other small jobs, plus cleanup, himself.  He only works on one job at a time actively (though he worked on planning ours in the evenings while actively building the previous house), so we always feel like we are forefront on his mind. We chose him based on recommendations and rapport as well as an obvious dedication to quality. He came and walked the ten-acre wooded property with us before we even put an offer in on it and gave several recommendations and caveats.  He is very experienced in rural building, septic systems and wells, etc., so gave us confidence to go with him. The main negatives of this kind of builder is that they are competing with other builders as well as homeowners for this same set of subcontractors, and our builder isn't always first in line.  Sometimes a sub would start on our job only to be pulled away on an emergency job elsewhere (for a day or week+), costing us time.  And some are in such great demand that we have had to wait weeks to be fit in to someone's schedule.  So, this kind of build can take a year or even more to complete, as opposed to the quicker process of a larger builder who employs his own dedicated subcontractors. During this unprecedented time with the pandemic, supply-chain slowdowns, and rapidly increasing prices, a cost-plus contract is not ideal.  We might never have gotten into this build had we known what was waiting down the road. In order to stay within budget, we had to cut several items we really wanted from the house (a metal roof, for example, and a shiplap kitchen ceiling).  And with every increase in price from a vendor, we are hurt, while our builder is actually helped financially due to his cut.  That doesn't really seem fair to me, but that's just one of the pitfalls of cost-plus in these unprecedented times. Still, given everything, we would have chosen this builder all over again.  We know that when we do move in, we are going to be getting a house of high-quality, built to exacting standards.  It just took a lot longer and cost more than we'd anticipated.  But we still have a good relationship with our builder two months prior to anticipated completion. Bottom line:  Lack of employees is not a deal killer, but there are some considerations to keep in mind, like the fact that your build might take longer than anticipated.  And we did consider the chance of our builder getting sick, especially with COVID running rampant.  A few of his subs did get COVID over the course of our build.  Our builder got vaccinated as soon as he was eligible, and he has stayed well, thank goodness!

My 2 cents, (and yes I have said part of this many times before)... The right builder is much more important than the right contract and relatively few builders use the AIA contracts. The AIA contracts are great, but if I were a builder the very last thing I would want to do is use a contract that I am not intimately familiar with, especially given the current construction market.  I suspect most builders would decline the change unless there is some significant benefit to them.  However, if your builder sees this as an opportunity to be recommended by, and regularly work with, your architect, then they may be amenable to the AIA contract. I would not write off a good fit for a builder simply because they refuse to use the AIA contract.  I typically tell people to have the builder's contract reviewed by an attorney (in this case maybe an attorney and your architect) to spot the possible risks and conflicts and then work to mitigate those risks. ETA: The contract itself should govern conflicts not create them.  There is significant potential for the builder to proceed in the manner he is familiar with even if that conflicts with the new contract terms.

Julia Child. That famous "licorice" scent? Never smelled it. Which *seems* strange (wait for it...keep reading) because I can detect that scent in other roses. I tried to grow JC three different times, own-root and grafted, obtained both potted and bare root. Not a hint of licorice in any of them. It's ironic, since I LOVE licorice. I normally can smell even the faintest of rose scents that others can't detect, but JC just smells faintly of soap to me :P Now for a bit of "nose science", and why I can't smell Julia, but you can: Our sense of smell is highly dependent on genetics. There are at least 1000 olfactory genes, and although humans possess them all, only about 350 of them are active and produce the proteins (olfactory receptors) that lock onto scent molecules . Each gene produces a discrete, different receptor protein, which contributes to our ability to identify many chemical compounds. These receptors are expressed in the cells of the the nose and sinuses, and the distribution of, total number of, or even lack of, certain types of receptors affects each person's ability to detect certain scents. Think of scent molecules as being the balls in a pinball machine. You only get points when the ball hits a target. OK, now each ball is a different color, and you only get points if the purple ball hits a purple target, regardless of how many other targets it hits, or how many points the targets *might potentially* give you. It doesn't matter how long the ball bounces around, until it hits a purple target, you don't get points. NOW imagine that in some pinball machines, there ARE no purple targets, but half the balls are purple. You never get any points from those balls. Your nose is the pinball machine, the balls are scent molecules, the targets are scent receptors, the points are your detection of the scent. If you lack the correct "target", you don't smell the scent, no matter how many purple balls (scent molecules) are bouncing around in the pinball machine (your nose). Since rose perfumes are a highly complex mixture of different chemicals (and the proportions change with time of day, age of bloom, humidity, temps, etc), depending on which receptors are active in your olfactory center, you may or may not smell all, some, or none of the various components of a particular perfume. Nose sensitivity is VERY variable person to person, being a spectrum, with the "nose-blindness" on one end, and "super noses" on the other. Nose blindness can be caused by things as disparate as allergies, age, dementia, and head trauma. Hyper-sensitivity to scents is called hyperosmia, and is common among the specialists that formulate new perfumes. These super noses are employed as commercial "spies" as well, as they can recreate "secret" recipes (food or perfume!) by taste and smell alone. A perfume specialist may be able to detect and identify up to 1000x more scents than the average person. In extreme cases, super noses have been known to even be able to identify the smell associated with Parkinson's disease. Of course it takes training to be able to put names to the scents and chemicals, but there's money to be had if your nose is that talented! So always take into account that each of us, as well as the roses we grow, are individuals with different abilities, sensitivities and quirks. Going back to my inability to smell Julia Child, the thing to remember is that for most "smells", there is more than one chemical that can cause the perception of a particular scent, so you might not smell rose "A", but CAN smell rose "B", even though to someone else they smell alike! (It all depends on your pinball machine, hehe). John

We ate at my grandparent's house quite often, and their round dining table had to be at least 60" because at least 6 or 7 people sat around it comfortably, maybe 8 occasionally. Find a pool company that does pool inspections. Some companies specialize in pool inspections solely. There's no difference in a pool structure's design for indoor or outdoor locations. Indoor pools however require the room they are located in to have a properly outfitted HVAC system and a dehumidification system. The latter being the most important. A room that has improper air circulation and too much moisture can damage everything in that room. Indoor pools should have an automatic cover in place to further reduce moisture content in the air. Every indoor pool we build has an automatic cover as part of the project. It's great your are confident in your own abilities to see perhaps the obvious problems, but there are so many nuances you could overlook that only a pro would recognize.

Lacking any useful information, we can only consider the issue most likely to cause the spoiled foliage, and over-watering wins, hands down. A 5 stage 100 gallon per day reverse osmosis filtration system can be had for under $300 and you can install it (easily) yourself. An ionic exchange water softening system won't work because it exchanges Na and Cl ions for the minerals that make your water hard, Ca, Mg, Fe, etc. Hard water causes a build-up of (bi)carbonates in the grow medium and can increase media pH over time to the degree that many essential nutrients become unavailable for uptake. It would be best if you were fertilizing regularly with an acid-forming fertilizer, and flushing the grow medium each time you water, such that the entire soil column gets moistened and at least 20% of the total volume of water applied exits the drain, carrying any build-up of carbonates and other minerals nutrients with it. My suggestion would be to read this short piece I wrote about Good Growing Practices, and compare the information to whatever regimen you have established, to see where improvements might be made. You can also start monitoring moisture levels by using a 'tell' to 'tell' you when it's time to water. The more water your grow medium holds, the more critical getting your watering intervals spaced appropriately becomes . You can depot the plant and examine the roots. If roots are scraggly or dead, or they smell sour and unlike what fresh soil smells like, you're likely over-watering. If the damage is mostly in older leaves, it might be a fluoride toxicity as fluoride accumulates in tissue and can be eliminated from the plant only when affected leaves with the accumulation are shed or removed. Should you start using a water supply w/o fluoride, the new growth will show no symptoms of a fluoride toxicity, but affected leaves would continue to show damage until the affected leaves are shed or removed. Interesting comments from consultants and designers. 1) Aluminum is not advisable unless it is in an appropriate climate (warm), or is necessitated by some other factor such as being in a high rise condo building or something of that nature. Yes it is "thermally broken", however the limits of that are generally tested and destroyed in a cold climate as aluminum is very conductive. 2) Vinyl windows (much like wood, fiberglass, and metal) come in a variety of designs, quality tiers, and perfromance levels. Stating that you don't like a material becasue of the design is like stating that you don't like hamburgers because you had a bad one at McDonalds, or perhaps more than one. As for the original concern, @Marla, you may notice that windows of various materials don't paint "high friction" areas for obvious reasons. Many fiberglass and wood products will have vinyl jamb liners of another color, and/or similarly unpainted areas. This is generally considered the "guts" of the window, where hardware, fasteners, and other items that make the window operate (and with little regard to the appearance) are located. It just so happens these areas are typcally white on a vinyl window, on wood or fiberglass they may be beige or brown. If that would make a difference, you could check with the manufacturer of your choice to see if they'd apply the black coating to a different color vinyl extrusion such as beige or brown. Some may paint all surfaces in and out of the jambs, but there are more that do not than those that do. Lastly, its very odd for the warranty to be affected by adding grids. Ficus elastica - commonly, rubber tree. More information is needed re how you go about caring for this tree. It is not prudent to remove any foliage from a tree in such steep decline as leaves are the factories in which the plant makes it own food - sugar/ glucose. There is a direct relationship between how much store energy a propagule has in reserve and how likely the cutting is to strike (grow roots). Cuttings from trees essentially circling the drain are rarely successful. This is due to the fact that low levels of stored energy in the cuttings slows the rooting process, and propagation by cuttings is essentially a race to see whether or not roots can form and make a connection to the plant's vasculature before any of a number of fungal species clogs the plumbing and makes that impossible. My suggestion would be to begin a dialog here that provides you with information needed to improve the cultural conditions currently proving to be so limiting. Odds are high that you're over-watering, so any fresh start should include a thorough flushing of the grow medium to ensure any build-up of salts from tapwater and fertilizer solutions is corrected. Also, unless your pot is very shallow (5" or less) the advice to "water when the top inch or two of the soil feels dry" should be ignored as it serves better as a recipe for over-watering. In stead, use a wooden "tell" to "tell" you when it's time to water. See more about using a '"tell" below. After flushing the soil, it would be best to make regular fertilizing a part of your care regimen. Ask if you have interest in discussing how to go about fertilizing appropriately. This Overview of Good Growing Practicesshould help you avoid all of the most common issues growers face at some point in their journey to a green thumb. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

text: Your plant is showing trifoliate leaves. So what has happened is your rootstock has overgrown the edible variety.  If you see any growth with monofoliate leaves, that is what is left of your edible variety (kumquat).  If not, then the edible variety has died out. Rootstock, if allowed to grow shoots, will often out-compete the edible variety. Many of the trifoliate hybrids used as rootstock are semi-deciduous. Leaves will often turn yellow and drop all winter long. You're seeing normal winter leaf drop from rootstock.

I think it all depends on the type of granite or quartzite you select - many/most standard granites are fool-proof and make for super durable counters - there are many quartzites that are that way too (we've had Madre Perla for 10+ years and it's bulletproof). On the plus side that's probably not box blight, box blight would be a summer issue and it sounds like yours are coming out of a late planting and the strong possibility of winter damage. I would just leave it until May and it will either flush from the green branches or not... On the negative side the dead areas will be dead down into the center of the bush and when you eventually cut them out, even if the rest lives, it will be 'gappy' for a few years as it fills in.  Ask me how I know lol. To leave on a plus note, box is super easy from cuttings.  This summer you can clip a few branches off the ones you have, stick them in the ground and they'll likely root if partially shaded and watered every now and then. An update - last Sunday, being completely bored, I chopped up some of my hoyas (actually only 7 small cuttings) along with a couple of leafless vines. I mixed up some sphagnum orchid moss I purchased at Loews, along with some phalanopsis special mix, again at Loews, then I placed the cuttings in a prop box and put it in a sunny window on top of a heading mat. Every day I would remove the top to let in fresh air for a few minutes. Inside the box is really cozy. Warm, humid, the perfect growing environment. I expected to wait several weeks before seeing anything happening. The cuttings were placed in clear plastic cups I purchased at Dollar Tree, with a single hold melted into the side of each one. The hole was about .5" off the bottom and the lower portion of the cub had sphagnum moss in the bottom to help hold in moisture, then the rest filled with the mix from above. Checking them a few minutes ago, several have already rooted! My Hoya Kerry, which was a single leaf on a vine that had been sitting there for almost a year, has roots almost 1.5" long already, and rambling all over the top of the mix. A couple others have roots throughout the mix. I can't believe how quickly they've grown and rooted. If I lived in a warm humid environment there would be no hoya shortage and prices would be a few dollars per plant since they root so quickly and easily. I'd flood the market! There really shouldn't be a high cost to hoyas for this very reason, but I guess greed gets in the way. Anyway, my clippings are doing well and seem to be growing roots. Unfortunately, the vines I planted are not doing as well and have shriveled up. Maybe they just weren't viable enough when I started, or they needed a leaf for chlorophyll? I'll try another soon, but for now I just enjoy watching these grow. Oh what I wouldn't give for a warm year round humid greenhouse or an environment that supports this kind of growth. Ahh yes, my dream....

I had a similar construction method in my bathroom walls...tar paper and metal lath attached to the studs and then mortar "floated" onto the wall and a final finish coat of plaster. It makes for a very solid wall and was a beast to demo. Where I live for all walls except inside a shower the common practice is to use blueboard and apply a coat of finish plaster. In my shower I wanted to paint the ceiling as so when  with a 3 mil vapor barrier, cement board and then veneer plaster. Ask over a johnbridge.com as well. They will be able to recommend the materials you should use to patch your walls. But veneer plastering takes a lot of skill.

For the walls, rock lath is the correct answer. In my house, two layers of gypsum panels (the precursor to today's drywall) topped with a finish coat of plaster. Rock solid. Doesn't ding. Great sound insulation. Pain to demo/patch/cut holes in. Thickness in my house is 7/8"-- I usually make 3/8" wood furring strips and then fasten 1/2" drywall to that. You could also use 3/8" drywall on top of 1/2" drywall. If you're using any power tools to cut it, the poster above is correct, you'll need carbide or diamond tipped for the top layer plaster. It will ruin regular metal blades. That said, a regular drywall hand saw and a little elbow grease will get you right through it too (just requires more effort than cutting regular drywall). Regarding your baseboards, that is because there had been tile there. These bathrooms are mud bed construction. There are boards between the joists that are flush with them and form a subfloor, then tar paper, then wire mesh, then 1.25" of concrete. You can tile right over it and fill the hole with regular concrete. You can also tear it out and do a new subfloor if you have concerns about height, but that requires mores sweat and a couple trips to the dump. Just a sledgehammer and pry bar will get the job done, but use as light a touch as possible, or you will crack the plaster in surrounding rooms.

I've worked for a *major* Canadian drug store chain off and on since 1993. 22 years in total between four stores. I had a few jobs between stores, and took time off a couple times so it hasn't been steady. I remember one day working in the OTC section stocking the vitamins overhearing the pharmacist and tech talking about the new drugstore across the street being robbed twice since they opened. I think at the time, they were only open for a month. I don't remember what I said, but the pharmacist said, "we were just robbed!". I laughed and said, "no we weren't!" He told me to look at the front of the store and there was our cash manager talking to police! I walked up front and said, "were we just robbed?" and she nodded "yes". To this day, she does not remember our conversation. There was more, but I won't bore you with it. A man had come to her till and bought something to which she asked if that was everything. He replied, "I'll take all the cash in your drawer" and the tone in his voice was serious so she knew this wasn't someone cracking a joke. And believe me, some people thinks it's funny to say that to us. She gave him the cash and a carton of smokes and he ran out. Turns out he was from a group or drug store robbers that had hit about a dozen stores in the are within a month. Two weeks ago Thursday, I got off work at 7 p.m. I did a little shopping and left by 7:20. Forty minutes later, two people entered the store, forced their way into the pharmacy and forced the pharmacist to open the safe and they reached in and took all the drugs they came for. They knew what they wanted and only took those particular drugs. I watched the video of the robbery and my heart broke for both staff members. One was scratched by the knife the woman had on her. The other dragged the pharmacist out of the office as he was eating his dinner. He pulled him across the pharmacy to the safe. It took days for either of them to return to work. Both were shaken up pretty badly, and rightfully so. Fast forward to this past Thursday: 14 days later. I was in the back room re-organizing the pet food over stock. I put some items on a cart and walked out the back room and noticed two people in the aisle. All I could think was, "holy crap! They look EXACTLY like the two people who robbed us two weeks ago!" I put my cart in the next aisle and debated: could it be? Should I do a double take? What if I'm wrong and they think I'm racially profiling them? What if it is them and they have a weapon? What do I do?? I walked out of the aisle and took another look down the one they were in. They hadn't moved, yet looked so suspicious I decided to walk down yet another aisle (no way I was going in the same one) and headed for the front of the store. I saw our cashier supervisor walking towards me from the other end. In the meantime the two people had come out of the aisle and slowly started to walk ahead of me. I was trying to get her to look at me, but nope: she headed for the exit on a mission. That's when I saw my boss on her cell phone. For sure something was wrong! I said, "Are we being robbed?" She replied, "We already were, go to the pharmacy and make sure they're okay!" I pointed at the two people I was following and she nodded. I got to the back of the store and our pharmacist appeared okay. The one tech had mascara all down her cheeks, she had been crying. The other tech? I swore, using the F-bomb and said, "no (insert her name here) {f-bomb} again!" Yup, Twice in two weeks, this girl was thrown to the ground. This time, it was two men. One said he had a gun and he told the pharmacist if she didn't open the safe he would blow her head off. The safe will not open. It is on a delay timer. No amount of threats will open it faster. In the video I could see him trying to open the safe. Nothing. Just then, I see both the manager and assistant manager walk past. They know something is off. First: another staff member saw the two people I saw and alerted management. Nobody saw these two people come in. Anyway, as they walked past the pharmacy counter, they realized nobody was there. One looked over the counter and saw them on the ground. Just as she peeked over, the person at the safe told his partner to run and they bolted out of the store. Had I looked to my left as I came out of the backroom, I would have seen that. Instead I saw these two men who we are all 100% positive were with the two in the pharmacy. We think they were a backup plan. The cashier supervisor whose attention I was trying to get, was locking the store as my manager, assistant manager and pharmacy called 911. This happened in the middle of the afternoon! I told many people I didn't like working at night because of the crazies (we close at 10), but this set of crazies don't care about the time And they're all youths! We aren't the first store robbed by this group and we won't be the last. They're quick. The first time in and out in 4 1/2 minutes. Gone 90 seconds before police showed up. In that case a customer saw we were being robbed and his English was poor, but he said to the cashier "9-1-1!" and pointed at the pharmacy. But the robbers were too fast. So, the company sent in a therapist for us to talk to and all I can think is, "THERE'S NO AMOUNT OF WORDS THAT WILL MAKE ME FEEL SAFE AT WORK!" You can do all the voodoo mumbo jumbo and pretend to have empathy but the back of my head will always ALWAYS wonder if today is the day we get robbed again, and if the safe doesn't open who gets shot??? I keep checking on the back (we can't see them from the front). Our owner says a panic button may do more harm than good. Having it on the counter does 0 good. Having in your pocket can spook a robber. "why are your hands in your pocket?" Again, it could end poorly. But we can't have our safe unsecured anymore or this will be a daily thing. I don't think our tech will come back to work. It'll be a miracle if we see her again. Our pharmacist who was robbed the first time, decided not to work again last Thursday, or he would have been robbed a second time too. So, I'll go to work. I'll pay close attention to who is coming and going. And I'll keep my phone on me. I told my boss she can fire me, I don't care. We were told just on Sunday NO PHONES ON THE FLOOR. Well, I had nobody to call when I saw these two guys. Nobody to warn quickly. She said nothing. I could've texted her or another manager. But no phone.... Okay....... I got that off my chest. I did come home that night and had a drink to calm down. I'm okay. I'll go back to work. I need the $$. I just hope the police can finally find this group. There's more than four as the first time there was a woman, but not this time. And the tech is sure the one who tried to get the safe open is the same man who was there 2 weeks ago. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al

White pine grows on nearly all the soils within its range (71), but generally competes best on well drained sandy soils of low to medium site quality. These soils permit fair growth of white pine but not hardwoods. On these sandy sites, white pine regenerates naturally, competes easily, and can be managed most effectively and economically (40,47). On medium-textured soils (sandy loams), it will outproduce most other native commercial species in both volume and value (47). White pine also grows on fine sandy loams and silt-loam soils with either good or impeded drainage when there is no hardwood competition during the establishment period-as on old fields and pastures, bums, and blowdowns. It has been found on clay soils and on poorly drained or very poorly drained soils with surface mounds. It can be very productive on these sites but usually occurs only as individual trees or in small groups (47). This pine should not be planted in heavy clay soils. Poorly drained bottom land sites and upland depressions are also poor choices for planting (6). Pinus strobus L (usda.gov)

These photos are an electric Whirlpool unit.  It can be vented out the back, left, right, and bottom.  There's room to run the exhaust to the right under the heater box.  Models that can't route out one side or the other are obstructed by the electric element housing or the gas burner assembly to the respective direction. The 4" exhaust duct in the center is removed from the blower housing and either cut shorter and reused or replaced with a new shorter piece and a 90° elbow to the left or right (or bottom) for routing through a pre-scored knock-out on the side or bottom accordingly.  This model has a sound insulation panel on the left that also has a scored spot to be removed for left-side conversion. A conversion kit offered by the manufacturer may include everything needed.

I grow many Japanese maples in containers, several that are 20+ years old. They remain suited to container growth because they get repotted and root pruned regularly every 5 years or so. The OP's tree does not have to be planted in the ground and while the rootball is exposed, root pruning now before a new container is created will ensure it remains healthy and vigorous for another 5-10 years. It would have been ideal to have done this routinely in the past but it is a very doable go-around to do so now. btw, as far as Japanese maples are concerned, they are all "foo-foo" compared to other maple types :-) A 25 y,o, coral bark maple is a valuable tree! I would NOT recommend leaving the tree as-is. Exposing any of the feeder roots to sun or drying air will just cause dieback and could provide inroads for various root pathogens JM's are subject to.

Use LED tape/strip lights in an aluminum channel. If you want the lights to be as unobtrusive as possible you can can embed a flush-mount channel in the underside of the cabinet. Otherwise, just attach a surface-mount channel to the underside of the cabinet. Use a channel with a plastic diffuser to reduce reflections of the individual LEDs in the countertop. You can use one driver for all the lights; just run low-voltage wiring from the driver to the the three LED/channel sections. Connect the driver to the house wiring* and hide it inside a cabinet. No, you will not need gfi recepticals if you have a gfi breaker, the breaker will gfi protect all outlets on that circuit. “My dad is a plumber and is teaching us electrical“ sounds a little scary to me. ive seen a lot of plumbers electrical work, and while it wont burn down your house, a lot of little things are overlooked.

PLEASE don’t skimp with electrical circuits.  Plan for what you will be using and wire accordingly.  Workout equipment, heaters, etc. often require a dedicated circuit.  You’ll need others for lights, TV and other electrical apparatus.  Use sufficient guage wire and correct breakers.  IF in doubt at least have the connections made by a professional.

The reason for a GFI  breaker is that it protects the whole circuit and makes adding additional GFI receptacles unnecessary. If you want to protect just part of a circuit, you don't use a GFI breaker and you install one GFI receptacle, which also protects all other receptacles " downstream" from that location. Having more than one GFI  receptacle on a circuit is not advisable as it can lead to unnecessary tripping.

I have no idea what TV says or why that should mean anything... but even the company that makes the bra isn't trying to call it a cotton bra. Manufactuers have the thresholds of purity there, because a lot of consumers want to know what is in what they are wearing, and what they are paying for. Just like they want to know what's in their food, or being added to their gardens/fields, or used in working on their homes. Like when folks think quartz is stone for all intents and purpouses- but it isn't- its stone and plastic blend-  and manufacturing standards are in place so people aren't scammed thinking they are getting quartzite, which is all stone. Velveeta isn't cheese, it's a cheese product. Fabric manufacturing is the same way- industry standards. For some folks it does not matter much, and for others it matters a lot. Sometimes it's for non-physical reasons, sometimes for more physical ones. Like that bra could make a sensitive person break out in a rash, scaling, hives wearing it because it's not al all cotton bra. What an awful allergy to have considering how much synthetics are in a lot of clothing now. Some people have sensitivities to chemicals of fabric manufacturing like formaldehyde used in anti-wrinkle and a lot of proofings, or some dyes can trigger it. Some folks have issues with nickel- it's commonly used for studs on jeans and used in bra hooks and wires. Those folks have to find bras that are nickle-free. It's often not disclosed on labels or by manufacturers- yet.

The shower drains into your main drain-- there is a whole network of pipes buried under your slab. I just bought a house built in 1958 with a similar issue. I called the plumber about snaking/scoping and he said the P-trap (buried under the concrete-- see under your bathroom sink for an example) is probably corroded that any snaking would be be a temporary solution and clogs would keep coming back.  He told me he could replace the pipes, but it makes no sense to pay a plumber to dig, and that I should have someone else do the excavation for less money. I rented a jackhammer, busted out a 3 ft x 3 ft  square of the concrete, then used shovel, and once I hit pipe about 3 feet down, a garden trowel to dig out around the pipe and cut out and replaced the pipes myself. The plumber was right, and the P trap was completely clogged and rusty on the inside. It's a big job, but doesn't require a lot of skill. It will cost a lot (ballpark $5000ish) to have a professional do it, but a seasoned DIYer could tackle it for the cost of the jackhammer rental and the pipes. (Less than $200 all in).  Or you could go the hybrid route and get a handyman type to do the excavation and then call a plumber in to replace the pipes (which really, is the easiest part of the job-- could just have the handyman do it at that point).

If you start pruning now, any growth the plant puts on between now and June will be leggy. My suggestion would be to wait until June to prune and get into that habit. If you prune in June, all subsequent growth will be the tightest possible within the limitations imposed by indoor light. Summer growth is for pinching. Allow 2-3 leaves to grow on each branch, then pinch out the growing tip. This forces back-budding proximal to (behind) the the pinch. When fall comes, stop pinching and allow the plant to grow unencumbered by pinching/pruning until the following June, when all leggy growth that occurs between mid-fall to early June is removed. This is how to maximize ramification, which is a measure of leaf and branch density. It ensures the plant will be as full as it can be within the limiting influence of cultural conditions antithetical to high levels of ramification. While pruning and pinching are the surest way to ensure back-budding, very bright light, good air movement, and fertility at luxury levels (especially nitrogen) can also cause natural back-budding w/o pruning pinching. This works best when the plant vacations outdoors over the summer.  Pilea variegata ^^^ Al

Even if it's not the fastest or easiest, the best way to achieve any goal is to choose the route that best ensures success, and avoid choosing a path solely because it offers the chance of success. I'll provide you with an outline of the actions needed to return the plant to a much higher state of vitality (health), while making allowances for the plant's weakness and taking advantage of its coming strengths. First, some questions. Where do you live? Would you provide an image of the plant and pot, and perhaps an image of what's going on under the hemp mat? Has the plant ever been fully repotted (includes bare-rooting, root pruning, and a change of soil. Do you fertilize regularly? .... with what? .... when last? Does the pot have a drain hole? .... and, after watering do you allow the pot to sit in any effluent that exits the drain hole? When you water, do you ensure the entire soil column is moistened and a good measure of water flushes through the soil, carrying mineral build-up from tapwater and fertilizer solutions out of the pot? The plant definitely needs a hard pruning, but now isn't a good time to prune, and your plant is too weak to do the kind of pruning required to reduce the plant to a framework you can build on. IOW, between now and an appropriate time to prune (possibly as early as this coming June, if you live in the Northern Hemisphere), the best use of time would be by focusing on betterment of the plant's vitality so it's able to tolerate the hard pruning. To do that, I would: * Figure out a way you can flush the soil as you water. That will 'reset' the level of fertility to close to 0. * After flushing, fertilize with a full production strength solution. I highly recommend using Foliage-Pro 9-3-6, as it contains ALL nutrients essential to normal growth, from a single source. It has many other attributes as well. * Start using a 'tell' to 'tell' you when it's time to water. More re using a tell below. Move the plant outdoors as soon as night temps are reliably above 55*. This will make a big difference in the plant's level of vitality. Currently, on a 1-10 scale with 10 being the peak of health, your plant is probably a 3, so it needs your help. * The plant will respond very favorably to being outdoors. Once it's pushing some new growth, it can be repotted. The best timing of that depends on where you live, but it will be sometime in June for Ficus in the Northern Hemisphere. Leaves are individual factories where the plant's true food (sugar/glucose) is synthesized, so removing green leaves by way of pruning always represents a setback. That's fine when a plant is robust/healthy and it's ability to make food is at or approaching peak levels, but your tree is not a good candidate for any type of pruning other than pinching, and pinching will not provide you with the response required to fix the fact that all foliage on major branches is concentrated at branch tips where new extension growth occurs. That is occurring likely because the plant is very root-bound The plant's level of vitality is not a constant. All else equal, it will be weaker in late fall through early spring than at any other part of its growth cycle, which is why it's best to do serious work like hard pruning and repotting in the weeks immediately prior to the summer solstice. The reason is simple - your plant will tolerate the work better and recover faster when light is most intense and days longest Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Questions ..... or was that informational overload. Don't be shy about asking questions. If you're serious about honing your growing skills, the key will be gaining a better understanding of how your plant works and how to work WITH the plant's natural rhythms instead of just ignoring them. Al

- I'm guessing you would recommend replacing the pot with one that has a drainage hole? Should it also be smaller? In the immediate, the best course would be to add a couple of drain holes through the bottom where the bottom and sidewall meet, then flush the soil thoroughly by slowly pouring a volume of room temp water equal to at least 10X the volume of the pot through the soil. When that is completed situate the plant above a collection saucer so there is no pathway by which the effluent that exits the pot can make its way back into the grow medium.  While you've done very well to keep the plant alive in a pot so large w/o a drain hole, there remains the fact that dissolved solids from fertilizer and tapwater have been accumulating in the soil for a very long time. This means that the TDS/EC (total dissolved solids and electrical conductivity ..... roughly the level of salts) levels in the soil solution are very high; and, even though the NPK ratio of the fertilizer is appropriate, it has undoubtedly become badly skewed over time. When that occurs, an access of one nutrient can cause a deficiency (antagonistic deficiency) of one or more of the other nutrients. - Do you think this is a good fertilizer? (see attached photo) There is no way to tell from the information on the label. All we know is it provides a slow release form of Nitrogen, phosphorous and potassium favorable to the plant. What is missing is which of the other 9 essential nutrients does it contain, if any. There are many fertilizers that contain only NPK, and those would be inappropriate for container culture. I have a large number of Ficus (40 or so,  not including a few dozen cuttings I started for some reason that will probably forever remain unclear to me. The Lord knows I don't need more plants, but propagating is pretty much a reflex for me. I use Foliage-Pro 9-3-6. It contains all nutrients (absorbed via the root pathway) essential to normal growth, from a single source. It has many other attributes as well, and would serve very well for almost everything you're apt to grow in a container.  - Should I use cactus soil as a replacement? Or just regular potting soil? You'll find that what the bag says a soil is appropriate for is more often than not misleading. Usually, if brand X makes an all purpose potting medium and one especially for cacti/succulents, the product for cacti/succulents will likely be not quite as bad for cacti/succulents as the all-purpose medium. Living where you do, you should have ready access to graded (for size) fir bark from Shasta Forest Products, from up Yreka way. Media for Ficus should be rather chunky. Growth should kick into second gear once the vernal equinox is behind you (Mar 21), but still, it's best for the plant if you repot after it has regained a good measure of vitality, and it's current ability to make food is about to peak. The plants natural defenses are a byproduct of its metabolism, so repotting w/o consideration of the timing can mean an unnecessarily long recovery during which the plant is more vulnerable to insect herbivory and attack by disease pathogens. - You mention putting it outside, is full shade OK? Had a quick look at the website and the installation instructions to get an idea as i'd not seen this range before and these are my honest opinions as a designer and supplier of true handleless kitchens. Looking at the design of the cabinets and the installation, for b+q to keep costs down, they are using their standard sized doors ie 715mm tall and then made the cabinets taller to accommodate the handle rail, this means that with a 40mm worktop the recommended height is 942mm which is very high, one option is to cut the legs down but check this doesn't affect dishwasher and other appliances. Cabinet sizes and drawer options are very limited, no option for standard split drawers as the only drawer fronts are pan drawer sizes. Usual cheap b+q hinges and drawer boxes. Cabinets are only in white, so if you opt for a dark door you will see white shadow lines everywhere and as the wall unit doors are flush with the base of the cabinet and you can't fit a pelmet you may well notice this if you have a seating area. B+q cabinet reviews are mixed, but many reports of poor quality control regarding cabinet widths, transport damage seems another issue, but note these are for the standard cabinet (has a top rail made of a bit of wire), the innova cabinets seem to be a new range B+q have a 25 year guarantee, but as this probably won't be made in 25 years time its pretty worthless. Doors, drawers and panels are a vinyl foil wrap, so depending on the foil, dark colours may show up greasy fingerprints which seem to be difficult to remove (shows more than light colours), again 25 year guarantee is optimistic and as with most of the sheds, they have a high turn over of door design so if the design is changed in a few years there won't be any back up stock. True handleless is harder to design, so if a designer isn't experienced with the product there's more chance of errors where things don't fit or the design doesn't work. True handleless is harder to fit with more components needed and with more unique features for the installer to be aware of, so for the inexperienced it can be a steep learning curve. I always advise customers who have their own installer that a good installer can make a cheap kitchen look hi end, but it won't last as fittings like hinges/drawers start to fail but an inexperienced/crap fitter can make a hi end expensive german kitchen look rubbish. Its really down to attention to detail and even more so with a true handleless design.

An AC can only cool. A heat pump can cool and provide heat. A heat pump is basically an AC running in reverse. It extracts heat from the outdoor air and supplies it to the house. This is called an air source heat pump. If you have a high efficiency gas furnace, then you can also install a heat pump. This is some time called a dual fuel system. The gas furnace has the same efficiency rating regardless of the outdoor temperature. The efficiency of the heat pump changes as the outdoor temperature drops. This is because cold air has less heat than warm air. The advantage of the heat pump is that you could save some money in heating costs. The cooling costs compared to an AC are about the same. The disadvantage is the initial installation cost is higher than an AC only system. Running the heat pump in the winter also creates more run time and potentially a shorter life on the equipment. If you post the cost of your natural gas and electricity, a calculation can be done to compare the operating costs of the furnace and heat pump.

I'd put good money on it being spider mites! For indoor ivy, the presence of spider mites is pretty much a foregone conclusion.....almost an inevitable occurrence, even with very experienced ivy growers :-) The white on the upper leaf surface is stippling or the patterning resulting from their tiny sucking little mouth parts and the dark specks on the underside is mite poop. The first is permanent and the second will wash off easily. I'd suspect there will also be some telltale webbing here and there as well. The only way to keep spider mites at bay is to keep humidity high.....they dislike moisture. So spray the plant down when watering each time, either in the kitchen sink or bathtub. And maybe once or twice in between waterings as well now we are in winter and the plant does not have the same water requirements. Neem oil is also a safe and moderately effective miticide and can be used as a soil drench if the problem should escalate.

There is a difficulty in combining wind resistance or blocking ability and a tolerance for coastal conditions.....very few plants will measure up satisfactorily to both situations. The Sunset Western Garden book carries lists of plants well suited to both of these conditions in our area but provide very little overlap. A few native conifers offer the best solutions - shore pine (Pinus contorta, native to coastal areas), western red cedar (Thuja plicata) and Doug firs lead the list. You may want to fill in gaps with shrubs like Arbutus unedo, cistus, cotoneaster, escallonia and eleagnus. If shielded from salt spray, you could add ceanothus, Pacific wax myrtle, junipers, nandina, barberry and chamaecyparis. Here's a local publication that could be useful: Trees Against the Wind

3rd image from the top seems to reveal at least 180* of dead phloem tissue if not the entire cambium. Phloem is the tissue found on the outside of the vascular cambium. The phloem conducts photosynthate (the plant's true food, sugar/glucose made during photosynthesis) and other growth regulators/ chemical messengers from the top of the plant to the roots. The plant's xylem tissues are located inside of the vascular cambium and conduct water and nutrients from the roots to the top of the plant. As long as the xylem is still able to provide the top of the plant with water/nutrients, new leaves can continue to grow for a period and the plant can survive on stored energy reserves. Energy reserves operate much like a battery. The energy held in reserve is finite, When the lights are exhausted, it's 'lights out' for the plant. The cause of the issue is almost certainly to be an inappropriate grow medium or a hand too heavy on the watering can. If you haven't been watering over the sink and allowing the pot to stop draining before you return it to the cache pot, that too is an issue. The maim pot should never come in contact with the effluent that exits the drain hole. The plant appears to be beyond salvation at this point, but there is nothing stopping you from flushing the grow medium, getting your watering under control, and hoping for a reversal. Ask if you want more specific advice ..... in case you decide to try another ponytail. Al

Like rhizo, I have also been a professional horticulturist for many years. But unlike rhizo, I have been stung multiple times :-)) Sometimes it is unavoidable......sometimes not. The bee stings were my fault. Early with my first real garden, I was wandering the yard barefoot and stepped on a bee. Can't blame it for striking back! The second bee sting happened when a bee flew in/got caught in the top of my wellies and couldn't find its way out. I am not sensitive or allergic so no big deal. The major sting incident was not my fault. I was working on weeding a bed and pruning back a huge rose. The bed included a birdhouse on a tall pole. Unbeknownst to me, wasps had taken up residence in the birdhouse and took offense to me being in their territory and so close to the nest. When I heard the buzzing, I looked up but it was too late. I was attacked by the wasps and received at least 7 stings......on my head!! My scalp felt like it was on fire and I have never had quite so severe a headache! But ibuprofen, an ice pack and a rest, and I was good to go in a couple of hours. For a single sting, aloe verde or Benadryl applied to the sting as soon as possible will soothe and reduce any inflammation. Also cold or ice packs and an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen or aspirin can help. And if you have any adverse reaction, get to the ER or a doctor ASAP. btw, I took revenge on the wasps :-) The next evening at dusk, when they were all tucked away in their birdhouse squat, I nuked 'em with a long distance wasp spray! I also removed the birdhouse from the middle of my planting bed to discourage future colonies from setting up house. I have a very strong affinity for bees of all kinds and encourage them in my gardens. But I draw the line at wasps and hornets!!

Thank you for reaching out.  The tops placed in this kitchen are Shadow Storm Marble tops.  Just a couple of things to keep in mind when choosing Marble:   1.  Marble tops etch very easily - you have to keep any acidic food, liquid off the surface - even coffee.  If any acidic food or liquid sits on the surface - it will etch it so if you have a polished marble, it will become rough to the touch.  2. You want to make sure to get a really good sealer - we sell a 15 year sealer called DryTreat and it's the best on the market.  However, even sealing the surface will not prevent it from etching or scratching.  3.  Marble is a softer stone than granite so you will want to take great care in not dropping heavy objects on it (like iron or cast iron skillets or heavy pans), we never recommend cutting food directly on the top (like you can with granite) because it may scratch the surface.  You will also want to utilize trivets and pot holders - I wouldn't recommend placing any hot pots or utensils on it's surface.  Although Marble tops look amazing it kitchens, they require much maintenance and care in keeping beautiful.  We hope this information will help you!

(An impeller technically is an agitator ... any device in the drum that swirls/moves the water and clothes is an agitator.) There's a lower-end Amana (manufactured by Whirlpool) model with a true dual-action agitator that regular fins on the base and a spiral upper section that rotates one direction to push the clothes down.  Majority, if not all, of the other brands and models have a fake auger that doesn't turn separately in one direction.  It rotates back-and-forth with the base and jiggles the clothes both up and down to no effect of promoting rollover. Speed Queen model TC5 has a regular agitator but it doesn't have a spiral auger.  It's a popular choice among people looking for an "old-style" toploader ... but be aware that it has no control for multiple fill levels.  All the cycles fill to one standard level (Normal Eco = 13 gals; Heavy Duty, Perm Press, Delicate = 14.5 gals; Bulky/Sheets = 16 gals) or a slightly higher level with Deep Fill option selected (16 gals Normal Eco, 19 gals all the others).   Can't get less than 13 gals for a small load or single item.

Older impeller models had stronger wash action.  Latest designs nowadays are lethargic, either because the speeds are reduced or the impellers are lower-profile than earlier versions. This is a 13yo model that works nicely.  Fourteen shirts in this load on HE (low-fill) mode.  The beginning shower is a pretreatment function.  The wash period begins at 7:10.  Takes a couple mins to get the load mixed-up and moving.

There has been enough interest over the past year or so in identifying faucet sellers that offer kitchen sprays (called "wands" in industry-speak) made of brass or stainless that we are in the process of compiling a directory. It will not be ready, however, until later this year. Unfortunately, plastic wands have become very common for two reasons (1) they don't get hot in use, and (2) they are a lot cheaper. The problem is that they are also more prone to failure, so much so that many companies that provide them do not include them in their lifetime warranties. All metal wands do tend to get uncomfortably hot when very hot water is run through them. We have through diligent and painstaking research over many years, however, found the solution. Don't run very hot water through the wand. No one needs to rinse with scalding water. Faucet companies are working on other solutions. Commercial pre-rinse faucets often feature a rubber sleeve over the wand. In2aqua and other companies are experimenting with hybrid wands in which an outer shell of metal is lined with plastic as insulation. At the moment the best course for avoiding plastic wands is to call customer service and ask what the wand is made of. If they won't say or don't know, move on to the next company. Keep in mind, however, that even if the shell of the wand is metal, the innards are likely plastic. It has been many years since we last saw an all-metal sprayer.

text: I routinely do twinning on almost all of my veggies. It's insurance that, if one plant croaks, there won't be a gap. Very true that you won't get optimal production out of both plants, but between the two of them, you'll get production that will rival one solitary plant. Two plants close together behave, in terms of soil nutrition, pretty much as two stems on one plant.

"Peppers tolerate close company well and it helps to protect the fruit from sun scald." I agree. Lacking any additional support, close spacing also help the plants to support each other. It also conserves soil moisture (which is important for good peppers) and helps to keep the weeds down. When planting large numbers of peppers, I too use alternating rows; but more closely than above. I use rows 12" apart, and plants 24" apart, in alternating positions row-to-row...  which equals about 17" between adjacent plants. "As the moss increases, the foliage/flowers have been decreasing." This can be a bit of a chicken and the egg situation. Often any decline in vitality of a tree festooned with Spanish moss is due to other environmental or cultural causes, not the moss itself. The moss proliferates because the tree is already in decline. This is very similar to trees heavily laden with lichen...it is not the lichen that is causing the decline but only its ability to take advantage of better, more open growing conditions to spread more aggressively. So in short, it may be a reverse cause and effect. The moss is not causing the decline but only taking advantage of it. btw, crape myrtles are a popular host tree for this epiphyte.

FWIW, it's been reported that the 'common' belief that MSG causes headaches/allergic reactions is a myth that was instigated by a single man in 1960s: "A little backstory sheds light on MSG's unsavory reputation. It all started in 1968, when a letter appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine, purportedly from a Dr. Robert Ho Man Kwok, expressing concern that Chinese food had made him sick. He contended that the monosodium glutamate in Chinese food was responsible for symptoms like headache, dizziness, numbness, and weakness. (It was later revealed that the letter was, in fact, written by an imposter as a prank.)... ...In reality, much of the early research on MSG had significant flaws. According to a 2020 study, most research that showed its supposedly harmful effects was fraught with poor design and small sample size. Many studies also gave subjects extremely high amounts of MSG you'd never find in a normal diet. More current research tells a different (and much more positive) story. For example, you may be surprised to learn that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has placed MSG in their "GRAS" category—aka "generally recognized as safe"—for years now. According to the FDA, science hasn't been able to consistently trigger any adverse symptoms from MSG consumption. The really interesting part: this holds true even in people who claim to have an MSG sensitivity. In terms of specific reactions to MSG, the good news continues. A 2016 systematic review in the Journal of Headache Painfoundno correlation between eating foods high in MSG and developing headaches. You can rest easy about MSG's effects on your brain, too. Despite some scary-sounding claims that this ingredient could cause the death of your brain cells, scientific evidence shows that MSG doesn't cross the blood-brain barrier. The take-home message: it's extremely unlikely that a plate of beef and broccoli will disrupt your neurological function. As for weight gain (another common MSG concern), the research isn't perfectly clear-cut. According to a 2019 review, some studies have reported that high-MSG foods could increase hunger and even promote obesity, while others have shown the opposite effect. The deciding factor of whether MSG makes you fuller or hungrier may be the macronutrient content of a meal. What about MSG sensitivity? MSG is considered safe for the vast majority of the population, but as with any food, it's possible to have a sensitivity to it. Less than 1% of the general population is thought to have MSG sensitivity. For these people, eating large amounts could result in unpleasant symptoms like dizziness, headache, trouble breathing, or numbness. If you consistently experience symptoms like these after eating high-MSG foods, you may want to scale back on them. Not sure if MSG is causing your issues? A food journal can be a helpful tool for finding answers. That said, you're likely already eating foods with MSG without even realizing it! Numerous whole foods like tomatoes, mushrooms, and aged cheeses naturally contain monosodium glutamate—and the body doesn't distinguish between natural and synthetic forms. Whether it comes from a fresh tomato or a bowl of ramen, your GI tract breaks down sodium and glutamate in the same way...." https://www.msn.com/en-us/health/nutrition/the-surprising-truth-about-msg-you-need-to-know/ar-AATvax7

i have the chip of first snowfall and love it but wondering how silver cloud compares? Two very interesting colors to compare because of where they sit in the Blue Hue Family. The difference between hue angle and Munsell hue family skews more in this region of the color wheel. But it doesn't matter because the notations still accurately describe how the colors differ in color appearance. Which is... Hue Family is where we see the most difference, second is Chroma. Silver Cloud has more Chroma and is more colorful. First Snowfall is more grayed, muted, less Chroma. Silver Cloud is more towards the middle of the Blue hue family so you know to look for greenish. First Snowfall is at the end of the Blue hue family, over near the purple-blue hue family so you know to look for overtones of purple/purple-blue. The Blue Hue Family neighborhood in the Munsell color system (which is what all my notations and color wheel are about) has an interesting idiosyncrasy. The middle, 5B, has a degree of greenishness to it; it's not a true primary blue. You'll find a primary blue around 245 to 250 degrees. It's explained in detail in this short video: https://youtu.be/-qNYL7PGCyg

You really shouldn't see cracks in the grout of a shower surround that was done properly, no matter how much humidity has changed in the house. Change of plane(wall corners, wall meeting floor, etc.) should = caulk not grout to allow for movement. Aside from moisture resistance, cement board/kerdi/etc. is also there to act as a decoupling layer, with the express purpose of isolating tile from the movement of the framing. Something, fundamentally, is wrong with your tile install on your shower, or the grout wouldn't crack. Either that or you have had MASSIVE movement in the framing for some reason, in which case if it was really that big to the point of overwhelming your decoupling layer, it may well also have compromised whatever waterproofing membrane they used.

The cuphea is hardier than you might expect. Mine has overwintered outside - in a container - for the last 3 years. While a bit slow to get going again each year, it had minimal dieback so can obviously take some colder temps, certainly a few good frosts. This past December we experienced a week of really cold weather....got down to about 25F (-4C) and never got above freezing for most of that time. The cuphea looks very dead at the moment and I fear a whole week of severe cold (and snow and ice) was far too much for it. It really does need some heat to kick into life again and as much sun as you can muster but I think it should be fine. Just don't expect a fast recovery :-) As an aside, I have NO room to overwinter anything iffy indoors so any temperennials I grow have to be able to withstand a PNW winter outside. Most have fared very well under this proposition but this past December freeze has pretty much wiped them all out - cuphea, bilbergia, pineapple sage, coprosma, hanging begonias and fancy leaf geraniums. 3 years is pretty good innings for these so I'm not too upset. Will replace the cuphea and try something different for the others. I am most miffed about the bilbergia as that was a gift (much older than 3 years) and will be hard to replace.

If the Dahlia survived, I have high hopes for the Lantana too.  But there are so many diff kinds of Lantana, generalizing may not be totally accurate.  Those floppy ground-cover types with names seem a lot less stalwart than a sturdy, upright L. camara.  The floppies leaf-out later in my yard than the big L. camara shrubs. If your Geranium is a Pelargonium, it could be worthwhile to put that by a sunny S window and keep watering as you do for it over summer.  I tried that for the first time this past winter and my plant started blooming again before going back outside.  That's a great head-start that I've never had overwintering one of those before.  If it keeps looking as good as it did when it went back outside, I should end up with a massive specimen by the end of the outside season.

GG, if you try the Billbergia again, try a spot that is sheltered from most of the rain if you have a spot like that.  I have good results with several kinds of Billbergia in protected spots like that, & a lot more frostbite on more exposed plants.  I was pleasantly surprised to see that they can survive for the 3 coldest months with virtually no water.  I have no scientific evidence but it's logical that if not full of water, being frozen would be less damaging.  Didn't think there would be enough light for blooms where I put them, which was supposed to be temporary at the time, but it has been the past 2 years so I am leaving that patch under a mini garden that has loose brick walls around the legs on 3 sides.  They don't get full of fallen leaves down there.

A radon mitigation system can be installed in existing homes, whether they are 1 year or 80 years old, without tearing up anything. A certified installer will simply test the "communication" of the subbase; meaning how well air can travel under the slab. It does not have to have gravel, or even a gas impermeable membrane to perform. You may wind up with 1 strategically placed extraction point or 3, it will be based on communication testing and the layout of your foundation. The system is based on pressures, which is to say you create a vacuum under the slab, which allows extraction of possibly radon-laced air prior to entering the building envelope.

I renovated my kitchen about nine years ago, and installed a Wolf 48" all gas range (4 burners + griddle) and one Gaggenau electric oven (side opening) and a Wolf warming drawer. But, I have to say that I rarely use the gas oven in my range because it takes significantly longer to heat up and the space is large.  Very large.  It also has no self-clean.  So for everyday cooking I turn to the Gaggenau.  I have been extremely happy with the Gaggenau, and the Wolf despite rarely using the oven (except holidays, big meals with company).  The Gaggenau is particularly easy because I don't have to bend over to move items in and out of the oven. I actually do use my warming drawer frequently to heat dishes, proof dough and keep meals warm when a family member misses a hot meal.  I am very happy my warming drawer is under my wall oven, and not at floor level -- I have the wall oven at counter height, then a drawer underneath for glass baking dishes (about 5" H), then the warming drawer and, at the bottom, another drawer for other baking dishes.  This placement encourages me to use this appliance more frequently because it is not a pain to get to. If I were to do it over again, I probably would not get the range but instead two Gaggenau wall ovens.  I also would likely go with induction because it heats as well or better than gas, and works better at very low temperatures.  I picked the range because of its looks, and at the time there were not any full surface induction tops (i.e., you can move your pots around the surface to heat anywhere vs. one particular place -- that feature was coming out about a year later -- and I have not researched it).

Sean, As an avid golfer, also sometimes golf course landscaper when called upon and having owned property in four different golf course communities .....and at the moment living across from an artificial putting green which allowed me to closely watch its installation several years ago....here are a few thoughts. The putting green holds up well to weather/wildlife. That is not the problem. As you talk with various pros make an attempt to play on one of their putting green products. This is what you are watching for. During installation there will be lots of rolling/smoothing etc. to prepare a proper base for the artificial grass. And, rolling again as it is installed. To the dedicated golfer this is a frustrating situation. Rather than putting 'to the hole' you find yourself putting to correct a poor installation. Hard to explain. Discuss it with installers as you meet with them. This is why you should 'try out' putting greens they have installed. It is an expensive toy!

I would think there is more than lack of insulation creating that much condensation. Any water intrusion will now trickle into a neighbor's unit. I would suspect there is some element of water intrusion to cause water as I also had significant efflorescensce caused by the intrusion and not by lack of insulation.
