Compost is NOT soil! It is only partially decomposed organic matter and while an excellent soil amendment, it is not intended to be - nor does it function well - as a stand alone planting medium. Because it takes years for compost to be fully 'finished', it continues to decompose and you can expect your 12 inches of compost to reduce to somewhere around 6-8 inches over the course of a year and more as time goes on. According to ARS recommendations, an ideal planting soil for rhodies is a 50-50 mix of a mineral based soil and organic matter. The soil itself is less critical than the OM added but a sandy loam seems to be a common feature, likely due to its fast draining characteristics. The OM should consist of some combination of peat moss, pine or fir bark (favored), compost or shredded leaf mold. The peat and bark should insure a desired pH of around 5.5-6.0 (slightly higher is okay).

I can understand your frustration.  With this extremely busy market, I am also limiting my jobs to new construction or whole-house remodels.  It can be difficult to manage a lot of smaller jobs so many designers are focusing on fewer larger jobs.  Another reason is that remodeling is very challenging right now with the supply chain issues.  With some appliances taking up to a year, it can be very difficult to schedule contractors so far out.  And then you have to order and store everything else very far in advance to avoid major price increases.  New construction builds have a much longer timeline so they are a little easier to manage right now. My advice is to be very flexible with your timeline.  If you tell a designer you want it started or done by a certain date, they may not want to take the risk of your job not finishing on time.  Be prepared that a remodel you plan for this year may not start production until next year. Also, a designer may have architectural or structural engineer resources for your ceiling, so start with finding a designer who is experienced in construction design and hold off on contacting architects on your own. Finally, do not get too hung up on finding a designer who has the look you want in their profile. A firm with multiple designers may also be better able to accommodate you.

Avocado is not normally a good bonsai candidate because of its long internodes and large leaves that don't reduce well. This means that to create a believable bonsai specimen with leaves proportionate to the composition's o/a size, the tree would need to be very large. Every tree in a pot (that isn't circling the drain) is a good candidate for full repots which include root pruning; but, the closest thing I saw to mention of bonsai is one posters comment about 'bonsai root pruning'. There is no such thing. Root pruning is root pruning, period. That all bonsai practitioners, having advanced beyond the beginner stage, practice root pruning comes from the knowledge that root congestion can rob a tree of massive amounts of its potential in terms of growth rate, vitality levels, appearance, and yields where applicable. So, root pruning, like dividing, is a practice that will benefit anyone growing any perennial plant in a pot over the long term. Also, I have seen admonitions that a number of particular plants don't like root work. I have never found that to be the case, even for plants said not to tolerate the practice well. Too, it's not necessarily about what plants like; more so, it's about what they need. Root pruning is an essential part of the care regimen of all trees and most other perennials in pots, IF the grower is intent on offering the plants (s)he grows the best opportunity to realize as much of their genetic potential as possible. Planning the repotting/ root pruning sessions for the segment of the growth cycle when the plant is certain to recover fastest seldom leads to issues caused by anything other than inappropriate care during the repotting session. Pam (Gardengal) gave good advice about fertilizing, and I too use Foliage-Pro 9-3-6. She knows that in order to offer precise advice about fertilizing it's essential that the advisor has good knowledge of the medium you use and your watering habits. BTW, Ken - regularly pruning the roots of containerized trees does not keep trees small - just the opposite. If you have 2 trees that are exactly the same genetically and all cultural conditions are equal, the tree that is root-pruned as needed will be many times larger after 10 years than the tree whose roots were ignored or was simply potted up. A full repot (with root pruning) ensures all stress/limitations associated with tight roots is relieved entirely; whereas, potting up is a half measure which ensures the stress of root congestion in the center of the root mass is perpetual, even if the plant is at some point planted out (in the landscape). Living areas above garages are indeed more difficult to condition because they are typically constructed over unconditioned garage bays and have sloped ceiling areas which limit insulation options. On a retrofit basis, you can use injection foam in the joist bays without the need to tear out the drywall.  I suspect your rim joist is poorly air sealed, so insulating that area would be a priority.  You indicated that you have spray foam in the knee walls, but if there are other walls which have batt insulation, make sure they have an air barrier on the back side (plywood, OSB sheathing or house wrap.)  Fiberglass batts don't work well unless air can be trapped in the stud or joist cavity. You'll be more comfortable if you have either a HVAC unit dedicated to the space (mini splits tend to work well in this application) or a multi-zoned central system with the room over the garage controlled by a separate thermostat.

While there are outliers, in general unsanded grout should be used in joints less than 1/8" wide. If your joints are wider, that's a concern. Based on the visible voids and pinholes, it looks like they might have not packed the joints fully, or used too much water in the mix or cleanup. Insufficiently mixing the grout, or not allowing it to slake after mixing, can also cause negative results. Grouting over existing grout, it can be done but it's best done within a couple of days, and only because the joints were raked out too deeply during the cleanup. Grouting ful joints where the grout is cracked might not provide the results you are looking for. The second coat will only be as good as what it's being installed over. And it it's a only thin veneer or schmear, meh. You may end up with a blotchy installation due to one coat here and a second coat over there. It'd have been better worksmanship for them to have caulked and not grouted the seam between the tile and the tub, as well as the other changes-in-plane in the shower; wall-to-wall corners for example. With the cracked tile being close to a corner, there is a chance that there was too much mud buildup in the corners when the backerboard seams were mudded and taped. When the tile was placed there, it might not have been fully bedded in thinset. If the tile is bridging a hollow behind it, it might have cracked (or a stress riser created) when they tapped it down to bed it, or it might have cracked (or the stress riser formed into a visible crack) due to differential bond stresses on each side of the hollow as the thinset cured. Sometimes we've had people pose photos of linear cracks through the tile field, with the cracks located over the seams in the tile backerboard. That's typically an indication that they did not  mud and tape that joints in the backerboard. Differential movement/stresses then cause the cracks in the tile right over those seams. There's still a bit of grout haze showing in a few of the photos. Depending on how well they did the grout cleanup, a hard buffing with a microfiber might take care of that. If it's worse, there are commercial products to help with that. I hope you get it resolved to your satisfaction.

When you use large format tiles, you must have flat walls.  It may be that your wall needed to be rebuilt so that it is flat.  Or maybe the tile setter just did not know what he was doing.  I can see that he did not apply the mortar properly because of the gaps.  90%of the back surface of the tile should be covered, applied with a notched trowel.  The wall is also covered with mortar with a notched trowel and then the tile is pressed into the mortar.  The two surfaces of mortar are stuck together and it would take an effort to pull the tile off.  Yours has gaps that allow you to peek down behind the tile.  Not right. If the wall was not straight, then you should have paid the workers to shim out the studs to get them even, then installed the wall surface.  If you plan to never get those walls wet, it might be okay to put tile on drywall (I am no expert, cannot say for sure).  But, if there is also tile over drywall in your shower, it must be torn out and redone.  Even using basic cement board alone for walls in a shower is wrong.  There are several methods for building a shower, but all of them require a step to waterproof the shower.  Waterproofing can be a sheet of plastic properly installed behind cement board, or a membrane applied according to manufacturer’s specifications, or a surface treatment on top of the cement board like Red Guard, applied to the right thickness and using the right tape over the seams and screw heads, or it can be any one of many products applied correctly.  The reason I bring up shower waterproofing is that tile people who do rotten jobs will often skip the waterproofing or do it incorrectly.  If the guy can’t back butter a tile, can he do waterproofing correctly?

I've in the past when a customer has requested taller worktop height, i've offered 200mm tall legs and plinth and kept standard sized base units at 720mm, but this also keeps the costs down. The other way to add height is to alter the worktop height, with wood worktops a half decent fitter could increase the worktop thickness easily by sandwiching strips underneath so you could have a prep area of raised worktop, for granite and quartz its quite easy to make it look much thicker in fabrication (except for curves) But looking at german kitchens, I sometimes copy Nobilia cabinet sizes, they have XL base cabinet sizes at 792mm tall and then they offer plinth heights of 70, 100, 150 and 200mm, they don't though add extra drawers, but just change the size of the facia's, so in theory you could have a 992 tall unit with a 40mm worktop. The limitations though are the doors available and how much a designer can think outside the box. Many of the doors i use are available in made to measure sizes so i can get my cabinets made to suit and its not as expensive as it sounds. With regards to selling the property afterwards, i go into a lot of kitchens to survey and when i say to clients your kitchen units are high or low they really don't realise, i then explain and show them how a 'standard' kitchen would be and give them the option of keeping the height they're used to, explain how it would look and the options to get it or changing to a 'standard' height. In general, to assure full capture of rising and expanding cooking plumes, one needs an overhead hood with an entry aperture that extends beyond the edges of possible pans used on hobs by the amount of expansion at the height of the hood above the cooktop.  Induction cooking does not relieve one of this necessity, it only relieves one of the extra plume components from gas combustion that rise with the cooking plume. Further, the actual airflow rate must be sufficient to achieve containment of the captured plumes before they can reflect out of the hood.  (See a bazillion threads here on this topic.) Downdraft collectors and pop-up side-draft collectors can only handle very low velocity cooking plumes such as from poaching or other water based light cooking, and maybe low simmering of such as bacon.  Otherwise, the momentum of the cooking plumes is too high to redirect them sideways or force a U-turn.  (See dozens of threads here commenting on this.) Ignoring all this, whether another down-draft or side-draft assembly can connect to the existing ducting depends on details within your cabinetry.  Whether a modern pop-up side-draft unit can work, even ineffectively, with whatever duct size you have would be a question that the installation directions for representative units might answer.  Broan and Wolf make such devices, as I recall, as well as others.

An "up-draft" (hood) is always preferable to trying to collect from the side or down.  Go for a route to the outside if at all possible. For recirculating (ductless), the only model well described here is the VaH ARS.  See https://www.houzz.com/discussions/2347276/vent-a-hood-ductless-ars-range-hood-update#n=65.  Note that unlike these thin under cabinet ductless hoods with some stab at a filtering system, the VaH ARS has a filter pack above the hood in a duct style assembly. I believe Broan/NuTone/Best also have filtering recirculating hoods that should be evaluated for whatever flow and overlap options there are.  I haven't evaluated these or searched out other manufacturers. The disadvantage of even the best recirculating units is less than desirable flow under heavy duty cooking conditions (commercial recirculating is likely an exception).  The advantage is no make-up air is needed to keep house pressure close to the outside pressure.  Window ventilation is desirable for dilution of any gasses that get through the filtering.

A note about the aluminum wiring issue that Austin Air brought up: The big problem with aluminum wiring was connections with outlets and such on branch circuits. Properly installed aluminum wiring when used for feeders generally weren't the issue.  The reason is that the larger feeders connected to lugs that were designed for aluminum wire and were properly cleaned, anti-oxidant applied and the lugs properly tightened. Your electrician can advise you on your panel. If there is aluminum branch wiring you will want to consider replacement. Again - if the wiring to outlets and such are aluminum, that's the highest risk. Aluminum circuits to furnace / water heater / stove / dryer should be inspected at the terminations for overheating / oxidation as well as making sure anti-oxidation compound was used and the lugs are tight.  These circuits are low-moderate risk as long as they were done properly and were not improperly modified. Aluminum wires can not be wire nutted with copper wire as I believe was done on your installation.  Consider replacement of these circuits particularly if any updates / changes are going to be made or have been made. Large aluminum service entrance cables should be inspected at the terminations for signs of overheating / oxidation (aluminum oxide is white) - but service entrance cables are much lower risk because they were typically installed properly. The electrician should also look for anti-oxidation compound and insure the lugs are still tight. Any new circuits - such as the one to your furnace / AC should be done in copper just to avoid issues.

My procedure is to look for any appliance part, electrical or non-electrical, on the open internet. What I have found is that there is no one site to satisfy all needs, every time. I usually determine the correct P/N via the appliance parts sites, then google the P/N and search for the best price. Notice if other sites use a shortened or modified P/N, this may be the common P/N that the part is sold under. Microwaves with exterior venting can help with that as well but I agree, the look is awful, and microwaves sit lower over your stove making it feel like you're cooking in a box. Keep your range where it is. Get an exterior vented hood. Preferably min 600 CFM if it works for you. Put your microwave under counter in the peninsula. Hi Ally, I don't have Caesarstone but 100% feel your pain as we've just been through a very similar situation with Dekton (Cosentino). TBH it's been three months of nightmare as Cosentino claimed there was nothing wrong with it (I'm afraid my opinion of them now is that they are cowboys), but we went through our fitters to get it sorted (which eventually resulted in them refinishing the surface of our worktop). We've now finally been able to draw a line under the whole sorry episode but it's been very stressful. I would advise you to carefully read the Consumer Rights Act and write down all the reasons why your worktop is not satisfactory to you/fit for purpose. To my mind the number one attribute of a kitchen worktop is that it is hygienic and easy to clean, it sounds very much like yours isn't. It also needs to meet the description given in the marketing literature, and again it sounds like that isn't the case. Once you've got your arguments together, contact your worktop retailer in writing. There are template letters available online (Consumer Rights Association website I think). You need to go through the retailer rather than the manufacturer as that's how Act works. Good luck!

Trees shouldn't be watered as frequently as grass so I don't like to have grass immediately around the base of my trees. If you want plants around the tree, they should be planted at the same time, so you don't damage surface roots when the tree becomes more established.  Crape Myrtles prefer full so presumably the plants you choose to go around the tree tolerate full sun but could also tolerate some shade. As the tree grows in size, it will cast more shade. David's Viburnum is an option but you will want to choose based on your climate and exposure.

The tree would be happier without grass up to the trunk. Less human/machinery  interaction and less risk of water/fertiliser/herbicide damage if those are applied to your grass. But there should not be a 'mound' of soil. The bed should be at grade and should not be heaped up against the trunk. if you like mulch do a mulch bed. Or plant the bed with low stuff.

Wood comes from trees, Glass is made with sand, and acrylic (Plexiglass) is a petroleum based product. Oil today is over $100 a barrel... U.S. plastics are mostly from natural gas and not crude oil.  Plastic feedstocks, from both natural gas and crude oil, are by-products and so are only loosely associated with the price of oil and/or natural gas. Also, when there is the least bit of a breeze, air will blow through the fireplace and cause it to smoke and burn erratically. Most see through fireplaces outdoors are relatively useless because of this and people find they can only burn them enjoyably if they have glass doors on both sides and the doors are closed when there is any breeze. So, you loose even more heat, but don't get the smoke. I fully agree with mojavemaria.  UC Verde buffalo grass would be ideal as long as it gets full sun most of the day.  It comes as plugs, not stolons, so you should buy a plugging tool to make your life much easier when you install.  I would not add any topsoil assuming you have adequate drainage away from the house.  If you plant any trees or shrubs between the buffalo and the sun, then the buffalo will die from the shade of the plants, so keep that in mind and don't waste plugs on the north, east, or west side of other landscaping.  Make those areas into garden beds of some sort. I also agree with the rock/stone on the side yard.  Buffalo will not get enough sun to grow on the side and the watering would be a headache.  If you use stone, use a chipped style of stone.  You might drive to the materials lot at Whitewater on I-10 and check out what they have.  I would want something like you see in the upper picture below only smaller (note the quarter in the lower right of the picture.  You can get it much smaller.   Chipped stone will eventually interlock and not slip around like rounded rocks.  I have used the 1/4" chipped stone in landscaping around paver stepping stones. @The Little House 23 I think what you might not be understanding is that "concrete" is actually a formula made from different ingredients, and the actual proportion of those ingredients changes quite a lot from one vendor to another.   If you do not get key aspects of that formula correct, it makes the concrete defective, for almost any application.  For example, the water to concrete ratio is under 35%, the concrete becomes brittle.   If the water to concrete ratio is too high, the concrete becomes porous and has a shorter lifetime. The nature of the failure here suggests the concrete itself was made incorrectly.   So I would spend time finding who made it and what formula did they use.  I suspect that will give you clues.

The points from which leaves grow (nodes) on this plant are extremely close together and the base of the leaves overlap somewhat, so when you remove a dead/dying leaf, part of the proximal part of the leaf (the base) remains attached to the stem and dries up. In both of the images you supplied in your original post, the stem is not exposed. What can be seen is only the persistent vestiges of the proximal ends of the dead or dying leaves, still attached to the stem. When you remove an older leaf by pulling it off (as opposed to removal using scissors, you often expose the proximal end of the leaf/leaves immediately above the one you remove, which will look different because condition under the protective older leaf would have been more moist and shaded from light. The area that appears white and scaly is a combination of dust and mineral residues left behind. It looks like the plant has been outdoors or when you water, water is collecting in the leaf axils (crotch formed by the leaf and stem). As the water evaporates, the minerals that were dissolved in the water are left behind, much like the scale that builds up on a tea kettle over time. I took your original post to mean it was actually the stem that was affected, but the images belie that idea. I don't really see anything I'd be concerned about, but I would plan a full repot (includes bare-rooting, root pruning, and a complete change of soil) sometime just before Father's Day or the Summer Solstice. This Overview of Good Growing Practices should be very helpful. Al

How about I have a 48 and it is too big? Which is the truth. For going on 13 years in 2 houses. The 48 is there for mostly visual appeal. Sure - the large surface is helpful sometimes. But it also means that it is a longer reach for things. Want a frying pan - it is on one end of the range. What if you want it on the opposite end? Need some garlic - that is on the right side. But I want it on the left. Salt shaker, oils etc etc. Behind you - that is probably a sink/DW/trash. Doesn't matter the setup, a larger range makes things you need further away. Admit that the best thing for cooking is a 36 inch cooktop and that you are getting a range because it looks good/cool/impressive. Then realize that the vast majority of people get by with a 36 inch or less. So a 60 inch range is on the large side for practicality for a residential kitchen.

It really depends on how you cook, how many cooks are in the house, the space available, and your budget.  I just looked at the Wolf 60" ranges, and all of them offer 6 burners, with options for charbroilers, infrared griddles and French tops.  All offer 2 approximately 30" ovens.  So what you're getting over a 6-burner 36" range  are the different cooktops and an extra oven.  Only you can determine if that is worth the extra space and cost. As for the 48" ranges, there's more flexibility.  They offer 4, 6 or 8 burners and varying grilles/griddles, broilers, and French top.  There is one small and one larger oven. I have a 6-burner range top and wall ovens, which suits my cooking style just fine.  But we are empty-nesters who entertain mostly on the holidays, and not for very large groups.

FWIW, the term 'range' is believed to come from medieval castle/manor cook zones where there were a swath of hearths to deal with cooking the various menu items at the same time. From a HVAC point of view, please note that no matter the number of burners operating at once, the required air flow into the hood is driven by the highest velocity cooking plume.  Because we can't tailor the hood aperture to what is being cooked and larger cooktops need larger hoods, larger hoods need higher air flow rate (CFM) to meet the air velocity requirement over the entire hood entry area. Along with this hood CFM requirement, there is a matching requirement for make-up air, which may require a complex system, or may only require a simple system, but integrating it in a residence is rarely simple.  So assume that as one grows the cooktop, the HVAC cost growth will continue to be commensurate that of the range cost growth.

We rejected the 48 “ Thermador range because you had to have a griddle, so it still only had 6 burners. And we rented a vacation house that had one, and the griddle was pathetic. We chose a 48” Blue Star, which we love, especially because you can pull off the grate and use a wok! The downside is that the ovens are gas, not electric. If I was more of a baker, I would probably add a wall oven.

Keep in mind that a 48" range will need a 54" hood, and a 60" range will need a 66" hood, and the required ductwork for hoods of either of those sizes, and a makeup air system.  I am saying this in case you have not budgeted for the hood when budgeting for your range.  Also, you will forego the upper cabinets to fit the hood.

Some spouts screw on using tapered pipe threads, some slide on and have an O-ring to seal to the OD of the copper pipe with a set screw to hold the spout in place. I've used both. The O-ring variety is easier, IMO A properly prepared and soldered joint is quite strong. I've tried to unscrew a copper threaded fitting that ended up twisting and breaking off the copper pipe without disturbing the soldered connection. (This was an expansion tank fitting, not a bathtub!) Make sure things are firmly attached inside the wall - use a drop ear elbow that is fully support and securely fixed to the structure. And, you don't need to screw the threaded spouts on super tight - the spout connection doesn't have to resist 100 psi continuous pressure; the pressure it experiences is intermittent and low. Fill the threads with pipe dope and just screw it on until snug and you'll be fine when/if removal time comes.

Just use a tub spout elbow from the mixing valve, not a drop ear elbow that will have another connection.   You can test for leaks at rough-in, then once your surround is done, you just cut it off the proper length. You don't have to worry about a MIP adapter or threaded stub length and maybe unknown surround thickness. Then you can use a slip-on spout, much easier. You don't really ever have to worry about your soldered connection at the mixing valve (or even a male doped fitting), it's the internal pieces of the spout that would ever sieze from long term leaking and mineral build-up, but those are all pretty much plastic and need teflon on any threads anyway.

I have rented a Terramite T5C which is a very small backhoe several times. i also used to own a John Deere 450 which weighed maybe 4 times as much and could lift a yard/ton of dirt in one pass. The Teramite would be very inexpensive it only has about a 20 HP engine but it gets the job done. I used it to dig up my septic drain system and then rebury it. I also used it after we rebuilt our house to connect the down spouts into the existing french drain. I'm thinking you could use it like an excavator to pull up dirt and then move it with the loader bucket. The advantage of it is the rental price. My rental shop still has it, but they're closed, but I think the rental was a few hundred dollars a day. One thing I hated about this machine is every time you go from digging to using the bucket you need to reverse the seat and this machines seat was a hassle to spin around. The John Deere loader had the advantage that you could do the digging and lifting in one pass, assuming your moving dirt in a truck. It will also load any dump truck regardless of its height. Also an advantage is that it has diggers (poking out in front of the loader bucket) A disadvantage is the rental cost. Another is that it's a track machine so does a lot of tearing up the ground and the driveway. The machine I owned was built in the 1960's mine was a JD 450, each time they revised the machine over the decades the added a letter to the model number. JD 450A, JD450B. It's possible you could buy one cheaper than renting one and then sell it for a net zero cost. I paid $7500 for mine. The hardest part of learning how to use these machines is learning how to dig. The backhoe is easy to learn. The loaders you've got to learn to tilt the loader bucket so that it's angled into the dirt as you move forward. I picked up on that when I said how would I do this with a shovel. Angle it into the ground and push with my foot. I think you might be best renting a Track skid loader like the John Deere 317G. Maybe not this machine but something similar hopefully with diggers. I use that as an example as my rental dealer has one on his web page. edit: My dealer delivers and picks up his machines as part of the rental charge.

If this kitchen is the top floor of the house, you can probably vent the hood (or OTR microwave) straight up through the roof. In which case you can put it anywhere. My favorite U layout is sink on the window wall, range on the narrow middle of the U, and fridge at the end of the other long U leg. That gives you the most continuous prep space. A fridge at the bottom midle of the U really chops of the countertop. And it means that the snackers have to cross through the entire prep zone to get their juice or plate of leftovers. Put the fridge at the outer end of the long wall opposite the window. Put your microwave shelf beside it. Snackers can pivot between fridge, microwave, and sink, and never cross into the prep zone between sink and range.

You can start with Goof Off to see if it will remove some of the stain. I refinish wood floors and the norm is that we do not repaint. We don't charge anything for paint and we don't do any painting. It's stated on every proposal. Some refinishers are more tidy than others but it's unrealistic to expect they sand, stain and poly next to adjacent surfaces and not have some transfer. It could have all been masked off at extra expense but stain often gets drawn up behind the tape, necessitating a repaint. Sometimes the finish seems to make the tape stick more aggressively, pulling of paint. To me it comes down to a matter of money. If you have a faux finished surface and masking is more economical we do that (and charge for it). If you're already repainting or having new trim installed (like shoemold) that requires painting after, I wouldn't mask. Since your walls are freshly painted, Goof Off and a touchup will probably suffice. You can use yellow Frog Tape to mask against the floor when painting but follow instructions and don't leave it on too long. When removing it, do so slowly and pull back against the tape rather than pulling up. "I did not want to have to replace the spindles, but since they are now in such bad shape I am wondering if that would be easier/less expensive at this point.." "they could maybe do something where the last couple of feet of supply ducting is a little bit bigger than normal but some kind of insulation would go inside (?) the duct" I have a rooftop packaged heatpump. I can confirm that insulation inside any duct is possible. There's insulation inside the exterior ducts that run between my heatpump and the point where the ducts penetrate the roof to reach the interior.

A few things... - Eliminate straight in line connections. This may sometimes require an extra couple of bends to create offsets. - Insulation within the ducts. - Silencers (e.g., from Fantech) work quite well. - Hang duct w/ perf strapping and don't let duct or fittings come in contact w/ framing or structural members of the house. - Insulation in walls. - Hang drywall w/ iso-channel, or do double layer w/ green glue or use pre-made acoustic drywall. ------------- Also (reduce noise at source!): - Sound damping materials in rooms that will have a lot of noise or that you want to be quiet. - Eliminate parallel surfaces. EG, ceiling sloped 5° so it's not parallel w/ floor. Opposing walls similarly un-parallel by a few °.

These are two sink materials have very different appearances, so aesthetically only you can decide which you prefer.  Fireclay is certainly more beautiful IMHO.  But I like the ease of stainless, and being free of worrying about chips, cracks, wine stains, and boiling water.  Having said that, stainless steel will scratch. To me, it's one more thing to clean, with nooks and crannies, and the rubber feet sometimes come off. If you decide on stainless steel, I would not get the Vigo.  I don't like the Vigo apron front because the front is curved and thick.  The big advantage of an apron front sink is the ergonomics of being able to stand right up against the sink, as opposed to an undermount sink where there is a strip of counter in front, which makes you have to bend slightly which can be uncomfortable over time for some people.  But the Vigo apron front is curved and thick and so defeats the benefit of an apron front sink. If you decide on the stainless steel apron front, I like the Elkay Crosstown EFRUFF3417RDBG.  It is the "taller apron" of 10", 16 gauge stainless steel, and has the corner drain.  Once you have a corner drain, you never go back to a center drain.  Alternatively, I also like the Elkay Crosstown ECTRUF30179RC which has a shorter apron of 6-5/8", and is 18 gauge.  The height of the apron is personal preference and what fits in your kitchen. "1) How long do dry peas and beans remain viable for germination & growth? Will they be reasonably good next season?" If properly dried, placed in an air-tight container, and stored in a cool dry location, beans & peas will have good germination for at least 2-3 years. Some of my saved bean seed still has fair germination even after 6-7 years. If sealed in an air-tight container & refrigerated, the seeds will probably be good until they run out. *** If you use refrigerated or frozen storage, be sure to warm the container to room temperature before opening. Otherwise moisture can condense on the seeds, which will quickly destroy them. The same is true of seed received in the mail during freezing conditions. "2) If I want to save seeds from this year's plants, do I just let the  pods go on maturing on the vines as long as possible or until they are  brown and dry and then shell out the seeds?" If possible, allow the pods to dry on the plant before harvesting for seed. Be sure to keep those pods (and any shelled-out seeds) in a well-ventilated area, to prevent mold. If the seeds have dried for at least several weeks in a low-humidity environment, they can be stored. In a humid environment, the use of desiccant may be necessary for the seeds to reach the proper low moisture level. "3) If I grow several types of peas and their varieties (snow peas/snap  peas/ shelling peas) and several types of beans and their varieties   (Pole beans/long beans)  would they cross pollinate, at least within the  varieties, and the seeds will no longer be predictable?  If cross  pollination is a problem then is there a way to save pea and bean seeds  true to the parent plant?" Beans & peas are both self-pollinating, but different varieties in the same species can cross if pollinators are active. In my experience, that is more likely with peas, perhaps due to their more conspicuous blossoms. You can reduce the chance of peas crossing by staggered plantings, 10-14 days apart, starting with the earliest & working toward the latest. Staggered plantings will work with bush beans too; but that is less effective with pole beans, since they flower over a longer period. For them, the distances quoted by @John D Zn6a PIT Pa will reduce crossing. I've used 20-30' between different pole beans for years, and have had less than 5% crossing (zero the last 2 years). Several other strategies can reduce crossing, such as the use of flowering crops in between, harvesting only pods from the first flowers (when pollinators may have been less active) or harvesting seed only from the center of the row. As a rule, you can assume seed is pure if you grow only one variety of each species. This includes peas (Pisum sativum), common beans (Phaseolus vulgaris), limas (Phaseolus lunatus), runner beans (Phaseolus coccineus), and yardlong beans or cowpeas (Vigna unguiculata). The one caveat is that bees really like limas & runner beans, so if neighbors nearby grow a different variety, those still might cross to a limited degree. @katyajini, I admire the enthusiasm you show in your posts; you should have a great garden this year!

Hi, Dane, I grew up in what is now a 200-year old farm house with similar issues to what you have with yours.  It wasn't in our family for generations.  To have one that has been in your family for five generations is really special. With respect to priorities, I suggest they are twofold:  1.) life safety/occupant health, and 2.) longevity of the structure.  If you've got a new roof and the shell is reasonably weather tight, that buys a lot of time for the structure.  I'd get the whole house professionally re-wired as soon as possible and install smoke detectors to meet current code requirements.  Receptacles can be usually be retrofit without the need to completely remove the wall finishes.  I'm in the keep-the-plaster camp wherever it is feasible. Since you're removing old trim work, I suggest you test the paint and take appropriate precautions if it contains lead.  If it does contain lead, there's no need to panic; you home isn't a hazardous materials site.  It just implies certain care when removing finishes and repainting.

Where does OP say he is removing old trim - refinishing yes, but not removing.  Shellac is easily removed with steel wool + denatured alcohol - there is no need to remove, and in fact its not recommended cos damage to plaster is likely and then you find that getting it to fit back on can be problematic.  Houses move and settle over a hundred years ad the woodwork with move and twist with the house, so you take it off and it might not fit very well back on!  Ask me how I know this LOL. Re electrical, any electrician who knows old houses will not have a problem with plaster and lath still up, and knows how to fish wire through the walls and wont charge more for doing it that way.  You may though want to ask about their old house expertise though before getting quote from them - as you can see from this thread, the guys whose business model is "total gut job" are going to recommend that approach, cos that's what they do and for THEM it may be more time consuming and expensive to take another approach.   It won't be for another guy whose business model is old houses.  Similarly, don't ask a window salesman about how to repair your old windows because they are only going to tell you to get rid of them. If your house is as solid as you say it would be a mistake to totally gut it for no reason. Plaster and lath in good condition is the superior product - soundproof, solid, more insulating.  Your approach doesnt have to be all or nothing - yeah that water damaged ceiling looks pretty nasty so yeah, take that one down and have a drywall ceiling, while doing simple crack repair everywhere else. Finally, there's a lot of old house specific diy videos online -  Youtube (eg plaster and mortar repair, wood finishing, wood rot repair, window reglazing etc.  A lot of this is VERY doable by the average detail oriented home owner!  Time consuming yes, but very rewarding.

Can you support a 10-inch  circular duct?  Or a large enough rectangular duct to be equivalent in pressure loss to a 10-inch round duct?  I can't tell from the drawing where the duct actually is as it follows the "4-inch" wall to the outside. VaH Magic Lung "equivalent CFM" depends on there not being a set of baffles in the hood to degrade conventional blower flow with pressure loss.  However, like the conventional blowers, the VaH blower is susceptible, perhaps more so, to other pressure losses.  These include the duct length and bend pressure losses, and the pressure loss from imperfect MUA.  (Even a screened window has a pressure loss as an MUA source.) 42 x 27 = 1134sq. in. (counting what is likely a control surface and not intake aperture) = 7.9 sq. ft. One would like to achieve 90 CFM/sq. ft. or 710 CFM.  If you do a good job on the MUA and the ducting, particularly the turn, your VaH may achieve close to this flow rate.  Note that this hood's spec sheet shows that you will need to limit the static pressure loss to about 0.2 inches of water column to meet this actual flow rate.  Your HVAC person will need to evaluate whether your actual ducting, along with the performance of your selected MUA system, causes the house to outside differential pressure to stay below this value. MUA is a separate system.  It takes outside air from somewhere, such as the roof, and injects it into the kitchen space or some space connected to the kitchen.  It will likely require filtering of dust and bugs, and heating.  If the household has no combustion appliances that take air from any space connected to the kitchen, then a passive (no blower) design might (!) be adequate.  Otherwise, it requires a blower (active MUA) that roughly approximates the hood blower in putting air into the house to replace that which is removed.  With the VaH, I would plan on the strong possibility of requiring an 'active' MUA system. Please review a number of MUA threads here, including those in @opaone's links.

You do NOT want trees right next to your house. First, the roots can cause damage to the foundation. Second, detritus from leaves and twigs will accumulate on your roof. There are tall shrubs you could use on the corners, but many are also wide. I can't tell how wide your current bed is, but you may need to widen it. If a shrub is expected to mature at 5' wide, you need a 5' wide bed with the shrub planted 2 & 1/2' from the house. Regardless, a wider bed also allows you room for low edging shrubs or perennials. Remember that all new plants will be small when first planted. Fill in behind and around them with annuals until they get established. Evergreen azaleas have more sun tolerant varieties, but they are only reliably hardy to zone 6, whereas deciduous azalea varieties are hardy to zone 4. Below is how I would redo this bed. Okay... Can it be done? Yes, anything CAN be done. Can it be done at anything like a reasonable cost? Probably not. Even if that's not a load bearing wall you will be into significant construction on the floor below and even more so on the floor above. Depending on how the floor joists are oriented you are also looking at bulkheads, etc.

Even if that's not a load bearing wall you will be into significant construction on the floor below and even more so on the floor above. Having had the significant pleasure of plumbing several 3 story, townhouses one summer, I submit it is difficult to make a guess on this.  For all we know that wall is running parallel to the joists and sitting over a garage/utility space .  So this could be a massive problem or nothing big at all. The townhouses we did were ground floor utility room, garage and storage.  This was over the living area, with the sleeping area above that.  Because the townhouses were rather narrow and long, the load bearing walls were the common walls and the plumbing wall was parallel to the joists.  Moving the plumbing in those townhouses would be easy, as you could just run them in the joist cavity towards the common wall.  You would have to put some type of pipe chase in but that could be as little as 6" deep.  Since it was over a utility room the work below would be no big deal.

(the plywood base) To attach the slats, you'll want to 'fir' out that plywood so that slats can be anchored to them.  As stated, run the fir out supports vertically, properly spaced. (you'll want to figure out the lengths you're using, and place your vertical slats to coordinate and add proper support and symmetry. It is hard to tell from your photo if it just callused or if there is some rot. When cutting, you should make sure you cut all rot off. Best is to keep cutting off slices until the flesh is of uniform color - no black spots/lines remaining. Then it needs to callus - for how long depends on thickness of the plant; how much moisture is in it; temps where the plant is. It may help to dust lightly with a fungicide (sulfur; or ground cinnamon), may not be needed. Usually, few days is enough. Pot up in well draining mix. I would not water until there are roots forming - usually new growth starts by then. But at least 1week. That worked for me in the past. After, start watering as any other succulent.

Looks like you've got a pachycereus marginatus there. The rot may have stopped, but it may be worth cutting again, with a sharp, sterilised blade, approx 2-3" above the current cut. I'd then lay it on it's side for about a day in an area that receives gentle but consistent airflow to encourage the callous to form. Then stand it back up, on top of a dry, very gritty mix and give it as much bright indirect light as you can. Bonus points if you can increase the rH to between 50-75% (this will aid in rooting generally speaking but it's not necessary). The humidity portion is also only helpful if you can maintain some airflow. Stagnant humidity will aid bacteria/fungal growth more than your cactus. From there it's a waiting game. These cacti are generally very hardy and prolific, but yours has had a go of it already so you've got to keep in mind that it's not starting from the most optimal conditions. I've no doubt you'll be able to turn it around, but it will take some time and extra attention until it gets reestablished. Try not to jostle it or constantly pull it up to check and see if it has roots. If after about a week and a half to two weeks it seems stable (as in it hasn't wrinkled super dramatically and the rot hasn't moved further up the cactus) you could try lightly watering or spraying the soil near the base of the cactus. This bare amount of moisture can assist some baby roots that may be poking out or encourage some if none have started yet. It can be tricky though because moisture is exactly what the fungi and bacteria associated w/ rot also love, so try to avoid getting the base of the cactus wet if you do choose to add some moisture. You can also just wait and hope the cactus throws some roots out in search of moisture. Good luck.

In years past I volunteered with my local Habitat for Humanity affiliate and removed materials for reuse. At this time, they no longer have an established program for reclaiming material but they will accept donated wood after nails have been removed. The website GPAElgin.org has a section with many preservation articles including a link to a method for removing flooring. If you work carefully you shoud be abe to get 90% usable boards. You coud even reinstall the boards in your house and buy extra boards to fill in closets or reinstall in a smaller area.There are a couple different approaches but most important is finding the direction because it is removed starting with the last installed board. Be warned that it is possible that the direction switches, often in hallway or closet. Start the project by setting a saw to 3/4 depth and cut down the midde of a row then pull the pieces out. My preferred method was using at least two prybars and forcing them under the boards unti the nails start to loosen. I have also used wood wedges for this step. Loosen the entire width of the flooring before starting to remove any boards. Once I get going, I usually just force the prybars in by hand rather than hammering. Be careful not to use too much force or go too quickly or you will end up breaking the tongues off. Use each row to loosen the next so after removing the boards it is easy to get under the next row. Put the boards behind you until you have a good quantity then switch modes and move the boards to your processing area. Next step is removing the nails which is quite a bit of work but essential to manage moving and storing. Try to hammer the nails back through the tongue and grab them with round nose pliers and use the board edges for leverage to get the nails out. When you have enough boards put them up on saw horses in sets. I use four boards wide and three rows high, long boards on the outsides, fill in middle with short ones. Force the boards tightly together and shrink wrap the bundle.  Stack bundles flat on top of boards or bricks for air circulation.  If you get the bundles tight you can move them easily without the boards shifting or falling out.

Was the pool filled with a garden hose or was water trucked in? We truck water in on every job. Filling the pool quickly is the best way. Was any sequestering agent added during the fill? Was the water chemistry checked and balanced daily for 2 weeks after fill? The first 72 hours after filling is paramount regarding properly balancing the water. The pool must be brushed twice a day for two weeks. More brushing is even better. The plaster takes 28 days to fully cure. No salt can be added for at least that time. It's recommended to even wait a season prior to firing up a salt system. No auto cleaners or wheeled vac heads for the same time period or longer if you can. Acid should always be diluted with the pool water and poured in the deeper section uniformly. Straight acid is heavier than water and can go directly to the surface and cause damage. For now, have your water professionally tested. Keep your chlorine at zero if you can. If you really need to add chlorine, add liquid and keep a low residual. pH and Total Alkalinity should be 7.2-7.6 and 100 PPM respectively. Any higher on either can cause scale. Calcium Hardness max 400 PPM. Also, any higher will create scale. Using a scale remover/controller either Jack's Magic products or Easy Care Beautec. The plaster is not fully cured so some of the color variations may disappear over time and become uniform. Your not the only one with this issue. Most of the time it's caused by improper start up procedures and mismanagement of chemistry. Sometimes plaster crews add too much calcium in their mix and it causes discoloration. The French Gray and other colors that are dark or darker, tend to have color variations.

We did one in Ohio for my mother. These are governed by state jurisdiction. We used an attorney who did hundreds of these, and I want to say it cost us about $3,000, and was a very efficient process. The basic gist is that in exchange for footing the bill for nursing home care (which was $8k/month in my mother's case), the government will take ownership of whatever estate remains in place at the time of the person's death. The funds remain in the individual's accounts -so my mother's credit union and savings and checking looked just like they always did, and she had full access to them. She/we were allowed to use those funds to provide for her care for the remainder of her life. These expenses could include all living expenses, travel, a new computer or tv, etc. The only real restriction is that the person cannot give the money away as gifts (including paying for grandchildren's college bills, etc.).

If I understand the planned design, the spa is under water as part of the pool level? While it is a nice, sleek look, there is only one way to truly separate the spa from the pool when in the spa mode using this design. Builders have installed a collection tank that allows the water level to drop down below the rim of the spa, so it can run and heat independently when set is SPA. Otherwise, your just heating the water from the pool and the spa together, and it won't reach temperature. The collection tank must be sized accordingly to handle the volume of the water needed to drop down to the spa level. It's a tricky set up and a lot of calculations are required. There is additional plumbing and pumps to make this happen. Plus and additional structure of gunite must shot, or a fiberglass tank must be used. Consider a perimeter overflow spa that is set 2"-3" above the pool water. The top is constantly wet and provides a nice look. And, you can heat the spa independently without the worries of interference of the pool water.

Yes. First, it is never suggested to fertilize something newly planted. The plants are already under stress from transplanting and will not assimilate the added nutrients properly. Second, it is also never recommended to amend an individual planting hole, Use the indigenous soil only....what comes out of the hole is all that goes back in. Use any amendments instead as a top dressing. Finally, fertilizer spikes of any kind are hugely inefficient. They concentrate nutrients to a specific point rather than distribute them throughout the root zone where the feeder roots can properly access them. If you have them, you can use them but grind them up first and then sprinkle on the soil surface around the drip line. But wait to do so until next spring.

Yep!! The tree roots will not stay within the original planting hole anyway so what is the point of amending it? It affects water percolation and drainage, doesn't help with establishment and can actually impede or delay proper establishment, so just don't do it :-) But I would take the time to remove all the weeds, grass and other stuff growing there and then mulch well after planting to make sure  they don't immediately overtake the new young tree. The attention to weeding and mulching (and watering) in its first year is far more important to the long-term health of the tree than any amending or fertilizing will accomplish!

If there are still parts of the plant that have heathy, green, firm leaves and trunk, it may still recuperate, but it's going to take some time to recuperate from the damage. I agree with what was said immediately above. Don't try to 'pep it up' by fertilizing until it is pushing new growth. It's highly likely the plant will eventually straighten out (if you provide the cultural conditions it likes). It likes temps in the 70s (Fahrenheit), very bright light (but acclimate to any VERY bright spots gradually over a 2 week span), regular fertilizing (Foliage-Pro 9-3-6 is a superb fertilizer for ficus and nearly all other houseplants), and you would do well to monitor moisture levels deep in the pot by using a wooden tell. If the pot is less than 5" deep, do not trust the advice to 'water when the top inch or two of the soil feels dry to touch', as it is little more than directions on how to chronically over-water. More about making/using a 'tell' below. This is especially important while the plant is essentially leafless. This short piece re How to Care for Ficus in Containers over the long term should prove very helpful. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source – photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water – so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16” (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48” (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Best luck ..... any other questions? Al

It appears to be gray, but, it doesnt look like caulk to me, it looks like grout, and it should never have been grouted, it should have been caulked.  All that has to be picked out of there, before you can redo it.  You want to use a caulk with silicone in it.  If any part of what you need to be caulked is also painted, you need a caulk with silicone that can be painted.  It will say paintable on the tube.  Buy the best quality caulk, you can find.  It will be less work in the long run.  Please post pictures here in the comments, and take more of them, so we can see the entire area.

It looks like someone tried to caulk over a grouted corner. You should scrape out what you can of the grout in there - get a tool with a sharp point and scrape it out (it won't be easy) . Rub your fingers down the tiles to remove the light strip of caulk that IS on the tile - like dried glue. Then get a good silicone based caulk in a fairly light gray. When clean and dry, tape down each side of the corner about 1/8" from the corner.  Press and seal the edge of the tape (blue painters). Run your caulk bead down between the tape - using a pretty small tip. I use a popsicle stick to then "tool" the caulk (you may remove quite a bit if you made the hole too big in the tube) .  if you do it right, you can have one smooth motion - keeping the stick at the same angle.  The key to a clean job is to match the curvature of the popsicle stick as closely as possible to where the tape edge is - that will give you a straight, smooth, perfect line. Remove tape and let harden.

Any name brand silicone caulk will do - and get paintable if you want - but you don't need it in a shower corner.  ;-) If you tape and use the dry tooling - you can be a pro with practice.  ;-) . That method provides a much crisper caulk line than the "wet your finger and smooth" approach.

14" is a major blunder. I hear similar stories like this and it just amazes me. This is poor or lack thereof, communication with the excavating crew and the PB's site supervisor or project manager on proposed finished depth. No blame on shotcrete crew as they shoot only what they are given. Any additional concrete for those areas must be reinforced with rebar or the new pour will definitely crack. The structural engineer should be involved to recommend the correct schedule of steel, size and the layout. Generally, thicknesses over 6", should be reinforced. Pouring concrete from a mixer is acceptable provided the surface is Saturated Surface Dry, SSD. It's wet to the point where it's not puddling, but wet enough to accept new material without pulling the moisture/water from the new pour. To me, too bad it costs extra to shoot the material rather than pour it. The builder is responsible for the correction at his expense. I would insist on shooting the material as it is applied at a high velocity ensuring proper bonding. Also, the new rebar should be bonded electrically with the original rebar. In order to achieve this, at least one spot of the original rebar must be exposed to secure a bond clamp which in turn can be bonded to the new rebar with a #8 copper wire. This is per NEC Code section 680. Hopefully this information is helpful and resolves the issue.

The size fuses you can use depend on the wire size.  Fuses typically have a number indicating the amperage, and are color-coded, too. But even if you had markings on the existing fuses, it's no guarantee that they were the right size.  Sometimes people replaced fuses with ones that were larger so they could run more stuff without the fuse blowing. Unfortunately, overloading a circuit like that can cause a fire. If there is no marking/label on the box or the 2 blocks that you pulled, the only safe thing to do is have an electrician or a knowledgeable friend take a look and determine the wire gauge of the circuits coming into the fuse box, which would then allow you to determine the maximum size fuses you can safely use.  If you can post a couple of closeup pictures of what you are dealing with -- the fuses, the blocks, and the box itself -- it may help you get some additional comments. By the way, 60A are rather large fuses, and since this is likely an old fuse box, they may or may not be oversized for what you have depending on which positions they would occupy.

My 1895 vintage house had a fuse box with two 60 Amp cartridge fuses, one for each leg of the 240-Volt service. There were 6 15A screw fuses and two larger ones (I don't remember what size) for the 240V DHW heater. 60A meter panel. (There was another, abandoned empty fuse box).

Kudzu has it right: Typical was 60 amp mains and 30 amp for the range or water heater. The amp rating was generally on the metal parts of the fuse also. If you find an amperage rating on the fuses and they match the typical, I'd say you were safe. That said, the only way to know for sure is to have someone determine what size the wire is. Another option is the Ottomanson Softy Stair Treads, which are made of soft, low-pile nylon and have a non-slip backing. I believe that is White Fantasy quartzite.  There is a granite called White Fantasy, but it does not look like that.  With quartzite, it is hard to know whether it is true quartzite, or whether it will behave more like marble in the way of etching and staining.  Some quartzites like Taj Mahal are impervious to etching, staining and scratching. You would need to test it first.  Get a sample, and drip some lemon juice or vinegar on it, and see if it etches.  If you cannot bring home a sample, try scratching the edge of one of the slabs with a knife.  Real quartzite will not scratch or will perhaps have a faint scratch.  But marble will scratch easily, as it would as your counter when you drag a plate across it or similar.  If it shows itself not to be true quartzite, then it is up to you whether you want to live with a more marble-type of stone. Here is a pic of White Fantasy granite:  Edited to add:  if that OP slab is more of a marble, your stoneyard's recommendation to "seal every 2-3 years" is complete BS.  It would need to be sealed minimum once a year, and more like twice a year.  Furthermore, sealing protects against staining, but not etching.  Between that BS recommendation, and telling you the stone is granite when it isn't, I would find a different stoneyard.  This one seems sketch.

I would do your research and understand what you’re getting.  It’s highly unlikely that it is granite (no such thing as soft granite, slab yards often misidentify their inventory) but more likely marble.  I recommend researching the difference between marble, granite, and quartzite (many marbles are also referred to as soft quartzite and again, no such thing).  There are some great stone threads on here tyat explain the difference.  If it’s a marble, as I suspect, it may etch, which sealing won’t protect you from.  It’s best to get a sample of the slab and test it. Stone identification resource thread from a geologist

Welcome to the Hell named Paint!  Your problem is it's definition. That could very well be Believable Buff.  Colors change in different lighting and sometimes just the orientation of the light.  If this is a pro-photo, as it seems to be, it will also be "processed" and the color you see is in fact different.  When we all look at even the same color over the internet, we are rarely actually seeing the same color - monitors are just that different from each other in how they portray color.  That's why questions like yours are difficult to answer.  The color they used may not be the color you need to produce the same effect as shown in the photo you're looking at. I am repainting with SW Steamed Milk.  I put a test patch on a wall, stood in the same room with the same lighting a few feet from the wall, held the chip in my hand and swore it was a different color.  Walked the chip up to the test patch and it was the same.  Color can vary by time of day and location in the room. Start by getting chips. Yes, you can grow ES hydrangea in full sun under the right conditions. It is not the summer sun they mind as much as the heat.  In direct sun with the heat, they will likely wilt during the day and perk back up in the evening. A little bit of that kind of stress won't hurt them much as long as you are not in drought conditions. The red leaves may be a feature of the particular cultivar you have. Some of them do have a reddish tint to them that can be highlighted due to environmental conditions. Planting any shrub too close to the house is bad form and not a wise move. Limelight is a much larger shrub than an ES hydrangea and not likely to be a good alternative for most foundation plantings. Your biggest problem with a H. macrophylla cultivar in your zone is going to be late spring freezes. If they break dormancy in an early warm spell and then get frozen to the ground, you will lose that year's bloom. They bloom on older wood and don't have enough time to regrow and bloom in one season of growth. In my southern zone 6 that warm then back to freeze cycle is common and H. macrophylla to a large extent have one good bloom year out of four. The key is they cannot get frozen after breaking dormancy in the spring.

One of the key attributes of many tropical plants is big, bold foliage and there are a number of quite hardy zone 7 plants that can help promote that look: hardy bananas, Fatsia japonica, gunnera, rodgersia, Phormium tenax, Lobelia tupa, palms, hardy ginger and even a number of larger ferns. I'd add cannas to the mix, although they will need to be dug and stored for winter. Adding annuals/non-hardies like castor bean, brugmansia (will need winter storage), datura, dahlias, lilies and other summer blooming bulbs, begonias, cerinthe (honeywort) and coleus should provide a lot of tropical looking color.

After 35 years of gardening in TN between Nashville and Chattanooga, the following perennials did well for me and others. Dwarf palmetto, needle palm, Japanese fiber banana, canna, butterfly ginger, elephant ears, yellow groove bamboo, and yellow brugmansia. I see you have a gas stove.  Whenever you are using it, you are burning fossil fuels inside your home.  If you're not using your exhaust, you are polluting the inside of your home.  Opening doors and windows doesn't necessarily fix that, or at least not as well as a vent fan does.  That fan is probably rated at 650 CFM, which means it's designed to move 650 cubic feet per minute of air.  that would replace all the air in a medium kitchen in about 2 minutes.  They are also designed to be turned on just before cooking, so you establish a stream of air right from your stove up through the vent.  Opening a door or window will just push that dirty air throughout your house. That being said, if you had an electric or induction cooktop, you could do without a vent fan, but you still wouldn't want to, and it may be against code.  They help removing moisture, odors, the occasional smoke from even a sautee.  I would leave it alone or get a different style hood, although I personally think your hood is a nice one.

Yes, your kitchen would definitely look ligher and more open without a heavy island hood. When you are ready for a more extensive remodel, consider moving the cooktop to the wall cabinets, and the sink to the island. Better sightlines, and people sitting at the bar benefit from being close to the water, not the flames.

Gas cooking has been more and more in the news due to the indoor pollution it creates. Nitrogen dioxide is the main culprit and I'd be using that exhaust fan even if I was boiling water for a cup of tea. Airborne food particulates are their own source of health problems, and direct ventilation to the out of doors is a must for your health due to the fuel plus food vapors . Long term effects are not fully understood, but the gas alone can be a lung and eye irritant, and the NO2 travels throughout the home. Some references state that the indoor pollution levels created by gas stoves would be illegal if the levels were outside (no one regulates indoor air quality).

Heat and moisture naturally move upwards.  I've never run across an oven that vented the baking cavity from the bottom.  That is not to say they don't exist but it would need to be fan-forced to make the air move against its natural inclination.  A fan to cool electronics is a different thing, it does not vent the oven cavity. Citing the specific model involved would be helpful.

Your plumber is right, turn the setpoint down.  What's happening is you're turning down the hot flow so much to reduce the temperature to what you want at the faucet or shower that the tankless may turn off.  It requires a specific volume of water flow through it to activate and stay on.  Turning down the set temperature will allow you to run *more* hot water flow (which is at at a lower temperature) so the tankless stays on. I set mine at 103°F to 105°F as the "normal" temp for showering so that I run ONLY hot water at the faucet with no cold water mixed in.  Never had a shower go cold in 17+ years of having the tankless unit.  Mine is easily accessible in a broom closet in my laundry room so I can easily raise it temporarily for dishes or washing clothes (I never wash clothes in cold water).  If yours isn't as accessible for adjustment then you'll need slightly higher temps as I said above.

These protruding growths appear to be galls, rather than symptoms of oedema. There was another recent thread I noticed that had images showing similar growths on the leaves, which I also believe was misdiagnosed as oedema, but I lost track of it before I could comment. More often than not, galls on leaves as a result of egg-laying or feeding activity of insects which feed on sap, but many gall types are caused by bacteria, fungi, or nematodes. While unsightly, the issue is usually more about aesthetics than actually injury to the plant. On the off-chance it is oedema, here is something I wrote that should help you prevent recurrence: Oedema Oedema (aka edema) is a physiological disorder that can affect all terrestrial plants. It occurs when the plant takes up more water than it can rid itself of via the process of transpiration. The word itself means 'swelling', which is usually the first symptom, and comes in the form of pale blisters or water-filled bumps on foliage. Under a variety of circumstances/cultural conditions, a plant's internal water pressure (turgidity) can become so high that some leaf cells rupture and leak their contents into inter-cellular spaces in leaf tissue, creating wet or weepy areas. Symptoms vary by plant, but as the malady progresses, areas of the leaf turn yellow, brown, brown with reddish overtones or even black, with older damage appearing as corky/ scaly/ ridged patches, or wart/gall-like bumpy growth. Symptoms are seen more frequently in plants that are fleshy, are usually more pronounced on the underside of leaves, and older/lower leaves are more likely to be affected than younger/upper leaves. Oedema is most common in houseplants during the winter/early spring months, is driven primarily by excessive water retention in the soil, and can be intensified via several additional cultural influences. Cool temperatures, high humidity levels, low light conditions, or partial defoliation can individually or collectively act to intensify the problem, as can anything else that slows transpiration. Nutritional deficiencies of Ca and Mg are also known contributors to the malady. Some things that can help you prevent oedema: * Increase light levels and temperature * Monitor water needs carefully – avoid over-watering. I'd heartily recommend a soil with drainage so sharp (fast) that when you to water to beyond the saturation point you needn't worry about prolonged periods of soil saturation wrecking root health/function. Your soil choice should be a key that unlocks the solutions to many potential problems. * Avoid misting or getting water on foliage. It slows transpiration and increases turgidity. * Water as soon as you get up in the AM. When stomata close in preparation for the dark cycle, turgidity builds. If you water early in the day, it gives the plant an opportunity to remove (for its own needs) some of the excess water in the soil. * Put a fan in the room or otherwise increase air flow/circulation. Avoid over-crowding your plants. ********************************************************************************* Limiting how much water your planting can hold can go a long way toward preventing poor root function, root diseases, and physiological disorders like oedema. Compare B to A below to see how simply tipping your pot after a thorough watering can significantly reduce how much water the planting can hold. Figure % illustrates how valuable over-turning an empty pot in the bottom of the main container can be when it comes to reducing water retention.  Also, if the planting is of manageable size, you can eliminate ALL excess water using this simple maneuver, which puts Newton's First Law of Motion to work: Newton's First Law For conventional container culture, it's a given that saturated/partially saturated media rob roots of the oxygen they need to function normally and efficiently. At best, soil saturation robs your plants of immense measure of potential in areas like growth, appearance, yields, ….. At worst, plants unable to cope with the strain of drought stress caused by saturated media  will succumb to it. This isn't a 'scare tactic, it's a very simple and straightforward observation that will be difficult to disagree with a straight face. Newton's First Law of Motion states that an object will remain either at rest, or in motion at a uniform rate and in a straight line unless acted upon by an external offsetting force. In this case, we will designate the 'object' as excess water in your potting medium. At risk of my being redundant, the 'law' can be seen as a simple statement about inertia, that objects will remain in motion and in a straight line unless a force acts to change the motion. To put the law to work for you/your plantings, you should water to beyond the point of total soil saturation - so the medium has been completely saturated and at least 15-20% of the water you have applied has exited the pot. Unless your soil is purposefully constructed to eliminate all/nearly all excess water, it's extremely probable, when the pot has stopped draining, there will be too much water in the potting medium for the plants' liking. To eliminate this excess water: immediately after a thorough watering, hold the pot in one hand over the sink, lawn, or over-sleeping significant other and move it downward, then sharply reverse the direction to upward. You'll immediately note that a good measure of 'excess' water will “continue downward in a straight line” and exit the drain hole. The sharper the reversal of direction, the more water exits the drain hole. When you have repeated the exercise until water no longer exits the drain hole on the reversal of direction, you will have eliminated all excess water and your plants will regard you with a newfound sense of awe. Never water houseplants according to a schedule :-) Water only as required and that can vary widely by plant type, soil media and the size of the container. The best way of determining when to water is by using a 'tell' or a long wooden skewer that you can insert down into the base of the container. If it comes out completely dry, it's time to water. If it comes out with some soil granules attached, keep an eye on it and evaluate again in a couple of days. If it comes out damp or with the soil firmly attached, wait to water until it dries. btw, you will get much more detailed info if you were to post your question in the subject appropriate forums.....like the House Plants, Container Gardening or Foliage Plants forums. The two you picked are very generalized, catch-all forums that rarely get attention from the serious gardeners.
