That didn't happen in a couple of days from over-watering or poor drainage. I too, suspect chill injury as the underlying cause as the symptoms are classic It helps to know where you live ...... or at least a large city near you. Was it carried from the store w/o the minimal protection of a bag covering the foliage, or carried to a cold car? Plant's needn't be subjected to freezing temps before chill injury occurs. It can occur at temps as high as 50* if the drop in temperature is sudden enough. Al

There's only one degree of dead, so if it's no longer viable, it's sure to stay that way. OTOH, the woody parts of plants are better able to handle cold than the roots and foliage. It's a good bet the duration of the too cold temps was short enough that the root/soil mass was largely unaffected. If the tree has enough energy to push a new flush of growth to where some of the new leaves are able to reach about 75% of their maturity (the break-even point where the leaves are able to create more food/energy than they are using to grow), the tree should recover to the degree that the only thing you'll have to remind you of the set-back is the memory.  Even if the upper part of the trunk has been damaged, the plant should come back from the base. There are 2 things that should be mentioned. The first is, be sure you monitor soil moisture levels carefully. 1) The tree will use only a fraction of the amount of water you might expect it to because transpirational water loss w/o leaves will be almost nil. DAMP or MOIST are the operational words, and there should be no room for WET or SOGGY. 2) If the growing tip of the main stem has lost viability, you might get several branches competing for position as the new leader. Your decision then will be whether or not you want a tree with a single trunk or a clump with a number of trunks. If you want a single trunk, rub off the unwanted sprouts as soon as they occur, which will force the tree to expend all its energy on the trunk you choose. Al Al

The "pure" Gallicas (those that do not have a lot of China genes in them) are extremely Blackspot resistant. In fact, I have never seen Blackspot on any of the true Gallicas. 'Charles de Mills' does not Blackspot. It mildews on new growth later in the season, but its rare to have a serious case of it. The Hybrid Gallicas - like 'Cardinal de Richelieu'  - are much more likely to suffer from Blackspot, but fortunately there aren't a lot of those. Its a shame that "Chucky M" is such a bully in the garden - I think this variety is the clear winner in terms of suckering. It has the ability to take over vast volumes of real estate if left unchecked. Plan to have a root barrier or some alternative, to keep it in bounds. One of the pieces of it I planted in 1999 has now expanded to a thicket about 30 X 30 feet, and still going. You've been forewarned. All of that aside, its one of the most exquisitely shaped of the whole OGR family of roses.

The mosaic will conform to the slope. Balance the layout to the walls and cut the tiles to meet the drain grate. I suggest pre cutting the entire shower floor before mixing the setting mortar. This will allow you to concentrate on the installation and decrease the concern of the mortar skinning over while making cuts. (Sorry this is a long...and involved story.) When I lived on the bayou, I raised and released several raccoons.   I rehabbed wildlife, but I preferred possums and armadillos, because they aren't territorial and easier to release.   Plus, there were already so many raccoons there.   My partner did the raccoons.   She was out of town and a new baby came in, and so I took it, and decided to go ahead and raise it.   The baby wasn't newborn, but she didn't have her eyes open yet.   I had trouble getting her to take a bottle.   I had a dog that had puppies about a year previously. I found the dog dumped out on the highway, and knew she had puppies, but none with her.   I saw her for a couple of days, and I felt bad for her, and I brought her home.   Later I found out she had belonged to the hog hunter down the road from me.   He got her to hunt hogs, and she wouldn't hunt.   He hauled her off and dumped her.   She had pups, and he stomped them and threw them in the bayou.  (More about Karma in a minute....) So I put the dog in the box with the baby raccoon and let it nurse her...of course, she had no milk, but then the baby would take the bottle.   After a few days, her milk came back in, and she raised the baby coon.   The coon never bonded with me...but she did bond with the dog.   The raccoon...that I just called Baby Coon, lived in my house for two years.   She slept on the top shelf in my closet, which I emptied out and gave to her.   At least she used a litter box.   I tried several times to release her....put her outside, but she wouldn't go.   She would sit in the window and look out a lot though.   So, one day I unlatched the screen and pushed her out.   She did come around to the back door and came back in, but after a couple of days she decided she liked being outside.   Plus, I put out food for the raccoons, and she had what the rehabbers would refer to as a "soft release".    She wasn't taken to a strange (to her) place and dropped off.   She blended in with the others and that was that. Before the baby coon was weaned though, the hog hunter stole the dog and hauled her off.   I looked for her for two days.   I put it on Facebook, asking for people in the area to look for her.  Miraculously, someone did find the dog (Tricia), and I (and Baby Coon) went to get her, and all was well. He is also the person who stole my pet hog and sold her.   That was Piggy Sue that I often had mentioned here.   I had raised her and had her spayed.   She was very tame and a big pet.  When they went to weigh her, she got away from them, and they shot her, which I am glad of, because she was very sweet, and had never been mistreated, and I would rather she have a quick end, than be subject to more stress and cruelty.   I didn't find this out for a month, but when I did, I went to the hog buyer and he told me about it. Anyway....Karma.    The guy went to work for a ranch in Bellville.   He was an alcoholic and always doing stupid things.   He decided to ride his horse into the house.   His girlfriend got mad at him.   So he came back in, and they got in an argument.    Being hot headed, and stupid, he punched the glass door, and his arm went through, and cut an artery in his arm pit, and he bled to death before they could get him to a hospital. The problem with humidification is that the indoor relative humidity is a function of both the evaporation rate of the humidifier and the air infiltration (leakage) rate for the home.   Under conditions where the outdoor air is cold and doesn't contain much moisture and the air leakage rate is high, your humidifier may not be able to move the r.h. needle.   I suspect that's what is happening.   If you know the air changes per hour from a blower door test, and the evaporation rate (flowrate supplied to the humidifier minus the flowrate of the water going down the drain) you can run the numbers and determine if that's indeed the case.

That sure doesn’t look like any soapstone I’ve ever seen.  Soft soapstone can scratch, but unless serously/purposely gouged, should not develop such deep scratches wide enough to collect crud. Our soapstone counters are 6 years old, show no evidence of any wear and tear.  It is a very hard variety called, Belvedere. "The electrician put the fridge outlet directly behind where the fridge is" This is correct. I checked the spec sheets for three refrigerators. Depending on the appliance, a 1-2" gap behind the refrigerator is required. There will be space for the cable and plug in this gap. Don't get a recessed outlet; there won't be room for the cable with its 90-degree prongs in the recess.

In the case of surface conduit and a metallic box, one might be able rotate the box so that it puts the receptacle to one side.  Then one would only have the box width taking up wall gap space, and that should be close to the desirable 2-inches for the rest of the area behind the fridge. Some conduit offset increase may be needed.

"No, why do you ask?" Because unless conduit is required or it's a brick wall, the obvious answer is to put the outlet IN the wall - not outside it. I've wired several plaster homes from the 1880's to the 1940's and NEVER had to run wire on the outside of the wall or demo the plaster.

The 200amp service for the entire building is probably misunderstood. No way could 12 furnaces, water heaters, refs, microwaves, and/or toaster ovens work on 200amps. You probably have a 200amp service for common areas for the building, and each unit has their own service of 100amp (maybe 60amp if old). The basement flooding issue is a localized one. Certainly climate change causes more severe storms, but that issue is still for that unit or the entire property. If you have water problems, then that should be addressed regardless of whether it used to happen once every 10 years or now 3 times a season because of changing weather patterns.

Any building located at the bottom of a hill needs to have had drainage features and a system designed and engineered in advance of construction to handle the expected runoff and saturated ground. As part of the building plan. It sounds like the problem could be that the drainage design was inadequate, was improperly built, or has deteriorated. No matter what the reason, fixing the problem needs expertise. I hope you're able to engage the right resources to assess the problems and fix them. From your brief description, that's your immediate need. Leave dealing with climate change as a topic for cocktail party chit chat.

Folks, Thanks for the feedback so far. Clarification on the electrical situation: The building has a 200 amp service. This means that the building gets a maximum of 200 amps at any given time. There are individual electrical panels for each of the 12 units. Each panel pulls in about 60 to 100 amps at any given time. When the trustees were looking into this whole issue last year, they informed us that: "It is theoretically possible for the demand from the individual units to vastly outstrip our 200 amp capacity if usage spikes across all units at the same time (e.g., 12 x 60 = 720 amps)." So far, according to a survey done in the building, electrical usage is not to the level where it's a safety issue. But this will need to be monitored yearly.

The time to keep an eye on your camellia flower bud production starts in the summer and ends when the last bloom opens. Observe if no flower buds develop or if they develop and not open as both scenarios have different causes. Check soil minerals (problems due to sandy soil for example), the amount of sunlight in spring/summer, unusual weather conditions (temperature that gyrate more than 30-40 degrees in one day, etc.), pests, inconsistent watering, etc. Maintain the soil as evenly moist as you can with no long periods of dry soil, wet soil, dry again, etc... Water when the soil feels dry if you insert a finger into several spots and the soil feels dry at a depth of 4". That is the typical depth of camellia's shallow, tiny and fibrous roots. Here in Texas, drip irrigation does not exactly keep the top 4" of the soil properly moist so, in the summer, I sometimes hand water. Make sure that the drip goes all around the plant so the roots on the back get some moisture in the summer. I keep watering during dry winters too. Lack of mulch may dry the top 4" easily in your summer months. With a smaller root system or with a weaker DNA, this plant may suffer more than the others.

Like roses, most camellia cultivars are very complex hybrids, and react to conditions differently depending on their heritage. Are all three plants in the same exposure? Are they getting consistent moisture? Camellias are VERY sensitive to inconsistent water availability and it can cause what is called "bud blast". Do the leaves show any signs of sun stress? C. japonica will not tolerate full sun in most places. Cameillia sasanqua is more sun tolerant. What is the soil pH? Camellias demand acidic soil, and it can and will affect bud formation, though too high a pH usually causes chlorosis before it affects bud set. If you don't know your soil pH, there are fairly cheap test kits you can purchase, as well as the hand held soil meters. But the most accurate method is to send a sample to your university/state extension office or a commercial lab. How is the drainage? Camellias like to be moist, but never, ever soggy. The root ball should normally be planted a little high, and heavily mulched, to avoid roots ever sitting in water-logged soil. Check for infestations of camellia scale. Sometimes a bad case can stress the plant into premature bloom or bud drop. These are just a few things that can affect bloom quality, though I don't know for sure that any will cause your exact problem. But I would address any cultural problems and see if that solves the issue. John EDIT. I can't really tell from the photos if your plants are mulched. Camellias love cool roots, and a mulch also helps maintain that evenly moist soil they prefer. Something light and airy, laid on fairly thick is ideal. I use pine needles. Most wood mulch actually forms an impenetrable water barrier if allowed to dry thoroughly. Water will pass through pine needles even when they are desiccated. Never let camellia roots be exposed.

Are we talking curtains or drapes?  If curtains (usually a thin, light fabric) I would probably do TWO 50” panels per 35” window.  If drapes (usually a heavier fabric), one might be enough. I just bought and hung 100” wide drapes (single panels) on my 44” wide bedroom windows.  The rods are mounted 1” outside the window frames and the drapes look nicely full. You can always cover some of the wall with your curtains/drapes if you think the panels are too wide.  You don’t have to mount the curtain rod right at edge of the window frames.

Assume, based on the centered chandelier that this is a dining room?  (So no need to close the draperies as in a bedroom…)  It looks like you have enough wall space to hang a rod so that the drapes can only slightly overlap the window edge on each side, so that the windows look wider.   50” wide drapes will “compress” to as little as maybe 17” depending on the pleating header type and look plenty full.   I would keep the fabric simple - no strong pattern or color contrast, so the drapes are a soft background and not an alarming distraction with so many windows.

Meant to add - they will not look too bunched at all, as long as the rod is set wide enough - something that is expandable to a total of 35” + maybe 20”max on either side - so 75”.  Depending on the pleated header type.  You will want to experiment with the exact width before putting up the rods.  Also I would keep the “finials” (or whatever they are called) on the ends of the rods very simple - no big balls or anything.

There are many reasons for this.   The key issue is that cellars are underground and built in wet soil and bricks and mortar are porous.   You can make sure the problem isn’t as bad by checking external drains are doing their job and wicking rainwater and bath water away to the road- cracked pipe may contribute to your issue. But most likely your cellar has capillary suction which moves moisture through porous walls. The water can be drawn upward through floors too. This effect creates the ring of dampness seen at the base of many basement walls. Basically it’s normal when heat rises in the rooms above for this suction to occur and your dehumidifier is likely doing the same thing. The solution is to make the floors and walls non porous.   It’s an expensive job that needs a specialist builder but it will gain you an additional habitable space.

The layout doesn't make sense to how I am familiar with basements being finished: - Kitchen: The bar area should be adjacent to at least the gaming area. The Kitchen is down the hall and walled in. It reminds me of the back kitchen in an assembly hall or funeral home, a room you may step in temporarily but not hang out and use as part of the main congregation space. - Sump: Not sure what you are saying about being near a sump pump. Is the plumbing roughed in already? Do you have an ejector pit (sump pump is for ground water)? Plumbing doesn't have to revolve immediately around an ejector pit, it can be run under the floor from somewhere else. - Mechanical room: Seems really small, like 4x6. If you have a furnace + water heater that isn't realistic. - Storage: Basements always need to have room for storage. Things that do not fit on a shelf in a closet upstairs or in the garage. - Windows: Take advantage of windows and doors. Which of the two windows is the emergency escape window that the bedroom has to have? Wouldn't the Living area be a better transition to be placed at the door if you plan on using it for an indoor/outdoor connection, and better to receive natural light than a gaming area? - Bath: Door does not work. - Media Room: Being 10' wide seems too restrictive to be walled off as a space. If you want theater seats centered on the screen, then a 10' wide room limits you to a front row of 2 seats, maybe a row of 3 if you tighten the aisle so you have to shimmy around the seat. - Ceiling: Ductwork, beams, and columns should always be considered in design layout.
